Beijing shuts tourist sites, suspends bus services as heavy rain continues

Aamir Latif
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
Heavy rain continued to lash the Chinese capital Beijing on Wednesday, forcing authorities to shut tourist attractions, suspend bus services and construction work and evacuate residents from high-risk areas, state media reported.
The city closed over 300 tourist and camping sites and suspended operations at more than 4,100 rural homestays.
Some 250 bus routes were halted, while trains on 10 subway lines were ordered to run at reduced speeds. All sightseeing boat services were also suspended, Xinhua News Agency reported.
Residents in mountainous villages, low-lying areas and other places at risk of flooding and geological disasters were evacuated, authorities said.
More than 5,000 elderly people were also evacuated from care facilities.
Beijing recorded an average of 23.5 millimeters of rain from noon Tuesday to Wednesday morning.
All 3,357 construction sites across the city were also ordered to suspend work as authorities stepped up flood-control measures, with reservoirs releasing water in advance to create additional storage capacity.
Renewing its orange alert for torrential rain Wednesday, the National Meteorological Center forecast heavy rain across a broad swath of the country through Thursday morning.

10th Baltic Film Days bring the best of new Latvian and Lithuanian cinema
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12

10th Baltic Film Days bring the best of new Latvian and Lithuanian cinema
The Baltic Film Days will take place from August 25–26, bringing recent major Latvian and Lithuanian films to the screen at Tallinn's Sõprus Cinema.
The program will feature a selection of Latvian and Lithuanian feature films from the past year, as well as a documentary and a program of short films. Selected screenings will be followed by meetings with the filmmakers, offering audiences an opportunity to discuss the films' themes in greater depth and hear the filmmakers share their knowledge and experience.
The event will also take place simultaneously in Latvia and Lithuania, celebrating the cultural distinctiveness of the Baltic states and marking the anniversary of the Baltic Way.
"The Visitor"
Director: Vytautas Katkus
As summer comes to an end in Šventoji, the Lithuanian seaside town draws its last warm breath. Danielius, a new father, leaves his family life in Norway behind and returns to Lithuania to sell his late parents' apartment. He reconnects with childhood friends, their relatives and new residents. He wanders alone through the forest, settling into quiet routines, candid conversations and playful games in nearly deserted places where few words are spoken. Everything here has changed.
It feels as though director Vytautas Katkus merely glanced at the screenplay before setting it aside and improvising. Shooting on 16 mm film, he captures poetic moments with friends, most of whom are not actors. "The Visitor" drifts along in the irreversible flow of time and undoubtedly deserves to be seen more than once.
"Flesh, Blood, Even a Heart"
Director: Alise Zariņa
When you think positively, the universe responds. This gentle, feel-good coming-of-age dramedy for 30-somethings follows Liv, a passionate woman struggling with body insecurities. She carries her past lightly and never judges others. She loves water flowers and has a soft spot for poodles, despite never having owned a dog. Once, Liv dreamed of being a Barbie and still hopes her loving, somewhat old-fashioned husband finds her irresistible, even if their kisses are few and far between.
Everything changes when Liv receives a sudden call: her estranged father is in a coma and undergoing intensive therapy. Her awkward, cynical mother remains stuck in the past with rigid rules and sees the stroke as a random attempt to escape. Liv wants to speak to her father, but each visit leaves her lost in the maze-like corridors of the brutalist hospital.
"Dog of God"
Directors: Raitis Abele, Lauris Ābele
It seems our southern neighbors have really hit their stride when it comes to animation. While their "Flow" captivated mass audiences and even the American Academy, the Ābele brothers' nightmarish offering is aimed primarily at genre fans and anyone with a taste for more perverse humor that pushes the boundaries of good taste. And there is plenty of it here — a great deal, in fact!
The film is set in the village of Zaube in Livonia in the late 17th century where everyone seems to be gripped by an inexplicable delirium, awaiting the arrival of evil. A witch trial culminates in the testimony of an old man branded a werewolf who claims he travels to hell to battle the devil and his witches in order to ensure a good harvest. But this bodes well for no one.
"Renovation"
Director: Gabriele Urbonaite
Translator Ilona and tour guide Matas plan to move in together after two years as a couple. They move into a new apartment just as renovations begin on the building. The constant drilling and hammering soon become exhausting.
Ilona's sharp-tongued mother visits to voice her disappointment over her daughter's unfulfilled potential, comparing her with former classmate Laura who has earned a doctorate and is now engaged. Ilona could have made many different choices. She resents Matas reminding her that she will soon turn 30 and dodges any talk of marriage.
One sunny day, Oleg, a Ukrainian construction worker, unexpectedly enters Ilona's life via the neighboring apartment's balcony and changes it profoundly. A painter before the war, Oleg knows the work of Lithuania's most famous artist and composer, Čiurlionis. Hoping to impress him, Ilona pretends to be a poet. Their encounters become more frequent and the air fills with unspoken attraction. Oleg tells Ilona that if she truly loves Matas, she should talk to him.
"A Goodnight Kiss"
Director: Giedrė Žickytė
Following her widely acclaimed film "The Jump," Giedrė Žickytė returns with her most heartfelt documentary to date. It is impossible to remain indifferent to the story of Irena Veisaitė. She was a writer, human rights activist and one of Lithuania's most perceptive and wise women who warned of the wars that continue to shape our world today.
A Holocaust survivor, Irena lost her parents and found refuge with a Christian family during the Soviet occupation of Lithuania. She died in 2020 while the film was in pre-production. Her death prompted Žickytė to seek new ways to bring to life Irena's moving memories of her two mothers, her lifelong friendship with Estonian composer Arvo Pärt and her guiding principle: to live without revenge or hatred.
Exploring Irena's story through archival footage, photographs and old interviews inspired Žickytė to uncover previously untold stories of Jewish Vilnius, once known as the Jerusalem of the North.
"Red Code Blue"
Director: Oskars Rupenheits
This independently produced crime drama authentically transports viewers back to the dangerous, frantic and uncertain 1990s. Riga is consumed by lawlessness and chaos, marked by high-stakes chases, intense interrogations and shootouts between rival gangs, reckless punks, corrupt agents and ruthless cops. In this harsh world, honesty and loyalty are punished without hesitation.
Young and idealistic investigator Romans Skulte struggles from his very first shift to find his footing in the brutal, cold labyrinth of newly independent Latvia. Drug traffickers and violent gangsters rule the desolate streets under the covert protection of high-ranking officials. Those who show initiative pay a heavy price. Young cadets quickly learn that trust is a liability, even among close friends, as traitors and informants lurk at every turn.
Cunning Georgian smugglers are deeply entrenched in a frightened society, while an aggressive Armenian mafia fearlessly stakes its claim. This slow-burn police thriller is packed with nerve-wracking heists, betrayals, extortions, bribes and relentless pursuits. All characters are fictional, though inspired by real-life investigations. In his debut lead role, Raitis Sturmanis brings to mind a young Charlie Sheen.
--
Editor: Kaspar Viilup, Marcus Turovski

Another win for Democrats’ anti-Israel left as Peggy Flanagan takes Minnesota Senate primary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:09:54 UTC
14:09:54 KST

Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a progressive Democrat who has accused Israel of “genocide” and said she would have voted to cut off military aid to the Jewish state, won the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate on Tuesday, handing the party’s anti-Israel left another high-profile victory.
Flanagan defeated centrist Rep. Angie Craig, a supporter of Israel who had received endorsements from the pro-Israel group AIPAC in previous elections and whose position on the Jewish state became a point of attack during the primary.
The result came just one week after progressive Abdul El-Sayed won a bitter Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, further underscoring the strength of the party’s left flank in contests where Israel and U.S. support for the Jewish state have become increasingly divisive issues.
Flanagan will face former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, who won the Republican Senate primary on Tuesday.
The Democratic contest to replace retiring Sen. Tina Smith pitted two sharply different wings of the party against one another.
Craig lined up endorsements from establishment Democrats including House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, former Speaker Nancy Pelosi and senators from competitive states. She pointed to her record of winning closely fought elections in a suburban Twin Cities district and presented herself as a candidate capable of appealing to swing voters.
Flanagan, meanwhile, was backed by prominent progressives including Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, as well as Smith.
Israel emerged as one of the defining fault lines between the candidates.
Flanagan has accused Israel of committing “genocide” and said she would have voted for legislation seeking to cut off U.S. military assistance to the country.
Craig was among the minority of House Democrats who voted against that effort, maintaining her support for U.S. military assistance to Israel.
Flanagan also repeatedly highlighted Craig’s past endorsements from AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, and sought to cast the race as a fight against the influence of wealthy donors and outside groups.
She emphasized during the campaign that she did not accept “AIPAC money.”
AIPAC, however, did not endorse Craig in the Senate primary and did not directly spend money on her behalf in the race.
Craig’s past support from the organization nevertheless became a political liability among progressive voters, reflecting the widening divide inside the Democratic Party over Israel.
“I love that she doesn’t take any corporate money, she doesn’t take any money from AIPAC,” Flanagan supporter Andrea Ropella said. “The things that she says, she believes in and she stands for.”
The race was also shaped heavily by immigration policy and the Trump administration’s enforcement campaign in Minnesota.
Flanagan attacked Craig for voting for the Laken Riley Act, a Trump-backed immigration measure passed early in the president’s second term. Craig later repudiated her support after federal immigration officers shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.
The killings, both captured on camera, fueled a backlash against Trump’s immigration policies and became a major issue in the closing stages of the primary.
Gov. Tim Walz declined to endorse either Democrat, although his wife, Gwen Walz, endorsed Craig late last month, a move viewed as a notable break with Flanagan, who has served as Walz’s running mate and governing partner for two terms.
On the Republican side, Tafoya emerged from a crowded field despite Trump declining to endorse a Senate candidate. She had support from the national GOP and defeated rivals including Marine veteran and former Navy SEAL Adam Schwarze and conservative commentator Royce White.
Republicans also held a closely watched gubernatorial primary in which state House Speaker Lisa Demuth defeated Mike Lindell, the MyPillow founder and longtime Trump ally.
Trump had endorsed Lindell and wrote on social media Tuesday that he “deserves a BIG WIN.”
Lindell has been one of the most persistent promoters of false claims that Trump’s 2020 election defeat was fraudulent. Some Minnesota Republicans had openly questioned whether his polarizing profile would make him unelectable in a general election.
Demuth will face Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who defeated six opponents to secure her party’s gubernatorial nomination.
Republicans have not won a statewide race in Minnesota since 2006, but they hope a major public-funds fraud scandal will give them an opening this year.
At least 65 people have been convicted in overlapping food-fraud cases stemming from investigations launched during the Biden administration. One former nonprofit leader was sentenced in May to 42 years in prison in connection with a $250 million fraud scheme.
Trump has cited the scandals in defending a sweeping immigration crackdown in Minnesota, which he initially said would focus on the state’s large Somali community.
For Democrats, however, Flanagan’s victory is likely to draw broader attention because of what it signals about the party’s internal battle over Israel.
Her win follows other recent successes by progressive candidates willing to sharply challenge longstanding Democratic support for the Jewish state, while candidates identified with the party establishment and the pro-Israel camp face growing pressure from primary voters.

Extreme heat grips Hong Kong as labour groups urge district-level index
Parts of northern Hong Kong including Yuen Long and Ta Kwu Ling surpass 35 degrees before noon
Hong Kong remained gripped by extreme heat on Wednesday with temperatures reaching 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) in parts of the city, prompting labour representatives to urge authorities to introduce a district-level index to better protect outdoor workers.
The Very Hot Weather Warning and the Amber Heat Stress at Work Warning have been in effect since Wednesday morning, with parts of northern Hong Kong including Yuen Long and Ta Kwu Ling already surpassing 35 degrees before noon, according to the Hong Kong Observatory.
The sustained heat followed Sunday’s record-breaking 36.9 degrees – the highest since the Observatory began keeping records in 1884. Yet the lowest-level amber heat stress alert for outdoor workers remained in place, drawing criticism of the Labour Department’s Heat Stress at Work Warning System.
Li Wing-foo, chairman of the Staffs and Workers Union of Hong Kong Civil Airlines, said heat stress warnings should be issued at a district level rather than relying solely on territory-wide readings.
He noted that areas such as the northern New Territories and the airport apron could run far hotter than urban stations.
“The airport apron is wide open and fully exposed. It should have its own independent reading so employers can roll out targeted protections for staff,” he told a radio programme.

Solar eclipse followed by meteor shower: Portugal prepares to watch two rare events
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:05:53 UTC
14:05:53 KST

In some parts of the country, the Moon will completely cover the Sun, plunging onlookers into a sci-fi-like scene. Find out all about the total solar eclipse, followed by a meteor shower.
Today the national team are not playing, the prime minister is not addressing the country, there are no COVID-19 press conferences, but the country will still stop at the same time to look at the same thing: the total eclipse of the Sun.
Around 19:30, in the Bragança region, the total eclipse of the Sun will occur, meaning day will turn into night as the Sun is covered by the Moon. As well as getting darker, ambient noise drops, the temperature changes and many more shadows are cast.
This will be an astronomical spectacle nobody will want to miss, not least because it is highly unusual and the last total eclipse visible from mainland Portugal took place in 1912.
But the eclipse will not be the only phenomenon to amaze this evening. From 21:30 on Wednesday, about an hour after the eclipse ends in mainland Portugal, there will also be a meteor shower. These meteors, known as the Perseids, leave a trail of light as they pass through the atmosphere.
This is an annual meteor shower, usually active from mid-July until the end of August. The peak generally occurs around 12 and 13 August.
As the Moon will be practically new, the sky will be very dark and conditions will be especially favourable for observing the phenomenon. However, for the best possible viewing experience, experts recommend finding a dark place with an unobstructed horizon.
Activity is expected to increase between midnight and 02:00, but the most favourable period to try to spot the highest number of meteors will be between 02:00 and 05:00 in the early hours of the 13th, when the Perseus constellation, the point from which the meteors appear to radiate, rises higher in the sky.
The best places to watch the phenomenon are Dark Sky Alqueva in the Alentejo, the world’s first certified dark-sky territory; in the North, the Montesinho and Bragança area in Trás-os-Montes; in the Serra da Estrela, Peneda-Gerês or any high, inland area away from settlements.
For an even more exciting experience, a few tricks also help, and it is essential to avoid looking at screens for 20 to 30 minutes beforehand so that your eyes adapt to the darkness and can focus on the meteor shower.
Back to the eclipse: Euronews has compiled everything you need to know about the phenomenon:
What is a solar eclipse?
The astronomical phenomenon known as an "eclipse" occurs when one celestial body blocks the light from another. In the case of a solar eclipse, the Moon completely or partially covers the light of the Sun, producing what is known as the "diamond ring", which lasts only a few seconds.
Where can I see the eclipse?
The eclipse will be visible across the country; however, it will not look the same in all regions. The total eclipse, which corresponds to 100%, will be visible only in the Montesinho Natural Park, in Bragança.
The deep partial eclipse, with between 92% and 99% coverage, can be observed throughout mainland Portugal.
On the islands, the Azores and Madeira, the percentage is much lower, between 74% and 77%.
It is advisable to watch the moment from a wide-open space, without many buildings in front.
What time does it happen?
The eclipse will begin at around 18:33 and end at around 20:23, lasting roughly two hours. Its maximum will be reached close to 19:30. The total eclipse phase lasts just 25 seconds.
Can I watch it without protection?
No! You must never look directly at the Sun during the phenomenon. There is only one safe way to see the eclipse: using proper eclipse viewing glasses. The phenomenon must not be watched with sunglasses, through telescopes or with the naked eye, as it can cause eye damage. Direct sunlight does not cause immediate pain, but it can burn the retina, leading to later consequences such as permanent loss of vision.
The organisations responsible also warn about the use of cameras and mobile phones, which can likewise be damaged if used without suitable filters.
In Portugal, ZEISS launched a campaign offering free eclipse glasses across the country. All you had to do was go to an optician in the Club de Visão network, after registering in advance. However, the initiative was limited to existing stock and it is no longer possible to obtain them free of charge.
You can buy eclipse glasses, but the optics community has set out some key features to check that you are purchasing the right model. The glasses must have ISO 12312-2 or ISO 12312-2:2015 certification for solar observation, as well as the CE marking printed on the frame. They must also ensure the blocking of UV, IR and intense visible light. They should be prefabricated and ready to use, with no assembly required.
You can buy the glasses in pharmacies, some supermarkets and online shops such as Astroshop, Telescopiomania, ESTUDIOPT, Aff Camera Store or Sol & Salvo, which sell these glasses for prices ranging from 2.90 to 3.25 euros per unit. These shops also offer packs for families or groups of friends.
Are there places where I can watch together with other people?
Yes. On the platform https://eclipse2026.pt (source in Portuguese) hundreds of events taking place on the day of the eclipse are listed. Some no longer accept participants, as they required prior registration. Even so, here are some of these initiatives, from north to south of the country, where you can still try to take part free of charge:
- Faro and Albufeira
Promoted by the Centro Ciência Viva do Algarve, there will be guided sessions for observing the partial solar eclipse in Faro and Albufeira. In Faro, the event will take place in the Parque Ribeirinho from 18:30. Admission is free and the minimum age for participants is 12.
In Albufeira, it will be held in the parish of Paderne, at the parish castle. The event is free and will continue into the night with observation of a Perseid meteor shower.
- Tavira
- "Solar Eclipse and Night-time Observation of Celestial Bodies"
Organised by the Centro Ciência Viva de Tavira in partnership with Tavira municipality, it will take place in Praça da República. Admission is free and the minimum age is 3.
"During the activity, there will be a brief explanation of how solar eclipses form and discussions will be held on the importance of scientific research and observing the sky," the organisers say.
- "Solar Eclipse at Praia do Arraial" and "Solar Eclipse at Praia do Barril"
Both events are organised by the Centro Ciência Viva de Tavira and are free of charge. They start at 18:30, but it is advisable to arrive a little earlier. At Praia do Arraial, the minimum age to take part is 5. At Praia do Barril, it is 3.
- Oeiras The partial solar eclipse will also be visible from Santo Amaro beach in Oeiras. Here, the phenomenon is expected to reach around 95%.
The event is organised by the local authority, which has prepared a festive afternoon from 16:00, combining a summer party atmosphere with observation of the phenomenon.
As well as a DJ set, a large screen will be installed to show the eclipse live, allowing everyone to follow it without risk to their eyesight. The session will be accompanied by explanations of what is being seen.
- Enxara do Bispo (Mafra)
"When the sky darkens: Understanding the Solar Eclipse and how to observe it safely" is one of the initiatives taking place in the late afternoon of the 12th. It is organised by the Associação Astronómica Horizonte Estelar, with the meeting point set for the churchyard at 17:00. The event lasts 3 hours and 30 minutes. Before the eclipse, there will be a theoretical introduction to the phenomenon and, during it, explanations will be given to participants. The minimum age to take part is 6.
- Porto
"Solar Eclipse 2026 at Time Out Market Porto" is organised by the market, which invites everyone to gather in the outdoor square, with a privileged view of the Clérigos Tower. The event starts at 18:00 and runs for 3 hours.
The organisers say that "to mark the occasion, a themed cocktail called 'Eclipse' has been created. With the purchase of this cocktail, a pair of solar viewing glasses will be offered, while stocks last."
- Vila do Conde
Organised by the Centro Ciência Viva de Vila do Conde, the eclipse can be observed in a group from the seafront, in front of the Farol restaurant. Admission is free and the event starts at 16:00. The recommended minimum age to observe the phenomenon is 6.
There are also private initiatives organised by groups of friends on social media pages. Check whether anything is being organised in your area.

Anxious dogs and silent birds: What happens to animals during a total solar eclipse?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:02:16 UTC
14:02:16 KST

Today's rare solar eclipse is thrilling for humans, but animals will face something they can't prepare for: sudden confusing darkness in the middle of the day.
Once day seemingly and unexpectedly turns to night, many animals will likely feel confused, disorientated or stressed - thankfully, for just a few minutes.
Animals, both wild and domesticated, rely on important environmental cues - like light and temperature - to help them navigate their daily lives. As light fades and temperatures drop, these cues suddenly change.
Scientists who have studied animal behaviour during eclipses have a fairly clear picture of what tends to happen - even if not every animal reacts the same way.
How different species react to eclipses
People observing a total solar eclipse often notice the sudden silence. Birds that sing throughout the day frequently stop the moment darkness falls, as though evening has arrived hours early. Nocturnal animals, such as owls, can do the opposite and become active, behaving as though dusk has begun.
Many - from zoo mammals to bees and other insects - interpret the sudden darkness as nightfall. Elephants have been seen heading straight for their night-time dens, treating the eclipse as their usual lock-up signal. Others show clearer signs of stress: gorillas have charged the glass of their enclosures, while giraffes have paced and swayed.
House pets may be worried too. Dogs and cats often pace, whine or hide during totality - a response some researchers compare to how pets react to fireworks or thunderstorms.
Normality returns within minutes
Total darkness itself is brief - lasting only a few minutes. As sunlight returns, the animal behaviour reverts just as suddenly.
Birds often burst into song, reportedly singing even louder than they would at a normal dawn. Within a short time, most animals settle back into their ordinary daytime routines, as if nothing unusual had happened at all.

Worried your child is a loner? A new study says playing alone may be just fine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

What matters may not be how much time a child spends alone, but whether they still feel they belong.
The child happily doing their own thing at recess may not need rescuing from the sidelines.
A new study suggests some children who play alone simply prefer their own company.
Researchers at the University of Georgia in the United States found that children who often chose to play alone could still be happy with their friendships and place within a wider peer group, particularly when they felt confident that they belonged.
The study surveyed 473 students between nine and eleven years old at several elementary schools in the US state of Georgia.
Children were asked which classmates tended to play alone despite getting along well with others. They also reported how important they thought it was to belong, and how satisfied they were with their friendships and their position within their class.
Here, researchers found an important distinction between children who preferred spending time alone but still valued belonging, and those who placed little importance on fitting in.
Children in the first group were generally satisfied with both their individual friendships and their wider peer relationships. These children may accept enough invitations to remain socially connected while still feeling comfortable turning down activities when they would rather be alone.
“They prefer to be alone and do their own thing rather than playing with their peers, but they still have that other flip side of getting along well with others,” Rachael Pfanz, the study’s corresponding author and an elementary school psychologist, said in a press release.
Children who did not consider belonging important, however, were more likely to report poorer relationships with both friends and classmates.
Researchers suggest that children who regularly reject invitations may eventually receive fewer of them, leaving them increasingly isolated and dissatisfied with their social lives.
“There are things we do because we know what’s good for us,” said Michele Lease, a professor of educational psychology at the University of Georgia and co-author of the study.
“Social interaction is the same way. Turning down invitations, like avoiding exercise, leads to poorer outcomes.”
The findings also suggest adults should be cautious about assuming that children who play alone need to be pushed into large group activities.
Instead, researchers suggest introducing children to smaller groups of peers with similar interests or behaviours.
“Maybe don’t ask them to go join the big soccer game right away on the playground,” Pfanz said. “That’s a little overwhelming if they’re already preferring to play alone.”
The research team said the findings are particularly relevant for children in fourth and fifth grade, when friendship groups tend to become more established and children are increasingly able to identify which classmates are choosing solitude and which are becoming excluded.

All-British chocolate bar made by scientists using Reading-grown cocoa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:00:19 UTC
14:00:19 KST

The late queen was the only person in history to have ever eaten a chocolate bar made with 100% British ingredients, after she was given one as a six-year-old in 1932 by the confectioner Rowntree’s.
The bar was created from a glasshouse-grown cocoa plant, at Rowntree’s headquarters in York.
But now, others could have the same experience after scientists at the University of Reading created a bar with cocoa beans grown in Berkshire.
The bar was crafted to celebrate the university’s 100th anniversary, made with cocoa grown from plants in the institute’s collection.
The UK makes some of the world’s best chocolate in a market worth £10.4bn, but the industry is entirely reliant on imported cocoa.
Maha Khan, a master’s student at the university, decided to make a bar with cocoa from Reading. She harvested, fermented, and processed the beans at the university’s food department.
She said: “It has been amazing to follow the entire chocolate-making process, from pod to bean to bar, without leaving Reading.
“This British bar of chocolate highlights the precarious nature of our food supplies. Cocoa plants are very sensitive to changes in temperature and rainfall, and climate change is already causing problems in countries that produce most of the world’s cocoa. Protecting different varieties is vital if farmers need hardier plants that can cope with a changing climate.
“I hope this shows people just how much work goes into the chocolate we enjoy, and how important it is to protect cocoa farmers and communities around the world.”
She said the chocolate is “delicious”, adding that it had a very rich flavour: “It’s incredible to taste the complexity of the flavour profiles as the cocoa is made from plants originating from over 300 varieties grown here. It was also really interesting to taste the raw cacao before it gets processed – the beans are coated in a white flesh that tastes like lychee and isn’t something many people in this country get to try.”
As well as being somewhat of a stunt, the university hopes that this can highlight the importance of its work in preserving different varieties of cocoa, which could be resistant to changes in weather brought by climate breakdown, as well as pests and diseases made more common by a heating planet.
Reading has more than 300 types of cocoa plant at its international cocoa quarantine centre, which handles 97% of the world’s international movement of cocoa plants.
Chocolate prices have risen in recent years as high temperatures in regions where cocoa is grown have stunted the growth of plants. Extreme rainfall made more likely by climate breakdown has also drowned crops across Africa.
The bar is currently a limited edition, with only six made so far, but Khan said there are hopes to ramp up production, depending on the availability of the beans – a single cocoa pod can take six months to grow.
She hopes to give one to the Princess of Wales: “We haven’t decided yet who will get to eat the chocolate. As the last British chocolate made was eaten by the future queen in 1932, it would be fitting if the next bar was a gift to another future queen, the Princess of Wales, who, like the chocolate, was also born in Reading.”

Tarte tatin, spicy pork chops and crumble: Ravinder Bhogal’s gooseberry recipes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:00:19 UTC
14:00:19 KST

In the summer glut of saccharine fruits such as strawberries and peaches, gooseberries may not be the ones you reach for first. But behind their strange burr of fine fuzz, these translucent, marble-like fruits offer a complex, defiant flavour. They are juicy, fragrant, a little sweet (especially the red ones that come along later in the season), but, overall, they are raspishly sour. Like rhubarb, they need sweetening if you’re using them in compotes or desserts, but their natural tartness offers a wonderful contrast and cuts through cheese, fatty meat such as pork or oily fish such as mackerel.
Spiced pork chops with fennel, tarragon and gooseberry salad (pictured top)
The addition of tart fruit in the salad helps to cut through the fattiness of the meat.
Prep 15 min
Marinate 20 min
Pickle 10 min
 Cook 30 min
 Serves 4
2 tsp sea salt
  2 tsp fennel seeds
2 tbsp coriander seeds
  1 tsp black peppercorns
  1 tsp caster sugar
  ½ tsp paprika
  1 tsp dried oregano
  4 pork chops
  2 tbsp olive oil
  25g butter
  4 garlic cloves, unpeeled and bashed flat
For the salad
3 tbsp white-wine vinegar
  1 tbsp caster sugar, or honey
  Sea salt and black pepper
  1 tsp coriander seeds, toasted and very lightly crushed
2 fennel bulbs, trimmed and very finely sliced from top to base (preferably with a mandoline)
1 cucumber, peeled and sliced into long ribbons with a vegetable peeler or mandoline
1 banana shallot, peeled and very finely sliced
200g gooseberries
25g tarragon, leaves picked
25g mint, leaves picked and finely chopped
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
Put the salt, fennel seeds, coriander seeds, pepper and sugar in a mortar and grind to a fine powder. Add the paprika and oregano, and grind again. Pat the chops dry with kitchen paper, then press the spice mix all over the meat. Leave to marinate at room temperature for 20 minutes.
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/350F/gas 6. Heat the oil and butter in an ovenproof frying pan and add the garlic. Using tongs, hold the chops skin-side down in the pan for five minutes to crisp up and render the fat. Once the fat is a lovely amber colour, fry the chops for three minutes on each side, basting as you go, then transfer to the oven for six minutes, or until cooked all the way through. Rest the meat for five minutes.
Meanwhile, make the salad. Mix the vinegar and caster sugar in a mixing bowl until the sugar has dissolved, then season well with salt and pepper. Add the coriander seeds, fennel, cucumber and shallot, and set aside to lightly pickle for 10 minutes. Finally, add the gooseberries and herbs and drizzle over the olive oil. Toss well and serve with the pork chops.
Gooseberry tarte tatin with goat’s cheese
A savoury take on the classic apple tarte tatin. This version features a wonderful partnership between tart gooseberries and funky goat’s cheese. Serve with some dressed salad leaves and toasted hazelnuts for crunch.
Prep 10 min
 Cook 55 min
 Serves 6
40g butter
A few sprigs of thyme
2½ tbsp runny honey
3 tbsp apple cider vinegar
Sea salt and black pepper
  750g gooseberries, topped and tailed
Plain flour, for dusting
500g block puff pastry
  150g soft goat’s cheese
 Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/425F/gas 6. Put a 20cm ovenproof frying pan on a medium heat and melt the butter. Once the butter has completely melted, add the thyme and fry briefly for 30 seconds, then stir in the honey and vinegar and season well.
Once the glaze has thickened and caramelised, remove the pan from the heat and leave to cool for eight to 10 minutes. Add the gooseberries and stir to coat.
On a floured work surface, roll out the pastry to 3mm thick, then cut out a circle slightly larger than the pan. Cover the gooseberries with the pastry, using your fingers to carefully tuck it in at the edges. Bake for 30-35 minutes, or until crisp and golden on top.
Remove from the oven and leave to cool for at least five minutes before carefully inverting on to a serving plate. Serve hot or cold, scattered with crumbled goat’s cheese and more black pepper.
Gooseberry crumble custard cake
The sour fruit offers a welcome respite in this nursery-sweet cake layered with custard. Raspberries would also work well here.
Prep 5 min
 Cook 1 hr 20 min, plus cooling
 Chill 4 hr
 Serves 12
300g unsalted butter, plus extra to grease tin
300g golden caster sugar
  5 medium eggs
  300g plain flour
  2 tsp baking powder
  150ml milk
  400g gooseberries
  500ml fresh vanilla custard
For the crumble
200g plain flour
  125g chilled butter 
  125g golden caster sugar
  A fat pinch of sea salt
  70g flaked almonds
  Finely grated zest of 1 lemon
Heat the oven to 160C (140C fan)/325F/gas 3. For the crumble topping, rub the flour and butter between your fingertips to a breadcrumb-like consistency, then mix in the sugar, salt, almonds, and lemon zest. Chill until needed.
Grease a 20cm x 30cm rectangular cake tin with butter, then line it with baking paper.
In a stand mixer or with an electric whisk, beat the butter and caster sugar until light and fluffy. Add the eggs one at a time, beating each one in thoroughly, then sift in the flour and baking powder. Pour in the milk, gently fold in, then add half the gooseberries.
Spread half the gooseberry batter evenly into the lined tin, then pour the custard on top. Carefully spread the rest of the batter on top, then dot with the remaining gooseberries.
Sprinkle with the crumble mixture, then bake for about an hour, until golden but still a bit wobbly in the centre. Leave to cool in the tin, then chill for at least four hours, and ideally overnight. Cut into 12 rectangles and serve.

China’s quant funds have an edge on foreign rivals, even as Beijing curbs trading speed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

China’s quant funds have an edge on foreign rivals, even as Beijing curbs trading speed
Top US quant teams unable to beat native competitors in mainland China unlike in Japan or India, despite regulatory clampdown on trading
“If a top US quant team goes to Japan or India, they can beat virtually all the native quants,” Xia Chun, founder and chief economist at Chinese financial research firm Wiselink Group and former finance professor at the University of Hong Kong, told the South China Morning Post this week.
The reason, Xia said, lies in China’s unique valuation logic for state-owned enterprises, whose state-backed financing advantages create pricing dynamics that traditional foreign models fail to capture.
Frequent administrative policy interventions such as initial public offering suspensions and policy-driven trading halts become trading signals that outside models struggle to replicate, he added.
The comments from Xia, who has also advised the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), came as Beijing tightens its grip on the quant trading industry. On the night of July 31, stock exchanges in Shanghai and Shenzhen cut the dedicated local-network queues that let quant funds’ co-located servers receive price feeds tens to hundreds of microseconds ahead of other participants.

Winding trails and coastal treks: Three of Europe’s best autumn hikes, according to Lonely Planet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

In its new guide book, Lonely Planet has picked out some of the best hikes around the world. Here we take a look at three of the top European options for hiking this autumn.
With the arrival of autumn comes a spectacular transformation of scenery and the opportunity to lace up your walking boots and to be at one with nature.
Hiking has become one of the most popular outdoor activities and in Europe we’re spoiled for choice when it comes to trails and routes to tackle.
In its new guide book – "Where to Go When: Hiking" – Lonely Planet has showcased more than 90 of the world's best hikes and the months to explore them in, from "micro walks and multi-day treks to pilgrimage routes and mountainous rambles".
Here we take a look at three of the featured hikes in Europe to do during the cooler autumn months, plus other popular options further afield.
Three of Europe’s best autumn hikes
Premužić Trail, Croatia (challenging)
Winding through Croatia's Northern Velebit National Park, the Premužić Trail is “one of Europe's finest examples of dry-stone engineering”, said Lonely Planet. Crafted pathways weave through rugged landscapes, passing wildflower meadows and shepherds' huts with views across the Adriatic Sea. September offers pleasant temperatures, snow-free trails and warm coastal waters, making it the “perfect time to discover this dramatic corner of Croatia”.
Coast to Coast Path, England (moderate/challenging)
Follow in the footsteps of fell-walking legend Alfred Wainwright with this west-to-east walk across England, which starts from the Cumbrian village of St Bees to Robin Hood’s Bay in Yorkshire. Going through three National Parks, this iconic route has recently been awarded National Trail status and now has clearer signage, better accessibility and is managed to a higher environmental standard. Lonely Planet recommends doing the English Coast to Coast Path in October.
Via Francigena, Swiss Alps and Northern Italy (moderate)
The Via Francigena is a pilgrimage from Bourg-Saint-Pierre in the Swiss Alps, through Italy’s Aosta Valley all the way to Rome. Hike in “historic, holy footsteps” and savour stunning panoramic mountain views, flower filled meadows and the cultural and culinary delights of Italy’s diverse regions.
Three of the best international autumn hikes
Choquequirao – Southern Peru (challenging)
For travellers seeking an alternative to the busy Inca Trail, Choquequirao is a 15th-century Inca site that’s sometimes described as “Machu Picchu's lesser-known sister”, with a fraction of the visitors. The demanding route descends deep into the flower-filled Apurímac Canyon before climbing steeply back towards the ruins, “rewarding hikers with ceremonial platforms, temples, ritual baths and intricate llama carvings etched into its ancient terraces”. September is one of the best times to visit, with warm, clear days arriving after the peak tourist season.
Quilotoa Loop, Ecuador (easy)
Explore Ecuador's Andean highlands on a gentle and rewarding journey through traditional villages and rolling mountain landscapes before reaching the "breathtaking" Laguna Quilotoa. Nestled within the crater of an extinct volcano, the emerald-green lake is celebrated for its Indigenous culture and striking scenery. As well as crisp blue-sky mornings and lush green hillsides, November offers quieter trails and plenty of time to explore local artisan stores.
Langtang and Helambu Trek, Northern Nepal (challenging)
Journey through one of Nepal's most spectacular Himalayan regions, where dense forests, sacred lakes and centuries-old Buddhist monasteries can be found beneath snow-capped peaks. Rich in Tibetan culture, the Langtang and Helambu valleys also “tell a story of resilience”, with tourism continuing to support communities rebuilding after the 2015 earthquake. November is among the best months to trek here, bringing dry, clear days, comfortable temperatures and unbeatable mountain views.

Lithuania is getting ready for EU Council presidency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Lithuania is in the final stretch of preparations to take over the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of next year – a six-month stint that will bring hundreds of meetings, and thousands of visiting officials, to Vilnius. But even as workers scramble to renovate parliament and repave city streets, the capital is about to become slightly harder to reach by air.
A parliament under repair
Workers, not lawmakers, have become the regular fixture at Lithuania's parliament, the Seimas, this summer.
Corridors are being refurbished, the historic Hall of March 11 – where Lithuania's 1990 declaration of independence was signed – is being restored, and previously unused spaces are being converted, all at a cost of around €1.2 million.
Visiting delegations are set to arrive through the courtyard, which is also being tidied up, though parliament received only a single bid when it put the courtyard work out to tender. Contractors, it turns out, aren't queuing up for jobs that must be squeezed into the narrow gaps between sessions.
The fact that the Hall of March 11 is a listed heritage space doesn't help either, as renovators' hands are largely tied.
"Everything here counts as cultural heritage – absolutely everything, the tables, the plasterwork, all of it," said parliamentary Chancellor Algirdas Stončaitis.
"This is the first refurbishment the hall has had since it was originally built," he added. Walls, benches, carpeting, lighting and ventilation have all been redone.
Other spaces are getting attention for the first time since the Soviet era, including the main cloakroom and a set of public toilets nearby – "five in total," Stončaitis noted, "but let's be clear, they won't be gold-plated."
Some stairwells will be repainted and the press centre lightly refreshed, though he added a wry aside that the building's appearance is getting more attention than the substance behind it.
Speaker Juozas Olekas, watching the work from his office window, framed it as ordinary housekeeping ahead of company: "Everyone tidies their house before guests come – that's essentially what's happening here too."
He pointed to accessibility improvements for people with disabilities as one substantive change amid the cosmetic ones, and said he expects everything to be ready by the autumn session.
The city has learned from experience, too. When Vilnius hosted a NATO leaders' summit three years ago, authorities faced criticism for cosmetic fixes – old trolleybuses hidden from view, street lamps given a quick coat of paint.
This time, Mayor Valdas Benkunskas says the approach will be different: "We're not repainting the lamp posts, we're replacing them with new ones."
The cost of preparation is already running over budget. More than €140 million was earmarked for the presidency, but Finance Minister Taurimas Valys says that won't be enough.
"More costs keep surfacing – there are procedures in some areas that were previously overlooked," he said.
Around 300 events are planned over the six-month presidency, with the largest – just like during the NATO summit – held at the Litexpo exhibition centre.
Heads of state, government and ministers from across the EU are expected to pass through the capital.
What Lithuania wants to prioritise
Valys says tackling inflation will be one focus, though he's candid about the limits of what a rotating presidency can actually achieve.
"We're second-from-last in the bloc on inflation, but we're not alone in this, and we can't fight it alone," he said before acknowledging that interest rates, not EU presidency initiatives, remain the primary lever in the long run.
The minister will also be involved in the early stages of negotiations over the EU's next seven-year budget, a process that requires balancing competing national interests.
"Naturally, we can't publicly play up any one position," he said.
The social security and labour minister, Inga Ruginienė, has named demographics – code, in an EU context increasingly worried about ageing populations, for boosting birth rates – as a priority.
Asked whether that might extend to matchmaking events for young people (a previous minister had floated the idea of a singles disco), Ruginienė laughed it off: "I do like to dance. If you join in, we'll dance together."
She says more substantive proposals on parental leave are coming this autumn, though she declined to give details, saying only that they'll go beyond "cosmetic adjustments."
The interior minister, Martynas Katelynas, has flagged migration as a priority. He suggested that the EU's new Migration and Asylum Pact, which took effect in June and introduces tighter border checks and a burden-sharing mechanism for asylum seekers among member states, already has shortcomings.
"The pact shouldn't come at the expense of states' security, and I think going forward we'll need to take account of the realities on the ground, in the world and in Europe, without trying to be holier than the Pope," he said.
The opposition isn't attacking the government's agenda outright, framing the preparations instead as the product of continuity in the civil service rather than the current governing coalition.
"Regardless of the change of political teams in government, the state apparatus is preparing the substance well," said Radvilė Morkūnaitė-Mikulėnienė, a member of the parliament's European affairs committee.
Getting there may be harder
Despite the preparations, reaching Vilnius during the presidency could get trickier. Latvia's airBaltic, which has been under financial strain, is cutting its winter routes from Vilnius to Berlin and Dubai, and reducing flights to Tallinn as well.

Israeli raids, demolitions continue as UN warns West Bank at breaking point
Israeli forces arrest 23 Palestinians and demolish the home of a man killed in a confrontation with Israeli settlers in July.
Israeli forces have continued their crackdown in the occupied West Bank, arresting at least 23 Palestinians and demolishing several homes, as the United Nations warned that the situation in the territory was at a “breaking point”.
The arrests and demolitions on Tuesday came as dozens of Israeli settlers continued raids on Palestinian villages, including one in Khirbet ar-Ras al-Ahmar, where a water pipeline was destroyed.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Concerns mount over integrity of Israel’s upcoming October elections
- list 2 of 4Israel is ‘trying to make Palestine disappear’: The Elders
- list 3 of 4Israel demolishes home of Palestinian killed during settler attack
- list 4 of 4In Gaza’s tents, widows face war’s harshest realities alone
According to the Palestinian Wafa news agency, those detained included two children, one of whom had a disability, as well as a man who was taken while he was grazing his livestock in al-Hadidiyah in the northern Jordan Valley.
At least 11 others were arrested in the Jenin governorate, while five were detained in the Bethlehem area.
In the village of Tal, southwest of Nablus, Israeli forces demolished the family home of Farouq Ramadan, one of four Palestinians killed during a confrontation with Israeli settlers on July 24. Two Israelis were also killed in the incident.
Israel maintains a policy of demolishing the homes belonging to relatives of Palestinians involved in attacks against Israelis, an approach human rights groups have condemned as collective punishment.
Near Yatta in the Hebron governorate, Israeli forces also demolished the home of Ibrahim Mifleh al-Atimin and filled in a water well, displacing nine members of his family, according to Wafa.
Attacks, demolitions
Israeli soldiers demolished 12 commercial warehouses in the village of Anza and bulldozed an agricultural facility in Yarza, east of Tubas. In Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, they issued demolition notices for the Khallat al-Dabaa school, as well as several homes and agricultural structures.
According to UN figures, Israel has demolished an average of 122 Palestinian buildings every month this year.
Separately, dozens of settlers attacked a group of Palestinians ploughing their lands in Al-Mughayyir, wounding six people, including three children and two women.
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Al-Mughayyir, said the settlers also burned part of the valley and attacked nearby homes.
“Upwards of 60 percent of Al-Mughayyir’s land has been confiscated by the Israeli army, while Israeli settlers have set up at least 11 illegal outposts in the village, barring the farmers from their land,” she said.
“Some 119 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have been uprooted by this very dynamic in the past three years. Palestinians are treated as trespassers in their own land, while Israeli settlers slash, burn, and steal the land with impunity,” she added.
In Burqa, northwest of Nablus, six Palestinians, including two children, were wounded after Israeli forces assaulted residents during a raid, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent. Settlers also raided the Nablus-area villages of Awarta, Osarin and Sarra.
The attacks form part of a sharp escalation in violence by Israeli forces and settlers across the occupied West Bank as Israel gears up for a parliamentary election in October.
UN warns of ‘de facto annexation’
Addressing the UN Security Council on Tuesday, Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov said the West Bank was at “breaking point”.
He said Israeli forces and settlers have killed 76 Palestinians, including 18 children, in the occupied West Bank so far this year, while about 3,800 Palestinians – nearly half of them children – have been displaced by settler violence, demolitions and evictions.
The UN has documented more than 1,430 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage across roughly 260 Palestinian communities in 2026, many carried out in the presence of Israeli forces, Alakbarov said. Since January 2023, 127 Palestinian communities have been fully or partially displaced, including 47 completely uprooted, affecting more than 6,390 people.
Alakbarov said settler attacks, once concentrated mainly in Area C, where Israel holds full civil and security control, are increasingly spreading into Areas A and B.
Israeli authorities have also advanced or approved roughly 12,360 settlement housing units across the West Bank this year, including 5,160 in occupied East Jerusalem, he said.
“These are interconnected steps, not isolated developments,” Alakbarov said, warning that they were reshaping the occupied West Bank, weakening Palestinian governance and advancing “de facto annexation”.

As Ukrinform reported, as of 22:00 on August 11, there had been 185 combat engagements along the front, with the largest number of Russian attacks recorded in the Kostiantynivka sector.

The half-year results "represent a positive indicator" of progress in implementing the targets of the country's unified financial expenditure agreement, the ministry said.

Oil and gas exports are Libya's main source of revenue, but production has been repeatedly disrupted in recent years by conflict and political instability. ■

Police described the devices as three aluminum pipe bombs and a tennis ball bomb containing an explosive, gunpowder and steel ball bearings. While none detonated, police described them as “viable” IEDs.
The father was killed in a gunbattle with police and the son was wounded.
Naveed Akram has not entered pleas to the charges that include murder, attempted murder and committing a terrorist act.

Unknown Publisher

13:51:24 KST

US military operations in 2025 killed 153 civilians and wounded 243, a US official said on Tuesday, citing Pentagon assessments.
This compares with a Pentagon assessment that two civilians were killed and two were injured by US military operations in 2024.
A Pentagon report submitted to the US Congress and published by US media said that all the death and injury tolls against civilians recorded in 2025 were due to three US strikes in Yemen.
The Pentagon report said the US Central Command (CENTCOM) had assessed that the three strikes in April 2025 in Yemen "more likely than not" resulted in civilian harm.
The Pentagon report also said that as of February 2026, there were 15 other incidents in Yemen that CENTCOM was currently assessing in response to reports received through non-governmental organizations.
The US military says it aims to degrade the capabilities of Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen.
Casualties from US strikes in Caribbean, East Pacific aren't included
The Pentagon report did not include any casualties from US strikes in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.
The report said as of February 1, 2026, the US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) assessed that "there were no incidents in which civilian casualties more likely than not resulted from US military operations in the US SOUTHCOM area of responsibility in 2025."
President Donald Trump's administration has struck vessels that it accuses of transporting narcotics in the Eastern Pacific, casting its targets as "narco-terrorists."
The US military's strikes on such vessels have killed more than 200 people since September 2025, according to a tally of death tolls published after each strike.
Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International consider such strikes unlawful extrajudicial killings. The American Civil Liberties Union casts the assertions by the Trump administration against those it targets as "unsubstantiated, fear-mongering claims."

Ukraine’s first domestically built CBRN scout vehicle just replaced Soviet jeep with no armor at all
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:45:08 UTC
13:45:08 KST

Ukraine is retiring a Soviet chemical-scout vehicle in favor of one it built itself. Ukraine's National Guard has received the first Ukrainian radiation and chemical reconnaissance vehicles on the armored Tisa chassis, replacing the outdated Soviet UAZ-469RKh, National Guard commander Oleksandr Pivnenko announced.
The vehicle is a step in Ukraine's shift from Soviet legacy equipment to its own modern designs. Developed to National Guard specifications for current battlefield conditions, the armored scout allows crews to survey and monitor contaminated zones without leaving the protected vehicle.
What the vehicle does
The vehicle carries radiation and chemical reconnaissance instruments, an automated system for collecting and processing information, a weather station, modern communications, and satellite navigation, all of which enable real-time data collection and transmission to assess a situation and make decisions faster.
The mission is early warning of invisible threats. The task of chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) units is to detect radiation, chemical, and biological threats in time, determine the extent of contamination, and quickly pass the information to command.
"The safety of soldiers, the completion of combat tasks, and the protection of the civilian population depend on the speed and accuracy of this work," Pivnenko said.
The armored base is the upgrade
The Tisa chassis is what sets the new vehicle apart from its Soviet predecessor. The light-armored Tisa is built on the Toyota Land Cruiser 79 platform and meets the NATO STANAG 4569 protection standard, providing ballistic and mine protection that the open-topped UAZ never offered.
The vehicle is equipped for hard conditions. It carries night-vision systems and air ventilation and filtration systems, letting the crew work in contaminated or dangerous environments while staying protected. The filtration matters especially for a CBRN vehicle: it lets the crew operate inside a sealed, over-pressured cabin in exactly the toxic zones the vehicle is sent to scout.

Russia turns to India for petrol as Ukraine pummels refineries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:45:00 UTC
13:45:00 KST

Russia turns to India for petrol as Ukraine pummels refineries
MOSCOW – Russia has started importing petrol from as far away as India, as Ukrainian attacks on its refineries trigger severe local shortages.
It is the first time Moscow has imported the motor fuel from the South Asian nation, according to Kpler data, with the lengthy journey required an indication of how dire the crunch is becoming.
The first shipment was received on Aug 5, and more may be on the way. According to Kpler. Indian processor Nayara Energy – backed by Rosneft, Russia’s top oil producer – has emerged as a source of the fuel, which is being moved on a chain of Russian-linked tankers via transfers off Egypt.
“The emergence of Indian barrels is particularly notable,” said Sumit Ritolia, lead analyst at Kpler.
The cargoes, which complement continued imports from Belarus and other neighbouring markets, highlight “the severity of the current domestic petrol imbalance, and the extent to which lower refinery runs are reshaping Russia’s traditional product trade flows”, he said.
The global energy market is coping with the fallout from two major conflicts, as Kyiv presses on with its assault on Russia’s refineries, while the US and Iran continue to face off in the Middle East.
The combined disruptions have acted to tighten fuel markets, with Moscow – traditionally a supplier of fuels overseas – banning both petrol and diesel exports to prioritise local users.
Following a wave of attacks, EA Analytics estimated that Russia’s crude-processing rates were running at 3.6 million barrels a day in July, about a third below the seasonal norm.
Since then, Kyiv has intensified strikes, hitting five processors last week and at least two more this week.
Russia’s Energy Ministry, India’s Oil Ministry, and Nayara’s communications team did not respond to Bloomberg requests for comment.
Since getting sanctioned by the European Union in July 2025, Nayara has been relying on so-called dark-fleet tankers and trans-shipment operations to receive its crude, and export fuels.
Its 400,000 barrel-a-day refinery at Vadinar on India’s west coast also needs to widen its export market, after a key buyer, Hindustan Petroleum, recently started producing more of its own fuel in the region.
For the inaugural shipment, Russian-flagged products tanker Cyclone (formerly Agni) loaded a 42,000 tonne petrol cargo from Vadinar on June 18, ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg shows.
The fuel was then transferred to the Oman-flagged Garnet at Damietta Port, off Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, on July 6. That vessel then reached Russia in early August.
More petrol may follow. The products tanker Varg loaded nearly 40,000 tonnes of the fuel at Vadinar on July 6 and likely conducted a ship-to-ship transfer at Damietta in late July, based on changes in its draft, according to Kpler.
Ship-to-ship transfers, or STS, typically take place so that individual vessels can cut travel times.
No receiving vessel has been confirmed, though Kpler identified Beast as a possibility.
The vessel was at Damietta and recorded an increase in draft on July 30 and 31.
Beast had signalled Morocco’s Tangier as a destination, but has since gone beyond that port and is now sailing north in the Atlantic Ocean, with its cargo intact, the data shows.
Another products tanker, Cameroon-flagged Photon, also left Vadinar on July 13 before transferring its petrol cargo at Damietta to the Russia-flagged Talisman on July 28 and 29, the data shows.
These ships were classed on the Russian register, with the exception of Garnet.
All of them have been sanctioned by the European Union, with Garnet and Talisman also being targeted by the US.
“The final destination of Talisman and Beast remain unconfirmed but, the emerging trading pattern suggests Damietta STS hub continues to facilitate the movement of Indian-origin petrol toward Russian import channels,” Kpler said. BLOOMBERG

Palestinian students and staff sue Columbia University alleging discrimination

Palestinian students and staff sue Columbia University alleging discrimination
- Palestinian students and staff have sued Columbia University for alleged discrimination and unfair disciplinary actions since late 2023.
- Columbia suspended over 65 students in May 2025 after pro-Palestinian protests amid federal funding cuts linked to accusations of antisemitism.
- The university paid over $200 million to resolve federal probes, while free speech groups criticised its crackdown on protests involving arrests and expulsions.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – A group of current and former Palestinian students and staff have sued Columbia University, alleging discriminatory treatment by the school against its Palestinian community since late 2023, according to a court filing in New York.
The lawsuit said the university failed to protect its Palestinian members from harassment and targeted them through what it cast as “unfair and biased disciplinary hearings”.
Columbia has previously denied being discriminatory and has condemned hate. Local media reported that it declined to comment on pending litigation. It did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Protests took place at Columbia and around the US after the start of Israel’s assault on Gaza following a deadly Palestinian Hamas attack in October 2023.
Protesters demanded an end to US support for its ally and called for the divestment of funds by universities from companies supporting Israel.
In May 2025, Columbia suspended more than 65 students for their role in shutting down the university’s main library in a pro-Palestinian demonstration.
That demonstration came as the university was negotiating with President Donald Trump’s administration, which had cut its federal funding after accusing the university of tolerating antisemitism during pro-Palestinian protests.
Protesters, including some Jewish groups, say opposing Israel’s assault on Gaza and its occupation of Palestinian territories is not antisemitic and advocacy for Palestinian rights should not be conflated with supporting extremism.
Columbia agreed to pay over $200 million (S$256 million) to the US government to resolve federal probes and restore most of the federal funding in July 2025.
Free speech groups condemned Columbia’s protest crackdown in which students faced arrests, suspensions, expulsions and degree revocations. REUTERS

Mass evacuations in Beijing as Typhoon Dolphin brings more torrential rain to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:43:19 UTC
13:43:19 KST

Thousands of people have been evacuated from areas at risk of flooding and landslides in Beijing, as the remnants of Typhoon Dolphin continue to bring torrential rain to northern and central China.
Forecasters warned on Tuesday that the Chinese capital could receive more than 150mm of rain over the following 24 hours, with some districts forecast to exceed 200mm – more than one-third of Beijing’s average annual rainfall of 528mm.
Beijing remained under an orange rainstorm warning, the second-highest level, on Wednesday, with the heaviest rainfall expected across the morning.
Authorities closed hundreds of tourist attractions and campsites on Wednesday, with more than 1,300 tourists evacuated or turned away. Meanwhile, over 5,000 elderly people were moved from care facilities and about 1,800 people living around construction projects in mountainous or riverside areas were relocated.
The rain also disrupted Wednesday morning’s commute. Official local media reported that 250 bus routes had been suspended and trains were running at reduced speeds on 10 metro lines.
Dolphin, the strongest typhoon to hit China so far this year, has weakened after making landfall in the eastern province of Zhejiang on Sunday, but its remnants have continued to draw large amounts of tropical moisture deep inland and drench central and northern parts of the country.
The neighbouring Hebei province was also on alert for mountain floods, landslides and other geological hazards. Authorities said they had dispatched 623 teams to mountainous areas and equipped more than 2,100 at-risk villages with satellite phones or satellite messaging terminals to maintain communications during emergencies, according to state media.
In the central province of Henan, authorities raised the warning for torrential rain to the highest-level red alert on Wednesday morning, as downpours continue to batter large swathes of the province. More heavy rain was forecast through Thursday morning, with 24-hour rainfall totals of up to 350mm expected in some areas.
Classes, business operations and non-essential outdoor activities have been suspended in the affected areas of Henan. Residents were told to avoid deep flood waters and evacuate immediately if vehicles stall in water, state media reports.
China, the world’s second-largest economy, is increasingly exposed to destructive weather events that scientists link to climate change. This year is proving particularly tough due to the emergence of the El Niño weather pattern that is driving up temperatures and fuelling more frequent and intense typhoons.
Rainfall records have also been broken elsewhere in central China. Wugang in Henan received 209.5mm in a day and Xiangyang in neighbouring Hubei recorded 169.1mm, both the highest single-day rainfall totals for August, according to state media.
Reuters contributed to this report

NDA MPs participate in 'Tiranga Yatra' rally in Delhi
NEW DELHI: Vice President CP Radhakrishnan on Wednesday flagged off a “Har Ghar Tiranga” bike rally in the national capital ahead of Independence Day celebrations on August 15.The rally, organised as part of the ongoing “Har Ghar Tiranga” campaign, saw participation from MPs of the ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA) and a large number of supporters carrying the national flag. The rally is scheduled to cover the stretch from Bharat Mandapam to Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium.
Addressing participants, Radhakrishnan noted that the various activities organised under the campaign may differ in form but carry the same sentiment of national belonging.“In Tiranga Yatra, bike rallies, cultural programmes, the activities are different but the sentiment they carry is the same, that is the collective sense of belonging... I urge each one of you to actively engage in this campaign and inspire every citizen to hoist the Tricolour with pride,” ANI quoted him as saying.The vice president also emphasised the unity of the country, declaring, “Bharat is one, and it will be one forever.”He paid tribute to Pingali Venkayya, who designed the national flag, and recalled Hansa Mehta, who led a group of 72 women who presented the first National Flag of independent India to Dr Rajendra Prasad, the country’s first president.
Several NDA MPs attended the rally. BJP MP Tarun Chugh highlighted the enthusiasm of young people and their resolve to contribute towards the goal of a developed India.“Under the leadership of PM Modi, the youth have come out today with the resolution of ‘Viksit Bharat’. Tiranga is the pride of India. Under PM Modi, India will realise the resolve to become a developed India,” Chugh said.Union minister of state for Home Nityanand Rai highlighted the significance of the national flag, describing the Tricolour as a sentiment deeply connected with the country and its people.“The Tiranga is our pride, and it is more precious to us than our life,” Rai said.BJP MP Ramvir Singh Bidhuri pointed to the participation of a large number of MPs in response to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for the Tiranga Yatra.“In response to PM Modi's call, a large number of MPs are joining this Tiranga Yatra today, and the Vice President will inaugurate this Tiranga Yatra. The journey will go from Bharat Mandapam to the Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium, and a spectacular celebration is visible here,” Bidhuri said.
The “Har Ghar Tiranga” campaign is being held across the country ahead of Independence Day, encouraging citizens, public representatives and organisations to display the national flag.The Delhi rally is part of a series of programmes being organised in the capital to mark Independence Day, with the Tricolour at the centre of celebrations aimed at strengthening the sense of unity and national pride.

Delimitation row: CM Vijay moves resolution to freeze Lok Sabha Seats at 543

Tamil Nadu assembly backs 543 Lok Sabha seat freeze
Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Wednesday moved a special resolution in the state Assembly urging the Centre to permanently retain the Lok Sabha’s strength at 543 seats.Days after convening a meeting of parties supporting his government, including the Congress and the Left parties that extend support from outside, Vijay moved the resolution in the Assembly urging the Centre to maintain the Lok Sabha-Rajya Sabha seat ratio at 2.2:1.The government-sponsored resolution urged the Centre to implement 33 per cent reservation for women in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections without delay, based on the existing strength of 543 seats."The 33% reservation for women should be implemented in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections itself, based on the existing 543 constituencies. The 33% reservation for women should not be delayed any further. In Tamil Nadu, more women have voted than men. Providing reservation for women is not a concession; it is a matter of social justice. The 33% reservation for women must be implemented without any further delay," Vijay said in the assembly.The resolution noted that the population of states, including Tamil Nadu, and the Union Territories has not been counted for more than five decades, with the next census scheduled for 2026."All the states including Tamil Nadu and the people / elected representatives of the union territories have not had their population counted for more than 50 years.
The next census to count the population was supposed to be held in 2026. Therefore, since the delimitation of constituencies has not been carried out for the last 50 years, based on the 2011 population census, the constituencies should be delimited and the number of Lok Sabha and Assembly members should be increased from 550 to 850 by bringing in a constitutional amendment Bill," the resolution stated.Also read: Delimitation decoded: What the Centre tried to do, why opposition shot it down & what happens nextLast week, a meeting convened by Vijay with Tamil Nadu MPs from alliance and friendly parties decided to oppose the Union government’s proposed delimitation exercise in its entirety.The meeting was boycotted by the main opposition DMK and the AIADMK, with the former calling the deliberations a “farce” and the latter describing them as a “hurriedly staged drama”.The MPs had demanded that the ratio of seats between the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha be maintained at 2.2:1. They also unanimously agreed to adopt a resolution in the state Assembly to permanently safeguard the interests of Tamil Nadu and other southern states in the delimitation process.Meanwhile, the AIADMK called the meeting a “hurriedly staged drama”, pointing out that no fresh delimitation Bill had been introduced in Parliament and that there had been no official announcement on the exercise.While the Congress and other opposition parties have supported the Women's Reservation Bill, they have opposed linking its implementation to the delimitation exercise and have demanded that the two be delinked.
The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023, was passed by both Houses of Parliament. However, its implementation has not moved forward after the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill fell in the Lok Sabha on April 17, failing to secure the constitutionally required two-thirds majority of members present and voting.The Bill had linked the implementation of 33% reservation for women in legislatures to the delimitation of Lok Sabha constituencies.

Two people were killed and two more injured in Kherson as a result of a massive drone attack
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of August 12, Russian forces launched a massive drone attack on Kherson. Two civilians were killed and two injured; homes and equipment were damaged.
Enemy forces massively attacked Kherson with strike drones during the night of August 12, killing two civilians and injuring two more people. This was reported by the Kherson Regional Prosecutor’s Office, UNN writes.
Details
The attack damaged apartment buildings and private houses, garages, and cars. Specialized equipment belonging to the rescue service was also damaged.
Following the attack, which resulted in deaths, prosecutors launched a pretrial investigation under Part 2 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine—on the facts of a war crime.
Law enforcement officers are currently clarifying information about the victims and continue documenting the consequences of the Russian strike.

South Korea calls on North Korea to cease missile launches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:33:52 UTC
13:33:52 KST

SEOUL, August 12. /TASS/. The authorities of the Republic of Korea are calling on North Korea to stop ballistic missile launches, the South Korean presidential administration has stated.
At approximately 6:00 a.m. local time [21 p.m. August 11 GMT], North Korea launched a ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the Sea of Japan, which flew over 700 km. "North Korea's ballistic missile launches are a provocation that violates UN Security Council resolutions. We call for their immediate cessation," the administration said.
The National Security Office at the presidential office held an emergency meeting with representatives of the Ministry of Defense and the Joint Chiefs of Staff. They "assessed the impact of the launch on the country's security and issued necessary orders."
The Yonhap agency suggests that the launch may have been related to the US-South Korea military exercise Ulchi Freedom Shield, which is set to begin on August 17.
The previous missile launch by Pyongyang took place on August 6; the missile launched at that time also fell outside Japan’s EEZ.
