Male redback's bizarre death somersault during sex is in its genes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
23:08:04 UTC
08:08:04 KST

Male redback spider's dramatic death somersault during sex coded in its DNA
In short:
Researchers have spotted a genetic source for the bizarre sexual cannibalism behaviour of the redback spider.
Male spiders, which somersault onto their partners' mouths to be eaten while mating, appear to inherit this trait via sex chromosomes.
What's next?
Genetic data and courtship information could help to conserve a related threatened New Zealand spider, the katipō.
Male redback spiders live fast and die young, ending their lives in a gory ritual of sexual cannibalism.
Female spiders eat their male partners while they mate, and males appear to encourage this behaviour, with their final act being a dramatic somersault onto the female's jaws.
A new study, published in Biology Letters, has pointed to a genetic source for this behaviour.
The researchers compared the activity of the Australian redback to its close, but non-cannibalistic cousin, New Zealand's katipō.
By breeding the two species together, the researchers, who are based at the University of Hamburg in Germany, learned more about the DNA behind the self-sacrificing somersault.
"Our interest in these spiders was sparked by the fact that two closely related sister species show very different mating systems," lead researcher Kardelen Uludağ said.
"This is very uncommon in animals. 
"Due to their close relatedness, the two species can be crossed and this provides the perfect opportunity to study the genetic inheritance of male sacrificial behaviour."
Bruno Alves Buzatto, a behavioural ecologist at Flinders University who wasn't involved in the research, said the findings were "very striking".
"It supports the idea that being killed during copulation and cannibalised can actually lead to the male's advantage,"
The self-sacrificial redback backflip
Loading...
Redback spiders (Latrodectus hasselti) are "monogynous": meaning male spiders mate with only one female over their lifetime.
This mating ritual is quite intricate, featuring a "somersault" so that the males' large abdomens are right next to the females' fangs for ease of biting.
Then, the male redbacks constrict their abdomens, which makes them look like they're being squeezed, so they can cheat death for long as possible.
The secret sex lives of redback spiders have been documented for decades, including research by scientists at the University of Toronto seen in the video from ABC TV's Catalyst program in 2010:
Loading...
Dr Buzatto said the self-sacrificing death dance gave males an evolutionary advantage: it improved their chances of offspring.
"The process of being cannibalised increases the time that they mate with the female. Being able to transfer more sperm to the female's spermatheca, which is the organ that the females use to store sperm, provides an advantage."
Female redbacks can store sperm and use it to lay eggs for up to two years after mating.
The katipō (Latrodectus katipo), a venomous spider native to New Zealand, is very closely related to the redback.
But katipō spiders don't engage in this cannibalistic mating ritual. Instead, males and females tend to mate with each other multiple times.
Cor Vink, an entomologist at Lincoln University in New Zealand who assisted with the study, said katipō evolved from redback spiders about 100,000–200,000 years ago: a blink of an eye in evolutionary terms.
"In that small amount of time, that whole behaviour is lost," Dr Vink said.
"It's really interesting when behaviours like that can be lost. We don't know enough about how behaviours are coded in the DNA of invertebrates."
Cross-breeding spiders to test genetics
The researchers bred male redbacks and female katipō together to see how mating behaviours were displayed in their offspring.
Dr Vink collected both species of spider from different sites in New Zealand, where the redback spider is an invasive species.
"We collected adult redbacks and then fed them up, took them back, grabbed their egg sacks and then they got sent to Germany. We did the same thing with the katipō as well," he said.
Both redbacks and katipō bites can require antivenom, but there haven’t been any recorded deaths in decades (for redbacks) or centuries (for katipō).
Dr Vink said both spider species were "shy and retiring", but he and his fellow collectors wore gloves as an extra precaution.
"When they bite you, you won't die, you'll just feel like you're going to,"
"It's a pretty horrible experience from what I've been told and I'm not willing to find out what it's like."
Once the spider eggs had made it to Germany, the researchers bred male redbacks and female katipō together and reared male hybrids to maturity.
Then, they added the hybrids to webs built by, and housing, female katipō, filming their behaviour with infrared cameras.
They analysed the footage from 104 mating rituals, looking for signs of both the somersault trick and the abdominal constriction.
Roughly half the hybrids performed the life-ending somersault while mating.
Because of the way they'd bred male redbacks with female katipō, this 50/50 split allowed the researchers to conclude the somersault trait was inherited on a spider sex chromosome.
But the other behaviour — the abdominal wiggle — wasn't displayed as clearly, suggesting the genetics for this trait were more complicated.
This surprised the researchers, who were expecting both traits to have a common genetic source.
Michael Kasumovic, an evolutionary biologist at the University of New South Wales who wasn't involved in the research, said this was a neat finding.
"Given how important both traits are to survival, we would guess that they should be strongly linked together. But they aren't, and that suggests they evolved independently. And that's really cool," he said.
"This study highlights that maybe we need to think about how different species interact and how that can lead to new traits evolving and new species appearing."
Dr Buzatto said he wasn't surprised by the study's findings.
"We know that a lot of very complex behaviours can be encoded by some fairly simple genetic basis."
But he said spider sex chromosomes were very complicated, and differed from species to species, meaning there was still much to learn.
"I feel like the more we look, the more weird and surprising things we'll find with spiders," Dr Buzatto said.
"We've probably only described and documented a quarter of the spiders that exist, maybe a third, we're not too sure … That really opens people's minds to why we find all these crazy, unusual, surprising behaviours and life histories in these animals."
Genetic research to conserve NZ's spiders
Dr Vink said this genetic research could help to protect the katipō, which is in decline in New Zealand — in part because of the redback spider.
In New Zealand, redback spiders are predating on and threatening several native species like skinks and beetles.
But the biggest threat to the rare katipō is that the two spiders can interbreed and create hybrids.
"In New Zealand, we have a very real danger of losing a species through hybridisation,"
In his own research, Dr Vink is studying redback spider pheromones to see if they can be used to control populations.
"The idea is that if we can attract enough males using the pheromone, we can reduce the male population, which will crash the overall population because males can only mate once," he said.
Research into courtship and genetics can help with this conservation technique, alongside giving researchers more data to track katipō and redback populations.

Households living near new power pylons will have £250 a year taken off their energy bills as the UK government prepares to push ahead with more than 40 grid upgrade projects across the country.
The government has promised hundreds of thousands of homes living within 500 metres of new grid infrastructure a saving of up to £2,500 on their energy bills over 10 years in return for “hosting vital infrastructure” which will help the UK transition away from fossil fuels.
One of the biggest grid upgrade drives since the 1960s will mean communities in over 40 locations across the country will be eligible for the payments as the government hopes to prevent a backlash against increased the building of pylons and substations.
Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said the multibillion-pound upgrades, which will be paid for through household energy bills, were “a vital part of how we deliver secure, homegrown energy and unlock economic growth across the country”.
“It is a moment of national renewal – upgrading what was built largely in the 1960s for the modern age and is our route to bringing down electricity bills for households across the country,” he said.
“It’s vital we build again as a country and we are determined those communities which host pylons should benefit which is why we’re bringing down the energy bills of those hosting this vital national infrastructure,” Shanks added.
Grid companies are expected to spend up to £77bn over five years to build the new networks and power lines needed to carry renewable electricity, often generated offshore or in more remote parts of the country, to urban areas with high electricity demand.
The government confirmed the sweetener for local communities near these projects after ruling out proposals to run the new cables underground.
It said that research, commissioned by the department for energy and net zero (DESNZ), found that “building pylons remains the most cost-effective way of upgrading Britain’s outdated electricity networks” and would provide “the best value for bill-payers”.
The eligible households can expect to receive their energy bill discountsautomatically every six months via their energy supplier. The discounts will begin next year.
The government has also called on grid companies including National Grid, SSE and Scottish Power to plough millions into a fund which will be used to support projects which benefit the local communities.
Some of the biggest beneficiaries will be those living close to National Grid’s Bramford-to-Twinstead grid reinforcement project which will receive more than £4m in payments to fund community projects.
In Scotland, communities near Scottish Power’s Chirmorie overhead line project would be eligible for about £2.4m of community benefit funding.
At present, constraints in the country’s ageing grid network mean that wind and solar farms are paid to stop generating electricity if there is not enough demand in the local area to absorb the power.
The electricity system operator also pays gas plants to fire up to meet demand, and buys electricity imported from the continent via high-voltage power cables. These payments are expected to total £3bn by 2030.

Male redback spiders invite cannibalism through a ‘self-sacrificial somersault’ during sex – but why?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
23:01:12 UTC
08:01:12 KST

If you think you’ve had a bad one-night stand, spare a thought for the male redback spider, whose sole reproductive partner eats him after sex.
Male redbacks appear to invite this cannibalism through a “self-sacrificial somersault”, with new research shedding light on the genetic basis of the behaviour.
The redback, also known as the Australian black widow, is one of two monogynous widow spider species – meaning that males typically only mate with a single female.
During copulation, a male redback uses his pedipalps – two arm-like appendages – to transfer sperm to the larger female’s two sperm storage organs. He also somersaults into the jaws of the female.
“He’s pumping sperm, he flips his abdomen right over into her mouthparts and then he constricts his abdomen … to make it hard for the female to get a purchase on his abdomen. That lets him survive the first mating,” said Cor Vink, an associate professor and spider expert at Lincoln University in New Zealand.
The self-sacrificial flip is thought to help maximise reproductive success, but the males risk being eaten before they are able to transfer sperm to the female’s second storage organ.
“Ideally, males should mate with the same female two times because females have two separate sperm storage organs,” said Kardelen Özgün Uludag of the University of Hamburg, the study’s first author.
“A male needs to inseminate and plug both of them, so that he can sire all of the offspring she produces.
“If a male dies after the first mating, another male can mate with the same female and then half of the female’s offspring would be from the second male.”
To avoid becoming a post-coital meal, previous research has found that some males have developed the survival tactic of mating with immature females not yet experienced in eating their partners.
The venomous redback spider is widespread throughout Australia and has been unintentionally introduced to other countries including New Zealand, Japan and the United Arab Emirates.
Redbacks are closely related to the New Zealand katipō, which do not engage in sexual cannibalism. “In the katipō, the male inseminates the female and runs off the web – that’s the same for most widow spiders,” Vink said. “The term widow is actually a misnomer.”
Of the 31 species of widow spider, male sacrificial behaviour is only usually observed in redbacks and brown widows.
In a study published in Biology Letters on Wednesday, German researchers investigated the genetic basis for why redback males perform a “self-sacrificial somersault” during mating, but katipō males do not.
To do so, they bred female katipō with male redbacks to determine how many offspring inherited the somersaulting behaviour. Close to half of their third-generation offspring also somersaulted, leading the scientists to conclude that the behaviour was linked to a specific location on the spider’s X chromosome.
“It is quite remarkable that a highly complex phenotype such as somersaulting, which may lead to partial reproductive isolation, can have such a simple genetic basis,” the researchers noted.
“Our work shows that this highly complex cannibalistic behaviour can evolve rapidly, with very few genetic changes,” Uludag said.
In New Zealand, Vink has found evidence that interbreeding between native katipō and invasive redbacks occurs in the wild. “This is a concern because we could lose our endemic protected species just through hybridisation,” he said.
Vink, who sourced the katipō spiders for the study but was not otherwise involved in the research, described the work as an “elegant paper” that shed light on the redback’s “weird mating behaviour”.
Katipō are thought to have diverged genetically from redbacks about 100,000 years ago. “It’s really neat that they’ve lost this behaviour in 100,000 to 200,000 years,” Vink said.
“The more we know about the interbreeding, the more we know about what we can do to combat redbacks and katipō interbreeding in New Zealand,” he added.

Romania tested the Sahara cruise missile for the first time, aiming to make it the &quot;smartest in the world&quot;
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
01:59:07 EEST
07:59:07 KST

Romania tested the Sahara cruise missile for the first time, aiming to make it the "smartest in the world"
Kyiv • UNN
Romanian company Oves Enterprise conducted the first tests of the Sahara cruise missile, which they plan to make the "smartest in the world." The missile weighs 55 kg, has a 10 kg warhead and a range of up to 200 km, and is also equipped with the Nemesis AI artificial intelligence system.
The Romanian private company Oves Enterprise reported the first successful tests of the Sahara cruise missile, which is being developed as a long-range weapon. Defense Express reports this, according to UNN.
Details
The company stated that its goal is "to create the smartest cruise missile in the world." At the same time, no video of the actual test was released, and the report was accompanied by artistic depictions of the missile's flight and a tank being hit.
According to preliminary data, the Sahara weighs approximately 55 kg, has a 10-kg warhead, and a range of up to 200 km. It is planned for use against tanks, air defense systems, ammunition depots, command posts, and communications systems.
The Romanian missile has received artificial intelligence
The developers are also working on longer-range versions of the Sahara. They are expected to have ranges of 500-600 km and 900-1,100 km, respectively, and may also receive more powerful warheads.
One of the missile's features is reportedly the Nemesis AI artificial intelligence system. It is intended to ensure rapid adaptation to the flight mission and increase the satellite navigation system's resistance to interference.
At the same time, Defense Express notes that the use of artificial intelligence in modern missiles is already becoming common practice. Therefore, the claim that this is the "smartest" missile in the world should currently be viewed primarily as the company's marketing statement.
The Sahara project became known in the autumn of 2025. The development is a private initiative of Oves Enterprise: by that time, €1 million had already been invested in the project, while another €2 million was planned for testing and further development of the missile.

Iran is going to become a member of the BRICS Bank, Governor of the Central Bank of Iran Abdolnaser Hemmati said, state media reported on Tuesday evening.
BRICS is an organization made up of eleven countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. It is an economic and geopolitical bloc that focuses on trade and development.
The New Development Bank (BRICS Bank) is a "multilateral development bank established by BRICS with the purpose of mobilizing resources for infrastructure and sustainable development projects in emerging markets and developing countries," its website explains.
Hemmati announced that Iran was set to join the BRICS Bank in the near future, Iran's semi-official Tasnim News Agency reported.
Iran expects the BRICS Bank to provide economic benefits
"Productive cooperation has commenced between our country and India in the areas of monetary affairs, banking, and the digital economy," Hemmati said.
The next BRICS Summit will take place in September. The governor said, "The BRICS summit offers a prime opportunity to meet with officials from member nations with whom our country maintains its most extensive monetary and banking exchanges and interactions," Tasnim reported.
"We believe that BRICS member nations can conduct trade using their national currencies, and we are pursuing bilateral and trilateral monetary cooperation with these members."
Iran's economy in crisis after war with US
Iran’s wartime economic crisis has triggered mass layoffs across multiple industries, with Iranian officials estimating that some two million people have lost work “directly or indirectly” due to the conflict and a prolonged nationwide internet blackout, according to a report by The New York Times.
Businesses across Iran have begun laying off workers as the country’s economy struggles under the combined pressure of war-related disruptions, sanctions, infrastructure damage, and the government-imposed internet blackout.
Iranian Deputy Labor Minister Gholamhossein Mohammadi said the conflict had already resulted in the loss of more than one million jobs and left another two million people “directly or indirectly unemployed,” according to statements given to Tasnim.
Asher Smith contributed to this report.

John Gotti’s grandson kept trying to delay prison to donate kidney to mother. A judge said enough.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:53:02 UTC
07:53:02 KST

John Gotti’s grandson kept trying to delay prison to donate kidney to mother. A judge said enough
NEW YORK (AP) — Late mob boss John Gotti ’s reality TV star grandson has reported to federal prison after trying to stave off his sentence on fraud charges by saying he was going to donate a kidney to his ailing mother, Victoria Gotti.
The Federal Bureau of Prisons confirmed Tuesday that Carmine Agnello began his 15-month prison term the previous day at the Federal Correctional Institution Fairton in southern New Jersey.
Agnello, who starred on “ Growing Up Gotti ” in the mid-2000s, was originally scheduled to report to prison in July. But U.S. District Court Judge Nusrat Choudhury agreed to delay that until Sept. 18, saying it would allow enough time to recover from the surgery, presuming that happened by Aug. 10 as Agnello suggested
Agnello’s lawyers have said in court filings that Victoria Gotti, the daughter of the former head of New York’s Gambino crime family, suffers from chronic kidney disease.
On Monday, though, with no operation in sight, Choudhury ordered Agnello to surrender immediately to federal authorities.
“Because there is no concrete evidence that an organ transplant will be scheduled to take place at any time between today and Sept. 18, 2026, the request for another deferral of Mr. Agnello’s self-surrender is unjustified,” the judge said.
Agnello lawyer Robert Beltrani said in a letter that surgeons needed more time to set a date for the operation because Gotti was dealing with infections.
“It is undisputed that Carmine is a great match for Ms. Gotti,” he said. “He is simply asking the Court to allow him to remain available to his mother during this very limited period while her doctors determine whether and when she can proceed with transplant.”
Prosecutors objected, noting that a medical report attached to the defendant’s letter said doctors were working to “identify the etiology and the proper treatment” for Gotti’s recurring infections and no transplant could happen until they are fully treated.
“Clearly, the transplant surgery is not imminent,” said Joseph Nocella, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of New York.
Nocella’s office declined to comment further, and lawyers for Agnello did not immediately respond to email messages. Nor did Gotti, an author and former columnist for the New York Post.
Agnello pleaded guilty in 2024 to wire fraud after prosecutors said he fraudulently obtained $1.1 million in loans from a federal program meant to help small businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic.
A resident of Long Island, he obtained the loans on behalf of his company, Crown Auto Parts & Recycling LLC, but lied about how many people it employed, his criminal record and his plans for the funds, prosecutors said.
The company ceased operations before Agnello applied for the loan, which he ultimately used on other ventures including a $420,000 investment in a cryptocurrency business, prosecutors said.
Agnello, now 40, was a teen when he and his brothers briefly rose to fame sporting gel-spiked hairdos on “Growing up Gotti,” which followed the family’s life on Long Island.
His grandfather earned the nicknames “Teflon Don” and “Dapper Don” for his flamboyant style and ability to beat some of the criminal charges he faced over the years. He died in a Missouri federal prison in 2002 at age 61.
The New Jersey lockup where Agnello is now incarcerated has housed some notable inmates over the years.
Most recently disgraced former New York Congressman George Santos served less than three months of a more than seven-year sentence there before President Donald Trump granted him clemency last year.

====================================================================================================

Why the elaborate ruse Trump used in Turkey isn’t like other secret presidential trips
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:53:02 UTC
07:53:02 KST

Trump says Secret Service and the military wanted him off Air Force One in Turkey due to threat
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he slipped away from Air Force One after a trip last month in Turkey because the Secret Service and military wanted him on a “different plane” due to a threat that he insisted didn’t scare him.
Trump downplayed the extraordinary nature of the subterfuge involved in his flight, which saw him stow away in an airport catering container to sneak onto another plane while Air Force One was sent into the sky, essentially as a decoy.
He also downplayed the risk to the people — White House officials, security and support staff, and reporters — he left on the plane.
“They wanted me to go on a different flight, different plane,” Trump told reporters after returning from an event in Ohio, saying he had little choice in the matter.
“I guess there was a threat out there. I didn’t really ask too much about it,” he said. “I get a lot of threats.”
His comments confirmed a report that first appeared in The Washington Post saying that Trump, following a NATO summit last month, was spirited onto a different plane because of a credible threat from Iran. The action was kept secret for weeks, until the newspaper’s story.
“I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk,” Trump said Tuesday, who did not provide many details about the action. But he said the incident did not scare him.
“I don’t worry about anything, to be honest,” Trump said. “Whatever it is. You know my attitude? Whatever!”
Presidents often take secret trips — but not like this
Commanders in chief have sometimes kept overseas trips covert for security reasons, with schedules and logistics kept classified until after for safety reasons. But the fact that Trump’s whereabouts were concealed at the time and for weeks afterward is believed to be unprecedented.
“We have absolutely seen the president fly on unmarked or decoy planes before, into Iraq, Afghanistan, other war-zone-like places,” said Garrett M. Graff, author of “Raven Rock: The Story of the U.S. Government’s Secret Plan to Save Itself — While the Rest of Us Die.”
“But this was an ongoing secret that I don’t think we’ve ever seen before.”
After hiding in the catering vehicle and being moved to the other plane, Trump stopped in Britain, sneaked back aboard the presidential plane undetected, and even later scoffed when asked about potential danger.
“If I go, you go. Right?” he told reporters then — gliding past the fact that if the plane had been shot down, the president wouldn’t have been aboard.
Many details about what happened remain unknown
The president’s flight out of Turkey made headlines at the time because he had arrived aboard a luxury jet gifted by Qatar, which was not equipped with some of the same missile detection and countermeasure systems found on older presidential jets.
Trump ended up traveling in a smaller government aircraft from Turkey to the United Kingdom, only to secretly reboard the decoy jet, then descend from it and climb back aboard the Qatari plane.
Presidents have regularly tested the confines of their office, pushing their security advisers to visit war zones as a show of American presence and their own leadership. Usually, this happens in the form of trips that aren’t announced until the president is deemed to be out of harm’s way.
What’s different this time is that Trump was covertly separated from the rest of his travelers — including the press pool meant to provide independent coverage of the president and his actions — and, instead of informing the public about what occurred once the risk had passed, the White House still hasn’t fully revealed what took place.
Graff said the presence of the White House press corps is as much about protecting “the presidency and democracy” as it is about covering the story.
“This shows that the White House just fundamentally doesn’t understand how important that role is,” he said.
Officials have gone to great lengths to keep presidents safe on covert trips before
In 2023, a motorcade pulled away from the White House around 3:30 a.m. on a Sunday, and President Joe Biden later boarded an Air Force C-32, a modified Boeing 757 normally used for domestic trips to smaller airports, and flew to Poland. Biden then took a secret, 10-hour overnight train ride to Kyiv meant to show solidarity with Ukraine after Russia’s invasion.
A press pool at the White House had been expecting a quiet Sunday for Biden in Washington. However, two journalists went to Ukraine with him and documented the trip, capturing images of Biden and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy walking together.
In Trump’s first term, he made a secret Thanksgiving trip to Afghanistan in 2019, when officials kept a separate press pool and decoy plane in Florida to maintain the illusion that the president was spending the holiday at his Mar-a-Lago estate.
Instead, Trump and another group of reporters flew to the U.S. military base at Bagram, where the president served turkey to troops, gave a speech and met with Afghanistan’s then-president, Ashraf Ghani, while journalists documented what was occurring.
When President George W. Bush made his first trip to Iraq in 2003, news was not released until he was in the air on the way back to the United States. President Barack Obama made a furtive nighttime visit to Afghanistan in 2010, when he was meant to be spending the weekend at Camp David.
Other risky trips featured presidential misdirection
President Bill Clinton went secretly from India to Pakistan in 2000, attempting to calm tensions in the disputed Kashmir region. He was seen talking with officials in front of a military plane that he appeared to board. Instead, Clinton ducked around the front of the aircraft to another jet parked nearby.
Both planes took off for Islamabad, as did a third jet painted with the familiar baby blue markings of Air Force One.
Joe Lockhart, a White House press secretary for Clinton, noted that reporters knew the president was on one of the planes, “but not which one.” He said he and other officials had briefed the press pool ahead of time and “although they didn’t know all the details, it was made clear” that Clinton “was not going to travel on the plane they were on.
“There was no attempt to hide anything, much less lie about it later,” Lockhart wrote on social media.
Bush was visiting an elementary school in Sarasota, Florida, during the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001, and, after all commercial air traffic was grounded, officials wanted to move him to an undisclosed location.
The full White House traveling press pool flew with Bush from Florida to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana, where officials reduced the number of reporters and staff on the plane. Bush and the smaller traveling party next flew to Nebraska’s Offutt Air Force Base before eventually returning to Washington.
Bush’s location remained secret throughout the day. However, the White House did not suggest that the president was somewhere he was not — unlike when Trump was whisked out of Turkey.
“You can imagine the different ways that this could have gone wrong, where, for a period of time, no one would have been able to independently corroborate the status of the U.S. president, or who was in charge of the U.S. government,” Graff said. “And that’s an incredibly dangerous moment for the world.”

The company is passing component price hikes down to customers, said Nitin Agrawal, its finance chief.

Meanwhile, competition is ramping. SpaceX has begun selling excess computing capacity, and Meta has considered launching a cloud business. Rival Nebius gained 5% in extended trading.
"Even with this increased competition, we're seeing demand, pricing and margin all expanding, which is a signal for the growth in the CoreWeave ... product, as well as our growth overall in an already massive TAM that exists," Agrawal said.
As of Tuesday's close, CoreWeave shares had gained 26% year to date, while the S&P 500 was up almost 13%. The stock debuted on Nasdaq in March 2025.

Industrial action by aviation unions in Nigeria disrupted domestic flight operations Tuesday in the commercial capital Lagos and the capital Abuja, leaving hundreds of passengers stranded at airports.
It was led by the National Union of Air Transport Employees (NUATE), the Air Transport Services Senior Staff Association of Nigeria (ATSSSAN) and the National Association of Aircraft Pilots and Engineers (NAAPE), with support from the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) and the Trade Union Congress (TUC).
The unions are protesting what they describe as anti-union practices by domestic airlines and the failure to remit a 5% Ticket Sales Charge (TSC) collected from passengers and owed to aviation agencies.
The action particularly disrupted the operations of Nigeria’s largest airline, Air Peace, after union members picketed its facilities at Murtala Muhammed Airport in Lagos and Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja.
Air Peace said the industrial action resulted in the barricading of entrances to its departure terminals, preventing scheduled flights from leaving Lagos and Abuja.
“The ongoing industrial action has resulted in the barricading of the entrances to our departure terminals at Murtala Muhammed Airport Terminal 1 (Alpha and Zulu Terminals) and Terminal 2 in Lagos, as well as the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport Terminal in Abuja,” the airline said in a statement.
It added that the disruption had “significantly affected” passengers travelling across its network and apologized to those stranded.
“Air Peace sincerely apologizes to all affected and stranded passengers for the disruption and inconvenience caused by circumstances beyond the airline’s control,” it said.
United Nigeria Airlines also suspended its flight operations, citing concerns over passenger and crew safety amid the industrial action.
“We regret to inform our valued passengers that we have temporarily suspended our flight operations due to the ongoing industrial action embarked upon by labor unions against domestic airlines,” it said.
“This decision was taken to protect the safety of our passengers and crew, which remains our priority at all times.”
The unions had earlier issued a three-day strike notice to airlines they accused of obstructing workers from joining unions and withholding the 5% TSC.
They said the remittance of the charge was necessary to enable aviation agencies to meet their financial obligations and implement negotiated conditions of service for workers.
The Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) said it was aware of the industrial action and its impact on passengers and other stakeholders.
The disruption comes during a period of heightened tension between aviation unions and domestic airlines over workers’ unionization and financial obligations to aviation agencies.
The unions have demanded that airline workers be allowed to join unions of their choice without intimidation, victimization or discrimination, while also calling for the immediate remittance of outstanding TSC revenues.
The action caused frustration among passengers at affected airports, with travelers facing uncertainty over their scheduled flights and alternative travel arrangements.

UNESCO: 2.4 million girls barred from school in Afghanistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:49:00 UTC
07:49:00 KST

UNESCO: 2.4 million girls barred from school in Afghanistan
August 12, 2026
Around 2.4 million girls in Afghanistan have been denied access to secondary education since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, UNESCO said Tuesday.
The figure has risen by about 200,000 since last year and could reach nearly four million by 2030 if the ban remains in place.
"Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls and women are formally banned from secondary and higher education," Hoda Jaberian, UNESCO’s program coordinator for education in emergencies, said.
"Five years is not a temporary interruption in a child’s education. It is clearly almost an entire secondary school cycle."
Why are Afghan girls banned from secondary schools and universities?
The Taliban seized power on August 15, 2021, as US and NATO forces withdrew after two decades of war.
They initially assured the international community that women would be allowed to continue studying.
But secondary schools were closed to girls in March 2022. Women were barred from universities in December that year.
The Taliban described both measures as temporary, but they remain in force.
The authorities say they respect women's rights in line with their interpretation of Islamic law and Afghan culture. They have also insisted the issue is a domestic matter.
Restrictions extend beyond education. Women face limits on employment and movement and have been barred from public parks, gyms and beauty salons.
The UN has described the broader system of restrictions as “gender apartheid.” Russia is the only country to formally recognize the Taliban administration.
What has happened to girls' education since the Taliban takeover?
UNESCO says the restrictions have reversed two decades of progress.
Girls had very limited access to schooling in 2001. By 2021, nearly one million were enrolled in secondary education.
"Afghanistan had made really major progress in expanding girls’ access to education," Jaberian said. "But unfortunately, much of that progress now has been completely reversed."
UNESCO has called for the immediate and unconditional restoration of girls' and women's right to secondary and higher education.
The agency continues to support community-based education as well as literacy and skills programs, often held in community spaces or facilitators' homes.
How is the Taliban ban affecting Afghanistan's economy?
UNESCO estimates that excluding women from secondary and higher education could push around 600,000 women out of the workforce by 2066.
The restrictions could also cause cumulative income losses of 9.6 billion US dollars and increase the risk of early marriage.
The ban is also worsening a shortage of female teachers. UNESCO expects Afghanistan to face a deficit of more than 11,000 qualified female teachers by 2030.
"Many teachers have left the country and those who were in the system are banned from continuing teaching," Jaberian said.
She added that restrictions on women teaching boys had left some pupils with unqualified male teachers or no teachers at all.
How severe is Afghanistan's wider education crisis?
Afghanistan's education system is facing problems far beyond the ban on girls.
More than two million primary school children are already out of school for other reasons. More than 90% of 10-year-olds cannot read a simple text, while the national literacy rate stands at 37%.
Many schools are overcrowded and poorly equipped. Nearly half lack water, sanitation or heating.
The system is also under pressure from people returning to Afghanistan.
Three million people returned in 2025 alone, either voluntarily or forcibly. More than seven million have returned or been forced back since 2023.
Natural disasters have added to the crisis. Earthquakes, floods and other disasters have forced around 1,000 schools to close since 2021, UNESCO said.
Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

PBS Chief Paula Kerger on the Aftermath of Federal Funding Cuts—and What People Get Wrong About Public Media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:44:45 UTC
07:44:45 KST

Paula Kerger is navigating arguably the most challenging period of her 20-year tenure at the helm of the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS), which has more than 330 member stations. Last spring, President Donald Trump signed an executive order calling for all federal funding to PBS and NPR to be blocked, accusing the organizations of bias. Soon after, the Department of Education notified the Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB) that it was terminating the 2020-2025 Ready To Learn grant for educational content, affecting PBS as well as dozens of public television and radio stations. PBS and NPR sued, and in March this year a federal judge ruled that the executive order barring the federal funding violated the First Amendment.
But the organization must still grapple with a funding shortfall created by a Congressional vote to rescind around $1.1 billion in advance appropriated federal funding for PBS and NPR, and an entirely new landscape for public media. The CPB, which was created in 1967 as a nonpartisan nonprofit to direct federal appropriations to public television and radio stations, announced in January that it would officially dissolve. PBS has since reduced its budget by 21% and cut 15% of positions, or around 100 jobs.
It’s not the first time PBS has faced such a threat, Kerger says, pointing to Newt Gingrich's “Contract with America” platform in 1994. But his idea was a “three-year glide path to zero,” she says. By contrast, the latest move gave stations just three months to find alternative funding, since they were already expecting the appropriated funds for 2026 and 2027, she says.
Since the rescission, Kerger has been touring the U.S. and speaking with affected communities. “The light bulb went off,” she says of the public’s reaction. “It's like, ‘Oh, Viewers Like You. That means us.’” Since the July 2025 rescission, PBS has seen more than a million new memberships. Philanthropy and commercial partnerships are helping. And Kerger hopes to get “some level of government funding back,” particularly to support rural communities and infrastructure, she says.
Kerger says she is most concerned about the future of content for children. “The kids' media landscape right now is really scary. A lot of kids are on YouTube, and there is some good stuff on YouTube, but kids get caught in the algorithm and they end up in places they shouldn't. Not all of it is by educators—our stuff all is, and it's rigorously tested,” she says. PBS is also working on games and content for “the significant number of kids that are not in formal pre-K, and whose family may not have access to as much technology or broadband.”
TIME spoke with Kerger on July 15 about the aftermath of the funding pullback, what people get wrong about PBS, and what gives her hope about the future for the organization.
This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.
You've talked before about how some people don't understand what PBS is. What do people get wrong about PBS?
Media in most countries started out as government-based, and then commercial media came second, and we were the other way around here. So commercial media was actually a growing industry, and it was the first woman FCC commissioner—a woman by the name of Frieda Hennock—who was looking at what she was anticipating as something that was going to have an enormous impact on society, but that was all rooted in commercialism in the marketplace. She worried there would be limitations, that there would be things that would be in the public interest that [the] commercial marketplace wasn't going to take up, and so she lobbied to have spectrum put aside for both TV and radio, and that's how we began.
Flash forward to Lyndon Johnson. He was particularly taken with what the BBC was able to do in terms of bringing great culture and history to the public, and he thought that our country should have that. He recognized that this loose confederation of individual stations that were mostly doing local or educational stuff wasn't exactly it, and that with some support you could create something that was more akin to the BBC, and that's when he signed the Public Broadcasting Act. Part of that was to create a network [that] could pull all these individual stations together. The second part of it was to ensure that there was federal funding available for communities that would perhaps be challenged to have their own stations. And so our funding always looked like that up until we lost the money last year. The largest percentage of most of the money went to stations, not to PBS and NPR. I think that was a confusion with some members of Congress. I'm not sure they knew exactly what they were voting on.
Those that were in smaller communities would get a larger proportion of their budget from the federal government. In Alaska, there actually is no other media except public radio and public television stations. Almost half of their budget comes from the federal government. So, it sort of played out exactly as LBJ anticipated. Our stations are all locally owned, locally operated, locally governed. I don't tell anyone what to do, but everyone pays dues to PBS. We take that money, we raise some other money, leverage some additional money. We work with producers. We pull together a full schedule that we distribute. The whole broadcast infrastructure is all managed by PBS. The digital infrastructure that was built— apps, PBS.org that a lot of stations plug into—all built by PBS. Stations’ positions on cable and on places like YouTube TV, negotiated by PBS. The work that we do in schools, which is all distributed via broadband—free, all done by PBS. Stations then contribute their content, so that it is still very much bottom up, but the glue that pulls it all together is PBS.
Can you talk me through where things stand today with the funding pullback?
So last year was quite a year, and we're still navigating through quite a few things. It started out with the FCC saying, "We think you're running commercials.” We actually are not. What we are running is sponsorship credits. We actually had worked with the FCC to define what is appropriate for public media, and we've worked closely with every Administration. Then we had the executive order that was going to make it illegal for any federal money to come to PBS and NPR. We won that suit. And the government [missed] the deadline to appeal, so it stands.
And then, of course there was the rescission. The executive order took out a program that we have managed for 30 years, which has funded our kids' content: Ready To Learn. For many years, the Department of Education would fund programming out of PBS that was all built around what the Education Department's priorities were, whether that's literacy or math skills or executive function or, in the last round—which had been re-upped under the first Trump Administration—workforce preparedness. Now, you can decide what that means for preschool, but we interpreted it as giving kids a really good start on the basics, before they entered school, as a way of just helping to make sure that we were jump-starting them in their school career that would lead to a professional career. After the executive order, that money was gone.
Then in June we lost the House vote, and this money had been advance appropriated for 2026 and 2027…I worked with the Public Media Company and within a very short period of time, we were able to raise bridge funds. That helped stabilize smaller stations that I think, some of them, would have gone dark very quickly.
PBS have been working pretty deliberately to make sure that the public is aware that the funding is gone. In the time since the rescission, we’ve picked up more than a million new members, and most of those are people that didn't just write a check, but they agreed to give every month, so they've really signed up to be part of this. It has not solved all of our problems, but we're in at least a stable position right now.
What I've been really focused on is our business model moving forward. Obviously, I would really love to get some level of government funding back, and I would argue [that’s] infrastructure money. If we could get that back, that would make an enormous difference. In addition to being a broadcaster, we're also the backup system for the emergency alert for this country because we operate broadcast, so we can reach everywhere. It's not just the messages to the public, but it's also using our spectrum to get information to first responders. It's a stable platform. Data and so forth can be pushed out via broadcast very effectively and very efficiently.
The philanthropy is going to continue to be significant. We continue to look for production partners. We are streaming content on Amazon. So, some business revenue, some philanthropic investment, and the hope of trying to get at least some [funding] from the government. I think if we can get all those pieces aligned, we'll be in really strong shape.
Can you give an indication of the proportions of those different funding streams?
So historically, half of our money came from our stations, and a lot of that was contributed money. So I would say probably moving forward, I would assume that half of our money would continue to be contributed money, if we can manage this properly. Of the government money, it was 15% in aggregate. Whether some piece of that would come back, I can't even begin to quantify what that would mean. The rest of it would be some combination of increased foundation grants, as well as the contributed money. So a quarter of earned revenue, a quarter of high net worth and then foundation grants and individual giving. Individual giving is what's kept us anchored in communities. It's also what makes this so powerful, because everyone feels that they own it.
On the philanthropy side of things, how are you thinking about who you want to take funding from? You've said before that you don't really want billionaires.
There were a lot of people that said, “Don't you have a billionaire that could solve your problems?” If people want to make more generous contributions, that’s great. We have some big needs. I just think that this idea that someone is going to sail in and save you is not good, and it's particularly not good for media. Even if someone has the very best of intentions, there's always going to be that doubt of, is someone really directing, or does someone have a thumb on the scale, or so forth.
There are some people that really did step up this last year. I'm out talking to a lot of them, particularly around specific genres, and particularly around kids, right now. Kids have been impacted on so many different levels in the last couple of years, whether it's access to health care, there's so many children that have food insecurity now, and daycare circumstance—particularly high quality pre-K—has deteriorated, not improved. You just see that kids have borne the brunt of so much. We've got the history going all the way back to Fred Rogers and Sesame Street—we reach all those children. Our stations live in communities across the country. There are a lot of philanthropists that are looking at this, and these are areas that they care deeply about. So I'm hoping to continue to make that good case.
The current administration has turned its attention to some foundations as well. Is that a consideration when you're thinking about which foundations you will accept funding from?
I'll tell you what I pay attention to. One is, obviously, we have a firewall between our editorial and the contributed money, and that's really important. What I do pay attention to is not whether I'll take money from this foundation or that foundation for political reasons. What I do pay attention to is that we have a mix of donors that represent a range of interests, perspectives, geography, and so forth. I think there was a fallacy in the arguments around us and our funding that somehow we were left-leaning, or that we were funded by left-leaning organizations. Look at Ken Burns' recent series on the American Revolution. If you look at those funders, particularly the larger ones, you see people across the political spectrum. That's how it should be. We want all people engaged and involved. We're a public media service for the country, and we need to reflect the country in that way.
I think the combination of doing that with the larger contributions, as well as lots and lots of small contributions, that's really always been the bedrock of public broadcasting. Every year, I think 23 years in a row, we have fielded a study that ranks us most trusted of public institutions. YouGov has been doing a similar survey in the last years. Same thing. I think we're number two after the Weather Channel. I think part of it is that if you anchor your support in a lot of grassroots philanthropy, people have to trust you, and so we take all of this really super seriously.
And I would say that in the funding discussions in the last year, and actually on an ongoing basis, occasionally someone says—and believe me, I get these calls—”What, are you just catering to the Administration?” or “You're too hard on the Administration.” A lot of times I'll get those calls around the same broadcast, which is a little weird. People say, “Well I think you're biased” and it's like, OK, we do take this really seriously, can you give me an example? And oftentimes they can't.
Are these the sorts of conversations that you're having with members of Congress? What is it that they are expressing they're most concerned about?
Some, I think, were surprised when we were defunded that it actually affected their local station. Ironically, a lot of the legislators spend time at the stations. That's where a lot of them end up doing town halls and debates, and they come in for various community events. I went and visited a couple of the senators that had voted against us and some of them said, well it was really the advance appropriation we were trying to get rid of and we'll look at the regular appropriations process, and it's still a dance. There was a little movement this year in looking at the infrastructure money that I'm talking about, at least reopening the program that existed where that funding had flowed before. That's a really important first step. Government funds infrastructure—it makes sense to me.
What would it take to get that through?
Getting enough people to vote from both sides of the aisle. I don't know [that], out of this budget process, we’ll be successful, but we're going to just keep plugging away at it because I think as people are setting priorities, the important thing is to get on that list. One of the things, both helpful and not, is in this last year, for the most part, people haven't seen enormous change. Unless we get some help, I think it'll become apparent in this next year we’ll likely lose a few stations, and I think that will also get people's attention, particularly if it happens to be in your legislative district.
This isn’t the first time that PBS has faced these sorts of challenges, but to your mind, why do you think PBS has become a target in this moment?
Well, I think media in general has been a target. I frankly think that's part of why so many people have also stepped up. I think a lot of people are very concerned about the impact of what they're seeing and how it's affecting different media organizations. It's a challenging time for media anyway because of the changes in how people are consuming content, and so we have been very much involved over a number of years, in really looking at how do we meet people where they are. YouTube has been a great partner of ours, and they helped us get all of our stations on YouTube TV, and that's opened up other possibilities on other platforms. So it's been a complicated time to navigate through. People's patterns have shifted a lot.
Who are your audiences, in terms of demographics?
Depends on what you're watching. We have a very big audience under 5. We have a very large audience across demographics on digital. For example, the Frontline broadcast audience is well over 60. The YouTube audience is under 35 [and] is also global.
I'd say the one commonality for a PBS viewer is that [it’s] people that are curious about the world, just want to learn more. I've been talking a lot over this last year as we've rolled into the 250th [anniversary of the U.S.]. I've always been struck by what I view as our key values of our country. The pursuit of happiness. What does that mean? I think what it means is lifelong learning. It's this idea that anyone would have the opportunity to achieve their potential, and that's who we are, and so I think that for our viewers, that very much captures who watches.
Where would you like to see PBS over the next 10 or 15 years?
I feel like we have had a role in the life of people and families and communities across this country, and I am deeply committed to making sure that we continue to meet the needs of people that clearly will evolve over the next 10, 15 years. I think how we connect to people will continue to change. I think the power of a story well told is extraordinary, and so, however that story [is told], I want to make sure that we're there to do that. I think our place in local communities is pretty profound.
But I think for us to thrive, we also have to make sure that we're continuing to bring in new voices and new perspectives. Our focus is around making sure that we're educating and engaging and inspiring. I really hope that as we look forward over the next 10 to 15 years, that it will continue to also be a through line. We want to embrace that whole idea of pursuit of happiness and really ensure that people see possibility. And if we do that and we do it well, then I'll be really proud of what we've accomplished at PBS.

According to the EIA, disruptions in oil supplies caused by the war involving Iran and restrictions on operations in the Strait of Hormuz could continue until early 2027. This will lead to higher fuel prices and inflation worldwide.
The United States expects oil supply disruptions caused by the war surrounding Iran and restrictions on the operation of the Strait of Hormuz to last until early 2027. Bloomberg reports this, citing a forecast by the U.S. Energy Information Administration, writes UNN.
Details
According to EIA estimates, an average of 4.9 million barrels of oil per day passed through the Strait of Hormuz in the second quarter of 2026. By comparison, in the fourth quarter of 2025, before the start of the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran, the figure was 21.6 million barrels per day.
Oil edges lower amid Oman-Iran talks on the Strait of Hormuz - Reuters11.08.26, 17:23 • 3176 views
Despite a brief pause in hostilities, the situation in global energy markets remains tense. An agreement between Iran and Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz has not yet been reached, although officials report progress in the negotiations.
Fuel prices may rise
Due to the prolonged disruptions, consumers worldwide may face another increase in fuel prices and inflation. The EIA raised its forecast for gasoline and diesel prices in 2026 by 3.7% and 5.4%, respectively. The forecast for the retail price of gasoline in 2027 was also increased by 6.5% compared with the estimate from a month earlier.
The exact volume of oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz is difficult to determine in real time because vessels conceal data about their activities. At the same time, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that an average of about 9 million barrels of oil per day had passed through the strait over the past week.

According to an EIA estimate, the reduction in Middle East production decreased from 7.5 million barrels per day in June to approximately 5.5 million in July. At the same time, the figure could rise to 6.6 million barrels per day in the third quarter.
Several countries in the region cut production due to limited access to global markets, placing additional strain on available oil storage capacity.
If threats to vessels carrying Saudi oil in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait area do not lead to further production cuts, the EIA expects most oil flows and trading operations to return to prewar levels by early 2027.

EU has no idea who will pay for €90 bn Ukraine loan – MEP

Member states gave the green light to the scheme in April, with Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia securing exemptions.
On Monday, German MEP Fabio De Masi, who co-chairs the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance party, told the Berliner Zeitung that the “European Commission apparently doesn’t even know the extent to which EU member states will have to guarantee the Ukraine loan.”
He cited the commission’s response to his inquiry, which said that a “breakdown [of the financial burden] by member state” could not be provided.
De Masi said the funds, which are being backed by joint EU borrowing on the capital market, would end up enriching “corrupt oligarchs” in Ukraine.

Since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, the EU has given more than €216 billion to Kiev. Germany has spent over €43.3 billion, while earmarking an additional €57.6 billion in military aid for the coming years, thus emerging as Ukraine’s top backer within the bloc.
In late June, the European Commission began disbursing the first €3.2 billion tranche as part of the scheme, under which Ukraine is due to receive €30 billion in budgetary aid and €60 billion for its military needs in 2026 and 2027. The installment was soon followed by another 3.9 billion earmarked for drone procurement.
European Council head Antonio Costa previously said Ukraine would only need to pay back the money after it receives reparations from Russia following the conclusion of the conflict. Moscow has dismissed the notion as “detached from reality.”

GM reaches up to $4.5 billion parts deal designed to avoid supply chain troubles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:42:10 UTC
07:42:10 KST

DETROIT — General Motors has reached a unique, multibillion-dollar parts deal as it aims to preserve cash and prevent supply chain disruptions like ones that have hit the global automotive industry this decade.
In a public filing Tuesday, GM said the up to $4.5 billion purchasing facility includes a company called Procura Auto Parts that specializes in sourcing rare or critical parts. It will receive funding through a bank syndicate led by JPMorgan Chase and Banco Santander to prepay select suppliers on behalf of GM.
In return, GM will issue formal promises called irrevocable payment undertakings, or IPUs, to pay back the company after it uses the parts in production, no later than July 31, 2029. The deal allows GM to keep inventory costs off its books, while better securing future supply.
GM pays interest, plus an agreed-upon premium on what's used, as well as a customary annual fee on the unused portion during that year, according to the filing. For accounting purposes, the prepayments show up as an asset and each purchase is booked as unsecured debt, and the cash flows are shown as if GM paid suppliers directly, the filing said.
These payments are excluded from adjusted automotive free cash flow until GM actually buys the inventory. The company typically books the capital within 90 days of purchase.
GM declined to disclose what parts the company may be targeting. Problematic parts for the automotive industry have included semiconductor chips, including dynamic random access memory, rare earths and wire harnesses.
The deal follows years of global automotive supply chain issues and comes after GM and other automakers reevaluated their sourcing or parts following U.S. tariffs and a push to move away from Chinese companies.
GM established the deal with Procura and the banks on Friday, according to the filing.

Trump administration ends Medicaid, CHIP funding for child gender transitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:38:49 UTC
07:38:49 KST

Rabia İclal Turan
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced Tuesday that it is ending federal Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) funding for gender transition procedures for children and youth.
The final rule, implemented through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), ends federal funding for puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and surgical operations for children, which HHS describes as "experimental and life-altering sex-rejecting procedures that carry serious long-term health risks."
"Today, we are ending federal taxpayer funding for sex-rejecting procedures on children," HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said, citing "serious risks" and "irreversible harm."
CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said children "deserve our protection, not experimental interventions."
"By cutting off federal funds for these sex-rejecting procedures, we’re following the science, saving taxpayer dollars, and, most importantly, protecting children from potentially irreversible harm so they can truly flourish," Oz added.
Mental health coverage is unaffected, and children currently on hormone therapy will retain funding for up to six months. The rule takes effect Oct. 13.
President Donald Trump said he directed the move, writing on his Truth Social platform that the administration would not "pay for our innocent children to undergo these barbaric surgeries and practices, which result in unthinkable and irreversible harm to their young bodies."
"Thanks to our strong position and pressure on this issue over the past year and a half, dozens of U.S. hospitals have already ended this so-called ‘gender-affirming care,’ and we expect many more to follow," he added.
He linked the announcement to the midterm elections, saying: "Please remember this when you are casting your vote in the Midterm Elections in November."

Iran has announced plans to create a ballistic missile with a range of up to 15,000 km, which could potentially reach U.S. territory. Defense Express reports this, citing a statement by Abd al-Nabi Musavi Fard, a representative of Iran’s Supreme Leader, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the Iranian leadership representative made the statement during Friday prayers. Currently, Iran’s longest-range ballistic missile is considered to be the Khorramshahr, with a claimed range of up to 4,000 km.
Defense Express notes that transitioning from medium-range missiles to an intercontinental system with a range of 15,000 km would be a difficult technological step. To strike Washington and New York from Iranian territory, a range of at least approximately 10,000 km would be required.
Possible role of North Korea
Defense Express suggests that Iran may attempt to use North Korea’s existing missile technologies. The publication recalls that the Khorramshahr was developed on the basis of the North Korean Hwasong-10, which, in turn, originated from the Soviet R-27 ballistic missile.
North Korea already has several intercontinental ballistic missiles with a claimed range of approximately 15,000 km or more. In particular, the Hwasong-18’s range is estimated at approximately 15,000 km, while the Hwasong-19 is claimed to have a range of more than 17,000 km. The Hwasong-17’s range is estimated at approximately 15,000 km.
Defense Express suggests that Iran may obtain some of the necessary technologies through cooperation with North Korea. At the same time, the publication does not rule out the direct transfer of missile technologies by Russia, although this is currently an assumption rather than a confirmed fact.

====================================================================================================

Budget Instability Puts Golden Dome at Risk, Guetlein Warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:26:27 UTC
07:26:27 KST

HUNTSVILLE, Ala.—The four-star general in charge of the Pentagon’s Golden Dome program warned that uncertainty around the Pentagon’s $350 billion reconciliation request could slow progress on the homeland missile defense effort, a top priority for President Donald Trump.
To date, the Pentagon’s strategy for funding the $185 billion program has been to bypass the annual budget process and rely instead on a separate funding maneuver called reconciliation, which isn’t subject to standard appropriations rules and can be passed by a simple majority in both chambers of Congress.
That approach allowed the program to hit the ground running last year after Trump signed an executive order announcing the initiative, according to Golden Dome Director Gen. Michael Guetlein. As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed in 2025, Golden Dome received $25 billion—90 percent of which it has since obligated, Guetlein told an audience Aug. 11 at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium here.
This year, the Pentagon requested $17 billion for the effort as part of a proposed $350 billion reconciliation package and just $400 million in the normal “base” budget for fiscal 2027. This time around, though, there appears to be little political will to pass another spending bill via reconciliation, leaving Golden Dome without a clear path for near-term funding.
“We’ve got to figure out as a nation a different way of funding Golden Dome, at least for ‘27,” Guetlein said. “Both sides of the aisle, as well as the House and the Senate, are working through the math about how do you do this in ‘27. I will tell you that if they don’t figure it out, there is no Golden Dome because there is no funding.”
For now, the reconciliation process is stalled in Congress. The House approved a slimmed down $60 billion version of the White House’s proposal in July. It’s possible some Pentagon priorities initially included in reconciliation could be funded through a separate $67 billion Iran war supplemental, though that proposal is also in limbo.
Meanwhile, the prospects of passing a standard appropriations bill by the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30 have also dimmed. The House and Senate have passed separate versions of a continuing resolution that would provide stopgap funding to avoid a government shutdown. Guetlein noted that the continuing resolution—which freezes funding at the prior year’s levels—doesn’t provide relief for Golden Dome.
“A CR doesn’t help me under Golden Dome because I don’t have a top line to fall back to to get that percentage of the continuing resolution,” he said.
Speaking with reporters after his speech, Guetlein said the department is discussing contingency plans should reconciliation fail. One option is for the military services to take over funding some elements of the Golden Dome architecture. He pointed to the Space Force as an example, which has already invested heavily in Golden Dome-enabling capabilities like the Space Data Network and space-based missile warning and tracking satellites.
“Several of the space capabilities that we are investing in are also being invested in by the Space Force,” he said. “So, if Golden Dome is not able to continue to invest in those type of capabilities, then the Space Force could decide at that time to continue the investments.”
He added: “Because we have diversified execution of a lot of these capabilities, and a lot of these capabilities are already requested by combatant commands, there are some alternatives that we can pursue. We have not made any decisions on any pathway.”
Guetlein said he’s hopeful the department and Congress will find a way to fund the program in ‘27 given the urgency around bolstering U.S. defenses against missile threats and the capabilities he says the team has already proven.
During his speech, Guetlein highlighted recent milestones, which include breaking ground on the Golden Dome’s first operational site at Joint Expeditionary Base Fort Story, Va., and a major test event it conducted in June at White Sands Missile Range, N.M. Of note, Guetlein told reporters the Pentagon’s independent Director of Operational Test & Evaluation did not oversee the test; instead a “separate entity” is charged with leading validation efforts in close coordination with DOT&E.
Guetlein also reported progress on one of Golden Dome’s more ambitious technical lifts—demonstrating the integration of space-based interceptors to defeat missile threats at various phases of flight. The Space Force is leading a prize competition among 12 companies to incrementally showcase SBI capabilities with the goal of an initial capability by 2028.
Contractors have completed the first of those increments, dubbed Gate One, which focused on solidifying a design and conducting component-level testing. Guetlein said it appears all of the providers will move to Gate Two, where they will build a prototype. Those that progress to Gate Three must prove the capability works in space and then the Gate Four providers must show their interceptors can be integrated with the broader Golden Dome architecture.
“We have not put in any operational requests for production capabilities until after they prove through the prize-based competition that those capabilities are effective, but more importantly, that they’re scalable and affordable,” he said. “At that point, we will then make a decision if we are going to move into production or not.”

On Aug 9, the Indian government said the pilot in command of AI2379, which flew from Phuket to Delhi, would undergo a second round of drug screening to confirm whether he was under the influence of a psychoactive substance when the aircraft suddenly lost altitude.
The incident, which occurred on Aug 4 and is being probed by India’s Aircraft Accidents Investigation Bureau, left several passengers and cabin crew members injured.
Quake death toll tops 250, amid race to find survivors
Rescue crews on Aug 11 dug through mountains of rubble in western Colombia, shouting for quiet so they could listen for survivors still trapped under the buildings that collapsed in a powerful earthquake estimated to have killed at least 250 people.
The 7.4-magnitude quake, the most devastating to strike Colombia this century, tore through its coffee-growing heartland early on Aug 10, leaving apartment blocks, homes, schools and health centers cracked, leaning or flattened.
Separate reports from affected cities put the death toll at 254 on the morning of Aug 11, with 101 people killed in Pereira, deep in coffee country, and 95 in Cali, the country’s third-biggest city.
Ukraine gives US negotiators proposals for ending war
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug 11 that Ukraine had handed proposals to US negotiators for a plan to end the war with Moscow and suggested that Russia would use its parliamentary election in September as a pretext to declare a new mobilisation.
Zelensky’s announcement of fresh proposals for peace talks, largely stalled since the outbreak of the conflict with Iran, comes amid suggestions by both Russia and Ukraine that US negotiators would soon pay a visit to their two countries.
“We have conveyed our proposals to the American side,” Zelensky said, in his nightly video address.
Ash cloud from Sicily’s Mount Etna disrupts Malta flights
An ash cloud from Sicily’s Mount Etna volcano drifted over Malta on Aug 11, forcing airlines to cancel some flights to the Mediterranean island at the height of the tourism season.
“We’re currently experiencing flight disruptions due to volcanic ash clouds over the Maltese Islands following recent activity at Mount Etna,” Malta International Airport said in a Facebook message.
A spokesperson said 19 flights had been cancelled by mid-afternoon on Aug 11 and several other flights had been significantly delayed.
