“The process cannot be so slow that the next assembly elections would be due by the time the appeals are decided,” said CJI Surya Kant.
NEW DELHI: With nearly 34 lakh appeals pending adjudication before SIR appellate tribunals against deletion of voters’ names in West Bengal, Supreme Court Tuesday decided to take stock of their performance and suggested they speed up their work, saying the process cannot be unending, even though it was unwilling to set a deadline for decision on appeals.“The process cannot be so slow that the next assembly elections would be due by the time the appeals are decided,” said CJI Surya Kant responding to a petition complaining about the slow rate of disposal of appeals by those whose names were deleted from electoral rolls during their Special Intensive Revision (SIR).Petitioner and Congress leader Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury, through senior advocate Rauf Rahim said the progress in deciding appeals by the tribunals, set up on SC orders, is painfully slow and requires impetus to speed up disposal rate. Chowdhury said names of lakhs of poor people have been deleted from the voter list in Murshidabad and they do not have the wherewithal to approach SC.A bench of CJI Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, “These tribunals were constituted on our orders. A substantial time has elapsed since they started working. We must consider their performance keeping in mind the pendency and disposals. Immediate concern is to take stock.”
“Once we get the statistics, we would be able to provide it with guidance and information technology to help speed up the process,” Justice Bagchi said. The bench asked Election Commisson to give details of pendency and disposals by Aug 25, the next date of hearing.
Also read:Less than 1% appeals disposed of by Bengal SIR tribunals in 100 daysWhen Rahim said appeals are required to be decided early as WB govt has begun depriving deleted voters of benefits of welfare schemes, the bench said this is altogether a separate cause of action which should be adjudicated by Calcutta High Court. “If you expand the scope of this petition, we will send it to HC,” it said and declined to fix a timeline for disposal of appeals.Chowdhury said, “Several people whose names are deleted from voter lists have made appeal before the tribunals and are waiting for the fate of their cases. But the process and infrastructure of the tribunals is not sufficient for early disposal of such a huge number of appeals after giving proper opportunity of hearing.”

US lifts TikTok ban on government devices after ByteDance restructuring
Unknown

06:40:01 KST

US lifts TikTok ban on government devices after ByteDance restructuring
Justice Department says the app’s new US joint venture is no longer covered by the 2022 prohibition targeting app’s Chinese parent company
The White House has formally lifted the ban on TikTok on US government devices after the Justice Department determined that the version operated by the platform’s new US joint venture is no longer covered by a 2022 prohibition targeting applications controlled by its Chinese parent company, ByteDance.
The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), in a memo dated Monday, rescinded a 2023 directive that barred the use of TikTok on government devices over national security concerns arising from its links to China.
The move formally implements a July opinion from the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel concluding that the application operated by TikTok USDS Joint Venture LLC no longer qualified as a “covered application” under the No TikTok on Government Devices Act.
The opinion said US President Donald Trump had instructed that executive branch employees could download TikTok on official devices, although individual agencies retain discretion over its use and employees must comply with applicable workplace policies.

One Ukrainian soldier to 26 Russian occupiers: Military officer reports losses on Huliaipole front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:34:00 UTC
06:34:00 KST

One Ukrainian soldier to 26 Russian occupiers: Military officer reports losses on Huliaipole front
Dmytro Perun Filatov, commander of the First Separate Assault Regiment named after Dmytro Kotsyubailo, said this in an exclusive interview with Ukrainian Radio.
"At present, this section of the front is under control. The enemy’s attempts to conduct further offensive operations have been reduced to zero. The enemy does not stop attempting daily assaults, but has had no success. We have built an effective system of countermeasures. We are actively advancing despite the fact that the enemy is trying to attack intensively in this area.
"The main challenges we expect from the enemy are increased mobilization after the completion of the electoral process in Russia. It is likely to be carried out covertly in Russia. However, we do not rule out broader mobilization. We will not be able to compensate for this through increased mobilization ourselves, since the enemy has greater manpower resources. Therefore, we are trying to find methods of countering this and conducting the war through asymmetric actions," he emphasized.
Filatov also said that the casualty ratio on this section of the front is one Ukrainian soldier to 26 Russian occupiers.
"Our ratio has reached 1 (Ukrainian soldier) to 26 (Russian occupiers). In general, during combat operations, the average ratio of losses between attacking and defending units is 1 defender to 3 attackers or 1 defender to 4 attackers. In our case, we are finding methods that result in significantly higher Russian losses.
"We pay great attention to protecting our equipment and artillery, which puts significant pressure on the enemy. Our assault operations are not as rapid as they are traditionally understood to be. We are looking for ways to reach operational space so that a single offensive operation could advance 30–40 kilometers in depth. This is difficult, and not all of our units have such a ratio," said the commander of the First Separate Assault Regiment named after Dmytro Kotsyubailo, Dmytro Perun Filatov.
According to Ukrinform, the total combat losses of Russian forces since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, through August 11, 2026, amount to approximately 1,460,400 personnel, including 1,190 over the past day.

‘We’ve seen this somewhere in history before, haven’t we?’ Inside Russia’s plan to resettle 114,000 of its people in occupied Ukraine.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:30:46 UTC
06:30:46 KST

‘We’ve seen this somewhere in history before, haven’t we?’ Inside Russia’s plan to resettle 114,000 of its people in occupied Ukraine.
Over the next 20 years, Russian authorities plan to resettle nearly 114,000 Russians in the occupied Ukrainian territories. Despite the grim circumstances, some people really are moving there. The independent journalists’ cooperative Bereg took Melitopol as its example — a city in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region that Russian troops entered as early as February 25, 2022 — to understand what kind of people move from Russia to the seized regions, and what occupation means for Ukrainians. Bereg talked with Russians who have resettled there, with lifelong Melitopol residents, and with the Ukrainian nonviolent resistance movement Zla Mavka (“Angry Mavka”). Meduza is translating the story in full.
‘I thought, “God, my business is closed.” I didn’t yet know what they would do to my family’
Lyudmila Plachkova, 34, was born and raised in Melitopol. She left for Bulgaria because of the occupation. Officers of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) abducted her parents, Tatyana and Oleg.
We’re a family of entrepreneurs. In Melitopol, we lived through good times and bad. The city was alive and growing, and we grew with it — new businesses, public gardens, parks, and fairs kept appearing. The COVID years were hard on business, but we all helped one another.
In 2013, my parents rented a space and opened their own business: a café. My mom had worked as a cook and had always dreamed of a restaurant of her own. The café became her baby. We had no real capital, so we took out loans.
It was hard at first. I worked there as a waitress, and my dad did all the physical work himself. My mom’s friends, cooks themselves, took jobs in the kitchen. Eventually it all grew into a fairly successful venture — a large banquet hall, where you’re constantly dealing with guests. My mom was very outgoing, and everyone in town knew her. A lot of people came to the café partly because of her. They’d all say, “We want to see Tanya.” I think the café became popular because of how open she was.
My parents were always like two lovebirds, together all the time. In 2023, the business turned 10. That was part of why my mom didn’t want to leave [the occupied territory] while she still could. She’d grown too attached to it.
When they started bombing us [on February 24, 2022], I froze and didn’t know what to do. Then [Russian] troops took up positions outside Melitopol, waiting for the order to move in, since Ukrainian forces were still in the city.
My dad said there would be a mop-up phase, but I didn’t know what that meant or what they’d do to us. As a young woman, I was terrified, especially given the news from Bucha and the stories about Kadyrov’s men. At that point, we [Lyudmila, her husband, and several relatives and friends — Bereg’s note] moved in with my parents. We huddled together and waited. My parents lived near a school, and when things got really frightening, we’d go to the bomb shelter there. Somehow it was all easier to bear when we were together.
Then Mariupol happened, and people started fleeing that city. We helped where we could, gathering supplies and food for them. In March and April 2022, pro-Ukrainian rallies were held in Melitopol, and I went out to them.
Looting had started in the city, and it mattered to me to show that decent people lived there. We [the protesters] said we didn’t want Russia here, and at first the soldiers even told us they might leave soon. Later, once Russian flags started going up around the city, I realized nothing good would come of it.
Melitopol changed. Business owners and young people left. I remember my dad saying at one point, “We’re back in the 1990s.” Makeshift markets sprang up (half the entrepreneurs had gone), and a lot of people of “eastern nationalities” arrived. The streets filled with strangers. It’s a small city — a lot of faces used to be familiar. Moscow plates, Krasnodar plates… You’d walk around and realize this wasn’t your city anymore.
I had little direct contact with the occupiers before I left. I just watched our city fill up with people who’d never lived in it. It frightened me: strangers had arrived and started imposing new rules on me. Before I left [the occupied territory], I was afraid even to go outside.
Leaving was frightening too — there was no telling what to expect at filtration. Vasylivka was still open then, the only crossing into Ukraine. I was afraid to go through it after hearing terrifying stories about people being taken to a basement. And you had to travel under shelling. I didn’t risk it. Vasylivka was later closed, and we left through Crimea, Russia, and Turkey.
In Crimea, [FSB officers] questioned us. The filtration drags on, and you don’t know whether your husband will come out of it at all. You drive across Russia not knowing whether you’ll make it… In the end, surprisingly, my husband got through.
My husband had a clothing store; I had a decor studio. We had to close it all and leave. At the time, I thought, “God, my business is closed.” I didn’t yet know what they would do to my family.
Overnight into September 26, 2023, FSB officers broke into my parents’ apartment. I had already left by then. I later learned from my mom’s cellmates that she’d been beaten on the head with a mop.
My grandmother was home too. They locked her in a room and told her, “Don’t try anything.” After my parents were taken away, two FSB officers stayed behind to search the apartment. She sat locked in that room from 11 p.m. to 11 a.m., without food or water.
I think my mom and dad were taken because they refused to recognize Russian rule. They believed the occupation would end — my mom especially.
Shortly before the abduction, a post about my mom appeared on the Telegram channel Zhduny. It said she was pro-Ukrainian. That was the first warning sign.
My mom was sure they wouldn’t touch her — she wasn’t doing anything, just living her life. Besides, my grandmother had just come through surgery, and my parents couldn’t leave her alone. In our last conversation, my mom said that if nothing changed, they’d leave in November. She held out hope to the very end that the occupation would be pushed back. My mom was always a huge optimist.
Everything I know about what happened to my parents afterward, I learned from my mom’s cellmates. My parents were taken to a basement room in Melitopol, in the building the FSB now occupies. They were tortured in captivity. My dad was beaten, and my mom was made to watch. As I understand it, that’s how they tried to force a confession out of her.
From September 26 until her birthday on October 2, my mom was held in that basement room. As far as I understand, it had no windows and no doors, and they kept her there without food. She was then moved to a women’s cell. There was no water, no shower, and no toilet, and the temperature was around 10 degrees Celsius (50 degrees Fahrenheit). Many of the women were still in the summer clothes they were taken in. Guards would starve my mom, then give her scraps and tell her, “Be glad for the leftovers.” They made her learn the anthems of Russia and of the self-proclaimed Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics.
On February 8, 2024, my mom was brought to a hospital in Melitopol already in critical condition. She was in a coma, with no clothes on and bedsores on her body. Where she’d been before that is unknown — possibly another hospital. She was put in the infectious disease ward after being diagnosed with the flu. She wasn’t breathing on her own; she arrived already on a ventilator.
I think her condition [the coma — Bereg’s note] came from the blows to the head [during torture at interrogations] and the lack of timely medical care.
Her cellmates later told me my mom started feeling ill back in December. When she asked for help, she was told, “You’re not at a resort.” She was vomiting, couldn’t eat, and couldn’t even drink. She kept getting worse, and toward the end she just lay there. The women said they once begged the guards for a piece of bread, cut it into small pieces, and dried them for her, but she couldn’t even eat those.
By late December, my mom had stopped coming to. There was no help. She wasn’t brought up from the basement until early January, when she began foaming at the mouth.
An FSB investigator let my grandmother visit my mom in the hospital for 10 minutes at a time, under strict supervision. They even mounted cameras over her, [although she was] in a coma. The investigator said that once she recovered, she’d be tried for espionage. I don’t know whether he really believed she could recover…
My mom died on May 23, 2024. I couldn’t say goodbye — investigators made it clear to the family that if I came, they’d do the same to me. All of it broke my grandmother. She lost her daughter.
Very little is known about my dad. For a time he was held on the other side of a wall from my mom, and she heard him being tortured with electric shocks. Where he was taken after that is unknown. My mom’s cellmates said she believed to the end that he’d been released and was home. She looked for him, and managed to write him notes. Some of the guards — mostly Kadyrov’s men — told her he’d been let go. We don’t know where he is.
There’s hope that he’s all right… As far as that’s possible. He may be held incommunicado. There are a great many such people, held for years. People say there are penal colonies in the occupied territories where they’re kept for years on end, unable to say anything about themselves.
I’m sending inquiries to detention facilities and to the FSB. The Investigative Committee has opened a case to find my dad. Investigators there don’t say he’s in their custody. They often reply that we should wait — that we may learn something once he’s charged with something.
One time when we went to the local Investigative Committee, officials told us, “Well, you understand where he is [the FSB — Bereg’s note]. There’s nothing we can do.” They also said something like, “Today we’re here, and tomorrow we could be where your parents [ended up].” But these were all unofficial conversations.
Officially, they write that they know nothing and are searching. The FSB says, “We have no information on him; no one detained him.” Every detention facility says he isn’t there — though there are plenty of cases where people are being held and their relatives told otherwise.
I personally know of six cases of abduction, torture, or arbitrary deportation of civilians in Melitopol alone. Many of us have people close to us in captivity, held without charge and with no way to communicate. Some have gone missing. Others have been convicted — and they’re people we know. And we’re ordinary people.
What's known about the abduction and torture of Melitopol residents by Russian security forces
In October 2023, the independent Russian outlet iStories detailed the system of abductions, torture, and terror in Russian-occupied Melitopol.
Journalists described the abduction by Russian troops of school principals and teachers who, as of fall 2023, were still teaching to Ukrainian standards, along with residents suspected of partisan activity.
Maksym Ivanov, a 29-year-old landscape designer from Melitopol, was abducted while putting up flyers for Ukrainian Independence Day, the outlet reported. His ribs were broken during questioning at a police station, and he was then driven — with a bag over his head — to “the garages under the bridge,” where he was beaten with rebar and given electric shocks.
The mother of 24-year-old Melitopol resident Leonid Popov told iStories that Russian troops abducted and tortured her son three times. He had been diagnosed with schizophrenia earlier, and his health became critical in captivity. Three months after his abduction, Popov weighed 40 kilograms (88 pounds) at a height of 195 centimeters (6 feet 5 inches). The FSB later charged Popov with espionage; he faces up to 20 years in prison.
They’re simply destroying people and covering it up. I still can’t fully understand why they do it. I could understand it if this were about a pool of prisoners for military exchanges, but they’re taking civilians — not by the dozens, by the thousands. They charge them with nothing and don’t exchange them. Why? What kind of terrorism is this?
A classmate of my husband’s is now being held somewhere in Siberia, without charge and with no way to contact his family. He was taken in 2022.
After what happened to my parents, [people still in Melitopol] are afraid to talk to me. It can be dangerous — they’re hunting for “traitors” there.
Russian passports were introduced for everyone. If you don’t get one, you’re called in for a talk; an acquaintance of mine was deported over it. My parents never had Russian passports.
If the occupation ends, I’ll go back. Though that’s hard to imagine right now, because everything there is steeped in memories of my parents. I can’t look at photographs from there. It hurts too much. I’m 34 now, but my life stopped in 2023. The two people closest to me were taken from me, and I don’t understand how to go on living.
The Russians did what they set out to do. They frightened everyone and showed what they’re capable of. They broke me. They broke my family. My dad is being held somewhere, unable to say anything about himself, and I can’t find him or help him. That’s a particular kind of torture, when you can’t do anything. But I keep fighting. I’ve switched on my mom’s optimism, and I’m still looking for my dad. I believe he’s alive.
‘I never managed to get used to this lack of civilization’
Darya, 30, moved to Melitopol from Izhevsk but went back home a year later.
We moved at the start of 2025, when my youngest child was two months old. After nearly a year, we went back — we didn’t like it.
I’m probably not giving away any great secret if I say that plenty of people are moving to the “new territories.” The main reason is simple: military personnel qualify for their pensions faster there, because a day of service counts as two or three days. And pay overall is a bit higher than outside [the “new territories”].
My husband was in the military, and we moved so he could qualify for his pension sooner. I didn’t really have doubts about it. The idea came up fairly spontaneously and was settled in a single night: my husband suggested it, and I didn’t say no.
We have two children, our own apartment in Izhevsk, and my parents nearby. So when my husband brought me to Melitopol, to a house in the Semenivka neighborhood where everything was old and in terrible shape, of course I cried.
It was very hard for me to adjust. Then I started looking for an apartment in Melitopol itself and ran into catastrophic prices. Insane ones.
Melitopol wasn’t badly damaged [during Russia’s military offensive]. It’s just that all the buildings are old; there’s no new construction in the city. To rent a two-room apartment, you need 60,000 [rubles] up front, and landlords may ask for a deposit on top.
Because Avito wasn’t operating [in Melitopol] at the time, you had to look through Telegram channels, go to real estate agents, or find listings from owners. I ended up finding an apartment for 30,000 rubles, which counts as cheap there. It hadn’t been renovated — everything was Soviet-era — but you could live in it. In Izhevsk, for that same 30,000 rubles, I was renting out my own two-room apartment, perfectly renovated.
What surprised me was that no store in the city had reasonable prices. Selection was limited, and grocery prices were catastrophic — multiply [Izhevsk prices] by three. And a lot of the food was expired. The markets were very popular.
It also surprised me that there were practically no banks, and you had to pay cash for everything. Readjusting to the old way was hard. It felt like I’d gone back to the 1990s, to a complete absence of civilization.
The power went out fairly often, whenever there were incoming strikes. You get used to them, and in the end they’re not that frightening. But at those moments you can’t go to a store unless it has a generator. A beauty salon without a generator won’t take you either. Banks close. And no electricity means no water.
To see a doctor, you need a compulsory medical insurance policy, but a new one issued under the Russian system, because the insurer there is Russian.
I ran into one big problem: there isn’t enough medical staff. There simply are no doctors. My child is a year old, and we can’t see all the doctors [required for a checkup at that age]. There are no cardiologists at all, for instance — the nearest are in Crimea or Rostov. Traveling to another city just for a checkup… And I needed to see a neurologist myself; the earliest appointment was two months out. All in all, I wasn’t thrilled.
The locals treated me pretty well. We had good relations with people, and thankfully there were no misunderstandings. I didn’t ask about what had happened in the city before. It’s tactless. It’s not right. I’m for neutrality, after all.
In the end we decided to leave. The trouble with doctors wore us down, and besides, my husband had become a [military] retiree. And I never managed to get used to this lack of civilization.
‘Occupation means living in constant fear of searches, detentions, and denunciations’
An activist with the Ukrainian movement Zla Mavka, familiar with the situation in Melitopol.
For us, occupation isn’t a change of government — it’s living in constant fear. People are afraid to speak and afraid to move around. They lose their jobs, their homes, and contact with their families, as though their lives are being taken apart piece by piece. The most painful part is the sense that you can be stripped of everything you spent years building.
The occupation has changed almost every area of life. Above all, people have lost their sense of security. You live in constant fear of searches, detentions, denunciations, and persecution for no reason at all. Simply to keep everyone afraid.
People have lost their jobs and their access to decent medicines, reliable communications, banking services, and a working legal system. Prices have risen, goods are often in short supply, or the goods are there but of terrible quality (that goes for everything, textiles and food alike). Many go months without income; others survive on odd jobs or help from relatives.
Enormous pressure is applied through [the forced issuance of Russian] passports, and through education, medicine, and work. People were effectively made to take Russian documents, move their children into the Russian education system, and work under Russian rules. For many, the choice wasn’t between “good” and “bad” but between survival and even bigger problems.
Some residents were forced to leave, abandoning apartments, houses, businesses, and belongings.
The occupiers have built a system that forces owners to re-register their property under Russian law. If someone has left, can’t return, or refuses on principle to go through these procedures, the property is declared “ownerless.” It can then be handed to someone else or registered as state property of the occupation administration.
If someone hasn’t been seen at their home for a long time and the occupation administration notices, officials leave a warning that the documents need to be updated. A month or two later, they come back with paperwork putting the property on the administration’s books — a peculiar sort of privatization.
For people leaving because of the war, it means risking their only home. Many can’t come back just to handle paperwork because that could mean checks, filtration, or persecution.
Formally, this is presented as putting the registries in order, but for many Ukrainians it’s a mechanism that legalizes the confiscation of any property. It isn’t only the loss of money as such; it’s also a way to pressure people into either accepting Russian rules and resigning themselves, or facing the risk of losing what they own.
It’s especially cynical, because a person can lose a home for the very reason that war and occupation drove them out.
To me, this looks like a deliberate policy of pushing Ukrainians out and replacing the population. In effect, they’re simply driving Ukrainians out and settling the cities with their own citizens. We’ve seen this somewhere in history before, haven’t we?
Large-scale propaganda has become a problem of its own. The occupation authorities construct a picture of normal life, but it doesn’t reflect reality. It’s especially painful to watch Russians move into Melitopol — most of them gangsters and thieves of one kind or another. And they’re untouchable by local law enforcement.
‘Military vehicles drive around, but otherwise I forget where I am’
Ruslan, 34, came from Rostov-on-Don on a work assignment lasting several months.
I’m a surveyor, working on the construction of a gas distribution station. I came to Melitopol in early February and will be here until around winter, going home every couple of months.
Housing is a bit hard to find, but easier with a real estate agent. Everything here is priced in rubles. Prices vary: you can find a one- or two-room apartment for 30,000 [rubles a month], or pay 45,000. And the apartments are identical — as far as I can see, the price depends on whether the owners have the paperwork.
I need a lease and an extract from the state property register so the rent will be reimbursed [at work], but not everyone is willing to provide those documents. Plus, most places are rented by the day — apparently a lot of people come for short stays.
I had a hard time forming a first impression. I’d been driving a long time and was simply glad to have made it. When I drove in, it felt like an ordinary Russian city: small, quiet, clean.
The only difficulties on the ground were finding an apartment and repairing my car, which started breaking down while I was here. The repairs went fine in the end.
From what I noticed, the power went out about four times in two months. I wouldn’t say it was a problem for me. In some neighborhoods it may be worse than where I am. But I could have missed outages at night or while I was at work. The water [in my rental] was shut off once.
I’ve seen a couple of destroyed houses. Nothing else caught my eye. What makes Melitopol different from the life I’m used to is probably the curfew, from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m., plus stores and some businesses closing early. Sometimes you hear “pops” [drone strikes and air defense fire — Bereg’s note], and military vehicles drive around. And there are checkpoints on the way out of town. Otherwise I forget where I am. I live in Rostov, which gets hit often too, so I don’t see a big difference.
There’s a curfew here, and people observe it. Without a pass, you can be jailed for 24 hours and fined. Even alcohol is sold only until 8 p.m.
The people who come to the city are usually [military personnel and] civil servants. Or just people who decided to take a spot that had opened up. Many come from Krasnodar, Volgograd, and Rostov.
I think you need a Russian passport to live here.
I haven’t noticed problems with the locals, and blending in is possible. Not everyone can tell I’m not from here.
‘Sometimes you hear drones and explosions, but otherwise everything’s calm’
Timur (name changed), 29, came from Uzbekistan to earn money.
I came to Melitopol in February from Uzbekistan; back home I do decorative plastering. Before that I lived in Nizhny Novgorod, working as an electrician from August 2025 until January 1. I heard about the job in Melitopol from an acquaintance.
They’re planning to open a hospital here, and the developer, the Russian company Profstroy, brought in workers from Uzbekistan: electricians, plumbers, and concrete workers.
As an electrician, I was promised a steady salary of 110,000 rubles a month and a day off every two weeks. Shifts run 11 hours, nine on Sundays. They say the paperwork is dragging on because of the influx of migrant workers. On the job it’s all bearable — nobody leans on you or pushes you.
A lot of the people I work with are from Central Asia — probably 90%. Usually from Uzbekistan, but there are Tajiks too. Russians and Turks work here as well, mostly in management and as security guards.
It’s an ordinary old provincial city, a little dirty. There are sometimes problems with water, but everything comes back quickly. Same with electricity.
Sometimes you hear drones and explosions, but otherwise everything’s calm. Nobody hides from the drones — everyone’s used to them, I guess. I see them about once a day. There are more at night, but I’m usually asleep and don’t notice. They fly around, and that’s that.
At the construction site, the electricity and water get shut off for an hour or two, then come back on. They have generators.
The internet works very poorly here; even the “whitelisted” sites load slowly. You can’t always spend time on VK or RuTube the way you’d want.
Prices in Melitopol are a little higher than in Nizhny Novgorod. Housing is hard to find here, as in other Russian cities, and especially for Uzbek citizens. In that respect, I don’t see any difference from Nizhny Novgorod.
And then there’s the red tape. You have to carry all sorts of documents, so that if you’re detained, you can prove to the police that you’re here legally.
As for the Ukrainians, I don’t know anything about that.

How India’s government can be a good parent to its young people
While recent protests were triggered by irregularities in the national medical entrance exam, the quality of education more broadly warrants attention

At least 20 young people had taken their own lives after a retest for the medical entrance exam was announced, underlining how such exams have become life-or-death affairs, providing many young people with a rare chance of economic security in India’s hypercompetitive job market.
In both India and China, education is often a key pathway to social mobility. In social systems with perceived inequalities, fair admissions to elite higher education institutions are a safety valve for social discontent. Undermining that valve led to predictable social consequences in India.
In the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) tests for 15-year-olds in mathematics, science and reading, Singapore and East Asian economies have consistently ranked at the top. East Asian economic successes have been built on human capital development.
In the 2022 Pisa test results, Singapore, which has often been the top performer, led the world again. In 2018, when China’s regions of Shanghai, Beijing, Zhejiang and Jiangsu were assessed, they narrowly beat Singapore.

Elbit Systems order backlog hits $32 billion amid global defense boom

2026-08-11
21:30:01 UTC
06:30:01 KST

The war in Ukraine is already in its fifth year; Israel has been through two rounds of fighting with Iran within a year, and China continues to put pressure on the countries around it.
The result: another record quarter for Elbit Systems.
The manufacturer of Hermes drones, munitions, and intelligence systems reported a 16% increase in sales in the second quarter of the year to $2.3 billion, putting it on track for annual sales of $9 billion. Net profit rose even more sharply, jumping 40% to $173.6 million.
The company's order backlog reached an all-time high of $32 billion, compared with $23.8 billion a year earlier, a 33% increase.
Sales to the Defense Ministry continued to grow in the latest quarter, reaching 37% of the company's activity, driven by munitions, drones, and intelligence systems.
Increased sales of radio and command-and-control systems in Europe drive profits
Sales of C4I and cyber systems rose by about 11%, mainly due to increased sales of radio and command-and-control systems in Europe. Intelligence and electronic warfare sales increased by about 22%, primarily due to higher sales of land- and airborne high-power laser systems, electronic warfare systems, and naval systems in the Asia-Pacific region.
Land systems sales rose by about 32%, thanks to sales of munitions and ammunition in Israel. Drone sales, by contrast, fell by about 8%, mainly due to an unfavorable one-time project mix and a decline in sales of training systems and simulators in Europe, which was partly offset by increased sales of unmanned aerial vehicles in Israel.
Earnings per share stood at $3.61, compared with $2.69 in the corresponding quarter last year.
"Most of the new orders are from abroad, which indicates the demand and interest in our products. We presented the airborne laser for fighter jets and combat helicopters, which will help, among other things, deal with swarm attacks by UAVs and drones, and there is great interest in them,” Bezhalel "Butzi" Machlis, president and CEO of Elbit Systems, told Walla.
“At the same time, we are continuing to increase deliveries of the high-power laser to the Defense Ministry and Rafael. Hundreds of our engineers are employed on this."
Elbit container reportedly held up at a port due to boycotting
When questioned about a recent report indicating an Elbit container had been held up at a port as part of a boycott of Israel, Machlis said the incident was being investigated.
“Containers are sometimes delayed for all kinds of reasons. We have no problems in the supply chain. Since the days of the coronavirus pandemic, we have invested in building up inventories of raw materials and diversifying suppliers."
Machlis also noted that the Defense Ministry has yet to settle its debt with the company.
“Fortunately, Elbit is a strong company and benefits from payments from abroad that allow us to continue supplying the IDF and move up delivery schedules. I am confident that the debt will be paid, and we are in dialogue with the Defense and Finance ministries about it," he said.

US immigration officers could get electric-shock gloves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
21:30:00 UTC
06:30:00 KST

U.S. immigration agents could soon gain a new force option for confrontations, with authorities considering gloves designed to deliver painful electric shocks to people who resist officers.
ICE plans to spend up to $20 million to purchase thousands of "conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.
The devices are known as the G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky. They have been used in recent years by some jails and police departments.
DHS said Tuesday that it was working on a response to an Associated Press inquiry and offered no immediate comment. Jeff Niklaus, the founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, wrote in an email, "Unfortunately, we are unable to speak on this subject.”
The notice said the solicitation for a no-bid contract could be published as early as Friday.
Civil rights advocates expressed alarm at the plan, saying ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode. The gloves must be applied directly to someone's skin to deliver a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds, according to the company.
"It’s immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting,” said John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used. "If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool.”
Peters said he believed ICE’s planned purchase would likely be the largest from the company to date. He said he could envision ICE officers using the gloves to help remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses and in and out of detention facilities.
"For smaller officers or weaker officers or older officers, I think it has a great advantage” because it can produce faster takedowns and shorten confrontations, he said.
The manufacturer warns the device should not be used as punishment, against people merely exhibiting "verbal defiance or belligerence” or on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or elderly or disabled people.
Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, said the public should have no confidence that ICE officers will use the devices appropriately. She questioned why the devices would be necessary for civil immigration enforcement and noted those getting shocked might have no advance warning.
"ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” she said. "Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”
Supporters say the devices are generally used in specific jail and transport situations, rather than broadly to patrol on the streets. They have been used to subdue violent suspects who are refusing to get into squad cars and inmates who are harming themselves and threatening officers, according to Compliant Technologies.
Peters said he expected the devices to be misused by a small number of employees, as with other policing technologies, but he said they are unlikely to cause injuries. He said it would be important for ICE to have robust policies and training in place.
To use the device, officers must complete a course and be recertified every two years, the manufacturer says.

US President Donald Trump has endorsed embattled FIFA president Gianni Infantino, saying removing him as football's head would be a "terrible mistake".
Trump said a World Cup after Infantino "will never be as successful or profitable again".
Despite Trump's endorsement, US Soccer has backed the call for meaningful change at FIFA following Infantino's bid to sell off the World Cup.
Embattled FIFA leader Gianni Infantino has a powerful and vocal supporter — US President Donald Trump.
As football organisations around the world continue to call for the resignation of the FIFA president, post-World Cup, Trump blasted that idea in a message he posted to Truth Social on Monday night.
"FIFA would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing President Gianni Infantino," Trump wrote.
"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented. If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!"
UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North America, Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) banded together earlier in the week to release an open letter, signed by the president and general secretary of each organisation, urging Infantino's resignation.
Infantino has been under fire since last month's failed plan to launch the FIFA Forward Enterprise, which would have sold part of the World Cup's commercial rights to private investors to raise billions of dollars.
He apparently caused further damage by holding a crisis meeting last week in Morocco with some members of FIFA's management team.
"This recent meeting, where a select number of members of the FIFA Management Committee — not the full Committee — were summoned abroad, rather than leadership going to Zurich to address the heart of FIFA, its staff, only reinforces these concerns and represents a continuation of the very pattern of conduct that brought us to this moment," reads the letter from UEFA, CONCACAF and AFC.
"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him. There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness.
"These are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership. That is why we have taken this stance: not lightly and not alone, but together, and out of duty to the game we serve."
Also Monday, US Soccer and others issued their own statement backing CONCACAF.
"US Soccer, Canada Soccer, CFU (Caribbean Football Union) and UNCAF (Central American Football Union) stand together, along with our colleagues around the world, in calling for meaningful change that strengthens FIFA's governance, transparency and accountability," the statement read.
Infantino, 56, has served as FIFA president since his initial election on February 26, 2016. His current term runs through 2027, and he has announced his bid for re-election to extend his tenure to 2031.

Bears safety Coby Bryant to miss four to six months after knee surgery
LAKE FOREST, Ill. (AP) — Chicago Bears safety Coby Bryant will miss four to six months after he had surgery on his injured left knee, coach Ben Johnson said Tuesday.
Bryant, signed to a $40 million, three-year deal as a free agent this offseason, was expected to be an important part of a revamped Chicago secondary.
Johnson said Bryant had surgery Friday without disclosing details of the injury. He did not rule out the possibility that Bryant would return this season.
“I got to see him today,” Johnson said. “He’s going to be in a hurry to get back to help us out there at the end of the year.”
Bryant was hurt at practice on Aug. 3. ESPN initially reported that he could miss eight to 10 weeks, but the team never confirmed that timeline.
Chicago let All-Pro safety Kevin Byard leave for Buffalo in free agency and signed Bryant, who spent four years with the Seattle Seahawks. He was the starting free safety for last year’s Super Bowl-winning squad.
“Coby is the template for how we all want our team to play,” Johnson said. “He was a big part of offense, defense and special teams, the mentality, the mindset, his approach. We loved everything about him.
“It certainly takes us back a little bit but it also provides opportunity for other guys to fill that void and it might be guys we hope to prod along a little bit.”
Former Dallas and Tennessee safety Xavier Woods was signed last week and immediately went in as a replacement for Bryant. He intercepted quarterback Caleb Williams in his first full practice.
“He’s a veteran player, he’s played a lot of football, been in a few different schemes,” defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said. “He’s been a productive player.”
Woods played for Bears defensive backs coach Al Harris in Dallas at the start of his career.
“So there’s some familiarity there with him,” Allen said. “And, I just think, right now, we needed another veteran piece back there in the back end, specifically at the safety position.”
Several other Bears players are banged up
The news about Bryant comes as the Bears deal with several less serious injuries. Chicago is preparing to host Cleveland on Saturday in its first preseason game.
Wide receiver Luther Burden suffered a groin injury last week and Johnson said he’ll miss the rest of training camp and the preseason, but will return for the start of the regular season.
Johnson also updated the injury status of starting left tackle Ozzy Trapilo, who suffered a patellar tendon injury last January in a playoff victory over Green Bay. Trapilo is progressing well, and Johnson wouldn’t rule out his return to practice by the end of preseason.
The Bears have been practicing without defensive end Montez Sweat, left tackle Braxton Jones, backup safety/cornerback Cam Lewis and backup safety Elijah Hicks. All of those injuries except for Hicks are considered day-to-day. Starting slot cornerback Kyler Gordon remains on the physically unable to perform list after a calf injury before training camp.
The Bears turned to rookie fourth-round pick Malik Muhammad in the slot last week and he continues to work with the starters in that role.

Situation in West Bank requires urgent action: UN envoy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:18:08 CST
06:18:08 KST

UN Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov (on screens) speaks via a video link at a Security Council meeting at the UN headquarters in New York, Aug. 11, 2026. The situation in the West Bank must be treated as an emergency requiring urgent action, Alakbarov said Tuesday. (Eskinder Debebe/UN Photo/Handout via Xinhua)
UNITED NATIONS, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- The situation in the West Bank must be treated as an emergency requiring urgent action, UN Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov said Tuesday.
"The concern is not only the continued expansion of (Israeli) settlements, but the speed and systematic manner in which new facts are being created on the ground," he warned in a briefing to the Security Council.
New outposts are established, often with state support, and can be retroactively authorized or incorporated into the wider settlement system. From these outposts, settler violence and intimidation have driven the displacement of Palestinian communities, said Alakbarov.
The spread of agricultural and grazing outposts is deeply troubling as well. Requiring only a few settlers, they enable control over vast areas of land. Israeli monitoring organizations report that agricultural and pastoral outposts now exercise effective control over close to 20 percent of the West Bank, he said.
"We must be clear-eyed about what is taking place. These are interconnected steps, not isolated developments. They are reshaping the West Bank, weakening Palestinian governance and advancing de-facto annexation," said the envoy.
The stakes are high. If the West Bank continues to unravel, it will further erode the prospects for ending the Israeli occupation and realizing a negotiated Israeli-Palestinian peace based on the two-state solution, he warned.
"We must act now, collectively and determinedly, to ensure concrete steps are taken towards that objective. The UN remains committed to supporting all efforts in support of a lasting peace between Israelis and Palestinians based on 1967 lines, with Jerusalem as capital of both States, living side by side in peace and security," he said.
Alakbarov warned that the West Bank is at the breaking point, noting that the situation has not been a sudden deterioration but the result of decades of unresolved conflict that has deepened the unlawful Israeli occupation, driven the Palestinian Authority to the brink of collapse, and undermined the prospects for an independent, viable, and sovereign Palestinian state.
As of Monday, 76 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank in 2026, including 18 children, by Israeli forces or settlers. Three Israelis, including one civilian and two members of Israeli security forces, were killed in confrontations with Palestinians in the West Bank, the envoy noted.
Some 127 Palestinian communities have experienced full or partial displacement since January 2023, including 47 that have been entirely displaced, affecting more than 6,390 Palestinians. In 2026 alone, about 3,800 Palestinians, nearly half of them children, have been displaced due to settler violence, demolitions and evictions, he said.
Settler violence has reached unprecedented levels. So far this year, the UN has documented more than 1,430 incidents involving Israeli settlers that resulted in casualties, property damage or both, affecting approximately 260 Palestinian communities. Many incidents occurred in the presence of Israeli forces, said Alakbarov.
The pattern is clear. Palestinian populations are increasingly being forcibly displaced from villages across the West Bank before settlers seize the vacated land. Settler attacks, which were previously concentrated in Area C -- which is under full Israeli control -- are increasingly reported in Area B -- which is under Palestinian civil control and joint Israeli-Palestinian security control -- and even Area A -- which is under full Palestinian control, he said.
Alongside the mounting violence, Israel is significantly accelerating its settlement activities while consolidating its control across the occupied West Bank. Since the beginning of the year, Israeli planning authorities advanced or approved approximately 12,360 housing units in the occupied West Bank -- 7,200 housing units in Area C and 5,160 housing units in East Jerusalem, he said. ■

The situation in the West Bank must be treated as an emergency requiring urgent action, Alakbarov said Tuesday. (Eskinder Debebe/UN Photo/Handout via Xinhua)

Roundup: Fast-spreading Ebola outbreak claims over 2,000 lives in DR Congo

06:18:02 KST

KINSHASA, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- Ebola has killed more than 2,000 people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) less than three months after the outbreak was declared, while the epidemic has yet to reach its peak and continues to outpace efforts to contain it.
The country has recorded 4,381 confirmed cases, including 2,011 deaths, according to the latest figures released Tuesday by local health authorities. Cases have been reported in 53 health zones across Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces, with Ituri remaining the epicenter.
OVER 1,000 DEATHS IN LESS THAN A MONTH
The Ebola outbreak is escalating at an alarming rate in the DRC, with the confirmed deaths surpassing 1,000 in late July. The toll nearly doubled in just three weeks.
"Today the Ebola epidemic surpassed 2,000 deaths, half of these in the last 20 days," United Nations Senior Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis said Tuesday on social media, urging governments, aid organizations, donors and communities to "do more, and do it today."
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has warned that in the DRC, this epidemic "dwarfed prior Ebola events," including the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak.
"After 12 weeks, it's almost nine times more than the West Africa outbreak in terms of confirmed cases, and six times more than the West Africa outbreak in terms of deaths," Africa CDC Director General Jean Kaseya said at an online briefing on Aug. 6.
The rapid increase has been compounded by evidence that the virus may have been circulating for months before authorities recognized the outbreak.
The DRC formally declared the Ebola outbreak on May 15. However, genetic sequencing studies indicate that transmission may have begun as early as February, World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi said on Monday during a visit to Bunia, the capital of Ituri Province.
"We are chasing the virus. The virus is ahead of us," Janabi said.
According to the Africa CDC, only about 10 percent of expected contacts have been listed, while roughly 70 percent of those identified are being followed, well below the operational target of 95 percent.
UPCOMING MONTHS COULD BE DECISIVE
DRC Health Minister Roger Kamba recently told local media that the epidemic "has not yet reached its peak," and the coming months would be critical to slowing transmission and eventually bringing case numbers down.
Kamba said treatment centers in several affected areas still have available capacity, yet Ebola patients continue to remain in communities and, in some cases, seek medical care only when their condition has become severe, with community deaths complicating contact tracing and increasing the risk of further transmission.
Against that backdrop, the government and its partners are shifting toward a more aggressive community-based strategy.
Following a high-level meeting chaired by the DRC President Felix Tshisekedi on Aug. 5, the government called for a "village-centered" response, increasing community participation and bringing protection, care and information closer to affected populations.
The Africa CDC has said conventional contact tracing alone is no longer sufficient given the scale of unrecognized transmission. Response teams are therefore seeking to expand active case finding, including door-to-door searches by community health workers, while strengthening surveillance, treatment and engagement with local leaders.
Meanwhile, scientists are racing to add vaccines and therapeutics to the response.
The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a less common Ebola virus species for which there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment.
A WHO technical advisory group said in a report published on Aug. 7 that the Ervebo vaccine, which was developed to target Zaire virus, should be prioritized for inclusion in a randomized clinical trial in the context of the ongoing outbreak.
WHO Representative in the DRC Anne Ancia said that a large population in North Kivu got vaccinated with Ervebo during the country's 2018-2020 Ebola outbreak.
Information showed that previously vaccinated health workers infected with the Bundibugyo virus during the current outbreak survived and appeared to develop milder illness, she said, suggesting a possible cross-protective effect that still needs to be confirmed through further studies.
The current outbreak is the DRC's 17th Ebola outbreak since the virus was first identified in the country in 1976. It has become the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country and the second-largest globally, behind only the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic, according to the WHO. ■

Researchers develop contactless optical method, paving way for new light-, spin-based electronics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:17:59 CST
06:17:59 KST

JERUSALEM, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- Israeli researchers have developed a new contactless method to study how mirror-image materials respond differently to light, the Hebrew University of Jerusalem said in a statement on Tuesday.
The study, published in the journal Small, examined chiral two-dimensional materials that exist in two mirror-image forms.
The researchers used circularly polarized light to measure how electrical charges separate inside the materials without attaching metal contacts or building a complete electronic device.
The two forms responded differently depending on the direction in which the light rotated. One responded more strongly to right-circularly polarized light and the other to left-circularly polarized light. A mixture containing both forms showed no significant difference between the two types of light.
The findings suggest that the materials' unusual structure can act like a microscopic filter for electrons, affecting how they move and separate.
The researchers said the approach could help advance light detectors, spin-based electronics and other devices using polarized light, electrical charge and electron spin. ■

ACCRA, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- Over the past two decades, the value of Ghana's merchandise trade has increased nearly ninefold, according to a report released Tuesday by the Ghana Statistical Service.
The Ghana's Merchandise Trade 2004-2025 report said the country's trade value grew from 6 billion U.S. dollars in 2004 to 52.5 billion dollars in 2025.
Government Statistician Alhassan Iddrisu, who launched the report, said exports grew from 1.93 billion dollars in 2004 to 32 billion dollars in 2025, while imports, which stood at 4.1 billion dollars in 2004, increased to 20.5 billion dollars in 2025.
"For most of two decades, Ghana bought more than it sold. That situation, however, turned the corner in 2023, when Ghana swung from years of trade deficit to a record surplus -- and stayed positive through 2025, when the country posted its largest-ever surplus," Iddrisu said.
Of the 2025 trade surplus of 11.5 billion dollars, the official said exports accounted for 61 percent, with gold accounting for 63 percent of all exports in 2025, up from 39 percent in 2004.
According to Iddrisu, the cocoa, gold, and crude oil exporter earned 20.2 billion dollars from gold exports in 2025, as the country now earns more from gold than from cocoa and crude oil combined.
On imports, he said fuel purchases account for 26 percent of Ghana's total imports, urging the country to reverse the trend of shipping out crude oil and buying back refined fuel, and take steps to retain more of the value locally. ■

World records second-warmest July: WMO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:17:14 CST
06:17:14 KST

GENEVA, Aug. 11 (Xinhua) -- The world saw its joint second-warmest July on record, as extreme heat, persistent drought and wildfires affected large parts of the Northern Hemisphere while heavy rainfall and flooding hit other regions, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said Tuesday.
The global average surface air temperature in July was 1.47 degrees Celsius above the estimated pre-industrial average for 1850-1900, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service cited by the WMO.
Western Europe experienced its hottest June-July period on record, with extreme heat continuing into August and some countries now facing their fourth heatwave since May, the WMO said.
"What we have seen over the last few months is the combined effect of long-term warming with a persistent pattern of alternating high- and low-pressure systems stretching across the Northern Hemisphere," said John Kennedy, head of climate information at the WMO.
High-pressure systems are typically associated with high temperatures and dry conditions, while low-pressure systems tend to bring cooler and wetter weather, Kennedy said, adding that such high-pressure patterns can persist for days or even weeks, as seen this year.
In Western Europe, the prolonged spell of extreme heat continued as widespread dryness observed between March and June persisted and intensified, the WMO said.
Exceptionally low rainfall and soil moisture were reported in France, Spain, parts of Germany and Britain, as well as areas further east. The heat, low soil moisture and drought have taken a heavy toll on ecosystems and agriculture, lowered river levels, disrupted transport and energy production, and increased the risk of wildfires, according to the WMO.
July also saw exceptional wildfire activity across Western Europe in terms of both the area burned and emissions, the WMO said. ■

Child labourers among 18 killed in Egypt pick-up crash
At least 18 people, many of them children aged 13 to 14, were killed on Tuesday in northern Egypt when two pick-up trucks carrying agricultural day labourers crashed, a local medical source told news agency AFP.
Egypt's health ministry had earlier said there were 47 casualties, including around 30 injured, in the crash in the Dawawis area of Ismailia governorate.
Dangerously overcrowded pick-ups are a regular mode of transport for millions of Egyptian informal workers, despite the danger they pose, including to child labourers.
Jomana Waleed, a 16-year-old survivor of the crash, said her sister's last words were "I want to see mama".
"And then she stopped breathing, she was dead," she told AFP outside the Al-Qasasin Hospital, her eyes red with tears.
Waleed said she was asleep -- exhausted "because we have to wake up at 5:00 a.m." -- when the pick-up truck she and her siblings were in crashed.
"Next thing I knew we were flipped over on the ground," she said, her sister dying next to her.
Waleed was released from hospital Tuesday with a slight injury to her back, while her brother Mohamed was sent to another hospital, their grandmother Nour Ahmed Abdulkader told AFP.
Families gathered outside the Al-Qasasin Hospital in Ismailia Tuesday, AFP reported, desperate for news of their loved ones.
Child labour
A medical source told AFP that "most of the dead are children 13 and 14 years old", but could not immediately provide exact figures.
Local media Al-Masry Al-Youm reported the youngest victims were two 10-year-old girls.
At least 1.3 million minors are engaged in some form of child labour in Egypt, according to official figures, and children are regularly the victims of commuter accidents.
The workers, mostly from two villages in the Nile delta governorate of Sharqiya, were employed on an Ismailia farm, a local security source told AFP.
Local media reported that President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi had directed authorities to immediately investigate the cause of the crash.
Informal labour accounts for nearly 67 percent of employment in Egypt and almost the entire agricultural sector, according to the International Labour Organization.
Between eight and 13 million people are estimated to work as "irregular" day labourers -- mostly in agriculture, construction and manufacturing -- and lack robust wage and safety protections.
Road accidents are common in Egypt, where traffic rules are unevenly enforced and many roads are in poor repair.
Accidents often involve underage labourers travelling to work in rural areas.

Russia Frees US Marine Robert Gilman After More Than Four Years in Prison
Moscow has freed former US Marine Robert Gilman, who had been imprisoned in Russia since 2022, after Russian leader Vladimir Putin granted him a pardon on “humanitarian grounds,” Reuters reported on August 11.
His release follows growing international alarm over his deteriorating condition while in Russian custody. In late June, Gilman was transferred from a prison medical unit in Voronezh to a civilian psychiatric ward in a “dissociative stupor,” leaving him unable to communicate and reliant on tube feeding.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Advocacy groups have warned that he had been subjected to torture and mind-altering drugs. The White House and US State Department launched repeated appeals demanding his immediate release for emergency medical treatment in the United States.
The 32-year-old American is currently flying from Russia to Washington Dulles Airport aboard a State Department plane, accompanied by his mother, Nina, and four doctors evaluating him mid-flight.
A US official who spoke directly with Gilman reported that he was walking, talking, and appeared to be in “good shape” considering the circumstances, Reuters wrote.

Gilman, who served in the Marines from 2019 to 2020, was arrested in January 2022 while traveling by train in Russia’s Voronezh. Russian state media alleged he drunkenly kicked a police officer.
However, in an October 2024 op-ed, his father, Vladimir Gilman, asserted the charges were fabricated, stating his son had fallen ill, accidentally kicked the officer, and that the officer—who was uninjured and presented no evidence at trial—had actually dropped the charges.
Despite this, Gilman was sentenced to four and a half years in prison, becoming one of at least 10 Americans known to be held in Russian captivity, Reuters reported.
Gilman’s unilateral release marks a rare departure from Moscow’s usual diplomatic playbook, which typically requires high-stakes prisoner swaps to secure the freedom of detained Americans. In February 2025, for instance, the US secured the release of former embassy staffer Mark Fogel—who was serving a 14-year sentence over medical cannabis—only by exchanging him for Russian cybercrime kingpin Alexander Vinnik.
Vinnik had been extradited to the US on charges of laundering billions of dollars through a cryptocurrency exchange before being traded back to Moscow.

In the post, Zvook described the result plainly: "It worked. Not perfectly—there were challenges, valuable lessons, and improvements to identify. But the concept proved itself under operational conditions, opening new possibilities for future mobile deployments."
Mounting the sensors on a moving vehicle departs from Zvook's usual concept, in which the equipment sits on permanent structures such as telecommunications towers.
The company explained that the setup emerged during experimentation, after not every system performed as originally planned and engineers, soldiers, and partners reworked the arrangement on the spot.
Images released by Zvook show the sensor fitted to a military vehicle, its individual components, and the equipment in use, with one frame capturing the vehicle in motion.
Zvook is a Ukrainian passive acoustic sensor network built for the early detection of aerial threats, including low-altitude cruise missiles and drones.
Its sensors are equipped with microcomputers capable of running machine-learning algorithms and are typically deployed at fixed sites such as telecom towers.
A mobile array could extend early-warning coverage to areas that lack the standing infrastructure the system typically relies on.
Ukraine's push to detect low-flying threats by sound extends beyond a single developer. Another domestic company, ARes, unveiled a passive acoustic system in December 2025 that can flag FPV drones at 200 to 300 meters and Shahed drones from as far as 5 kilometers. The system has been trialed during actual Russian drone and missile strikes, tracking several targets at once with 360-degree coverage.

‘Forced to drink own urine’: Stranded Ukrainian soldiers vent frustration over lack of supplies (VIDEO)
A group of Ukrainian soldiers took to social media to say they were forced to drink their own urine due to Kiev’s failure to rotate or provide them with supplies. The soldiers urged Ukraine’s recently appointed top general, Mikhail Drapaty, to intervene, claiming their immediate command ignored their pleas.
The scandal erupted on Tuesday when the soldiers, claiming to be a fire support platoon with the 121st Territorial Defense Brigade, published their address on social media. The video features several men sitting inside a dark room, likely a basement, with the platoon commander, who identified himself as Anatoly Sischuk, reading out the address.
Sischuk claimed that his platoon was in one position in Zaporozhye Region, Russia for nearly four months, despite their command initially promising the unit that they would be there for four weeks. The soldiers replaced another unit, which was stationed for around eight months, he said.
The position turned out to be largely destroyed despite the command’s claims that the location had entrenchments, dugouts, and reserve positions ready. Apart from this, the platoon experienced severe supply shortages, with provisions delivered by drones in three to seven day intervals on average. The longest period without supply drops was 12 days, and the food was often rotten or spoiled and in insufficient amounts, according to Sischuk. The scarce supplies pushed the unit to take extreme measures, including drinking their own urine to survive, he said.
The 121st Brigade’s command was quick to respond to the allegations, insisting that the address of the soldiers “did not reflect all the circumstances.”
The command is seeking to replace the platoon with a new unit as soon as “an opportunity arises to perform the rotation safely,” it said in a statement.
The brigade also disputed the claims about scarce supplies, insisting that the unit received 27 nine-kilogram packages of provisions and medical supplies in a single month. It blamed any issues on weather conditions and the Russian military.
Drapaty – who was appointed to his role last month amid mass protests demanding the firing of his predecessor, Aleksandr Syrsky – has yet to respond to the platoon’s address. Syrsky became highly unpopular during the conflict with Russia. Critics accused him of gross disregard of soldiers’ lives and mass casualties sustained in assaults launched solely to appease the political leadership.

MOSCOW, August 11. /TASS/. The US Department of Energy has raised its outlook for an average Brent oil price in 2026 by 6%, to $86.81 per barrel from $81.91 per barrel, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) said in its report.
The report says that reduced oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz lower global oil inventories further in the coming months and keep crude oil prices near levels from the first week of August. In short:
Sione Fukofuka has been named Wallaroos head coach.
He will take on the role in 2027, with a transitional coaching team to lead the Wallaroos for the remainder of this year.
Fukofuka will be in charge of the Wallaroos at the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup, which will be hosted by Australia.
The Wallaroos have made another key appointment in the build-up to the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup with Sione Fukofuka named head coach.
Fukofuka will begin the role in 2027 after the Wallaroos become a full-time program.
He will work under Rugby Australia's (RA) director of women's high performance, Tim Walsh, who took on his newly created position last month.
Fukofuka was Scotland women's head coach until last week.
He was granted a release from his contract for family and personal reasons.
The 47-year-old will be returning home to Australia, having begun his coaching career while working as a teacher in the Queensland schools system.
He previously served as an assistant on the Wallaroos staff and was USA head coach between 2023-25.
"Although a difficult decision to leave the Scottish role, this opportunity allows me to be in Sydney closer to my family," Fukofuka said in an RA statement.
"I know many of the players and coaches well from my time in the Queensland and Australian systems and, as we transition to a full-time program this year, the opportunity for growth is enormous."
RA is determined the Wallaroos make an impression at the next Women's Rugby World Cup, which Australia will host.
They departed last year's tournament at the quarterfinal stage and are ranked ninth in the world.
The Wallaroos went winless during April's Pacific Four Series following losses to Canada (24-0), USA (33-12) and New Zealand (40-5).
But the move to full-time status will be a game changer for the Wallaroos in terms of improving on-field results.
The alignment of the Wallaroos and Australian sevens programs, under Walsh's guidance, will also make the squad competitive with the likes of New Zealand and reigning world champions England.
Walsh said he was confident the Wallaroos would make progress under Fukofuka, whose contract runs through until the end of the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup.
"Sione is a pioneer among international coaches of Pasifika heritage and a proud product of the Australian rugby coaching system," Walsh said.
"He is highly regarded by players and staff alike for his connection, team culture and driving high standards within the daily training environment.
"He is well-positioned to lead the Wallaroos into a new era and a generational opportunity presented by the home Rugby World Cup in 2029."
The Wallaroos still have six Tests to play this year, with a return bout against New Zealand coming up in Auckland on August 22.
The clash with New Zealand has historical significance as it will be the Wallaroos' 100th Test.
They head to Europe next month to play WXV Global Series Tests against England in Salford (September 13), France in Aix-en-Provence (September 20) and Scotland in Edinburgh (September 27).
The Wallaroos will later host Scotland in Sydney (October 17) and Canberra (October 23) as part of the WXV Global Series.
Vast coaching experience
Fukofuka took charge of Scotland last December.
Under his watch, Scotland finished fifth in this year's Women's Six Nations Championship with a 1-4 win-loss record.
Former Wallabies hooker and ACT Brumbies men's coach David Nucifora, now working as Scottish Rugby performance director, said Fukofuka left with the governing body's blessings.
Fukofuka moved to Scotland after stepping down as USA head coach following the 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup in England.
USA, which drew 31-31 with the Wallaroos in the pool stage, did not advance to the quarterfinals but Fukofuka was credited with improving the level of professionalism within the Eagles program during his tenure.
"Sione is a leader with a comprehensive knowledge of Australian and international systems and a reputation for creating world-class team environments and standards," RA chief executive Phil Waugh said.
As Fukofuka will not take the reins until next year, Walsh will oversee the Wallaroos' coaching transition team for the remainder of the Test season.
Walsh recently guided Australia to its World Championship victory in women's sevens, ending a successful second stint as head coach.
He coached Australia to a historic victory at the 2016 Rio Olympics during his first term.
The Wallaroos' coaching transition team includes NSW head coach Mike Ruthven, who led the Waratahs to the Super Rugby Women's title last month, and ex-Wallabies captain Ben Mowen.
Mowen currently works on the Brumbies' coaching staff.
Interim coaches Sam Needs and Gill Bourke have departed the Wallaroos' set-up.

2026-08-11

06:07:54 KST

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday that his wife, Rama Duwaji, will not receive NYPD protection during an upcoming trip to Syria and Lebanon, after his office initially claimed the department had “strongly” recommended that officers accompany her.
Mamdani told a local television station that the earlier statement had been the result of a “misunderstanding,” though he did not say what security arrangements, if any, would be in place for Duwaji during the trip.
His clarification came after the NYPD publicly contradicted City Hall over the planned visit, which is scheduled to begin September 20.
“Upon the strong recommendation of the NYPD, the First Lady’s security detail will be joining her when she travels to visit family in Syria and Lebanon,” mayoral spokesperson Dora Pekec had said.
But the department denied that any such escort would take place.
“The NYPD does not send officers to countries with level four travel advisories for discretionary reasons not linked to investigative work,” an NYPD spokesperson said early Tuesday.
“This is not an investigative trip, and therefore, NYPD personnel will not be traveling there for it.”
Both Syria and Lebanon are on the U.S. State Department’s Level 4 “Do Not Travel” list.
“It’s not official business. It’s not doing anything for the city,” a source with knowledge of the trip told the New York Post.
A source familiar with Duwaji’s security detail told the newspaper that the 29-year-old first lady, whom Mamdani has described as a “private person,” specifically requested NYPD protection after making another overseas trip last month without police security.
The conflicting statements sparked criticism over the prospect of taxpayer-funded protection for a private trip, as well as concern over sending New York police officers to countries carrying the highest-level U.S. travel warnings.
Former NYPD Commissioner Bill Bratton told the Post it would have been “ill-advised” for the department to take on such an assignment and said it would “definitely” put officers at risk to send them to Level 4 countries.
He added that such a mission would be expensive and would require significant assistance and cooperation from the federal government.
“There would be lots of hoops you’d have to go through for that kind of assignment,” Bratton said.
Duwaji’s trip is also expected to overlap with the 81st United Nations General Assembly, a period when NYPD resources are traditionally stretched because of the large number of world leaders and dignitaries in New York.
The issue is particularly sensitive after Mamdani urged New Yorkers last month to take to the streets to protest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during the UN gathering.
Duwaji, an American of Syrian descent and an illustrator, continues to describe herself as “Syrian” on her website.
Like her husband, she is known for strongly pro-Palestinian and anti-Israel views and has previously faced scrutiny over her social media activity.
A 2015 post attributed to her said Tel Aviv “shouldn’t exist in the first place” and referred to its residents as “occupiers.”
She also drew criticism after liking several Instagram posts following Hamas’ October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, including one praising the assault and another claiming that reports of rapes committed against Israeli hostages were a “mass hoax.”
Earlier this year, Duwaji apologized over older posts in which she had praised Palestinian militants, including Leila Khaled and members of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. She said those posts had been written when she was a teenager.
Before Mamdani clarified that no NYPD officers would accompany her, pro-Israel activist Dov Hikind sharply criticized the reported security arrangement.
Hikind, founder of Americans Against Antisemitism and a former New York state assemblyman, argued that the officers themselves, rather than Duwaji, could be placed in danger.
“We’re putting the officers at risk,” Hikind said. “They’ll be viewed as the bad guys. These are war zones.”
“Duwaji doesn’t need security. She’ll be welcomed as a hero and protected by Hezbollah, Hamas and the Houthis,” he added.
Mamdani’s later clarification effectively ended the immediate dispute over whether New York police officers would accompany his wife, though questions remain over how she will be protected during the Syria and Lebanon visit.
