A Vienna-based company has been caught supplying equipment used to manufacture engines for Russian missiles and fighter jets, in violation of EU sanctions.
Austria’s interior ministry disclosed the scheme in a statement on Monday, Aug. 10, saying the company falsified end-user certificates to supply the equipment to Russia, according to Reuters.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is unacceptable for high-precision European technology to be diverted towards the production of cruise missiles and air-defence systems,” said Jörg Leichtfried, Austria’s junior minister in charge of intelligence.
CNC machines and metalworking tools
The restricted equipment included specialized Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machines and metalworking tools capable of producing certain parts and components needed to sustain Russia’s war effort.
“We will continue to take decisive action,” Leichtfried said, particularly “against those actors who attempt to circumvent legal bans on supporting the Russian arms industry.”
The company, which the ministry did not identify, concealed its shipments through a network of shell companies based in Turkey, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Hong Kong, Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, South Korea, Poland, and Lithuania.
According to the ministry, its 28-year-old Belarusian director was arrested in May.
Authorities valued the seized equipment at about €140,000 ($162,000) on the day of the arrest. The unidentified suspect remains in custody as the investigation continues.
Germany Grants Ukraine’s State Emergency Service Nearly €6M in Robotic Firefighting Package
Equipment tracing back to Russian state conglomerate
Austrian authorities said the equipment was delivered to companies affiliated with Rostec – Russia’s state industrial conglomerate – and was used to produce military hardware.
The Russian embassy in Vienna declined Reuters’ request for comment, while Rostec did not respond.
According to the ministry, evidence collected during four raids conducted in August last year showed that more than €3.3 million ($3.8 million) in industrial goods had been delivered to Russian weapons producers since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
Case surfaces alongside new Canadian sanctions
The Austrian sanctions-evasion scheme was unveiled the same day Canada announced sanctions against Streit Group, an armored vehicle manufacturer headquartered in the UAE and run by Canadian-Russian businessman Guerman Goutorov.
Canada’s Foreign Minister Anita Anand accused the company of supplying Russia’s military-industrial complex, bypassing the 21st sanctions package the EU finalized against Russia on July 23.
Canada confirmed its sanctions on the company, saying that multiple credible reports show that armoured vehicles it manufactured have been used by the Russian National Guard (Rosgvardia).
“Streit Group continues to feed Russia’s war machine and the Putin regime’s unprovoked and unjustifiable war against Ukraine,” Global Affairs Canada said.
“Canada will continue to hold accountable individuals and entities that profit from the illegal, full-scale invasion,” Anand said on X.
By sanctioning the company, Canada is aligning with measures already adopted by Ukraine in 2023, alongside the EU and Switzerland in 2025, according to Global Affairs Canada.
Since 2014, Canada has sanctioned more than 3,500 individuals and entities linked to violations of Ukraine’s territorial integrity.
EU’s 21st sanctions package
The EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia adopted measures that include a pause of the automatic adjustment of the oil price cap mechanism until July 15, 2027, as well as port access bans for Russia’s “Shadow Fleet” tankers.
The EU also targeted more than 15 crypto-related service platforms based in non-EU countries, imposed a visa ban for soldiers who fought in Russia’s war, alongside transaction bans on 33 Russian financial institutions and four banks.
As of Aug. 7, the EU introduced new sanctions targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex, in response to Russia’s deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine.
Five additional individuals holding senior positions in Russian defense and military technology companies were sanctioned.

The European power system remains stable despite the heat and drought
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

The European power system remains stable despite the heat and drought
Kyiv • UNN
The European Commission confirmed that there are no short-term risks to electricity supplies in Europe. Solar generation and coordination among countries are helping to maintain the balance, but the situation remains tense.
Europe’s electricity system remains stable despite the heat and drought affecting the operation of energy infrastructure in some countries. This is stated on the European Commission’s website, UNN reports.
Details
Experts from the European Commission, EU countries, Ukraine, Moldova, the Energy Community Secretariat, and the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) held a special meeting of the Electricity Coordination Group. Participants discussed security of electricity supply amid extreme weather conditions.
Following the meeting, the group confirmed the absence of short-term risks to the adequacy of the electricity system. At the same time, the situation is expected to remain strained over the next week.
Electricity generation has declined in some EU countries due to low water levels or high water temperatures. At the same time, coordination between countries and the functioning of the single electricity market make it possible to direct electricity to the regions where it is most needed.
Solar generation is helping the energy system
High levels of solar power generation significantly helped reduce pressure on prices during the central hours of the day. However, the European Commission emphasized the need to further develop energy storage systems, which will make it possible to use surplus solar generation during the evening peak in consumption.
The meeting participants separately noted the effectiveness of voluntary measures to reduce electricity demand in some EU countries. In particular, in Hungary, such measures helped the energy system maintain balance under conditions of high load.
ENTSO-E also informed the Coordination Group about transmission system operators’ preparations for the solar eclipse on August 12. During the astronomical event, a temporary reduction in solar power generation is expected, requiring additional coordination of energy system operations.
The European Commission will continue to monitor the situation in European countries, coordinate the necessary actions, and maintain regular contact with the EU member states, ENTSO-E, and the Energy Community Secretariat.

📸Question Time in pictures
Albanese again pressed on melon gaffe in Question Time
The prime minister has been asked another question from the Coalition about that melon gaffe on the Bush Deep podcast.
Shadow Foreign Affairs Minister Ted O'Brien has asked the PM if he will apologise and own up to the gaffe.
"My question to the prime minister is whether or not he'll follow the example of someone else in this house, who has made it very clear, when he made a mistake, he owns up to it?" O'Brien asks.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has, as expected, sidestepped the question, instead talking up the government's work on the bilateral relationship with Japan.
"I have worked, the government has worked, to improve relations in our region and indeed, right around the world," Albanese says.
"Our relationship between Australia and Japan has never been stronger. We have never been more strategically aligned than we are today."
No plans to introduce sugar tax, Butler says
Oops, Speaker Milton Dick got the order of questions mixed up and let independent Sophie Scamps ask the next question, rather than the opposition.
"I will admit that I made the mistake there. When I make mistakes, I own up to them," he says, to Coalition laughter (presumably at the PM's expense).
Dick apologies to Scamps, and offers to give the call to Ted O'Brien as was originally planned. But Anthony Albanese interjects and says since we've already heard Scamps' question, let's just keep rolling.
Her question was about dental decay, and whether Australia would consider a sugar levy on sweetened beverages.
Health Minister Mark Butler says while sugar consumption is a significant public health issue, the government has no plans to introduce a UK-style tax.
PM flags amendments to Labor's gambling advertising changes
Independent MP Andrew Wilkie is up with a question about Labor's gambling advertising changes.
The Clarke MP has referred the government to the National Anti-Corruption Commission over its gambling advertising bill before parliament.
Wilkie asks the PM whether he thinks the government had been "inappropriately influenced" by the gambling lobby when it crafted its gambling advertising bill.
Leader of the House Tony Burke stands up, saying Wilkie's question would be better suited to a motion. Speaker Milton Dick asks the PM to only respond to the question.
Anthony Albanese acknowledges Wilkie's commitment to the issue, and says he expects there will be amendments to the bill.
The prime minister also denies the legislation before parliament has been influenced by the gambling lobby.
"We'll continue to promote the legislation that is before the parliament today. It hasn't been influenced, from certainly my position, has not been influenced by the way that is suggested," Albanese says.
"I expect there will be amendments to the legislation that I hope receive the support of the entire parliament."
Changes to older Australians' private health rebate 'necessary': Butler
As part of Labor's aged care reforms, the government is scrapping a Howard-era private health rebate for over-65s to redirect funding towards aged care services.
The Coalition has seized on the change in recent weeks, with Nationals frontbencher Anne Webster asking the health minister why he's "imposing another toxic tax on millions of older Australians".
Mark Butler says it's a hard but "necessary" decision to fund an expansion in aged care services, and it returns the private health rebate to its original design.
"To deliver more beds, to deliver more packages at home, and to deliver better care," he says.
"And one of the reasons why we had to do that, to the shadow minister's question, [is] the appalling state that the former government left the aged care system in, when we came to government."
PM quizzed on rent stress following federal budget
Independent MP Dai Le has asked the PM whether he will convene national cabinet to discuss rental stress in the wake of the government's budget.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says people currently negatively gearing a property will continue to be able to do so.
Under Labor's last federal budget, the negative gearing perk will be restricted to only new builds.
The prime minister has also talked up the government's cost of living measures.
"I do note that around 65,000 taxpayers in the member's electorate will benefit from the tax cuts that came in on 1 July, as a result of our re-election in May last year — tax cuts that wouldn't have been taken place, had the leader of the opposition been elected as a minister," Albanese says.
High migration figures not Labor's fault, PM argues
Nationals MP Allison Penfold is up next, asking if Labor's record on migration has "killed the Australian dream of home ownership".
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese takes this one, arguing the government has reduced the migration intake post-Covid.
He quotes a former immigration department secretary, Abul Rizvi, who said that the Coalition previously "stomped on the the accelerator" and increased migration figures:
"By 2031, Australia's population is expected to be 754,000 smaller than what the former Coalition government was forecasting prior to the pandemic."
Treasurer praises 'outstanding' Labor MP who raised concerns about budget changes
Liberal frontbencher Angie Bell has asked the treasurer about Labor MP Claire Clutterham's response to a constituent who emailed her raising concerns about the Labor's budget tax changes.
The Australian reported last week Clutterham, who represents the eastern Adelaide seat of Sturt, told the constituent over email she has "difficultly" understanding why Labor extended the capital gains tax changes beyond housing.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has leapt to Clutterham's defence, saying she's an "outstanding" local member.
He says it's not unusual for local members to relay their concerns raised by their constituents to ministers.
"That's how it's supposed to work. Now, the member for Sturt is not just a good local member, the member for Sturt is an outstanding local member," Chalmers says.
"One of the reasons why the member for Sturt is such a good local member is because the member for Sturt, and in conjunction with everyone in on this side of the House, is delivering tax cuts for every one of the working people in Sturt."
Liberal MP Aaron Violi has tried to table the Sturt MP's response to the constituent reported in The Australian. But he hasn't had any success.
Meanwhile, Labor MP Rob Mitchell has been ejected from the chamber for interjecting.
Key Event
Japan breaks silence on melon gaffe, plays down incident
Japan's government has broken its silence on the political furore over the prime minister's melons podcast comment, with Tokyo's ambassador in Canberra playing down the significance of the episode.
In a statement, Japan's ambassador to Australia Kazuhiro Suzuki told the ABC the Japanese government was "aware of the reporting in the media" on the podcast.
"We have been informed by the Australian side that Prime Minister Albanese did not make the comments in the way that has been reported," he said in a statement.
"In any case, the dinner hosted by Prime Minister Albanese during the prime minister's visit to Australia this May was held in a very relaxed atmosphere.
"We believe it helped build a personal trust relationship between the two leaders."
A squabble over a Barefoot Investor quote
We're back to talking about tax, specifically the changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount.
Nationals frontbencher Kevin Hogan makes reference to an answer Anthony Albanese gave yesterday, when he quoted the Barefoot Investor Scott Pape who called the schemes taxpayer-funded landlord welfare in an op-ed in the News Corp tabloids.
"Why is the prime minister attacking millions of aspirational Australians for trying to get ahead, just like he did," Hogan asks.
The PM accuses Hogan of misleading the house by misattributing Pape's quote to Albanese.
"If you have a problem, I suggest take it up with Mr Pape," he responds.
Julie Collins defends funding to H5 bird flu preparedness
Independent MP Nicolette Boele is up with the first question from the crossbench about the H5 bird flu that is spreading.
She's asked whether the government will commit $200 million over two years to build the resilience of critical bird species vulnerable to the bird flu.
Agriculture Minister Julie Collins says the government has invested $113 million in preparedness for the bird flu and $99 million for saving threatened species.
Yesterday, the minister announced the Commonwealth would release 1,500 vials of bird flu vaccines to begin vaccinating vulnerable birds.
She has defended the money released by federal Labor so far, and has welcomed the Victorian government's announcement today that they will begin a vaccination program.
"There has been a lot of preparedness done to make sure that as a government, we're doing everything we can do to protect our threatened species, and certainly from our government," Collins says.
"We know the biosecurity is the front line, but the vaccination and the vaccination program will also be complementary."
Key Event
PM dismisses referral of melon gaffe to AFP as a 'political stunt'
Can the prime minister assure the house that his office and his department weren't behind the apparent leak of communication between Australian and Japanese officials?
That's the question from Shadow Home Affairs Minister Ted O'Brien. It comes after reports of a diplomatic note that suggested Japanese officials saw no "ill intention" over Anthony Albanese's remarks on a comedy podcast last month.
The Coalition has since referred the correspondence's appearance in the media to the federal police.
The PM says he takes relationships with other nations seriously, before dismissing the referral as a "political stunt".
"The AFP is completely independent of the government and they'll undertake their work, and I'm confident about that," he said.
Angus Taylor tells PM to 'man up' and apologise to Japanese PM
And we're up and away. The first question is from Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, who has brought up the PM's appearance on the Bush Deep podcast.
Anthony Albanese gestured his hands in front of his chest when he was discussing a gift of crown melons from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on the podcast.
The opposition leader has asked the prime minister whether he will "man up" and apologise to Japan's prime minister for the gaffe.
Albanese has refused to apologise and instead promoted the Labor government's credentials on diplomacy with Japan.
"We take our relationships seriously, including our regular engagement with Japan. And that is why we will always put the national interest first and we continue to do so," Albanese says.
"The prime minister of Japan is a good friend of Australia. Prime Minister Takaichi is the third Japanese prime minister I have had dealings with, all of them have been constructive. She was a welcome guest here."

My blog co-captain Courtney Gould and I will bring you all the hot takes over the next 70 minutes or so from the House of Representatives.
Members are walking into the chamber as I type so let's settle in for questions without notice.

AFP Commissioner to hold meetings in Solomon Islands
There will be a small flurry of high-level Australian visitors to Solomon Islands over coming days.
AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett is set to hold a series of meetings and events in the Pacific island nation, which has drawn closer to Australia under the new Prime Minister Matthew Wale.
Like many Pacific island countries, Solomon Islands has been grappling with the increasingly sophisticated operations of international drug smuggling syndicates, which pose a sharp challenge to local police.
Defence Minister Richard Marles is also set to fly to Solomon Islands early next week.
He's expected to use the visit to open the new Australia-funded Western Border Outpost — which will be a key hub for Solomon Islands police and customs officials in the Western reaches of the country next to Bougainville.
Key Event
Pacific nations call for transparency over ballistic missile testing
Pacific foreign ministers have called for "transparency and reassurance" from China over its ballistic missile tests, after diplomatic wrangling at the region's pre-eminent diplomatic forum.
Australia and New Zealand were left frustrated last week when Kiribati and Naoero (formerly Nauru) refused to back a joint statement from all Pacific Islands Forum member nations criticising the test.
New Zealand's Foreign Minister Winston Peters even suggested China might have tried to influence the final statement through the two Pacific nations, which have warm ties with Beijing.
But in the wake of the meeting, officials seem to have hammered out a compromise, with the final outcomes statement referring to "recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) tests in the region".
"In light of concerns raised by a number of Pacific Islands Forum members, ministers called for transparency and reassurance," the statement says.
"They also emphasised the importance of all States conducting ICBM tests consistently with the Blue Pacific Ocean of Peace Declaration, the Treaty of Rarotonga, and respecting the sovereignty of Forum Members."
The word "China" does not appear in the section, and the statement is framed broadly enough for Pacific nations to say it's not solely aimed at Beijing.
But Australia will still be pleased to see a clear reference to the test in the final statement, after some tricky negotiations.
Key Event
Did Bragg freelance on his plan for the net overseas migration rate?
So as part of his speech, Andrew Bragg put a figure on what the opposition wants to bring the net overseas migration (NOM) figure down to.
He suggested a cut to under 180,000 over the next four years could occur by reducing the number of international students, backpackers, and post-study work visas.
So is that an actual opposition target, or just Bragg freelancing on policy?
Bragg says he thought it was "important to move the debate on towards where the numbers are probably going to hit".
"That's the range, and we look forward to backing that up with more to say later. But I think it's important that we keep the debate moving," he says.
Key Event
A 'simple house' with basic amenities but no energy efficiency requirements
Alright, back to housing. Andrew Bragg is asked about hisplan to drastically shrink the national construction code — specifically if the new code would include any energy efficiency requirements at all.
"It just has basic amenity standards. So it's a house. It won't fall down. It's secure. It won't burn down, but it doesn't have anything else in it. It's a simple house," he says.
Bragg says basic amenities would include a window in a room, for example. He refers to Maslow's hierarchy of needs to make his point.
"Maslow's hierarchy dictates to you [that] you need to build more cheap housing just to get the thing moving. And if people want optional extras, that's up to them," he says.
Australia shouldn't fear Trump in taxing tech giants: Bragg
But wait, there's more. Andrew Bragg is offering up policy ideas beyond his housing portfolio too.
On tax, the top tax rates for individuals are too high, Bragg says. He wants the top rate to be in the 30 per cent. Small business taxes are also too high, he adds.
"We need to get to a much flatter income tax system for people and all businesses," he says.
Australia should also "not be immobilised" by US President Donald Trump, he says, by getting a bigger deal on taxing big global corporations and not allowing them to use transfer pricing to shift profits elsewhere.
"We should tax these companies at the point they make revenue. A small business can't send its tax obligations to Ireland, so why should Meta or Netflix be allowed to avoid paying tax?" he says.
He thinks Australia is over mandates and rules. "You cannot legislate away inflation or abolish addiction and other social problems," he says.
Bragg also wants 5 per cent deposit scheme means tested for first home buyers.
Bragg wishes he stopped the Morrison-era 'madness'
Okay, so Andrew Bragg covered a lot of ground in his address, swinging from housing (his shadow portfolio) to offering up some frank thoughts on politics and the major parities.
The Liberal frontbencher thinks it's fair enough people are letting the major parties know they're unhappy with them. He likens Labor's national conference to North Korea.
But the Liberals have contributed to the problem too, he argues.
"The Liberal Party has contributed to our malaise by not being prepared to develop enough alternative policy and wear political risk," he says.
"For 20 years, Australian leadership, including under the custodians of liberalism, has too often been indolent."
Bragg, who was a backbencher in the Morrison government, tells the Press Club that he was "sorry that I didn't do more to stop the madness".
So how does he propose fragmentation is fixed? Through cutting the spin, being prepared to tell people bad news, and giving people all the information.
Bragg wants the Coalition to focus on the radical centre (coincidentally, that's the same phrase Anthony Albanese uses to describe the space Labor occupies).
"I call this the economic revolution. It's core to the renewal of liberalism. We have to become the radical centre — the free market with a safety net for those who really need it," he says.

Iran is ‘bleeding badly’: Trump bets economic pain will force Tehran to surrender
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:59:13 UTC
05:59:13 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump has not abandoned the military option against Iran, and given his unpredictable approach, could still return to explicit threats against Tehran. For now, however, he appears to be pursuing a different strategy: intensifying economic pressure in hopes that Iran’s deteriorating economy will eventually force the regime to compromise.
Trump has said he is “lowering the profile” of the confrontation and conducting only limited negotiations with Tehran, while repeatedly highlighting the damage inflicted on Iran after two wars and a U.S. naval blockade that has severely restricted its oil exports.
In an interview Tuesday with conservative television network Real America’s Voice, Trump outlined what he described as two “very powerful strategies” for dealing with Iran.
One, he said, would be to “hit them really, really hard,” an option he has so far avoided amid concern over possible Iranian retaliation against Gulf oil infrastructure and shortages of some U.S. munitions and interceptors.
The second is to defeat Iran economically by maintaining the blockade and sanctions.
Trump described that approach as simply allowing the pressure to continue while watching conditions inside Iran deteriorate.
“They have 300% inflation, their currency is worth almost nothing. They’re not paying their soldiers, their soldiers are leaving,” he said. “So you just keep it going, because it’s not sustainable.”
“Economically, they’re in chaos,” Trump added.
He also referred to Iranian assets frozen abroad, which Tehran has demanded be released as part of negotiations.
“They can’t borrow money. We control their money,” Trump said. “What they have, and they had a lot, we have total control of it. I’m their banker. I’m their banker!”
The central question is whether Iran’s leadership, which emerged from the latest war more radicalized and believes its ability to block the Strait of Hormuz gives it major strategic leverage, will eventually soften its position under economic pressure.
If it does not, and Trump ultimately decides to resume major military operations, some analysts believe such a move would be more likely after the November 3 U.S. midterm elections. Renewed fighting before then could further complicate Republican efforts to retain control of Congress.
Iran’s economy becomes ‘the main battlefield’
Iranian officials are not hiding the severity of the economic crisis, while hardship among ordinary citizens continues to deepen.
So far, however, there are few visible signs of renewed mass protest. Memories remain fresh of the brutal suppression of the enormous demonstrations that erupted in January over the economic crisis and soaring inflation.
Tens of thousands of protesters were killed in that crackdown by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its Basij militia, which emerged from the war with even greater influence and are now widely viewed as the real centers of power in Tehran.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, considered relatively moderate but politically weak, has repeatedly warned that the economic crisis could trigger “social instability,” effectively a renewed wave of protests.
Last month, amid a pause in mutual attacks between Iran and the United States, he declared that the economy had become the country’s “main battlefield.”
Pezeshkian said he recently raised the issue during a meeting with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei that lasted seven to eight hours.
“We discussed all the country’s issues, and naturally the main concerns were people’s living conditions, the state of the economy, employment, housing and the problems currently caused by the sanctions,” he told Iranian media Monday.
Rial at historic low, ‘misery index’ at record high
Iran’s economy has been in crisis for years, due in part to the sanctions Trump restored during his first term after withdrawing from the 2015 nuclear agreement in 2018.
But sanctions are only part of the story.
Economic mismanagement, corruption and the diversion of enormous resources toward the Revolutionary Guards and armed groups across the Middle East have also contributed to the country’s decline.
Conditions worsened sharply following last year’s war in June and deteriorated further during the current conflict, which began in late February and has now continued for six months without a clear end.
Over the past year, the decline appears to have accelerated across virtually every economic indicator.
According to the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s economy is expected to contract by 5.6% this year, its steepest decline since 1988.
Iranian authorities say annual inflation has reached 88.6%, while food prices have risen 130% in a single year.
The rial fell to a record low early this month of 1.9 million to the dollar. It has since recovered slightly to around 1.88 million per dollar, but remains roughly 20% weaker than at the start of the war.
Iran’s official statistics agency has also reported that the country’s “misery index,” which combines inflation and unemployment, hit a record 91.1 in the spring, more than double last year’s level.
Unemployment reportedly rose to around 7% in the first quarter of 2026.
Iranian statistics officials say the country lost 630,000 industrial jobs during that quarter. Deputy Labor Minister Gholam-Hossein Mohammadi has said the war has caused roughly 1 million job losses overall in a country of about 92 million people.
A major source of the economic damage has been Iran’s loss of oil-export capacity.
Exports were first disrupted during 40 days of fighting with Israel and the United States, and later by the American naval blockade.
The blockade began April 13, was suspended June 18 following a memorandum of understanding and resumed July 14 after that agreement collapsed.
Oil revenue accounted for around 11% of Iran’s GDP before the war.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies estimates the blockade is costing Iran’s economy around $435 million per day.
In a recent analysis, the Washington-based institute said Iran’s economy had already begun “unraveling” late last year and argued that the blockade was accelerating the process.
“The U.S. naval blockade has proven to be the most precise economic pressure tool deployed so far,” it said.
Iranians struggle to survive: ‘We’ve been forgotten’
Those figures translate into severe hardship for millions of Iranians, something the regime fears could eventually ignite another uprising.
Even ILNA, a semi-official news agency associated with a state-linked labor organization, has recently carried increasingly stark accounts of the crisis.
The government has warned that worsening conditions may force it to reduce fuel subsidies, a move that has triggered protests in the past.
Albert Baghezian, an economics professor in Tehran, told ILNA that the Iranian economy resembles “a patient suffering from severe bleeding.”
“Delivering a gasoline shock would be equivalent to a fatal blow to people’s livelihoods,” he said.
ILNA has reported that increasing numbers of Iranians are turning to credit applications that allow purchases to be paid off over longer periods.
A 29-year-old Tehran resident said he uses dozens of such apps “because you simply can’t afford to pay for everything at once.”
Other workers told the agency that around 40% of their salaries go toward rent and another 40% toward credit repayments.
Students are increasingly relying on the same services amid what ILNA described as an unpredictable employment outlook and unstable incomes.
But those credit systems also impose penalties and fees when payments are missed.
“The fines just keep piling up,” a man named Hossein said. “The fear that you won’t have money and will fall behind on payments really tortures you.”
Many Iranian workers are employed under temporary contracts or move repeatedly in and out of employment, further reducing their chances of keeping up with debt repayments.
Workers interviewed by ILNA said only a minority have health insurance, meaning even a relatively routine medical problem can wipe out their income.
Iran is also facing a rapidly worsening housing crisis.
Government figures show construction costs have doubled over the past year, feeding directly into higher rents.
Some local authorities have attempted to cap rent increases, including a 27% ceiling in Tehran Province, but such restrictions are often poorly enforced.
“Rental prices continue to rise, construction costs have surged, purchasing power has weakened and residential property transactions remain at a low point,” the Iranian news agency ISNA reported.
Labor organizations increasingly accuse the government of abandoning workers during the war.
“Iranian workers, and construction workers in particular, have been forgotten and left helpless at the mercy of fate,” said Hassan Azati, head of a construction workers’ union in Baneh.
“All their efforts are focused on one thing only: staying alive.”
Azati estimated that half of the construction workforce in Baneh lacks health insurance.
Some workers are so desperate, he said, that they have turned to work as kolbars, laborers who carry smuggled goods across Iran’s borders, sometimes through minefields left from the Iran-Iraq War.
Tehran refuses to yield: ‘Accept our conditions’
Despite the economic pressure, it remains far from certain that Iran’s hard-line leadership will compromise.
Tehran now views control over the Strait of Hormuz, through which about one-fifth of global oil consumption passed before the war, as a strategic asset comparable in importance to its nuclear program.
Last week, optimism briefly grew that an agreement to reopen the waterway could soon be reached.
Iran then declared that an arrangement with neighboring Oman would not be enough and presented Washington with a series of sweeping conditions.
Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s newly appointed secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, reiterated those demands Tuesday.
“The United States is the cause of instability in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman,” he said. “America endangered the entire region by imposing an illegal war on Iran.”
“The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen unless the United States changes its behavior and accepts Iran’s conditions.”
Rezaei said Washington must end the war, release frozen Iranian funds and end fighting across the region, including in Lebanon and Gaza, along with fulfilling additional demands conveyed through intermediaries.
“If an agreement is reached between Iran and Oman concerning passage through the Strait of Hormuz, that agreement will be separate from the issue of closing the strait,” he said.
What is unfolding now resembles a waiting game, with both Trump and Iran hoping the other side will give way first.
Richard Nephew, a Columbia University scholar who helped formulate Iran sanctions policy during the Obama administration, told the Associated Press that sanctions generally require significant time before producing political results.
He also argued that Trump has failed to define clear strategic objectives for the conflict.
“Trump has repeatedly weakened his own hand by using force insufficiently, articulating the objective unclearly and hesitating in negotiations,” Nephew said.
Trump continues to insist that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon remains his central goal.
But reports suggest he may ultimately accept a settlement without significant new restrictions on Iran’s nuclear program if Tehran agrees to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, allowing fuel prices to fall before the November midterms.
A U.S. official told The Wall Street Journal this week that reopening Hormuz is now the administration’s main policy focus.
Economic warfare requires patience
If Trump continues relying on economic warfare, an approach the White House previously called “Operation Economic Fury,” analysts say the pressure could eventually prove powerful.
But they also stress that it will take time.
“The central question is how far the United States is prepared to go to reduce Iran’s oil trade and threaten severe sanctions against third countries, and whether it has the patience to see if economic suffering causes the regime to change its behavior,” said Juan Zarate, a former national security official in the George W. Bush administration.
A senior U.S. administration official told the AP that American military action had already significantly reduced Iran’s ability to produce, sell and transport oil and other energy resources.
The official said that beyond the naval blockade and sanctions, Trump still has “additional options” that could be deployed over the coming weeks and months.
But continued economic warfare carries a political cost for Trump as well.
If Iran keeps disrupting tanker traffic through Hormuz, U.S. gasoline prices are likely to remain elevated heading into the November elections, a scenario that is increasingly worrying Republicans.
Recent polling suggests the GOP has lost what had long been one of its strongest advantages over Democrats: public confidence on the economy.
Democrats began leading Republicans on the issue in April, the first time they had done so since 2010.
A recent Fox News poll found 54% of respondents believed Democrats would handle the economy better, compared with 45% who preferred Republicans, Democrats’ strongest advantage on the issue since 2006.
Trump, in effect, appears to be betting that American voters can tolerate economic discomfort longer than Iran’s population can endure its far more severe crisis.
“It’s not just what the military can do,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday during a joint appearance with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
“We also have the strongest economy in the world. And when you have a motivated Treasury secretary who knows how to use many different levers because he knows how to do it, you can put enormous pressure on adversaries.”

US Senate minority leader calls for briefing on alleged Iranian threat to Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:57:59 UTC
05:57:59 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
11 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
The US Senate minority leader called Monday for an immediate congressional briefing on an alleged Iranian assassination threat against President Donald Trump and the measures reportedly taken to evacuate him from Türkiye.
“The Senate should be immediately briefed on the Iranian threats against the President,” as well as the “extraordinary measures” taken to get him out of Türkiye following a July NATO summit there, senior Democratic Senator Chuck Schumer said on US social media platform X.
“It is unacceptable that Congress was kept in the dark and instead learned about this serious threat through press reports,” he added.
Schumer also criticized the Trump administration over its handling of the conflict with Iran, accusing the president of putting US personnel “in harm’s way” by pursuing what he described as an unnecessary war.
He called on Congress to reassert its constitutional authority and work to end the conflict, saying Republicans should not prioritize Trump’s “luxury and vanity” over US security.
US media reported Monday that Trump secretly departed Türkiye aboard a military aircraft last month after an alleged Iranian threat against him emerged during his visit to the Turkish capital for a NATO summit.
According to The Washington Post, Trump initially boarded an older Air Force One aircraft visible to television cameras before being transferred to a smaller C-32A using an airport catering truck.
The maneuver was reportedly intended to conceal his location from the public, journalists, and some White House staff.
The operation came one night after US forces renewed strikes on Iran following a breakdown in negotiations between Washington and Tehran.

Latvia launches operation to counter illegal migration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:57:00 UTC
05:57:00 KST

Latvia launches operation to counter illegal migration
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by LSM, citing LETA.
The State Chancellery said the operation was launched at the initiative of Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, following an assessment of the situation by the defense and interior ministries, with the aim of ensuring the security of Latvia's eastern border.
The operation is coordinated by the State Chancellery's Crisis Management Center and primarily involves Latvia's Interior Ministry services — the State Border Guard and State Police — as well as the National Armed Forces.
The Latvian Defense Ministry will ensure the continued involvement of the National Armed Forces in supporting the State Border Guard by increasing the number of personnel deployed and providing additional logistical support, including expanding the use of new technologies such as drones, helicopters, and aircraft.
The State Border Guard, State Police, Military Intelligence and Security Service, State Security Service, and National Armed Forces will exchange operational information about attempts to cross the border illegally and the individuals involved, including possible participation in organizing illegal migration.
Latvia's Foreign Ministry will ensure cooperation and coordination with Lithuania, Estonia, and Poland on measures to restrict illegal border crossings and secondary migration flows.
The country's Justice Ministry will assess whether the sanctions provided for under the Criminal Law are sufficient for organizing illegal border crossings, facilitating illegal residence in Latvia, and abuses aimed at obtaining legal grounds to remain in the country, the report said.
In addition, the Latvian Cabinet of Ministers will consider establishing a special working group with specific tasks to more effectively counter hybrid threats and strengthen border-control capabilities. The move is intended to improve the effectiveness of measures to prevent border violations and ensure coordinated and consistent action with Lithuania, Estonia, Poland, and other countries in the region.
As part of the operation, modern technologies, including unmanned aerial systems, are expected to be used more actively to detect and detain illegal migrants and to protect Latvia's entire eastern border.
As Ukrinform reported, on the night before Tuesday, a tunnel dug by migrants was discovered for the first time near the Latvia-Belarus border in the area covered by the Silene border guard station.

US faults China over opaque overseas lending, warns of emerging-market debt risks
US State Department introduces tougher disclosure requirement covering sovereign loans, liabilities and collateral
3-MIN READ3-MIN
10
 Listen
Teresa Elena Frontadoin Washington
The United States has stepped up scrutiny of China’s overseas lending, warning that the lack of transparency surrounding Chinese loans could increase the risk of unexpected defaults and debt restructuring in emerging markets.
In its 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report, released on Tuesday, the US State Department said China had failed to meet its minimum transparency requirements, citing deficiencies in both its domestic finances and the disclosure of claims against foreign borrowers.
“China’s lack of transparency related to its foreign claims – including loans and other obligations held by state-owned and private commercial banks and state-owned enterprises – obscures the scale and terms of many sovereign liabilities,” the report said.
The lack of disclosure undermined accurate risk assessments and increased “the likelihood of unexpected defaults or debt restructuring in emerging markets”, it added.
The warning came as the department added a requirement that governments make public the terms and conditions of sovereign loans provided to foreign borrowers, including liabilities and collateralised assets.
The report did not say whether the new requirement was introduced specifically in response to China, a major source of financing for infrastructure and development projects across Asia, Africa, Latin America and other parts of the developing world.

Federal safety agency issues final report into 2025 blast that killed 2 at Pennsylvania steel plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:53:02 UTC
05:53:02 KST

Federal safety agency issues final report into 2025 blast that killed 2 at Pennsylvania steel plant
A federal safety agency recommended the development of written policies and procedures for flushing gas valves a year after a blast at a U.S. Steel plant near Pittsburgh killed two workers.
The U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board issued a final report into the August 2025 blast at Clairton Coke Works, which also injured 11 others, including contractors.
U.S. Steel has said the explosion happened when workers were flushing a gas valve with pressurized water in preparation for routine planned maintenance at the sprawling riverside industrial facility, the largest of its kind in the Western Hemisphere. The valve ruptured under intense pressure and released combustible coke oven gas.
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration previously fined the company a total of $118,214 and issued 10 citations. OSHA had said that U.S. Steel’s written procedures, practices and training to safely maintain equipment and flush the gas valve were incomplete, outdated or inadequate.
The Chemical Safety Board report recommended that U.S. Steel develop a written procedure for washing valves with pressurized water in order to minimize the operation’s hazards. It also recommended that an industrial cleaning contractor which used a pump truck to apply pressurized water to the valve develop written policies and procedures for cleaning piping systems containing flammable or toxic gas, and train its workers in such operations.
The Chemical Safety Board report found that when a valve would not close fully, U.S. Steel had a practice of injecting steam or high-pressure water into the cleanout port in an attempt to remove residue.
“U.S. Steel had no procedure for how to safely conduct this operation, but for at least three years before the incident, U.S. Steel employees had utilized pressurized water to clean valve seats on an ad hoc basis despite the lack of a formal procedure prescribing it,” according to the report’s executive summary.
Chemical Safety Board member Sylvia Johnson said the blast “was the result of workers routinely performing a task incorrectly over a period of years until it ultimately led to a catastrophic explosion.”
The valve that failed was more than 70 years old and made from cast iron, which the report said is widely recognized as a brittle material. Numerous safety publications either ban or warn against using cast iron equipment in certain hazardous applications, including for flammable substances such as coke oven gas.
The report also said the two workers who died and two of the five seriously injured workers were located around buildings directly above the coke oven gas piping. If these buildings were located in a different area of the facility away from coke ovens, “this incident could have been far less severe,” said Drew Sahli, the Chemical Safety Board investigator in charge.
Before the blast, Clairton Coke Works had a history of accidents and explosions, and some current and former workers there say poor management and underinvestment have exacerbated air pollution and undermined workplace safety, Pittsburgh’s Public Source and The Associated Press have found.
The blast came on top of a string of other accidents at the Clairton plant over time, as well as a long history of legal battles between U.S. Steel and Allegheny County regulators, who regularly accuse the company of flouting environmental rules at the facility.
The report noted that a similar gas oven explosion occurred at the Clairton plant in July 2010, injuring 14 U.S. Steel employees and six contractors. The report criticized U.S. Steel for failing to conduct a subsequent facility siting evaluation after that incident.

At Lindsay Clancy trial, focus turns to medications prescribed before she killed her 3 children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:53:02 UTC
05:53:02 KST

At Lindsay Clancy trial, focus turns to medications prescribed before she killed her 3 children
Lindsay Clancy messaged one of her caregivers less than two months before she killed her three young children in 2023 to say she was having “intrusive thoughts I never had before,” “feeling completely hopeless” and worried about becoming addicted to some medications.
Rebecca Jollotta, a psychiatric nurse practitioner at South Shore Health Perinatal Behavior Health Program, testified at the trial Tuesday she exchanged messages with Clancy regularly on a patient portal throughout in late November and December 2022. Much of their conversations revolved around Clancy reporting trouble sleeping, depressive symptoms she was having and her search for the right mix of medications to treat her symptoms.
Several times Clancy indicated to Jollotta either that she had not taken the full dose of a prescribed medication or that she wanted to reduce a dosage or change her prescription based on what she felt were intolerable side effects. Clancy also worried about being addicted to some medications like Ativan, but Jollotta said she was not.
___
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
___
Struggle to find the right medications
“I really don’t like the way I feel on the Remeron and I know that I can’t stick with taking it,” Clancy said in a December message asking to switch from the antidepressant, which also is used to treat anxiety and insomnia, to a previous prescription mix. “I started having very intrusive thoughts that I never had before.”
Jollotta tried to assure Clancy that having intrusive thoughts is common with someone diagnosed with postpartum depression and anxiety and encouraged her to give the Remeron more time to work since she had only been on it a few days.
“This could be some postpartum anxiety. And I wanted to familiarize her with the symptoms, so that she had them written down and she could report them to me,” Jollotta said.
Jollotta, who is among several providers that Lindsay and her former husband Patrick Clancy have sued over her care, repeatedly came up with alternative treatment plans for Clancy including a range of different medications, behavioral therapy, support groups and meditation. But she acknowledged that it was up to Clancy whether she chose to follow her advice.
“I’m only making recommendations based on my education experience, training and what I’m seeing in terms of symptoms,” Jollotta said. “The patient has the autonomy.”
During their virtual and in-person visits, Jollotta said, Clancy never talked of having a plan to harm herself or her children. She also never showed signs of psychosis or mania.
But Jollotta acknowledged that Clancy did report having thoughts of suicide. She also suggested that Clancy might have underlying bipolar disorder — due to her days of going without sleep. But Patrick Clancy denied that was the case.
Suicidal thoughts
In mid-December, Jollotta had a call with the couple and was told Clancy had her “worst day” and was “having persistent, intrusive thoughts of suicide.” Jollotta suggested she consider a higher level of care such as that offered by Massachusetts General Hospital. She settled on the Women and Infants Hospital postpartum program in Rhode Island t but was soon discharged — with advice to stop taking one of her antipsychotic medication.
Jollotta, who was going on vacation, said she was concerned that Clancy had been discharged from the hospital, telling her in a message that she could “could benefit from the groups and added support separate even from medication changes.”
She was worried the hospital wanted Clancy to go off Seroquel, the antipsychotic medications. Clancy was advised this could lead to “worsening of mood, worsening of sleep,” but she insisted on going off the medication. Jollotta agreed to slowly reduce the dosage.
During cross-examination Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington argued that Jollotta was not familiar with the care Clancy received elsewhere.
Jollotta never talked to one of Clancy’s psychiatrist, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, nor did she access Tuft’s medical records. She did not know how many times Clancy saw Tufts, noting that she only thought Tufts treated Clancy in September.
“Would it surprise you if I told you that she saw Dr. Tufts 14 times” during a four-month period ending in January, Reddington said.
Jollotta never talked to anyone from the Rhode Island hospital that admitted Clancy, nor did she have access to the records of McLean Hospital, a psychiatric facility that Clancy admitted herself into on New Year’s Eve.
“If you’re treating a person through all of this stuff that we’ve talked about and it’s now apparent that things have decompensated so bad that they have voluntarily admitted her to a locked ward in a mental institution, is it important to Rebecca Jollotta to find out what the diagnosis and treatment was of their patient?” Reddington said.
Jollotta agreed it was but acknowledged that she never did find out.
Killer, or someone who was mentally ill
Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty to murder charges in the deaths of Callan, Dawson and Cora Clancy, who ranged from 8 months to 5 years old. They were found in the basement of the family’s home in coastal Duxbury, Massachusetts, where their mother was lying in the yard. She had jumped from a second-story window, and she remains paralyzed from the waist down.
Prosecutors argue that the former labor and delivery nurse was an intentional killer who contrived to get her husband out of the house and then strangled the children with exercise bands on Jan. 24, 2023. Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham has urged jurors not to view the trial as “a public debate about women’s mental health and how the medical system treats women.”
Clancy’s attorneys do not dispute that she killed the children. But they say she should not be held criminally responsible because she was mentally ill, believing she heard voices ordering her to take their lives and her own.
The defense says she was in the grip of bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis, a rare postpregnancy condition that can alter a woman’s sense of reality. A forensic psychiatrist diagnosed Clancy with those conditions after the killings.

A ferry capsizes on Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba, leaving at least 15 people dead and 27 missing
HARARE, Zimbabwe (AP) — An overloaded ferry capsized on Zimbabwe ‘s Lake Kariba on Tuesday, killing at least 15 people and leaving 27 missing, the national disaster management agency said. It said 77 people were rescued and made it to a small island on the lake, with boats now being dispatched to bring the survivors back.
Zimbabwean state broadcaster ZBC published video of speedboats making their way to what appeared to be an overturned boat on the lake as a helicopter hovered overhead. An underwater team for search and rescue operations was deployed on the huge lake, which forms part of the border between Zimbabwe and neighboring Zambia.
The statement from Zimbabwe’s Civil Protection Unit said it could only confirm through registered ticket sales that there were 114 adult passengers onboard, along with five crew members. There could have been an unknown number of children below ticketing age who were onboard and not accounted for, it said.
The boat has a carrying capacity of 90 people, the agency said, adding its recommendation that the accident be officially declared a disaster.
Mutsa Murombedzi, a local member of Parliament, posted a video of what she said were people on shore waving off what appeared to be the ageing ferry at the start of its journey. She said rural communities use the boat to travel along the lake to the town of Kariba, a journey that usually takes about five hours.
Some people standing on the shore were also concerned about whether the ferry would survive strong waves on the lake, according to the video.
Earlier, Zimbabwe police had said a rescue operation was underway but did not give any other details.
Kariba is the largest man-made lake in the world by volume and was created in the late 1950s and early 1960s by building a dam wall to block the Zambezi River, resulting in a valley slowly filling with water to form a huge lake that’s now more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) long and up to 40 kilometers (25 miles) wide in places.
Zimbabwe and Zambia share the lake, with the official border between them in the middle of it.

UN says 2 staff arrested by Afghan intelligence agency

The country has been governed for almost five years by the Taliban authorities, which rule according to a strict interpretation of Islamic law.

Afghanistan has been hit hard by international aid cuts and faces multiple challenges, including the arrival of millions of its citizens from Iran and Pakistan in recent years.

Belarusian opposition politician and scientist Aliaksandr Milinkevich dies at 79
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:47:22 UTC
05:47:22 KST

The former Sakharov Prize laureate ran against Aliaksandr Lukashenka for the Belarusian presidency in 2006.
Aliaksandr Milinkevich, the physicist-turned-politician who united Belarus’s opposition forces to challenge Aliaksandr Lukashenka in the 2006 presidential election, has died at the age of 79.
His death was announced on Tuesday.
Milinkevich underwent a complicated operation to remove a blood clot from his carotid artery last year. He spent a prolonged period in critical condition and later underwent extensive rehabilitation.
From academia to politics
Milinkevich was born in 1947, in Grodno, Belarus. After graduating from the faculty of physics and mathematics at the Grodno Pedagogical Institute, he worked as a teacher at a local school. He later earned a PhD and became an associate professor at the same institution.
He went on to author dozens of academic works on quantum electronics and laser technology, as well as on Belarusian culture, art, education and more.
Around the time of the Soviet Union's collapse, he moved into the public sector, and from 1990 to 1996, he served as deputy chair of the Grodno city executive committee.
In 2001, he headed the campaign headquarters of Belarusian presidential candidate Semyon Domash, and five years later he ran for the presidency himself.
A pro-European challenger
In 2005, Milinkevich was chosen as the candidate of the opposition democratic forces, which stood as a united front against the Lukashenka regime. A pro-European vision for Belarus became a defining feature of his campaign.
The election campaign was marked by intense pressure on the opposition, including threats of criminal prosecution, disinformation campaigns in pro-government media, and arrests of opposition activists at rallies.
In the end, according to the official figures, Lukashenka took 83% of the vote, with Milinkevich receiving 6%. Both in the United States and in Europe, doubts remained over the reliability of the results and the legitimacy of Lukashenka's third term in office.
That same year, Milinkevich received the European Parliament’s Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought.
After the unprecedentedly harsh suppression of protests in Belarus in 2020, he left the country and lived in exile with his family.
He became an adviser to opposition leader in exile Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya and the founder of the "Free Belarusian University," with its headquarters in Warsaw.
'Return to the European family'
Immediately after the election, Milinkevich founded the civic movement "For Freedom," which he continued to lead for another decade.
The movement championed European values and advocated for the development of civil society in Belarus, free and fair elections, democratic rights and European standards of living.
"By our mentality, traditions, history, culture and language, we are Europeans. For me, it has never been a matter of choosing which way we should go, east or west. For me it has been about returning to the European family from which we were forcibly taken into an empire," he said in one interview.
For Milinkevich, the issue was ultimately existential - "about whether Belarusians will continue to exist in our own country. The master of the Kremlin does not recognise as a nation not only Ukrainians, but us as well," he said.
'A man of exceptional dignity'
Tsikhanouskaya has expressed her condolences to Milinkevich's family.
"A man of exceptional dignity, a kind soul and a brilliant mind, he was a true point of reference for many of us. For me, Aliaksandr was a source of support and wisdom, whose advice I always valued deeply," she wrote in a post on X.
"His devotion to Belarus, our language and culture, and his ability to unite and support people in the most difficult moments will remain with us," she added.
President of the European Parliament Roberta Metsola also responded to the news on social media, writing: "Aliaksandr Milinkevich dedicated his life to the fight for democracy in Belarus."
"His courage and legacy will stay with us. Europe continues to stand with the people of Belarus," Metsola said.
In a 2006 interview, Milinkevich told Euronews: “The humiliation people feel when living in fear, the violation of their dignity — this, I believe, is the root cause of all Belarus’s problems."
For years, he watched as Lukashenka’s regime crushed even the smallest expressions of dissent, stamping out any signs of resistance in Belarusian society. Yet he never lost his optimism. In fact, he said his faith in change had grown stronger after the events of 2020.
"We have experience, we had the fantastic year 2020, when everyone contributed to the Belarusian spirit and the desire to defend their 'self', truth, freedom. After 2020, I am an absolute optimist, because a completely different nation was born. People overcame their fear," he said.

Russia is recruiting women out of prisons to serve as front-line medics. A new investigation documents rape by commanders and criminal cases against the women who report it.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:43:42 UTC
05:43:42 KST

Russia is recruiting women out of prisons to serve as front-line medics. A new investigation documents rape by commanders and criminal cases against the women who report it.
‘You girls are a very powerful destabilizing factor’
In 2024, Russia’s Defense Ministry launched an experiment called “Choice,” according to a new investigation by the independent Russian news outlet Verstka. The military solicited volunteers at women’s penal colonies in several regions and assigned them to tactical medicine units to treat the wounded near the front.
The first group of convicted women was recruited in early 2024 from penal colonies in Russia’s Southern Federal District. “From what I was told, there was no selection process and no training, and the crowd there was… ‘Freedom for AUE’ types [a banned prison subculture that glorifies criminal life]. They were simply told, ‘Want freedom? Sign a contract.’ They thinned out fast. They wiped themselves out: drunken self-inflicted gunshot wounds, a grenade in a dugout, some died from drugs, some were killed out of jealousy… And a small number died carrying out combat missions,” a source told Verstka.
The next round of recruitment took place that fall in Russia’s Irkutsk region, where the women did receive two weeks of training in tactical medicine, taught by former fighters from the Russian mercenary group Wagner. One of the instructors said the women’s commitment was “ferocious.” At the final session, the instructors gave each woman a first-aid kit and advised them never to go anywhere near the front line.
“If women are ending up at war, that’s a sign things are seriously screwed up in the country. If I were a commander and was told women were being brought into my unit, I’d have fought it any way I could. You girls are a very powerful destabilizing factor. Men have been in the trenches for a third year now, and then they bring in women. Hormones will go through the roof, and no law and no army regulation will hold anything together. It’ll turn into chaos,” Verstka quoted one of the instructors as saying. The women did not heed the instructors’ advice, Verstka said.
A source familiar with the women who took the courses said their fates diverged: “Some got a taste of that illusion of freedom and went completely off the rails. Some started building a life for themselves. Some have already died. A small percentage really did try, in good faith, to earn their freedom. I’m talking, above all, about Lyudmila.”
‘You’re a convict, you don’t get that!’
Before her imprisonment, Lyudmila Poltarakova practiced aikido and competed in multi-discipline strength sports. She won the European armlifting championship and earned the Russian rank of International Master of Sports. In 2019, she was convicted on drug charges and sentenced to 15 years in prison after being detained while planting mephedrone dead drops. She pleaded guilty and said she hadn’t used drugs herself but sold them for money to help her brother and sister. After the trial, she was transferred under guard to Penal Colony No. 40 in the Irkutsk region.
One of Poltarakova’s acquaintances described her to Verstka this way: “Very intelligent, prone to calculated risk. She can walk right up to the edge if she’s thought through every move in advance. She doesn’t think like a woman, and she’s extremely strong in spirit, even compared to my comrades in arms. A heightened sense of justice.”
Poltarakova signed a contract, studied hard in the preparatory courses, and arrived in the annexed Luhansk region in early 2025 along with other women from the program. She was assigned to the 370th Medical Battalion and from there sent to the 12th Tank Regiment of the Kantemirovskaya Division, part of the 1st Tank Army, as a medical orderly. The regiment’s commander, Sergei Zhitkov — who goes by the call sign Oskol — began summoning her to his trench, ostensibly for medical massages. The first few times, that was all it amounted to, but later, according to Poltarakova, he began “getting handsy.”
“When he was turned down, he started yelling, asking why the hell her battalion commander had recommended her to him. It turned out that Oskol and [the commander of the 370th Medical Battalion, Ramazan] Mutalipov were old friends, and that it was Mutalipov who had sent Lyudmila to him, saying that she was fine and that he could fuck her,” an acquaintance of Poltarakova said, relaying her account.
Poltarakova later told acquaintances and a military investigator that Zhitkov raped her on February 14, 2025, and continued to do so for at least the whole of March. Many of their fellow soldiers witnessed the assaults, she said. “The whole 12th Regiment was talking about it. And when Oskol called our dugout one night in April and told us to go provide sexual services to the division commander, who had come to visit him, I couldn’t take it anymore. I started screaming, I had a breakdown,” Poltarakova said in a voice message to a friend.
Other medics who shared a dugout with Poltarakova witnessed the scene, as did the military police officers guarding it. According to Poltarakova, another woman was sent to Zhitkov that night, while she herself was sent back to the 370th Medical Battalion. Poltarakova signed a statement saying she had no complaints against Zhitkov. She did so voluntarily, fearing that publicity would “negatively affect her future service and her receipt of an award to expunge her conviction,” according to her testimony, which Verstka reviewed.
In June 2026, Poltarakova was wounded and ended up in a military hospital, where, she said, she began getting threatening phone calls demanding that she sign another statement saying she had no complaints against Zhitkov. She then filed a rape complaint with the deputy military prosecutor of the 1st Tank Army and made her story public on a pro-war Telegram channel.
“I can say that we’re all slaves with no rights. You want a medal for being wounded? You’re a convict, you don’t get that! They struck me off the list for a medal! … You want leave after eight months of hellish work on the front line? You’re a convict, you don’t get that! You just want to rest in the hospital after surviving at the front? You’re a convict, you don’t get that! No one has ever thrown my criminal record in my face this often! I’ve served honestly since the first days of my contract; I don’t hide in hospitals, I’m always on the front line. … They never humiliated me in the penal colony the way they have in the army,” she said in a video statement.
After filing the complaint, Poltarakova was told she was being sent on a combat mission — an order she refused, believing it was an attempt to get rid of her. She dropped out of contact on July 15, but not before telling acquaintances that military police had come for her at the hospital. Verstka later learned that Poltarakova was alive and on the front line. A criminal case has been opened against her for refusing the order to leave the hospital for a combat mission. No case has been opened over the rape. Zhitkov was promoted in 2025 to acting commander of the Kantemirovskaya Division.
‘A guy comes up to me and says he’ll throw a grenade into my dugout if I don’t put out’
Darya Chirukhina dropped out of contact at the same time as Poltarakova. Another former convict from the Irkutsk region, she had also been assigned to the 370th Medical Battalion and had spoken publicly about attempted sexual assault.
“I’m posted at an outpost where some guy comes up to me and says that he’s the brother of an FSB [Federal Security Service] officer and that he’ll throw a grenade into my dugout if I don’t put out. Who am I supposed to go to about this — you?” Chirukhina asked in a phone call with a sergeant major. At Chirukhina’s request, a recording of the call was posted in a military chat group.
She also complained about the workload and health problems: “Even in the penal colony, I had more rights when it came to dealing with my own affairs… I developed diabetes at the front. I asked the command for medical help again and again, and for six months they just turned me away. Our commanders used manipulation and pressure to make me file a formal refusal of treatment. When the top brass come to visit, they hide us on purpose so we don’t say anything we shouldn’t…”
Other women from the penal colonies who spoke with Verstka also described consensual relationships at the front that resulted in children. “Things get truly awful when it comes to the kids — the babies aren’t even a month old, and they take them away from the mothers. I sent the babies away [from military hospitals] myself, and I still feel sick about it,” one of the convicted women said.
Verstka’s sources among former inmates said they knew of at least three births at the front. The women who gave birth were threatened with having their children sent to an orphanage, but in the end managed to hand the infants over to distant relatives. They then continued to serve “under compulsion,” the sources claimed.

The death toll from the earthquake in Colombia has exceeded 250, and rescuers are searching for people under the rubble
Kyiv • UNN
An earthquake measuring 7.4 in magnitude struck western Colombia, killing at least 254 people. Rescuers continue searching beneath the debris, while operations in the Chocó region are hampered by a lack of communication.
The death toll from a powerful earthquake in western Colombia has risen to at least 254, while rescuers continue searching for people under the rubble of collapsed buildings. Reuters reports, as reported by UNN.
Details
A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck early on August 10, affecting the country's western regions, including the coffee-growing region. The powerful tremors damaged or destroyed residential buildings, schools, and medical facilities.
According to local authorities, 101 people were killed in Pereira and another 95 in Cali. The total number of victims is still being clarified, as communication with some affected areas remains unstable.
Rescuers worked overnight and on Tuesday, using cranes, excavators, and other equipment. In places where heavy machinery could not reach the rubble, people cleared the debris by hand and formed human chains to move it. Rescuers also asked those present to remain silent so they could hear possible signals from people trapped under the rubble.
The situation in the Chocó region is complicating rescue operations
In the forested areas of the department of Chocó, located near the earthquake's epicenter, some communities remain without electricity and basic services. Difficult terrain and communication problems are hindering rescue teams' access to the affected settlements.
The earthquake also caused significant damage to housing and rural infrastructure. Preliminary estimates indicate that more than 5,000 homes were damaged. The National Federation of Coffee Growers is working with local families to assess the damage caused to farms and the infrastructure of the coffee-growing region.
Nearly 100 aftershocks were recorded in the region following the main earthquake. Authorities continue the search-and-rescue operation, as the extent of the destruction in some areas has still not been fully determined.

During the day, on the Southern Slobozhanshchyna axis, Russian forces attacked Ukrainian positions six times near Lyman and Starytsia and in the directions of Okhrimivka and Vodiane. Two combat engagements are still ongoing.

In July, drones manufactured by General Cherry struck over 16,000 aerial targets.
The company reported this to Militarnyi.
The majority of the targets hit were enemy winged drones — more than 13,000. Another 3,000-plus were various types of copter drones.
At the end of the month, General Cherry’s products ranked second in the Delta system’s rating for the total number of targets struck and first for the number of E-points earned. The company also took second place for the number of targets struck during daylight hours.
At the same time, the manufacturer highlights the results of using FPV drones at night. In this category, General Cherry ranked third among all FPV systems in terms of the number of targets hit.
The company notes that this indicates a significant improvement in performance, as nighttime engagements were not previously one of the manufacturer’s strongest areas in the ranking.
Separately, General Cherry highlights the effectiveness of its systems in intercepting Russian Shahed-type strike UAVs and their counterparts.
The company has become the only manufacturer represented in the top of the ranking by two products at once — the General Cherry AIR Speed and General Cherry Bullet interceptors.
According to the manufacturer, in July these two types of interceptors together destroyed approximately 300 Shahed-like drones.
Thus, based on July’s results, General Cherry retained first place in E-scores within the Delta situational awareness system.
At the same time, the company ranked second in the total number of aerial targets engaged, and its FPV drones demonstrated a noticeable improvement in performance during nighttime operations.
Earlier, on August 3, it was reported that the French company Alta Ares and the Ukrainian drone manufacturer General Cherry signed a memorandum of understanding regarding cooperation in the development of interceptor drones.
