Moving, complex ‘Valley of Shadows’ explores culture clash in the Himalayas - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:01:17 UTC
05:01:17 KST

There have been many movies in recent years chronicling the journey of Westerners into Third World countries where they travel to engage with nature or seek spirituality and enlightenment. Most of these, however, have been one-note, with the foreign travelers meeting locals who are glowing with wisdom and virtue, or who turn out to be criminals engaged in drug trafficking or other illegal enterprises.
Given all that, I was happy to see Salvador Calvo’s Valley of Shadows – opening throughout Israel on Thursday – which does not feature stereotypes or offer easy answers. It tells the story of Quique (Miguel Herran), a Spanish tourist who undergoes a horrific ordeal in northern India and ends up spending months in a tiny isolated village.
His time there gives him an unusual insight into the lives of the inhabitants of this area, whose existence is ruled by the harshness of nature and their lack of resources. They accept the limitations imposed on them in a way that is initially very difficult for Quique to understand and accept.
Something of a classic hero’s journey
But through his experiences with them, he changes his perspective in a fundamental way. The story, which would otherwise be bleak, becomes something of a classic hero’s journey as he eventually transcends his own limitations to find courage he didn’t know he possessed.
The movie, which features gorgeous photography of the Himalayas, starts out as Quique is traveling with Clara (Susana Abaitua), his girlfriend, and her son, Lucas (Iván Renedo), to whom he is very attached. They are part of the young backpacker culture who want an authentic experience.
They cope with the thin air and stay without complaint in guesthouses with no showers, joining the locals for hot baths at public facilities. But it is not an easy time for them. Clara has had cancer, and Quique sees this trip as an opportunity for her to heal.
When they hear of a village that some tourists tell them they must see to fully experience all the Himalayas have to offer, he is eager to visit it, even though it is isolated and the path to it is challenging. Clara would like them to go to Goa so she can go surfing, but Quique persuades her to head for the village with him and Lucas, which he hopes will help her come back to herself after a mastectomy. She agrees reluctantly.
Quique is beaten by bandits and left for dead
INEVITABLY, THEY get lost and camp out for the night in a remote spot. It’s difficult to discuss this next section without revealing spoilers, but they are separated, and Quique is beaten by bandits and left for dead. A local trader picks him up and takes him back to his mountain village.
In a monastery there, he is treated with local remedies for his injuries, and when he regains consciousness, he is confused and barely able to walk. Frantically, he insists he must report what has happened to the police immediately.
The monk and his assistant, Prana (Alexandra Masangkay, who gives the movie’s standout performance), a young woman with an eye-patch that covers a serious injury of her own, insist that he make a contribution to their monastery, and he struggles to explain what happened to him and why he has no money.
Prana speaks English and Spanish and translates for the head monk. Quique learns to his dismay that there is no way to travel to any village with police for months, until the river freezes and it is possible to walk there. But he must report the crime and get in touch with their families, he insists, to which the locals shrug. There is nothing to be done right now.
Much of the rest of the movie is about Quique getting to know the villagers and absorbing their point of view. In many ways, this film is reminiscent of the movies by the director and Buddhist lama Khyentse Norbu, who made The Cup and Travelers & Magicians, and Pawo Choyning Dorji, the director of the Oscar-nominated Lunana: A Yak in the Classroom and The Monk and the Gun.
All of these movies are set in Bhutan and northern India and deal with the clash between Buddhist tradition, third-world realities, and Western culture. It’s high praise that Valley of Shadows brought to mind these films, which are among the most interesting movies of the past 25 years.
Valley of Shadows neither glorifies nor demonizes the local culture, and it makes it clear that tourists are putting themselves in danger by going off on their own in a place where their phones, cameras, and the contents of their wallets represent more money than most residents can hope to earn in years.
This is a reality that so many Westerners seem to ignore when they head off on their treks, and it’s true that most of the time, they return home safely. But the risk is real, and Valley of Shadows explores it.
By the end, we have learned so much about the villagers that our perspective on them has changed, as has Quique’s. Alejandro Hernandez’s script, which tells us exactly as much as we need to know at any point, is low-key but effective. Combined with the spectacular photography and compelling performances by the entire cast, many of whom are non-professionals, the movie takes us on a moving journey.

One week after notching a significant primary victory in a Midwestern purple state, pro-Palestinian progressives are looking to repeat their success in Wisconsin.
The Badger State’s chaotic Democratic primary for governor ends Tuesday with state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, polling comfortably in the lead. Despite the best efforts of the state’s Democratic establishment, and the concerns of Wisconsin Jewish groups, Hong appears well positioned to win the primary - leaving many in the state concerned about her electability in the general.
Hong’s record on Israel and antisemitism is of concern to Wisconsin Jews, as well as Democratic figureheads more broadly. She has appeared on livestream fundraisers with Hasan Piker, the left-wing strident Israel critic who has also rallied with Hong, as well as twice with Michael Beyer (“Mike from PA”), who has called Jewish identity “a constructed ethnicity, this demonic ethnicity, wholly invented.”
On one of her appearances with Beyer, Hong urged constituents to fundraise for people on the “front lines in Gaza.”
A poll of likely voters one week before the race, conducted by nonpartisan outlet State Navigate, showed Hong with a commanding lead. Forty-four percent of those surveyed said they favored Hong, twice the total who backed Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the next-closest candidate.
Only 17% of the same voter sample said they identified as democratic socialists, possibly indicating that Hong - whose platform has emphasized working families, healthcare, and data centers - has found wider appeal beyond her movement.
The party’s left flank is buoyed by Abdul El-Sayed’s victory last week in the US Senate primary in Michigan, and hopes that a repeat success is possible in a neighboring Great Lakes state with a similarly purple voting bloc. But El-Sayed performed far short of the comfortable victory many polling outlets had predicted, squeaking a winning margin of just under 1%.
Polls show Hong in wide lead despite early lack of name recognition
That may not be the case this time. Polling from Marquette Law School, considered the gold standard in the state, has also consistently shown Hong with a wide lead. Despite entering the race with little name recognition, Hong has benefitted from both a national progressive populist push and a crowded, musical-chairs Democratic field that burst with seven candidates at its peak.
The race has been whittled down to four candidates today, with Crowley having re-entered the field after previously suspending his campaign. The flip came after Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, the preferred candidate of Crowley and many other institutionalist Democrats, dropped out of the race following an accounting scandal. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, the party’s 2022 US Senate nominee and a once-promising figure in the state, also dropped out after failing to gain traction.
During her campaign, Hong apologized for having called the police on a vandalized Israeli flag in her district in December 2023, which at the time she had called “highly antisemitic” and urged to be investigated as a hate crime.
Explaining why she now regrets making the call, Hong recently told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, “The image was cropped and incomplete to misrepresent anti-Zionism as antisemitism – a distinction I take seriously.”
Hong’s impact on Israel policy as governor of Wisconsin would be limited. But she has called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government “genocidal” and pushed the state to overturn a ban on government contracts with businesses that boycott Israel. She has also criticized Wisconsin’s current moderate Democratic governor for backing the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)’s controversial definition of antisemitism.
DSA co-chair defends Oct. 8 Times Square rally in ‘New Yorker’ interview
Hong’s general-election success may hinge on the broader electorate’s views of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). This week a co-chair of the DSA drew further concern from Jewish Democrats after appearing in a viral interview on The New Yorker’s podcast. Megan Romer called the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel “largely inevitable” and said she “probably would have” joined a pro-Palestinian rally in New York the day after the attacks if she’d been able to attend.
Prior to Oct. 7, Hong’s state house campaigns had expressed some positive feelings toward Jews and Jewish causes. In January 2023, her campaign sold a Hebrew-language shirt, with proceeds going to Jewish Social Services of Madison.
“Team Hong has upped our commitment to uplifting multiculturalism,” Hong’s campaign wrote on Twitter at the time. She included praise of the symbolic significance of the number 18 in Hebrew and of the Hebrew phrase “L’chaim.”

Russia Halts Production of Geran-3 Jet-Powered Drones — DIU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:59:30 UTC
04:59:30 KST

Russia has halted production of the Geran-3 jet-powered kamikaze drones.
This was reported to Militarnyi by the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU).
The Geran-3 is a UAV developed using the airframe and components of the Geran-2. However, instead of a piston engine, it is powered by a Telefly JT80 jet engine.
The basic UAV airframe underwent only minimal modifications.
The propulsion system allows the drone to reach speeds of 300–370 km/h, while its operational range is up to 1,000 km.
The drone’s onboard equipment includes a SADRA inertial navigation system, an ADC pressure measurement unit, a PDU power distribution unit, and several other modules.
For navigation, the Geran-3 is equipped with a Kometa-M12 satellite navigation system resistant to electronic interference. It uses a 12-element CRPA adaptive antenna array.
This allows the UAV to counter the effects of electronic warfare systems.
According to the DIU, 45 foreign-made components have been identified in the Geran-3. Of these, 22 are manufactured in the United States, eight in China, seven in Switzerland, three in Germany, two in the United Kingdom, and one in Japan.
The Russians also installed a camera and video transmission system on the Geran-3 similar to those used on the Geran-2 of the “Ъ” series.
Overall, the Geran-3’s electronic architecture is almost identical to that of the gasoline-powered Geran-2 variants of the “Ы” series.
The Geran-3 family effectively served as a transitional stage toward the Geran-4. Its airframe was specifically designed to accommodate the Telefly LX-WP-160 jet engine.

US military fires on cargo vessel it said sought to break Iran blockade
CENTCOM says helicopter fired at engine room of Panama-flagged Vela Nova as US-Iran diplomacy remains stalled.
The United States military has said it fired on a ship attempting to break its blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf of Oman.
The attack on Tuesday comes amid a period of relative calm in the US-Israeli war with Iran, with attacks mostly paused since a 13-day escalation in July. That came after a ceasefire as part of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by the US and Iran in June appeared to collapse.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump took ‘secret flight’ from Turkiye to avoid Iran ‘threat’
- list 2 of 3Trump sends conflicting signals on Iran strategy
- list 3 of 3Iran, US set new conditions during Hormuz talks: What does this mean?
In a statement, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees the Middle East, said a Navy helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles at the Panama-flagged Vela Nova cargo vessel.
It said the vessel “attempted to transit the Gulf of Oman and violate the U.S. blockade against Iran by sailing toward an Iranian port”.
The attack targeted the ship’s engine room and disabled its steering gear, CENTCOM said, alleging the crew “ignored repeated warnings from American forces”.
It did not say if any crew members were wounded in the attack. In its statement on Tuesday, CENTCOM said US forces had disabled 55 commercial vessels throughout its blockade on Iranian ports, disabled three “non-compliant vessels”, and boarded two.
The US reimposed its naval blockade of Iranian ports amid the recent return to fighting, with Iran again reasserting its control over the Strait of Hormuz. Both of those conditions had been lifted as part of the June MoU, which was meant to launch renewed negotiations on a more lasting peace, as well as the future of crippling sanctions on Iran and its nuclear programme.
Efforts to return to an agreement have so far yielded little progress, with Trump on Monday appearing to up the ante as he called for reparations from Iran for “50 years” of damage. Tehran has previously called for reconstruction funding to be part of any deal, with the June MoU containing a preliminary plan for a $300bn fund.
The conflict has been further complicated in the latest bout of fighting by attacks by the Yemen-based Houthis on ships in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, another key trade route in the region.
Iran, for its part, has largely focused its diplomatic efforts on direct talks with Oman to determine new shipping lines in the Strait of Hormuz, an arterial waterway through which 20 percent of the world’s maritime fossil fuel trade transited prior to the war launched by the US and Israel on February 28.
Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency on Tuesday quoted Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, saying the Strait of Hormuz “will not be opened until the United States changes its behaviour and accepts Iran’s conditions”.
He maintained that any agreement with Oman would be “separate” from the issue of the strait’s closure.
Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, meanwhile, arrived in Tehran on Tuesday for talks with Iranian officials, in the latest effort towards wider mediation of the war.

Former Secret Service Agents: Trump’s Secret Plane Swap Unusual, Not Unprecedented
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:54:55 UTC
04:54:55 KST

The Trump administration's extraordinary maneuver to shield the President from an alleged assassination threat from Iran last month by secretly moving him to a different plane has raised new questions about how often the Secret Service resorts to such tactics. Former Secret Service agents tell TIME that such security measures, while rare, are not without precedent in the agency's playbook for handling credible threats.
Multiple outlets reported that the Trump administration orchestrated an elaborate plan to get Trump out of Turkey during the NATO summit on July 8, transporting him via a catering container to a military plane, after intelligence officials flagged a specific threat tied to Iran.
Moments before Trump was shuttled off the plane, he was seen by reporters boarding the original Air Force One instead of the new one donated by Qatar due to its lack of defensive capabilities. Reporters and White House staff on the aircraft were unaware of the fact that the President was not on the plane until after he had already switched planes again in Britain.
Jason Russell, a former Secret Service Agent who spent eight years protecting presidents and planning security details ahead of presidential trips, says that the President boarding Air Force One is normally the last thing that happens before the plane closes its door and begins taking off.
“For him [Trump] to get on a plane, and then have a catering truck pull up to the side of the plane, anybody who's actually paying any attention to how Air Force One operates, should have been, like, ‘That's strange,’” Russell said.
Russell explained that flying is usually deemed the safest way to transport a President because airspaces are normally severely restricted for Air Force One to pass by. Yet threats remain, including drone attacks and even surface-to-air missile attacks.
“Obviously, the Air Force One is equipped with some countermeasures and some security that hopefully never have to be used,” Russell says, adding that there's also an airspace security division within the Secret Service that regularly works with the military to ensure the president’s safety while traveling on air.
Robert McDonald, who spent 21 years with the Secret Service, including on the Presidential Protective Division and as a supervisory agent on then-Vice President Biden's detail, said the plane-swapping operation in Turkey reflects real-time improvisation by presidential security personnel rather than a standing procedure.
“I'm sure they started preparing as soon as they found out about the threat,” McDonald said in an interview. “I'm not sure they had the luxury of having many days or even potentially many hours.”
McDonald described the decision-making process around such operations as a joint effort among the Secret Service, the White House Military Office and White House staff, with "no one entity" holding more authority than the others.
The Department of Defense has referred questions from TIME to the White House. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
White House Pool Reporters Deceived
McDonald pushed back on the idea that Air Force One and the people still aboard it, including journalists, were left exposed. “I would find it incredibly hard to believe that those two planes weren't escorted or with other assets from allies or the U.S. Air Force in the area,” he said, adding that he doubted the people on the aircraft “were dangled out there and left to fend for themselves.”
The operation broke a White House tradition that presidents rarely travel without a group of reporters known as the White House pool, to ensure the public has an independent account of the president’s activities. Former President Barack Obama broke the tradition in 2010 by leaving the White House to attend his daughter’s soccer game without telling reporters. 
In 2000, President Bill Clinton secretly switched to an unmarked plane for a trip to Pakistan. At least one member of the White House pool, a reporter covering the trip for USA Today, was briefed on the operation beforehand, according to The Washington Post.
On the secrecy around the maneuver in Turkey—with even journalists traveling with Trump left in the dark—McDonald said limiting the circle of those informed is standard practice, especially now. “We're in a time now where instantaneous news articles are going out—TikTok, Instagram, Facebook,” he said. “That doesn't help the plan that the Secret Service needs to implement.”
Ultimately, McDonald said, judgments about the optics of the operation are secondary to its outcome. “Everybody that I'm aware of got home from that trip to Turkey," he said. "The bottom line is everybody got home safe. That's the main function of the Secret Service.”

Women coaches have almost tripled, but 'misogynistic and abusive' behaviour remains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:53:47 UTC
04:53:47 KST

Elite women coach numbers almost triple but 'misogynistic and abusive' behaviour still exists
If you asked generative AI to create an image of a sports coach, it would likely serve up a middle-aged white man.
And while rooted in stereotypes, it would not necessarily be inaccurate.
The picture is slowly changing in some sports, although not substantial enough yet to disturb the algorithm.
The Australian Institute of Sport found the number of female head coaches in funded sports has nearly tripled since starting its Women in High Performance Coaching project in 2021.
The number now sits at more than 25 per cent, but AIS Director Matti Clements told ABC Sport that is still not good enough.
"Maybe we've had a history where we've just had male coaches coaching our best athletes," she said.
"We want to make sure the right people are coaching our athletes at the right time, female or male coaches."
The AIS report found many women coaches have experienced bad behaviour, which was "in some cases appalling, misogynistic and abusive," as well as challenges managing careers alongside having a family, and difficulties even getting a foot in the door, let alone climbing the ladder.
It highlighted the need for leaders within the sporting sector to drive cultural change to address the barriers.
"As a system, we've had a real focus in the last couple of years of wellbeing being fundamental to high performance sport in this country," Clements said.
"If you look at wellbeing as a sustainable high-performance lever, that will encourage all different types of people to stay in our system, female coaches included.
"Perhaps historically, high-performance sport in this country has not been as welcoming for female coaches as it has been for male coaches."
Clements pointed out some of the strategies which have helped deliver positive results over the past four years include visibility of high profile coaches, having conversations at the highest levels, re-evaluating recruitment practices, and targeted development.
Sauvage leading the way
Louise Sauvage is one of Australia's most decorated Paralympians, and since retiring in 2004, has established herself as a leading coach in para wheelchair track and road racing.
She has noticed an evolution over the past 20 years.
"It's been really good to see that infrastructure and also the investment into women's coaching," she told ABC Sport.
"Our athletes are almost 50-50 male, female, so to have that balance is perfect.
"And I think women bring something a little different to the male coaches as well. So I think it's important that we encourage them to continue on in those roles and to show the identity and what we can bring as female coaches."
Sauvage is also one of very few elite coaches with disability across the Australian sporting landscape, and acknowledged it has not always been an easy path for her.
"I think some of the barriers were definitely identifying what you could or couldn't do or how the workarounds would work," she said.
"And also talking with your national sporting organisation and how you can get past them or what help you might need and then you can just be as effective as any other coach.
"I think it's about communication more than anything and not just looking at something [and saying] 'oh, I can't do that.'
"[You should ask] how can you do it? How can we make it work for you so that you can progress as a coach?"
She added having coaches with shared lived experiences was a valuable asset for athletes.
"They already know that I know how they're feeling or what they need because I've been there and I've done that," she said.
"But things evolve all the time, so I need to keep learning as well. But I really do think a lot of the athletes do appreciate that the understanding is already there."
The professional picture
The AIS report focused on sports it funds, largely rooted in the Olympic and Paralympic arena, but many of the issues raised prevail in the professional codes too.
Four of the 18 of AFLW head coaches are women, one of 12 in the NRLW, one of 11 in the A-League Women and two of eight in the WBBL (last season).
The WNBL is close to parity with four of the nine coaches women, and as the country's number one female participation sport, five of Super Netball's eight coaches were female last season.
Like the dearth of disabled coaches, there are also very few First Nations, or culturally diverse head coaches, across men's and women's sports.
Clements said diversity in coaching simply makes sense.
"The sports are seeing the value of it in terms of performance outcomes. So this is not just a nice to have, we're doing it because it feels good," she said.
"It absolutely is a competitive advantage and that's what's going to engage our sports to continue to focus on this because we want to have the best games ever in Brisbane and in order to do that we have to make sure we've got the best people coaching."

NEW DELHI: The Centre should scrap all existing inter-state border check posts within six months and replace the All India Tourist Permit with a unified All India Passenger Permit within a year, a parliamentary panel has recommended, pitching for a sweeping overhaul of the country’s bus transport system.The committee headed by JD(U) MP Sanjay Kumar Jha made the recommendations after consultations with govt departments, bus operators, passengers and other stakeholders to identify key hurdles facing the sector, which transports more passengers daily than Indian Railways.The panel noted that India has around 4.4 lakh buses, but only about 1.1 lakh are owned by govt entities, mainly state road transport undertakings. Panel further recommended that all bus terminals provide private operators “non-discriminatory access” to pick up passengers on payment of an entry fee, following the model at Delhi’s ISBT.It also proposed establishment of a National Bus Terminals Authority to develop and standardise terminal infrastructure and, where states agree, manage bus terminals and intermodal passenger hubs.Panel further recommended a unified online ticketing platform covering state-run and private bus operators for passenger convenience.It has proposed a citizen vigilance channel, modelled on Election Commission’s cVIGIL app, allowing passengers to file geo-tagged, time-stamped complaints—with photos or videos—about overloading, unsafe transport of schoolchildren, faulty safety equipment and poor sanitation in buses, terminals and halting points.Complaints would be automatically forwarded to the enforcement authority concerned for action within a prescribed timeframe, it said.

The site is one of several satellite encampments established from the nearby Tel Talpiot outpost in recent months.
Footage circulated Monday showed IDF soldiers praying alongside settlers staying at the Qusra site, whose presence has fueled tensions with Palestinian residents. Following publication of the footage, the IDF said commanders were investigating the incident and that disciplinary action would be taken depending on the findings.
Qusra council head Abd al-Azim Wadi told ynet that the situation had not changed since Monday.
“The settlers are still there. There are several outposts,” he said.

Looking to see the solar eclipse from North America? Here’s where and when to catch a sliver
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — Sorry, North America. After winning the cosmic lottery with a pair of coast-to-coast total solar eclipses, now it’s Europe’s turn.
But look skyward anyway Wednesday and, if you’re far enough north in the U.S. and Canada, you might savor a partial eclipse as the moon nibbles away at the sun.
Totality will begin near the North Pole, then streak southward across Greenland, Iceland, Spain and a patch of Portugal. Daytime darkness won’t last more than a couple minutes at best — shrimpy compared with North America’s epic 2024 eclipse — but it is continental Europe’s first encounter with totality since 1999. Spain gets a much longer shot at totality next August, along with North Africa and the Middle East.
For the U.S., the Great American Eclipse of 2017 kicked off the sun-vanishing mania with more than two minutes of totality from Oregon to South Carolina. The amount of totality almost doubled in 2024, racing diagonally from Mexico’s Pacific coast all the way past Newfoundland.
America’s next coast-to-coast total solar eclipse isn’t until 2045. So catch a partial now if you can, but don’t forget to protect your eyes with certified eclipse glasses.
Here’s a list of some U.S. and Canadian cities in position to see a partial solar eclipse on Wednesday if skies are clear, in alphabetical order, with local times and the amount of sun coverage provided by NASA:
—Anchorage, Alaska, with 28% coverage. Begins at 7:36 a.m. and ends at 9:09 a.m., peaking at 8:21 a.m.
—Bangor, Maine, with 24% coverage. Begins at 12:54 p.m. and ends at 2:49 p.m., peaking at 1:53 p.m.
—Detroit with 3% coverage. Begins at 1:03 p.m. and ends at 2:08 p.m., peaking at 1:36 p.m.
—Montreal, Quebec, with 18% coverage. Begins at 12:50 p.m. and ends at 2:38 p.m., peaking at 1:45 p.m.
—New York City with 9% coverage. Begins at 1:07 p.m. and ends at 2:38 p.m., peaking at 1:54 p.m.
—Philadelphia with 7% coverage. Begins at 1:11 p.m. and ends at 2:35 p.m., peaking at 1:53 p.m.
—St. Johns, Newfoundland and Labrador, with 53% coverage. Begins at 2:28 p.m. and ends at 4:37 p.m., peaking at 3:35 p.m.
—Toronto, Ontario, with 8% coverage. Begins at 12:55 p.m. and ends at 2:23 p.m., peaking at 1:40 p.m.
—Washington, D.C., with 4% coverage. Begins at 1:17 p.m. and ends at 2:27 p.m., peaking at 1:53 p.m.
—Winnipeg, Manitoba, with 5% coverage. Begins at 11:25 a.m. and ends at 12:40 p.m., peaking at 12:02 p.m.

Tiffany Haddish avoids more jail time by pleading guilty to a drunken driving charge in Georgia
FAYETTEVILLE, Ga. (AP) — Actor and comedian Tiffany Haddish avoided additional jail time Tuesday when she pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor alcohol-related driving charge that stemmed from her 2022 arrest in Georgia after someone called 911 about a driver asleep at the wheel at a traffic light.
Other charges were dropped. After entering the plea by video, Haddish was placed on 12 months’ probation and told to avoid drugs and alcohol and complete a substance abuse evaluation. She was credited for the brief time she spent in jail following her arrest.
Haddish’s films include the comedy “Girls Trip,” “Night School,” “Like a Boss” and “The Kitchen.” She wrote the New York Times bestseller “The Last Black Unicorn,” which earned a Grammy nomination for a subsequent audiobook she narrated. In 2018, she won an Emmy for her appearance on “Saturday Night Live” and a Grammy in 2021 for her special “Black Mitzvah.”
At around 2:30 a.m. on Jan. 14, 2022, someone called 911 to report seeing a person who appeared to be asleep in the driver’s seat of a white Ford Explorer with their foot on the brake in Peachtree City, about 30 miles (48 kilometers) south of Atlanta, according to a court filing. An officer spotted an SUV that matched the description given by the caller and stopped Haddish as she pulled into a neighborhood, according to a police report.
Haddish’s lawyers in May asked a judge to dismiss the case, arguing that waiting more than four years for the case to be resolved had caused personal and professional difficulties and violated her right to a speedy trial. Fayette County State Court Judge Jason Thompson rejected her arguments.
The judge found that Haddish and her attorneys had requested some of the delays, including a request for a delay so she could attend a fashion show in Morocco and a request to leave a hearing early to catch a flight. He wrote that she also did not show any evidence of having missed specific performing opportunities or of actual financial harm because of the delay.
Haddish also was arrested in November 2023 in Beverly Hills, California, on suspicion of driving under the influence after police received a call and said Haddish appeared to be slumped over the wheel of a vehicle while the engine was still running.
Haddish reached a plea deal with prosecutors in that case in February 2024, pleading no contest to a vehicle code violation, and the two misdemeanor DUI charges against her were dropped, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Details

The incident is currently being investigated by the State Security Division of the Central Department of Criminal Investigations in Hannover.

The White House has asked the Department of Justice to weigh new charges against a former Olympian accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, according to a person familiar with the matter, pushing to revive a case Donald Trump has fumed about ever since an ally dropped the case citing insufficient evidence.
Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, dropped the charges against the man, David Hearn, on 31 July, blaming a contractor for a flawed installation. In a 20-page filing dismissing the charges, Pirro’s office said it had received evidence that damage to the pool occurred before Hearn visited it, and that “it is difficult to attribute the widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool to vandalism, let alone to establish that fact beyond a reasonable doubt.” Hearn has maintained that he reached in the water to touch a piece of already detached lining while he was on a bike ride in June.
Trump has publicly rebuked Pirro for the decision and said she “choked”.

The justice department did not directly respond when asked whether it was considering filing new charges. “The Department of Justice follows the evidence when determining if crimes have been committed. We always evaluate any case based on the facts and the law,” a spokesperson said in an email.
The request from the White House to the justice department is itself extraordinary and underscores how Trump has moved to take control of the department and use it for his own ends. Traditionally, the justice department operates at an arm’s length from the White House to maintain impartiality and avoid the appearance of political interference.
The White House also did not directly address whether it asked the justice department to file new charges. A spokesperson referred a request for comment to the justice department and sent links to two recent Trump posts on Truth Social calling for Pirro to reconsider her decision and suggesting there was evidence against Hearn.
Lawyers representing Hearn said a request from the White House would be “another bizarre turn”.
“If true, it would mark a shocking first: a case that the DoJ lost by its own admission because it lacked the evidence to convict returning from the dead. This would add another bizarre turn to a sad chapter in the DOJ’s history and further harass an innocent man,” the lawyers, Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann and Steve Levin, said in a statement.

====================================================================================================

July’s Heat Made History. Trump’s Cuts Could Leave Us Less Prepared for What Comes Next
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:47:00 UTC
04:47:00 KST

July was the hottest month on record in the contiguous United States, with an average temperature of 76.9°F—the highest average ever recorded by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), going back to 1895. The previous record was shared by July 1936, during the Dust Bowl, and July 2012. Every state was at least 1 degree above its 20th-century average.
This type of observation can help communities prepare for and respond to extreme heat events. They can then take informed steps to prevent serious health issues that the World Health Organization (WHO) links to high temperatures, like heat stroke and cardiovascular disease, or even death.
But NOAA relies on federal funding in order to keep historic records, observe weather patterns, and produce informed forecasts.
The Trump Administration reduced NOAA’s workforce in 2025, and subsequently proposed steep cuts to the agency’s funding, hampering its ability to monitor weather conditions, analyze patterns, and provide forecasts.
The National Weather Service (NWS), which operates under NOAA, lost roughly 600 employees—about 15% of its workforce—through layoffs, buyouts and retirements. It must now respond to increasingly severe weather events—like hurricane season and wildfire season—with reduced resources. As a result, it announced last year that it was scaling back the tools used to track weather patterns, such as weather balloons.
The administration later proposed cutting NOAA’s overall budget by $1.6 billion, or roughly 26%, compared with fiscal year 2025.
“A leaner NOAA that focuses on core operational needs, eliminates unnecessary layers of bureaucracy, terminates nonessential grant programs, and ends activities that do not warrant a Federal role, will provide better value to the American public,” its budget summary stated.
The United States will likely continue struggling to reconcile diminishing resources with increasing extreme temperatures, as the United Nations World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warned Tuesday that periods of extreme heat will become more frequent, intense, and longer-lasting as climate change warms the planet.
How we know when heat is becoming dangerous
The NWS tracks weather in multiple ways—including the installation of surface stations at over 900 airports that provide 24/7 real-time surface weather observations, as well as weather balloons, marine buoys, and satellites.
Those observations feed forecast models that help meteorologists understand developing weather patterns and anticipate dangerous conditions.
“Extended periods of high day and nighttime temperature conditions create cumulative stress on the human body, increasing the risk of illness and death from heat exposure,” according to the WHO. In the United States, the NWS considers heat the leading weather-related killer. Globally, studies estimate that heat was associated with roughly 489,000 deaths annually between 2000 and 2019.
The health effects of heat waves were felt acutely this summer. Maryland’s Department of Health said that 2026 was its deadliest heat season on record, with a total of 50 heat-related fatalities since May. The state also recorded over 1,300 heat-related illnesses in that period. At the national level, the Washington Post reported that there were at least 70 deaths related to heat domes in July. And in Europe, officials said that there were more than 10,000 excess deaths during the continent’s record-breaking heat wave in June.
The NWS communicates the danger that high temperatures pose using a Heat Index that describes the “feels like” temperature to the human body based on a combination of heat and humidity. For consistency, it uses what’s called “apparent temperature,” referring to the temperature that the body “feels” in shady locations. Exposure to direct sunlight can increase values by up to 15°F.
With information from the NWS, local governments are better able to prepare infrastructure and warn vulnerable communities. At the same time, the agencies are better equipped to create and distribute useful resources, such as guidance on how to stay cool during heat waves.
But less accurate data, and less data collected overall, can prevent experts from accurately anticipating future events. Agencies might be less prepared to inform vulnerable communities or cooperate with local and state governments to ensure outreach and preparedness. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this is more likely to impact people with chronic medical conditions, children, and adults over 65.
What happens when weather agencies have fewer resources?
Cuts at NOAA and the Federal Emergency Management Agency have left the U.S. more vulnerable to the effects of extreme weather.
In May, for instance, lawmakers expressed concerns over the NWS’s failure to launch 75% of the weather balloons typically sent aloft in Kansas to help measure atmospheric conditions. These balloons carry a device called a radiosonde that is used to collect upper-atmosphere temperature, humidity, pressure, and wind information to support forecasting. NWS blamed staffing shortages, but Kansas Rep. Sharice Davids pointed out that those disruptions were occurring during tornado season.
“Kansans deserve transparency about what’s happening, why it’s happening and what’s being done to fix it,” Davids said in a statement. “Kansans deserve confidence that the systems meant to keep them safe are fully operational during tornado season and meteorologists deserve the reliable data they need to do their jobs.”
In order to preserve its work with fewer resources, NOAA has continued to evolve its use of technology. It has long used artificial intelligence and machine learning for “weather forecasting, climate modeling, and environmental monitoring.” And it announced a partnership with Google Cloud in July, explaining how the move is expected to “result in a modeling system that is more flexible and easy to update.”
That same month, China debuted Fenghe, an open-source large language model (LLM) for meteorological services. The government announced that the LLM “is trained on 50 million tokens of meteorological service data and integrated with authoritative weather datasets to support weather forecasting, risk assessment, and meteorological services.”
As NOAA faces an uncertain funding future, such tools could become increasingly important to its efforts to maintain forecasting capacity for an increasingly hot planet.

How does the man behind Russia’s most soothing cartoon dog end up with an 18+ horror hit? Leonid Shmelkov’s ‘Restlessness’ strands two travelers in a roadside hotel they can’t escape.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:44:02 UTC
04:44:02 KST

How does the man behind Russia’s most soothing cartoon dog end up with an 18+ horror hit? Leonid Shmelkov’s ‘Restlessness’ strands two travelers in a roadside hotel they can’t escape.
Nepokoy (“Restlessness”), a feature-length art-house animation for adults, is now playing in Russian theaters. That in itself is news: 18+ animation is a real rarity not only in Russia but worldwide. Nepokoy has already become a phenomenon: it’s the highest-grossing Russian animated film for adults, the living legend Yuri Norstein has praised it, and its heroine has been turned into a Dymkovo toy, a traditional Russian painted-clay folk figurine. Nepokoy’s director, Leonid Shmelkov, is known online for his viral animated clips about a dog named Andrei and the dog’s friends. The feature looks nothing like them: it’s a surreal story about travelers stranded in a mysterious hotel run by the eccentric Madam. The critic Anton Khitrov explains how to read this puzzle of a film — and why it became a hit.
Warning: This review contains spoilers. If you want to avoid them, read up to the next yellow banner, then come back once you’ve seen the film.
Had A24 released Nepokoy, movie buffs worldwide would already be snapping up the studio’s merchandise — tiger-print infinity scarves, pink bunny keychains. Slow-paced, unsettling, and not fully comprehensible on first viewing, the film is bound — despite all those qualities — to build a fan base. A Russian one, though, not yet an international one.
Leonid Shmelkov — who won Russia’s Nika Award and Berlin’s Crystal Bear for his short film Moy lichny los (“My Personal Moose”) — spent three and a half years making Nepokoy and showed it at several festivals in 2025, including the Moscow International Film Festival and the Big Cartoon Festival. The film has only now reached theaters; online, it will be available on Okko.
For all its originality, Nepokoy produces a sense of déjà vu at every turn, and each new review of it arrives with its own catalog of spotted references. Shmelkov himself cites Groundhog Day, the films of David Lynch, and Julio Cortázar’s story “House Taken Over” — a classic of magical realism about a brother and sister who live alone in their family’s city mansion but meekly abandon it as unnamed entities take over one room after another. There are far more sources than that, conscious and unconscious alike, from mythology and folklore to 19th- and 20th-century prose and contemporary cinema. Animation is in the mix too: the most obvious analog is Hayao Miyazaki’s Spirited Away. But in Shmelkov’s hands, everything is much darker.
The story opens with two travelers — the imperturbable Yasha and the perpetually drowsy Bernard — driving across Russia one hot summer in a car whose pink color is no accident. They turn off the road for the night at a roadside hotel called the Rose, lost among the fields. Its owner, a certain “Madam” — cheerful, talkative, and somehow a little too pushy — takes a distinct interest in Yasha.
By the next day, the travelers realize that they can’t leave the Rose and that something is off about the hotel itself. The longer they stay, the more marvels they find. One guest can teleport. Another turns into a little pyramid. A third is a tiger, though he walks on two legs. Little by little, the Rose’s residents start disappearing, and strange creatures overrun the surrounding fields — all of it set to the unbearably disquieting music of Sergei Kuryokhin, performed by Alexei Aigi’s ensemble 4’33”.
The new film has little in common with Shmelkov’s therapeutic reels about Andrei, though his followers will still find familiar touches — his characteristic gentle voice, for instance, which he lends to several characters, including the leads, Yasha and Madam. Much closer to Nepokoy is another of his works, the 2021 short Komnata s vidom na more (“A Room with a Sea View”), which is also available online. Visually it’s sparer than the feature — black-and-white with occasional flecks of red and green — but the character designs already hint at the future cast of Nepokoy. And the plot is all but identical.
The idea for the short seems to grow entirely out of observations of the frustration that sets in on vacation: you travel for the experience and find only boredom when you arrive. A traveler named Herbert checks into a rented room whose sea view is nominal at best — really just a narrow strip between buildings — and spends his hours moping in front of the television. Before long he meets a mysterious florist from the shop across the street, and she takes over his thoughts completely. Like Madam, she rules an enchanted kingdom of her own — a kingdom of plants — but in looks she is closer to Rita, another of the hotel’s residents: the same silence, the same wide eyes.
Still, Shmelkov has never worked in a visual language as complex and varied as the one in Nepokoy.
Nepokoy gives us a convincing portrait of the Russian backwoods, full of living detail: the road overgrown with gray weeds, the air swarming with flies — leave a car in the yard overnight and by morning you’ll find a couple of apples on the hood. In some scenes, the balance of stylization and realism is no less exact than the celebrated Studio Ghibli’s: a flock of sheep drawn as a single creature, many-headed and flowing, or the painstaking animation of food, from a meager hotel breakfast to a fantastical pomegranate that might have been borrowed from Sergei Parajanov.
The effect is all the more startling when the lifelike image suddenly gives way to a schematic, deliberately primitive one, as in the Andrei cartoons. Or, on the contrary, to detailed, intricate surrealist images, such as the imagined “eternal tiger” coiled into a ring like an ouroboros. Nepokoy has both ordinary-looking people and humanoid pink bunnies — frankly cartoonish creatures, a cross between the putti of Old Master paintings and the Hattifatteners from Tove Jansson’s books. They apparently embody Yasha’s unconscious — since they anticipate desires he doesn’t yet know he has.
The bunnies are the only characters the animators didn’t draw from life. For everyone else, they used rotoscoping, a retro technique, an old analog of today’s motion capture. It works like this: a live actor plays the character and is filmed; an artist then traces the movements, adjusting the proportions as needed (the textbook example is Walt Disney’s Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs). The characters in Nepokoy have cartoon faces and human everything else, so the facial expressions come out exaggerated while the body language is startlingly natural. The dancing is especially expressive; the choreography in Nepokoy, incidentally, is quite idiosyncratic — like something out of an experimental dance piece.
Spoilers start here!
Nepokoy’s plot and visual style are in fine harmony: the animation here is realism plus stylization, and the script is everyday life plus archetypes. Madam, for instance, is drawn, acted, and voiced in a way that lets you picture her at the register of your nearest supermarket. But is she human? Hardly. More likely she’s good at pretending.
A goddess or sorceress who keeps a mortal man as her lover by force is an ancient image with a rich history. Readers of Homer — and viewers of Christopher Nolan — will inevitably think of the nymph Calypso, who kept Odysseus from going home for seven years. Then there’s the legend of the German knight Tannhäuser, who spent those same seven years in the cave of the goddess Holda — Venus, in Richard Wagner’s opera. The most obvious Russian counterpart is Pavel Bazhov’s “The Stone Flower”: the Mistress of the Copper Mountain may not make Danila the Craftsman her husband, but everything else matches.
In all these stories, the hero is either across the sea or underground — in short, in the land of the dead. And since the world of the dead is an inverted world, it’s no surprise that a woman rules it, with patriarchal logic being what it is. To some extent, all these stories are about male fear of women in general and of women with power in particular. Nepokoy is no exception: in Shmelkov’s film, that fear takes the form of Madam — mocking, loud, demanding, with a short “masculine” haircut.
If the hero in all such stories is symbolically held in the land of the dead, does that make the Rose the afterlife? Not quite: the clue is in the title. The Russian word nepokoy — literally the absence of pokoy, rest — is bound up with unquiet souls, the ones stuck between life and death. That is the oldest horror story there is, familiar to just about every culture. So the Rose appears to mark the border between two worlds, like Baba Yaga’s hut in Russian folktales (another of the film’s many sources). Madam, with her big nose, even looks like her. The Rose’s eccentric guests die off one by one because they are, in fact, already dead: at some point they’re simply let through. And you can pass, it seems, only by understanding something about yourself.
Yasha, at any rate, understands a great deal before he’s allowed to leave the hotel. He meets his own fear, for instance, at the very start of the film, when he spots his pursuers from the car window: mysterious runners. There’s a whole crowd of them, and they’re something like zombies — vicious, frenzied, nearly indistinguishable from one another apart from the numbers on their shirts.
In time it becomes clear that the runners, it seems, are a projection straight out of Yasha’s head: this is how he sees human society. Tellingly, he admits that he loves cars and hates buses — implying, of course, that in a car he picks his own fellow passengers. Only after living at the Rose does Yasha realize that he, too, is one of the runners in some sense.
Seconds before the closing credits, the audience learns for the first time what year — roughly — Yasha and Bernard arrived at the Rose. Shmelkov conceived Nepokoy quite some time ago, in 2019, but he must have settled on the final shot much later — and if he didn’t, one can only marvel at his foresight. A hint will do in a review: if the Rose really is a refuge for unquiet souls, it won’t be short of guests.
Fantastical as it is, Nepokoy conveys the present condition of many of its viewers more precisely than a social media feed does. Shmelkov’s film answers not only Nolan’s The Odyssey but another international box-office hit, Kane Parsons’s Backrooms.
The internet legend behind that film popularized the term “liminal space.” Online, it’s taken to mean an empty, sinister room, preferably windowless. In the humanities, “liminal” simply means transitional, in-between. The Rose fits that definition perfectly. Millions of people are living in liminal space today: between freedom and prison, between normalcy and catastrophe, and, in the end, between their own country and someone else’s.
One more thing. For all the differences between Nepokoy and the Andrei reels, the secret of their relevance is one and the same: Shmelkov is not only a tremendous animator but a brilliant voice actor.
There is no weighty philosophical dialogue in his feature, only ordinary speech — as though you were eavesdropping on a conversation aboard a commuter train. There’s nothing mystical in Madam’s voice, and Yasha talks like a man who’s never surprised by anything, or who is surprised but doesn’t let it show. Sure, a tiger in the hotel, unusual. Sure, the old man turned into a little pyramid, terrific, thanks for showing us, but we really do have to go. The Rose’s other residents are even harder to faze. Yesterday’s paranormal is today’s normal: adaptation is the most natural human quality there is. Nepokoy may be a surrealist film, but in a way it’s realist, with no prefix attached.

The airport problem passengers rarely see — until their flight is delayed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:41:15 UTC
04:41:15 KST

IN BRIEF
- Australia's air traffic control workforce is in the spotlight amid days of flight delays and a near collision at Sydney Airport.
- Experts say the job is highly specialised and requires years of experience to ensure public safety is not compromised.
On Tuesday, many Australians arrived at the airport with their plane waiting on the tarmac and clear skies overhead — only to discover their flight had been delayed.
Around 200 flights moving through Melbourne and Perth Airports were forecast to experience delays, according to a daily plan issued by Airservices Australia.
In Sydney, 138 flights were expected to be impacted by ground delays of around 43 minutes, in part due to strong winds, the government-owned air traffic management organisation said.
Rob Sharp, CEO of Airservices Australia, acknowledged that flight delays and disruptions can cause "very high frustration levels" for passengers, airlines and airport partners alike.
Behind the scenes, delays are often used to ensure public safety is not compromised during what Sharp described as a "challenging period" for air traffic controllers.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We do this through effectively putting space between aircraft. But it does come at a cost, and that cost is delays," Sharp said during a press conference on Monday.
His comments follow significant delays to flights on Friday and Saturday last week. On Sunday, two passenger jets also narrowly avoided a ground collision at Sydney Airport, with the incident now under investigation.
It's left industry leaders and aviation experts questioning whether Australia's air traffic control workforce can keep up with aviation demands.
Who's in control?
Uğur Turhan is a senior lecturer in aviation at the University of New South Wales in Canberra. He said controllers are responsible for air traffic safety and efficiency, both on the ground and in the air.
"You cannot put somebody as a high-performing air-traffic controller in one day or one year ... generally, we think that five years' experience is a really good level to perform at high levels in complex traffic situations," Turhan told SBS News.
There are three types of controllers — tower controllers, terminal controllers and en route controllers — responsible for various stages of flights including take-off, landing and airspace movement.
While training programs vary, typically air traffic controllers train for 12 months before undergoing additional on-the-job training.
Australian air services manage more than 51 million square kilometres of airspace, equivalent to approximately 11 per cent of the world's airspace. This area is managed 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, Airservices Australia said.
Federal Transport Minister Catherine King believes the work of air traffic controllers is a "really stressful and difficult job".
"If you've been in an air traffic control tower, you've seen the number of flights they are managing, the complexities in how quickly they have to think. It's a really specialised job."
She held emergency meetings in Canberra on Monday following recent flight disruptions. King described her discussion with Sharp from Airservices Australia as "constructive" and said she felt "confident" the organisation was doing "everything they can to get on top of this".
Staff shortages
National disruptions due to air traffic control have fallen by 86 per cent over the past financial year, according to Airservices Australia. Ground delays caused by air services also reduced by 13 per cent.
The air traffic industry has recorded an uptick in staffing, with a record 109 new controllers employed last year. Sharp told the ABC's 7.30 on Monday there were now more than 1,070 air traffic controllers in Australia.
There are an additional 15 people in training, expected to join the workforce by the end of 2027, King said in a press conference on Monday. Experienced air traffic controllers have also been hired from overseas to work in Australia.
Sharp said the sector has traditionally relied on high staff overtime, which he does not believe is a "sustainable model" as Australian airports expand. He said new rostering systems are likely to ease staff burdens from September this year.
Turhan acknowledged the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the aviation industry too.
"Globally, we had COVID-19. We lost some manpower capability in aviation, not just for air traffic controllers. As I said, it is not easy to put someone, with a high performance level in [the job in] just one year; it takes time."
Between October 2021 and December 2022, more than 180 air traffic controllers accepted voluntary redundancies, according to online information published by the Brisbane Flight Path Community Alliance.
Turhan believes Sydney Airport is a particularly challenging environment for new air traffic controllers. It requires workers to train for two years, plus an additional two years to embed into the system, according to Sharp from Airservices Australia.
"It has a really complex layout ... and also it is operated by different domestic and international terminals," Turhan said.
"In Sydney Airport ... you cannot operate your flights during the night. So, during that limited time you should perform all traffic in a short time and traffic levels are not homogeneously distributed to the time. So, we have peak traffic."
A global issue?
Air traffic control is a highly competitive field which can offer high pay. The base salary for an initial trainee air traffic controller begins at $60,000, which increases to more than $171,000 for a Level 5 controller. Workers at a Level 10 classification can earn over $243,000, and supervisors more than $286,000.
Angus Mitchell, the chief commissioner of the Australian Transport Safety Bureau, said it's also considered a specialised profession.
"Airports are incredibly busy. You've got planes taking off, planes landing, planes being manoeuvred across crossing runways, across taxiways. It is a complex environment, but it needs to also be incredibly robust," Mitchell told SBS News.
"Even at low speeds, there can be very significant outcomes if planes come into contact with each other."
This complexity has fuelled a global shortage in air traffic controllers.
In July 2025, United States transportation secretary Sean Duffy told Congress it would cost US$31.5 billion ($44.6 billion) to fully modernise the country's air traffic control system. That same year, the Federal Aviation Administration told US media it was facing a shortage of around 3,000 air traffic controllers.
In July 2026, Singapore announced new air traffic controller recruits would receive a sign-on bonus of SGD$20,000 (approximately $22,100), as Changi Airport is expanded.
Parts of Europe, including Athens Airport in Greece, have experienced flight delays amidst seasonal summer travel peaks.
However, Turhan cautioned against comparing Australia's situation directly with Europe.
"In Australia, we have really broad and wide airspace. We have a few big airports but they are busy, and they're handling different kinds of traffic levels."
He is optimistic that discussions about Australia's air traffic control sector could eventually lead to reduced workloads, improved working conditions and fatigue management.

Venezuela and Israel resume consular services after 17-year diplomatic break
Venezuela and Israel have agreed to re-establish consular services in each country, both governments said on Tuesday, a dramatic shift in the South American nation's geopolitical alignment after it broke ties with Israel in 2009.
Venezuela, which ended relations 17 years ago over Israeli attacks in the Gaza Strip, has strengthened ties with Israel-allied Washington since the US captured President Nicolas Maduro in January, pushing it away from its historic alignment with Iran.
Venezuela's government, now led by Interim President Delcy Rodriguez, said an Israeli humanitarian delegation visited the country after deadly earthquakes in June and discussions took place among senior officials from both nations, leading to the deal to resume consular services.

Iran for years has allied itself with Venezuela, a fellow global oil producer that had similarly suffered under years of US sanctions, and condemned Washington's recent intervention in Caracas.

I used ice every day at work to chase a dopamine hit. After 10 years, the charade had to stop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:40:55 UTC
04:40:55 KST

What do extreme sports, doomscrolling, addiction, Parkinson's disease, and ADHD all have in common? Dopamine. This crucial neurotransmitter helps facilitate reward, motivation, memory and movement within the body, but are its effects always beneficial? Watch Insight episode Chasing Dopamine on SBS On Demand.
Content warning: This article references drug use and addiction.
When I was 18 years old at a party, someone offered me ice (crystal meth), and I said yes as I was fresh out of a breakup and wanted to escape reality.
Before I knew it, 10 years had passed, and I no longer recognised the woman that stood in front of the mirror.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
There were a few factors that went into me making that decision that night.
I didn't really know who I was and placed all my worth in what other people thought about me. And I actively avoided rejection or confrontation, which meant I had no boundaries and never said no. I also had a high appetite for risk, because I thought it would make me look cool and be liked.
For the next 10 years, I would smoke amphetamines every single day — chasing dopamine and trying to regulate my emotions in an unhealthy way.
Dopamine is a neurotransmitter in the brain that contributes to our motivation, reward systems, and habit development. Dopamine is not itself addictive, but the associated substances, behaviours or activities that cause the brain to release dopamine can be.
I liken smoking ice to the dopamine centre of your brain lighting up like a Christmas tree. Your dopamine receptors are the lights, and it takes so much power to light the tree. But you need more and more of the drug to reach the feeling of your first high, to power the lights. And with regular drug use over time, the dopamine receptors start to die off, and your brain needs more drugs to feel the same high.
I experienced a full spectrum in that decade: The hard times would send me further into my addiction, and I'd try escape the reality I had created for myself.
The good times would make me believe I didn't need to change — that I could manage it all. I would still go to work, look after my health in other ways, study at university, pay my rent and maintained my relationships with family.
But all the while, I would sneak off into the toilets to smoke a pipe — just to feel normal.
Keeping something like that hidden for long periods of time is exhausting because you can never keep up the charade. Eventually, the walls start to crumble around you.
The cycle of being able to keep it all together was getting shorter and shorter.
Things would be going "well" but then something would happen, and there would be a crash; I'd become dysfunctional with periods of couch surfing, hotel hopping, unemployment and being in unhealthy relationships.
And then I would seem to get it together again and then be highly functioning again.
Until I wasn't.
A fateful decision
One day, eight years into my addiction, I found myself sitting in my unregistered car, with no phone, no money, no job and no licence, feeling desperate.
It was in this moment I realised how I could make money quickly and get myself some power back.
I went to my dealer's house and asked to sell drugs for them. It was a poor decision that would change my life forever, for better and for worse.
And the newfound agency I felt as a drug dealer soon landed me in custody several times for supply of a dangerous drug, and my longest stint behind bars was 10 months.
The first time I was in a cell was terrifying. They strip searched me and took my shoes, which meant I was barefoot on the cold concrete.
They handed me a blanket that made me itch just by looking at it, and my bed: three small square mats, which slid apart during the night and exposed my body to the cold concrete.
As I lay in the cell with my itchy blanket, I thought about how I had reached this point in my life. I also thought of nothing and slept.
You would think this would be the time I would try and get myself together — to finally be rid of the drugs.
But for me, being incarcerated only pushed me further into that life, because now I was a criminal with no hope for the bright future I once believed I was going to have.
Chasing sobriety
I had tried many times to stop using drugs before, but it never stuck.
The stints would usually last one or two months. I would move from the Gold Coast back home to Moreton Bay, Queensland, to be with my mum and dad, convinced that I was only using because of the people I hung with.
I needed to understand why I sought out that world if I was ever going to get a handle on my addiction.
Coming off ice looks different for everyone.
For me, I would just sleep and eat for weeks on end. When my body had finally detoxed the drugs, what was left was a shell of a human — devoid of life.
I felt empty, like someone had turned down the volume for colour in my world — like my capacity to enjoy anything had died.
It was a feeling I had become scared to face, and so I stopped trying to get sober and continued using.
Establishing a new path forward
It wasn't until 2018, when I was in custody for the last time that things really started to change.
When you're sitting in a cell that's two by four metres for 22 hours a day with nothing to do, you soon realise that you must look inwards and work on yourself to not land back in custody.
So, I met with an incredible therapist weekly who taught me all the thing I needed to understand so I could stop masking my head noise with drugs. This included my behaviour patterns and understanding how I showed up in the world.
I also attended a narcotics support group and learnt that your brain has pathways for behaviour. In my case, when I learned new pathways (as in new ways to handle certain emotions) my brain stops telling me that I need to use drugs.
It's an oversimplified explanation — but all I needed to hold onto to break free of that life.
These days, my life looks worlds away from the girl sneaking to the work toilets to smoke drugs.
I had heard that your dopamine receptors die when you use ice, so I went through a time where I didn't think I'd feel happy again.
But slowly and surely, all the feelings a healthy brain lets you experience returned. Learning to emotionally regulate and sit with emotions joy, sadness, excitement, and pain has kept me from going back to drugs.
And despite everything that happened to me in that decade, I hadn't cried once. Being able to cry again was an experience I'll never forget.
These days, my life looks worlds away from the girl sneaking to the work toilets to smoke drugs.
I have built an entirely new life that doesn't require me to run from anything or occupy myself with anything or replace the drug use with anything. I worked through it and addressed the reasons why I was using drugs. I just replaced it with life and living life.
I'm a mum, a wife, a criminologist, and a whole person who experiences a whole life.
I also founded an advocacy organisation supporting women to break their cycles of incarceration, which is my main work. Going back into women's prisons and helping them is now a much healthier dopamine hit for me.
My joy now also comes from hearing my kids laugh, soaking up the sunshine with friends at lunch, or watching the beautiful colours of a sunset.

Release
- Trump said Russia has released Gilman.
- According to Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin released Gilman on a humanitarian basis, without exchanging him for a Russian prisoner.

Requests for pardon
- On August 6, Reuters quoted a US official as saying that the Washington administration had asked Russia to release Gilman.

Health problems
- On July 6, Gilman’s lawyer Irina Brazhnikova told TASS that his trials had been suspended due to him being hospitalized for treatment.

The Gilman case
- Gilman was detained in 2022 at the Voronezh railway station after being involved in a drunken brawl on the Sukhum-Moscow train.

- The court sentenced him to 4.5 years in a general regime penal colony, and in 2023 his sentence was reduced by one year.

- In 2024, Gilman was sentenced to seven years and one month of imprisonment in a high-security penal colony and a fine of 300,000 rubles ($3,660). In April 2025, the sentence was increased by one year.
- At the end of 2025, the Central District Court of Voronezh handed down another verdict to Gilman, who was accused of two counts of using force against employees of the Federal Penitentiary Service.
- Thus, on May 5 of the same year, Gilman attacked an employee of the Federal Penitentiary Service in protest of being sent to a penal colony from the pre-trial detention center.
- Despite the attempt to attack a pre-trial detention center employee, the next day he was transferred to a correctional colony. Gilman again attacked an employee of the Federal Penitentiary Service.
- Two more years of penal colony were added to his previously appointed term of imprisonment.
- In early July, Gilman's court proceedings in Voronezh were suspended because he was hospitalized.

It also warned that illegal settlers are increasingly using “archaeology and heritage claims” to justify the expansion of the occupation.
The United Kingdom expressed opposition to the reintroduction of the “E1” settlement project, which aims to bisect the occupied West Bank. Pakistan added that the “Crimson Thread” project is part of a broader effort to shatter Palestinian territorial contiguity.
France welcomed the PA’s upcoming legislative and presidential elections, while Russia argued that the American peace plan has “essentially stalled”. It noted a tragic toll, stating that, on average, one child has been killed in Gaza per day by Israeli forces over the last 300 days.
Liberia issued a stark warning that the council is presiding over the “slow-motion disappearance” of the two-state solution rather than enforcing it.

Staged vote with no real opposition
“[Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s plan is not particularly complicated,” Zelensky said.

Zelensky said the vote itself is part of the mobilization strategy.

As public fatigue grows and Russia’s economy continues to strain under war spending, a second, direct mobilization would carry heightened political risks for Putin.
Instead, Russia has increasingly relied on fraudulent recruitment schemes to draw in foreign fighters, particularly from third countries such as Colombia, Peru, and Bolivia – all with promises of well-paid civilian jobs, such as construction work or factory labor.

However, he did not disclose further details on what those measures would involve.
A broader pattern of Russia’s suppression
The move against Yabloko fits into Russia’s broader pattern of systematically suppressing progressive and liberal voices it associates with Western values.
Moscow has similarly promoted residency programs for foreigners who explicitly reject Western values and progressive social norms by issuing a “traditional values” visa scheme, framing itself as a refuge for those “under pressure” in liberal democracies.
Russia also continues to target its openly anti-war nationals, even those who remain in exile.
Yabloko’s removal from the upcoming elections, therefore, does not come as a surprise.

Meta and TikTok fail to halt thousands of social media addiction lawsuits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:23:20 UTC
04:23:20 KST

Meta and TikTok fail to halt thousands of social media addiction lawsuits
Thousands of lawsuits accusing major social media companies of fueling addiction and harming young users can move forward in the US after a federal appeals court rejected an attempt to halt the litigation.
The San Francisco-based Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed appeals by Meta and TikTok on Monday against earlier rulings that allowed more than 3,000 federal cases to proceed.
The companies sought to challenge the cases under Section 230, a US law that protects online platforms from some claims involving content posted by users.
The appeals court ruled that they could not use the law to stop the cases from moving forward at this stage, saying Section 230 “merely provides a defense to liability – not immunity from suit.” The ruling does not determine whether Meta, TikTok, and other companies are responsible for the alleged harms.
The lawsuits target Meta, Google, TikTok, Snap, and other companies and have been brought by individuals, school districts, US states, and local authorities. They accuse the platforms of using features designed to keep children and teenagers engaged, allegedly contributing to addiction, depression, anxiety, and other problems.
The court also rejected Meta’s bid to delay a separate case brought by 29 US state attorneys general. Jury selection is due to begin Wednesday, with the states accusing the company of improperly collecting children’s data, using features designed to keep young users engaged, and misleading consumers about the safety of its platforms. Meta denies the allegations.
The decision follows another setback for the industry in March, when a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google negligent in the first social media addiction case to reach a verdict. It awarded $6 million to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child. Both companies denied wrongdoing and have challenged the verdict.
The legal battles come as governments around the world tighten rules on children’s access to social media amid concerns over addictive features, harmful content, and weak age checks.
Last December, Australia became the first country to require major social media platforms to prevent people under 16 from holding accounts. Indonesia and Malaysia have since introduced restrictions for under-16s, and Britain has announced its own ban for next year. France has restricted access for children under 15, and the measure is due to take effect in September pending a constitutional review.
