Al Jazeera was not able to independently confirm the validity of the report.
In July, California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced that he was leading a coalition of 12 state attorneys general in an antitrust lawsuit to block the consolidation.
Should Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery combine, Bonta warned that the resulting company would control 27 percent of theatrically released films in the United States and a third of the country’s basic-cable output.
“Consolidation here not only leads to higher prices,” Bonta said. “It also leads to fewer opportunities for important stories to come to life, and fewer ways for audiences to encounter stories, ideas, and perspectives beyond their own experiences.”
But Variety reported that Ellison told Paramount’s senior executives that he would begin the process of moving the company out of California on October 1 if Bonta does not agree to settlement talks.
There could be downstream effects as well. The report also alleged that Ellison would pull Warner Bros Discovery out of California, too, if the $110bn merger goes through.
Variety indicated that Paramount is considering relocating to the US states of Tennessee, Texas or Georgia — none of which are involved in the ongoing antitrust lawsuit.
A growing enterprise
The dispute over Warner Bros Discovery’s fate stretches back to late 2025, when the company’s sale was first announced.
Critics quickly observed that the sale had the potential to shift the balance of power in Hollywood, with Warner Bros Discovery wielding influential properties including the news channel CNN, the production company New Line Cinema and the television-streaming service HBO.
The streaming giant Netflix initially emerged as a frontrunner to take over Warner Bros Discovery, but by February, Paramount succeeded in inking an agreement.
It was the second major merger Paramount had lined up in less than a year. In 2025, it had also succeeded in consolidating with the media production company Skydance, in a deal that generated scrutiny about the editorial independence of its subsidiaries.
Paramount’s decisions that year to cancel The Late Show with Stephen Colbert and enter into a $16m settlement with US President Donald Trump were widely perceived as efforts to curry government favour for the merger.
Paramount is considered a titan in US filmmaking and media production, as one of the oldest studios in the country. Its portfolio includes CBS News and Paramount Pictures.
A pair of lawsuits
The impending merger with Warner Bros Discovery has led to a fresh round of scrutiny for Ellison and the Paramount leadership.
Last week, Ellison addressed some of those concerns in an opinion column in The New York Times.
In it, he questioned whether the states’ antitrust lawsuit was “really about market share”, speculating that it was instead about control over major news outlets like CNN. He also sought to portray himself as politically independent.
“I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties; I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans,” Ellison wrote.
“When it comes to our news operations, I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views.”
But the states have argued that combining Warner Bros Discovery and Paramount would create a monopoly, stifling competition.
If the merger succeeds, the states say that only four distributors would control 86 percent of the country’s films.
The merger could also mean job losses. As of the end of 2025, the headcount at Paramount stood at 17,600, while Warner Bros Discovery had 35,500 employees.
A day after the 12 states filed their lawsuit, the Writers Guild of America (WGA) followed suit.
In its July 14 complaint, the guild argued that the merger would mean fewer jobs and more pressure on writers to accept less favourable working terms, owing to reduced competition in the media market.
“Writers will be paid less and have fewer employment opportunities,” the WGA complaint said.
In Los Angeles County alone, the merger could result in a loss of nearly 2,500 jobs, according to an analysis by the Los Angeles County Department of Economic Opportunity, published in June.
As many as 6,000 employees around the world could also see their positions cut.
By comparison, when the Paramount and Skydance merger was completed in 2025, the company laid off roughly 2,000 people.
Costly standoff
On July 24, Paramount Skydance agreed to pause the merger until a ruling in the states’ case is ultimately made or until June 1, 2027 — a move the WGA celebrated.
“It remains our view that this merger is unlawful, and we will continue the fight to block it,” WGA said at the time.
The WGA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Slowing the merger could be costly for Paramount Skydance. Under the terms of the merger, the company would have to pay a so-called ticking fee of $7m per day, or $650m per quarter, if the deal does not close by September 30.
But the standoff with Ellison could also be costly for California, which is experiencing a downturn in the number of productions filmed in the state. New York, another state involved in the lawsuit, could see a backlash, as it houses studios for CBS News and Paramount’s executive offices.
Representatives for the state of California and Paramount Skydance did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Paramount Skydance’s stock is trending upward on the heels of Tuesday’s report. The stock was up 0.4 percent in midday trading, while Warner Bros Discovery was up 1.1 percent.

Fire is both friend and foe for Australia's wildflowers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Fire is a friend and foe for Australian wildflowers. Climate change is shifting the balance
Crouched on the sandy soils of an urban bushland in Perth, ecologist Mark Brundrett points out a herd of green elephant ears.
The "ears" are a flush of fleshy little leaves, firmly attached to the ground, belonging to the red beak orchid (Pyrorchis nigricans).
The plant's Greek genus name, Pyrorchis, translates to "fire orchid". Its red and white flowers appear most often after a bushfire when its seeds can spread on the wind to new areas.
But when it goes without fire for a long time, the orchid clones itself — by making several new underground tubers from each leaf annually — with individuals known to spread out some 30 metres wide.
"There's a paradox in this orchid," says Dr Brundrett, an adjunct associate professor with the University of Western Austalia.
"This orchid needs fire to reproduce by seed, but it's harmed by fire when it wants to develop a large healthy colony."
So while fire makes the orchid flower, flames may also reduce the size of the plant or wipe it out completely if it is too intense or frequent.
In this particular patch of Warwick Bushland — a 63 hectare site of mixed jarrah and banksia woodland — the red beak orchids haven't been hit by a fire for three decades.
"If [the plant is] the same individual, it could be thousands of years old," Dr Brundrett says.
That contrasts with more frequently burnt parts of the small bushlands where there are smaller patches of red beak orchids with fewer tubers.
It's just one of the complex relationships between 17 different orchid species and fire that Dr Brundrett is studying in the small bushland.
"Some orchids are very tolerant of fire and some even benefit from it because they flower more," he says.
"But the downside is that there's more orchids that are harmed by fire than benefit from it."
Orchids are just one of many Australian plant groups and species that have evolved over millions of years to adapt to fires.
But the way that fire moves in the landscape is rapidly changing, so the question is whether strategies used by flowers in the past to survive will work in the future.
The threat from fire
Large bushfires in Australia, and globally, are thought to be getting more intense. Firefighters say they're also running hotter at night than in the past.
In the past six years there have been huge fires which have torn through entire national parks and beyond in one go.
For example, the 2019–20 Black Summer bushfires burnt more than 24 million hectares of land and half the ranges of about 800 different flora species. About 150 of these species had most of their range burn.
Many of these species are resilient to fire and some even rely on it.
After Black Summer, large drifts of flannel flowers (Actinotus sp) — one of Science Week's top 10 amazing wildflowers — sprang up en masse in the Sydney region.
Pink flannel flowers (A. forsythii), which rely on smoke to trigger growth, are among a group of plants known as fire ephemerals.
They follow the "live fast, die young" motto by trying to grow quickly and generate more seed that is stored in the soil for the next fire event.
The seeds of fire ephemerals are thought to be able to last for decades, if not a century, between fires. That means that sometimes, new species are found after fires in long-unburnt areas.
But scientists are concerned about other flower species that don't get enough time to recover before the next blaze comes through.
The long slender red and yellow flowers of the Christmas Bell ( Blandfordia sp) also appeared after Black Summer in the east.
Studies of B. grandiflora at a site near Port Macquarie, show flowering peaked after the second fire season, regardless of how often fires occur.
But it takes three years for the plant to develop from seed to flower, so fires more often than this may be detrimental to the species.
Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria seed scientist Rebecca Miller says there is a delicate balance in Australian ecosystems.
"With climate change, there's a shift in terms of the frequency and intensity and probably extent and scale of fires," she says.
"Which is problematic when you're working with threatened species that might have really restricted distributions and narrow ranges."
When fires take out big areas in one go, they can wipe out seed stock in the soil and put pressure on flora species that might only occur in a few areas.
"Things adapted to fire, whether they're regenerating from seed or whether they're re-sprouting from lignotubers or other storage structures within the plant, need time to regrow or grow to a reproductive stage,"
Unlike the red beak orchid and the Christmas bell which have lignotubers, some Australian flowering plants, such as alpine ash and many banksia species such as the mountain banksia (Banksia canei), have no fallback strategy for fire.
These plants, known as obligate seeders, rely on fire and can only regenerate from seed.
"So that if the frequency is too high, then they may not have reached that point and there may not be those seeds there to support regeneration after the next fire."
Off the back of the Black Summer, scientists analysed the threat of changing fire regimes to native species for the federal government.
Threatened species commissioner Fiona Fraser says climate-induced changes to fire intensity and frequency was one of the most pervasive threats to native animals and plants.
"In the period from September 2020 to February 2026, 80 bushfire affected plants have been listed as threatened under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, and 39 have been uplisted — changed to a higher category of extinction risk," Dr Fraser says.
"The Australian government is investing $800 million in the recovery of threatened species and ecological communities.
"This includes action to manage fire regimes and help build species resilience."
Seed collecting is no easy affair
Dr Miller's team tries to collect seeds, many from rare or threatened Victorian species, which can be used to grow new populations or supplement existing ones after fire.
While seed from some species may last hundreds of years in storage, Dr Miller says others lose viability after 10 to 15 years.
"We need to up our research into that area to understand the frequency or how quickly we need to use our collections and the frequency with which we may need to recollect," she says.
"We've got collections from over 1,500 species now."
Collecting itself can be tricky.
"Often they're in remote and quite inaccessible areas, they produce seed erratically, the timing of that seed production might be unpredictable and vary from year to year," Dr Miller says.
"So the resourcing for collection is problematic because it does take multiple visits for many of these species."
Dr Miller says inevitably, and unfortunately, there is picking and choosing when it comes to how the team prioritises species for collecting.
But there are a lot of significant successes.
One of the current programs at the RBGV, funded by the Victorian government, targets conservation for 24 species, including the rare rosella spider orchid.
"For eight of them, we're about to translocate populations and establish new populations, essentially, in the world for those," Dr Miller says.
"So that's come from seed collecting and germination trials, genetic research into the populations, extensive surveys of the populations, and identifying pollinators so that we know that we're establishing populations in areas where the pollinators exist."
What else can be done?
More baseline research is essential to preserve flower species.
Dr Brundrett says monitoring is necessary for adaptive approaches to managing threats like fire.
"But we need that for everything, we need it for the birds and the animals and the native plants," he said.
He also says we need to know more about other climate factors for species like orchids, like rainfall.
"The growing seasons [in south west WA] are shortening from both ends," Dr Brundrett says.
"I think we should be setting up what I call orchid climate observatories where anyone can just observe orchids in a particular area and … what that tells you is basically what's happening."
And he has one other suggestion.
"Ironically, possibly the way to protect them [orchids] is to do some small fuel reduction burns around them."

Adel Abdelrheem and Mohammad Sio

About 2,500 people were displaced from Geisan in Sudan’s Blue Nile state after clashes broke out in the town Tuesday, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
The IOM said field teams, working under its Displacement Tracking Matrix initiative, estimated that 500 families fled Geisan because of deteriorating security conditions.
Most have moved to other locations within the Geisan area, while others crossed the border into Ethiopia, it said.
The agency said the situation remained “tense and volatile” and that teams were closely monitoring developments on the ground.
Geisan authorities said earlier Tuesday that the army had repelled an attack on the town by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and their ally, the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North.

On July 10, the army said it had repelled an attack on the areas of Dim Saad and Yara in the Geisan district.
The army controls large parts of Blue Nile state, while the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North has been fighting the Sudanese government since 2011, seeking autonomy for the South Kordofan and Blue Nile regions.
The army and RSF have been at war since April 2023 over disagreements about integrating the paramilitary force into the military. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced 13 million and plunged the country into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

While Germany has not yet suffered the widespread production outages experienced during previous Rhine crises, traders said on Aug 11 that it was no longer possible to book some cargo shipments after weeks of drought and companies are increasingly reporting operational issues.
Chemicals company Covestro said the lack of transport capacity could not be offset fully despite shifting volumes to trucks and trains wherever possible and it has declared force majeure for products including polyether polyols used in mattresses and refrigerator insulation.
Companies face higher freight costs
The Rhine is one of Europe’s main arteries for transporting grains, fuels, minerals and manufactured goods, but its shallow waters are increasingly leaving companies facing higher freight costs and a lack of suitable alternatives.
“Alarm bells are ringing loudly: the extremely low water levels are increasingly pushing logistics and supply chains to their limits,” Wolfgang Grosse Entrup, chief executive officer of German chemical industry association VCI, told Reuters.
Production at rival Evonik’s Marl chemical park has been hampered by reduced cargoes, it said without disclosing further details.
State-owned utility Uniper, meanwhile, pointed to lower output at its German hydroelectric plants, chiming with similar comments from local rival EnBW last week.
Salzgitter, Germany’s second-largest steelmaker, said that the low Rhine levels had forced it to transport coal via train from Rotterdam to its HKM division.
“The current situation shows that we need to pay greater attention to waterways as part of our critical transport infrastructure,” Tim-Oliver Mueller, head of the German Construction Industry Federation, told Reuters.
“Low water levels cannot be prevented.”
He said certain construction materials could not easily be transported by road or rail because of capacity shortages and high volumes, with up to 150 trucks needed to replace a single barge.
At German agricultural trader RWZ, company executive Katharina Stelzer described the prospect of Rhine levels falling further as “catastrophic”.
Stelzer said that in normal years, the company usually shipped 50,000 metric tonnes or more from its water terminals in the German cities of Worms and Andernach in the months of July and August.
She said that RWZ has not even shipped 10 per cent of that volume in the comparable period this year and was switching to more expensive truck transport.
“If Rhine levels do not recover in October, things will get really challenging for us,” she said. REUTERS

UN warns Colombia earthquake toll could rise as remote areas remain unassessed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:24:04 UTC
03:24:04 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
The humanitarian effects of a powerful earthquake in Colombia could be significantly greater than currently reported as emergency teams have yet to fully assess remote and conflict-affected areas, the UN’s resident coordinator in the country warned Tuesday.
Maria Jose Torres Macho said the 7.4-magnitude earthquake, whose epicenter was in the Pacific region of Choco, has affected 14 of Colombia’s 32 departments.
“Everything that I’m reporting right now is going to be evolving as we speak, and we are constantly updating,” Torres Macho said at a UN briefing.
She said the effect of the earthquake was “bigger than they were expecting,” while noting that authorities have more information about damage in major cities than in rural and remote areas.
“We don’t know exactly what is the impact in the rural, remote areas,” she said. “There might be much more to report and to respond to.”
Search and rescue operations remain the priority, while humanitarian agencies are preparing assistance focused on temporary shelter, health, food security and protection.
Torres Macho said Choco and Valle del Cauca, including Cali, were among areas receiving humanitarian support.
She also said the UN is using remote-sensing technology to assess structural and socioeconomic damage, and is deploying additional staff from Bogota to affected regions.
“We have been invited by the national authorities to complement the national response,” she said, adding that existing resources are being realigned while additional humanitarian funding is being considered.
UN spokesman Farhan Haq said assessments were continuing and authorities reported thousands of injuries, with the death toll continuing to rise.
“Initial reports indicate that 12 departments have been impacted by the earthquake, with thousands of homes damaged and hundreds destroyed,” Haq told reporters.
Health and education facilities, as well as roads and airports, have also been affected, he said.
The government is leading and coordinating the response, while shelter, food, safe drinking water and health care are among the most urgent needs, according to Haq.
The World Food Program (WFP) is monitoring the situation and remains in contact with national authorities and humanitarian partners as assessments continue, he said.
Following a request from the government for international assistance, WFP has begun mobilizing support and stands ready to provide food assistance and cash-based response mechanisms to affected populations.
WFP said nearly 4,500 metric tons of food are available through pre-positioned stocks in Colombia, located close enough to affected areas to enable a rapid response if needed, according to Haq.

The Advisory Board for this fall’s COP31 UN climate change conference held its first online meeting Tuesday under Türkiye’s environment, urbanization, and climate change minister.
Speaking at the meeting, Murat Kurum – who also serves as COP31 president – presented Türkiye's vision for this year’s conference to focus on implementation, for action to replace rhetoric, and highlighted the 10-point COP31 Action Agenda and six global implementation goals.
Kurum also briefed participants on the diplomatic efforts carried out by the COP31 Presidency to date, saying negotiations will continue with the aim of holding a conference this November that leaves no one behind.

He said this year’s conference expects the participation of experts from around the world, adding that the board outlined the preparations, vision, and goals for COP31 during its online meeting.
"We will not leave COP31 as merely a conference; through common wisdom, dialogue, consensus and action, we will make it a key to the global fight against climate change," he added.
According to a ministry statement, the Advisory Board was established as part of preparations for COP31, which Türkiye will host in the southern city of Antalya on Nov. 9-20, bringing together senior officials and experts working on climate change from around the world.

Vikings pick Kyler Murray as their starting quarterback over J.J. McCarthy, AP source says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:23:02 UTC
03:23:02 KST

Vikings pick Murray as their starting QB over McCarthy, giving him the rest of camp to get ready
EAGAN, Minn. (AP) — The Minnesota Vikings have chosen Kyler Murray as their starting quarterback over J.J. McCarthy, the widely expected conclusion to what coach Kevin O’Connell pledged was a true competition.
O’Connell made the announcement before practice on Tuesday afternoon, giving Murray a full month of full-time repetitions with the first-team offense before the regular season begins on Sept. 13. O’Connell and general manager Nolan Teasley met with both players in the morning to discuss the decision.
“I didn’t come in here expecting to be handed the job or anything like that. I just expected to come here and compete,” Murray said after practice. “I’m very appreciative of how it was handled.”
With 87 starts over seven years in the NFL with the Arizona Cardinals, two Pro Bowl selections and a unique elusiveness that has fueled 3,193 career rushing yards, Murray was going to have to either get hurt or badly struggle with his grasp of O’Connell’s offense for McCarthy to keep the job.
An earlier end to the audition was always going to be ideal for Murray, too, in the familiarization process with a layered playbook that asks more of the quarterback than most teams in the league.
Based purely on performance in open-to-the-public practices, this depth chart battle was more even than not. But the Vikings have clearly been cognizant of the downside to splitting turns considering the value to Murray of maximizing his preseason time running the offense.
“It’s just the appropriate time now to allow our team and everybody clarity for exactly the direction we’re moving going forward,” O’Connell said.
Murray, who signed a one-year contract with the Vikings for the veteran minimum salary, will be the fourth starting quarterback in four season openers following McCarthy, Sam Darnold and Kirk Cousins.
“There’s moments in time where you know there’s comfort from Kyler in the scheme. He had some really high completion days where he was able to show some really, really good understanding of just putting the ball in play, playing with great timing, rhythm,” O’Connell said. “You guys have seen him be explosive when there’s opportunities there, but you’ve also seen him check the ball down and put the ball in play and get us from a first-and-10 to a second-and-3. And then, as you continued to look at the body of work through those 10 days, what jumped out is what could be.”
Both Murray and McCarthy will play in the first exhibition game on Saturday against the New York Giants, O’Connell said. McCarthy will be the second stringer, followed by Carson Wentz, who started five games last season while McCarthy was injured. Max Brosmer, who made two starts, is the other quarterback in camp.
McCarthy, who was not immediately made available for comment, was the 10th overall pick in the 2024 draft. He tore the meniscus in his right knee during the first exhibition game and underwent surgery that kept him sidelined for his entire rookie year while Darnold helped the Vikings rack up 14 wins.
After Darnold departed as a free agent for the eventual Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks, McCarthy inherited the job without any legitimate competition and struggled as a variety of injuries limited him to 10 starts.
“Look, he’s a young player with a whole bunch of outstanding things in his future,” O’Connell said, adding: “I know he’s going to continue to improve, and the long-term mindset of him as a Minnesota Viking and all the things that he’s brought here is still absolutely part of the long-term vision for sure. I’m excited to see him go do that and get to do it with him.”

Man charged with bomb threat against US consulate in Canada
The incident in Halifax, Nova Scotia, has heightened concern around US diplomatic security in Canada after recent Toronto shootings
Canadian police on Tuesday charged a man with making a bomb threat against the US consulate in Halifax, the latest security incident involving an American diplomatic post in Canada after two shootings at the US consulate in Toronto this year.
Several streets downtown were evacuated after Halifax Regional Police found a car linked to the suspect, Ali Assakereh, parked near the consulate on Monday morning. The vehicle contained a propane tank and containers believed to hold flammable liquids, police said
Police said Assakereh, 54, was scheduled to appear in provincial court on charges of uttering threats and public mischief. They said they learned of the threat on Sunday night.
An explosives expert later determined the items in the vehicle posed no threat to public safety, and the evacuation was lifted Monday afternoon.
A spokesperson for the US embassy in Ottawa said on Monday that US officials would not comment on a security matter while the police investigation was continuing.
The Halifax case follows two shootings this year at the US consulate in Toronto, Canada’s largest city.

Rights groups launch new legal challenge to Trump campaign against ICC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:18:44 UTC
03:18:44 KST

Rights groups launch new legal challenge to Trump campaign against ICC
Prominent organisation charge sanctions against international tribunal trample consitutional rights, hinder their work.
Four leading human rights groups have launched a new lawsuit against the Trump administration’s campaign against the International Criminal Court.
The new lawsuit filed on Tuesday charges that the administration’s wide-ranging sanctions against the international tribunal and organisations that cooperate with it risk treading on the constitutional rights of US citizens and groups. It adds to several previous legal challenges making similar claims.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Netanyahu vows to go to New York City despite ICC arrest warrant, Mamdani
- list 2 of 3Chad to join raft of withdrawals from International Criminal Court
- list 3 of 3What drove Venezuela’s decision to leave the ICC?
The four US-based groups – The American Friends Service Committee, the Centre for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch, and the Open Society Institute – charge the sanctions “force them to curtail a wide range of human rights and legal work”. That, in turn, violates their constitutional rights, including their freedom of speech and their right to due process.
The lawsuit further charges that Trump has exceeded his presidential authority “based on a pseudo ‘national emergency’ that has no basis in fact”, according to a Human Rights Watch statement.
“The US government’s efforts to dismantle the ICC and punish people seeking justice for grave human rights violations harm far more than the individuals and groups facing sanctions. It is an affront to all victims and survivors of war crimes and genocide,” said Joyce Ajlouny, general-secretary of the American Friends Service Committee.
“This executive order seeks to intimidate human rights defenders and deter people of conscience from advocating for the rights and dignity of others. We are joining this lawsuit because we refuse to stay silent when the pursuit of justice is criminalised.”
Trump escalated his approach towards the ICC upon taking office last year, issuing a sweeping executive order in February 2025 that authorised sanctions against the court’s prosecutors, judges and other officials, as well as individuals or groups that support the court’s investigations.
The executive order specifically cited the court’s issuance of arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for war crimes committed in Gaza, as well as an ongoing investigation into possible abuses committed by foreign forces in Afghanistan, including US military and intelligence personnel.
Since then, several ICC judges and prosecutors have been sanctioned by the US, along with an array of Palestinian rights groups that provided evidence to the court. It also sanctioned UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese.
Beyond the earlier lawsuit filed by the Washington, DC-based DAWN rights organisation and the Taxpayers Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG), ICC judges and Albanese’s family had previously sued the Trump administration in response to the sanctions, which included travel bans and restrictions on assets in the US.
Last month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio promised to increase the US pressure campaign to “disable” the ICC, accusing the court of “waging a war against our country, not with bullets or missiles, but with statutes, compacts, and the force of so-called international law”.
He pledged to increase “scrutiny” of how countries that receive US assistance approach the court and increase penalties on officials. At least one member state, Chad, cited pressure from Washington in recently announcing its withdrawal from the court.
International law experts have called the timing of the announcement perplexing, noting that, beyond the long-stalled Afghanistan investigation, no US citizens are known to currently be the subject of any investigations by the court. No US citizen has ever been prosecuted by the ICC.
The US is not a signatory to the ICC’s founding charter, the Rome Statute, and is therefore not subject to the court’s jurisdiction, although abuses committed on the territory of member states can be probed and potentially prosecuted.
Federal judges in Maine and New York ruled last year that Trump’s ICC executive order violated the constitutional rights of individual advocates and academics who provide expertise to the court.
In the latest lawsuit, the four human rights groups said the sanctions had stopped them “from continuing or undertaking activities like representing victims of war crimes as legal counsel, making legal and policy submissions to the ICC, and collaborating with the sanctioned Palestinian human rights groups to undertake litigation, coordinate advocacy campaigns, research human rights violations, or provide humanitarian aid”.
It noted that, due to the dominance of US financial and technological companies, sanctions are also chilling organisations that do not operate in the US.
“These sanctions are an assault on the rule of law, independent judges and prosecutors, and civil society in the United States and around the world,” James Goldston, executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, said in a statement.
“They betray historic US leadership in the cause of international justice and are a slap in the face to victims and survivors of grave crimes everywhere who depend on the ICC as a court of last resort.”

Sergey Nedovodin, St. Petersburg radio founder, dies at 61 after being beaten outside his Moscow home
Sergey Nedovodin, a founder and former executive director of the radio station Ekho Peterburga, has died at 61, the station’s Telegram channel reported.
Nedovodin had been in intensive care and unconscious since late June, the news outlet Rotonda said. He was hospitalized after being beaten in the Moscow region, where he had recently moved. His wife, Anna Shefner, said that on the evening of June 23, Nedovodin went outside after hearing a drunk neighbor loudly discussing something with a friend below his window, and reprimanded them. The neighbor and his friend then beat him. According to Nedovodin’s former colleague Anastasia Mironova, one of the neighbors identified himself as a “participant in the special military operation” — Russia’s term for its war in Ukraine.
“His condition is extremely serious. There are no prognoses at all. He has a bunch of complications: sepsis, a lung abscess. He hasn’t regained consciousness the entire time,” Shefner said of her husband’s condition in early August.
Shefner filed a police report, but as of August 7, no criminal case had been opened over the beating. Mironova, however, claims that a case has since been opened.
Nedovodin helped launch Ekho Peterburga in 1998. In the 2010s, he was a founder, minority shareholder, and executive director of the station and, for a time, also ran its website, according to the independent Telegram channel Astra. He left the station’s management in 2015 after a conflict with the now-shuttered independent Russian radio station Ekho Moskvy. In recent years, Nedovodin headed the research company SMR and the Living Future foundation, which, Rotonda reports, organizes patriotic events and cooperates with Russia’s Defense Ministry.

Lebanon becomes first Arab country to abolish death penalty as Hezbollah votes no
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:17:14 UTC
03:17:14 KST

Lebanon’s parliament voted Tuesday to abolish the death penalty, making the country the first in the Arab world to formally eliminate capital punishment.
Under the newly approved law, death sentences will be replaced with life imprisonment accompanied by hard labor.
Lebanon had effectively maintained a moratorium on executions since 2004, but the death penalty remained on the books and continued to be handed down in dozens of cases over the years. Those sentences were either not carried out or were later commuted.
Most members of Lebanon’s 128-seat parliament backed the measure. Hezbollah’s parliamentary bloc was the only faction to vote against it.
Lebanese Justice Minister Adel Nassar called the approval “a historic step.”
Human rights organizations, which had long urged Lebanon to turn its de facto moratorium into full abolition, also welcomed the vote.
Ramzi Kaiss, a Lebanon researcher at Human Rights Watch, said the move marked “a definitive break with a cruel punishment that should never have been imposed.”
“The death penalty is uniquely cruel and irreversible, and it is riddled with arbitrariness, bias and error,” he said.
However, questions remain over how the replacement sentence of aggravated hard labor will be implemented.
Lebanese law already allows courts to impose hard labor, but the punishment has rarely been carried out in recent years, in part because of limited resources and capacity in the country’s overcrowded prisons amid Lebanon’s continuing economic difficulties.
The abolition comes as parliament is also debating a controversial general amnesty bill, the broadest such measure since the end of Lebanon’s 15-year civil war in 1990.
The proposed amnesty could reduce sentences or lead to early release for convicted militants and drug traffickers, with several exceptions.
Relatives of Lebanese soldiers and members of the security forces who were killed or attacked by Islamist groups have repeatedly protested against the proposed legislation. Some have said they had hoped to see those responsible for killing their relatives executed rather than receive reduced prison terms.
Hezbollah did not immediately issue a formal response to the historic vote. Lebanon’s various religious institutions, some of whose court systems permit capital punishment, also did not immediately comment.
Hezbollah explained its opposition by arguing that the death penalty should not be abolished before lawmakers complete work on the general amnesty bill.
The group said that under the sequence currently proposed, some prisoners sentenced to death could effectively benefit twice: first by having their death sentences commuted to 28 years in prison, and then by seeing those terms reduced further, potentially to 17 years, under the amnesty law.
Hezbollah argues that such a sentence would be far too lenient for people convicted of attacks against its members who, in its view, should face much harsher punishment.

The son of ‘Orthodox oligarch’ Igor Altushkin (who funds Russian churches and a battalion in Ukraine) crashed the family Lamborghini into a house in Yekaterinburg, injuring a combat veteran
A purple Lamborghini crashed into a house at 1 Otradnaya Street in Yekaterinburg on the evening of August 11, according to news outlet E1.ru and the Telegram channel “Baza,” which has ties to Russia’s security services.
Paramedics and police arrived at the scene. Footage shows the sports car striking several scooters, though it’s unclear whether anyone was riding them at the time of the crash.
The Lamborghini belongs to Ural businessman Igor Altushkin, owner of the Russian Copper Company, according to media reports. His son, David, was behind the wheel and was injured.
Traffic police in the Sverdlovsk region said the driver lost control of the vehicle, injuring one pedestrian. The car has 16 speeding tickets on record, Mash reported.
“Baza” said two men were injured sitting on the porch when the sports car crashed into the house. One of them, who had recently returned from the war in Ukraine and was walking with crutches, suffered multiple fractures and a closed traumatic brain injury.
Timur Khalilov, 23, a former professional boxer, was also injured in a crash, the Telegram channel Ostorozhno, Novosti reported. Khalilov was arrested in the spring of 2025 on charges of kidnapping a resident of Samara. By the time of his arrest, according to the outlet, he had already signed a contract with Russia’s Ministry of Defense.
Altushkin has been called an “Orthodox oligarch” — he financed the construction and restoration of churches in the Sverdlovsk region and regularly donated expensive icons to the Russian Orthodox Church. In 2019, his attempt to build a church on the site of a park in Yekaterinburg sparked a wave of protests among local residents.
Forbes Russia estimates Altushkin’s fortune at $4.9 billion. The Moscow Times, an independent Russian news outlet, reported that he sponsors the “Ural” battalion — an assault unit of Russia’s Defense Ministry fighting in Ukraine’s Luhansk region.
Altushkin’s wife and one of his sons hold British citizenship, and the family owns a mansion and several apartments in London, according to data from the independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta.

Germany has delivered a €5.7 million ($6.6 million) package of firefighting equipment to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service, including robotic systems designed to operate in conditions deemed too dangerous for emergency personnel.
The German Embassy in Ukraine confirmed the handover to European Pravda on Tuesday, Aug. 11, detailing a shipment that combines remote-controlled systems with traditional emergency vehicles.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Amid Russia’s brutal war, the challenges facing Ukraine’s State Emergency Service have become even more difficult,” Katrin Buchholz, Germany’s Chargé d’Affaires, told European Pravda.
Robotic systems built for danger zones
The package centers on four robotic firefighting systems – the Alpha Robotics Wolf R1, LUF 60, LUF-CRV, and Magirus AirCore TAF60.
The robots are built to extinguish fires and operate in environments too risky for human rescuers. The AirCore TAF60, for instance, is a remote-controlled unit designed to spray nebulized water or foam over distances of up to 60 meters (about 197 feet) while staying clear of collapse or heat hazards.
According to European Pravda, the systems were delivered under the project “Support to the State and Municipal Emergency Management in Ukraine,” implemented by the German Society for International Cooperation (GIZ) on behalf of the German government.
In a broader effort to preserve emergency and military personnel, Ukraine has increasingly turned to robots for performing dangerous tasks.
Russia Preparing Mass Mobilization for Fall, Zelensky Says
According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense on June 9, ground robotic systems were reported to be a regular presence on the front line, performing logistical tasks and providing combat support, as well as helping with medical evacuation.
Part of a decade-long partnership
Other than the robots, Berlin also handed over fire tankers, a heavy evacuation tractor, trucks fitted with crane manipulators, buses and minibuses for personnel transport, portable fire pumps and booster pumps, and personal protective equipment for rescuers.
“Our partnership has lasted for more than 10 years and goes far beyond the transfer of equipment,” Buchholz said, adding that Germany-Ukraine ties consist of “strengthening institutions, sharing experience and developing joint capabilities.”
The handover follows a similar delivery in July, when Germany provided Ukraine’s State Emegency Service with 10 sets of rescue equipment intended to help pull survivors from rubble, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
Ukraine’s emergency responders have also been active abroad – in early August, a Ukrainian firefighting team helped extinguish a forest fire near a French town in the Gironde region, arriving after a 52-hour drive across Europe as part of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism.

Police in Spain bust network accused of trafficking migrant girls
- Spanish police dismantled a criminal network recruiting unaccompanied migrant girls from Gran Canaria and moving them to mainland Spain and France for sexual exploitation.
- The network used false identity and travel documents to exploit vulnerable girls and arranged their journeys, aiming to transfer them off the islands.
- Five people were arrested, two victims rescued, and concerns remain over the safety of many unaccompanied minors stranded in Ceuta after a mass border crossing from Morocco.
AI generated
MADRID - Spanish police said on Aug 11 they had dismantled a criminal ring accused of recruiting unaccompanied migrant girls from care centres on Gran Canaria, in Spain’s Canary Islands, and moving them to mainland Spain and France, where some were sexually exploited.
The operation comes as migration debates have returned to the forefront across Europe after a mass border crossing from Morocco into Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta in July left hundreds of unaccompanied minors stranded in the city.
The Guardia Civil said the investigation began after a migrant girl who had been under the care of authorities in Gran Canaria returned to Spain from France and told investigators she had been recruited with the promise of a job.
Investigators subsequently identified several similar cases involving girls who left care centres without their personal documents and were later linked to flights to mainland Spain, the Guardia Civil said in a statement.
The network allegedly exploited the girls’ vulnerability, offering to help them leave the Canary Islands while providing false identity or travel documents and arranging their journeys by air and land.
“All with the aim of facilitating their departure from the islands and subsequently transferring them to mainland Spain and France, where some of them are alleged to have been subjected to sexual exploitation,” the statement said.
The Guardia Civil said it rescued two victims and prevented four other minors from leaving the islands.
Five people were arrested, including one minor, following five searches across Gran Canaria.
Some 72,000 migrants breached Ceuta’s border in an unprecedented and deadly rush on July 30-31, with 70,000 having since returned to Morocco, according to Spanish government figures.
Spain’s Youth and Children Minister Sira Rego said Friday that 1,342 unaccompanied migrant minors had been registered in Ceuta following the mass influx from Morocco.
Aid groups have warned that the minors, many of whom are sleeping rough on the streets of Ceuta, are at risk of abuse and exploitation. AFP

Trump says NYC pied-à-terre tax 'must be stopped,' eyes federal block

2026-08-11
18:10:10 UTC
03:10:10 KST

President Donald Trump on Tuesday decried New York City's pied-à-terre tax and said he is exploring whether the federal government "has any legal right to avert this disaster, before it is too late."
The tax on nonprimary residences of wealthy owners "doesn't work in America, and must be stopped, NOW!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Trump's vow to seek federal intervention against the tax, which was pushed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani and passed by the New York State legislature in late May, came one day after a Staten Island judge temporarily blocked the new policy.
New York City government quickly filed a motion to seek an appeal of that order, placing the judge's order on hold.
Mamdani's office did not respond to CNBC's request for comment on Trump's threat to challenge the pied-à-terre tax. Asked about the ongoing lawsuit, the mayor's office referred CNBC to Mamdani's assurance at a Monday press conference that "we look forward to vigorously defend our city's position in court."
"We are confident in our position," Mamdani said. "And that is a confidence coming from both the legality of the City's actions as well as the importance of a surcharge on secondary homes worth more than $5 million, a surcharge that will help fund safer streets, that will help fund stronger schools, and it will help fund the city that New Yorkers deserve."
Trump, in his Tuesday morning post, called the tax a "dangerous political 'experiment' in New York will destroy what was once a great City and State."
Trump added that it's hard for him as president "to sit back and watch it happen, especially to a place I once loved."
Trump is a native New Yorker who lived in a penthouse in Manhattan's Trump Tower, but moved his primary residence to his Mar-a-Lago golf club in Florida in 2019. It is unclear whether Trump or his immediate family would be subject to the NYC tax.
Trump also asserted that the levy on second homes is spurring thousands of people to flee to more tax-friendly regions, canceling out any revenue that the policy might bring in.
The claim echoes other warnings that have followed the election of Mamdani, a democratic socialist who has vowed to make the city's richest pay more.
Citadel CEO Ken Griffin, for instance, threatened to move his business to Miami after Mamdani unveiled the pied-à-terre tax in a video that featured Griffin's ultraluxury Manhattan penthouse.
Griffin also suggested Citadel was reconsidering moving ahead with a pricey redevelopment of a Park Avenue building. Vornado CEO Steven Roth, however, said in a recent earnings call that Griffin was not abandoning his plans for the NYC building.
Some have shrugged off concerns that hiking taxes on the wealthy in New York, which already has among the nation's highest income tax rates, will push people out of the state. While some studies show New York's share of millionaires has declined in recent years, others dispute the idea that the rich flee high state taxes.
The pied-à-terre tax backed by Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul would raise taxes on second properties valued at $1 million or more, with more valuable residences facing higher rates.
Mamdani, who announced the policy on Tax Day, said it is expected to raise $500 million in revenue, though NYC Comptroller Mark Levine said weeks later that that estimate could fall to between $340 million and $380 million.
Last week, three NYC residents filed a lawsuit in New York Supreme Court challenging the city's distribution of a list showing the names, addresses and property values of hundreds of thousands of NYC homeowners. The suit also targets written notices the city mailed, informing 17,000 people on that list that they may be subject to the new tax.
The suit alleges that those actions "arbitrarily and capriciously foisted onto New York City residents the burden of proving they are not subject" to the tax, instead of the city first determining which properties are included.
On Monday, Judge Wayne Ozzi temporarily blocked the city from "taking any further action" in connection with the list or the mailed notices.
Hours later, an attorney for Mamdani said in a court filing that the city intends to file a motion for permission to appeal the ruling.
Doing so triggers an "automatic stay" of all proceedings to enforce Ozzi's order for the time being, the lawyer wrote.

Romania destroys drones drifting near major offshore gas project in the Black Sea
BUCHAREST, Aug 11 - Romanian army divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones drifting in the country's Black Sea exclusive economic zone near the offshore gas project Neptun Deep, Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Tuesday.
The NATO state shares a 614-km (382-mile) land border with Ukraine and has seen Russian drones repeatedly breach its airspace over the last four years, as well as mines floating in the Black Sea across key trade and energy routes.
In July, Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down three Russian drones breaching national airspace over three consecutive days after dozens of such incursions in the more than four years of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
On Tuesday, a civilian vessel working near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project spotted the drones, Miruta said. The minister did not specify the origin of the drones, but said Ukraine had confirmed they did not belong to its forces.
"For the safety of the shipping lane and the works being carried out around the platform, the decision was made to carry out a controlled destruction by detonation," Miruta said.
"The defence ministry contacted Ukrainian partners, who confirmed that the systems do not belong to them."
NATO states Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey, which share the Black Sea with Georgia, Russia and Ukraine, have neutralised more than 150 mines drifting across crucial trade lanes.
In July, the three states agreed to expand a joint task force that clears mines floating in the Black Sea to include missions to protect critical infrastructure.
All three countries have gas exploration or production projects in the Black Sea. Romania's Neptun Deep, jointly owned by OMV Petrom and state gas producer Romgaz, is due to come onstream in 2027 and make Romania the European Union's largest gas producer. REUTERS

Democrats clash again in Minnesota and Wisconsin primaries as big midterm races take shape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

03:05:12 KST

Progressives and moderates will face off again in Tuesday's Democratic primary elections in Wisconsin and Minnesota as the party decides whether to lurch further to the left or chart toward the middle after crushing losses to Republicans in 2024.
Populist progressives in recent months have capitalized on economic anger to defeat establishment Democratic candidates across the country, setting off a potentially seismic political shift within the party. Last week in Michigan, progressive former health official Abdul El-Sayed defeated the more moderate Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens in a primary to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich. — the latest stunning upset for longtime party power brokers who backed Stevens.
The progressive swell will be tested again on Tuesday as candidates in the mold of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., vie for gubernatorial and Senate nominations in Wisconsin and Minnesota against establishment-backed moderates.
Wisconsin
In Wisconsin, Francesca Hong is running to be the state's next governor and is the clear polling favorite heading into Election Day. Hong, who leads the field by double digits in recent polls, is endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America's Milwaukee chapter and is a staunch progressive. Some prominent Democrats such as Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., have endorsed Hong.
Some of Hong's past comments, including calling for the cancellation of Thanksgiving and abolishing the police, have garnered scrutiny in recent days. Hong has since distanced herself from both statements.
She is facing a field that includes the more moderate Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who is endorsed by retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Crowley had previously dropped out of the race, but reentered and scored Evers' endorsements as some Democrats fear Hong is too progressive to win the general election in the purple state.
Hong's platform includes offering universal childcare, creating publicly owned grocery stores, establishing a public option healthcare plan and launching a public bank. She has also called for raising taxes on the wealthy in Wisconsin to pay for more services.
The winner of the Democratic contest will likely face Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis., in the general election. Tiffany, who has served in the House since 2020, represents northern Wisconsin. He is a member of the ultra-conservative House Freedom Caucus.
Tiffany is proposing freezing property taxes, rolling back other tax increases and increasing energy production.
Republicans have seized on the surge of progressives in the Democratic Party, branding the party's left flank as "communists." None of the high-profile Democrats in key primaries this year support communist policies.
Minnesota
In Minnesota, progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and moderate Democratic Rep. Angie Craig are in a tight race for the nomination to succeed the retiring Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn.
Flanagan, who is the No. 2 official in the state behind retiring Gov. Tim Walz, is running a progressive campaign and has been endorsed by Smith and top lawmakers on the left such as Sanders and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass. She has also nabbed the endorsement of the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party — the official state Democratic Party — but unlike Hong, is not backed by the Twin Cities DSA chapter.
She's pushing for a universal healthcare plan known as Medicare for All, wants to dismantle Immigration and Customs Enforcement and seeks to halt offensive weapons sales to Israel.
Support for Israel has become a flashpoint for Democrats in primary contests as many on the left recoil from the Jewish state's conduct during the war in Gaza that was launched in response to Hamas' attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. Flanagan has called Israel's actions a "genocide."
Flanagan, however, has caught some flak for her proximity to Walz and the cascading social services fraud scandal that prompted the 2024 vice presidential candidate to abandon his reelection bid. Flanagan has expressed regret that the administration did not act faster, but has defended the governor's response and subsequent crackdown on fraud.
President Donald Trump and his Republican allies earlier this year seized on the fraud claims, some of which are years old, to launch an immigration crackdown and pause some Medicaid funding in Minnesota.
Craig, in a debate with Flanagan, said "Republicans are going to have a field day with you" over her connection to the fraud scandal.
Craig, meanwhile, is a moderate who flipped a Republican-held seat in 2018. She leapfrogged to the top minority slot on the House Agriculture Committee in this Congress, defeating several more senior candidates to secure the spot.
She contends that her ability to win a purple district makes her the best candidate against a Republican in what's expected to be a tight election. Craig has scored endorsements from House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.
While Craig does not support Medicare for All, she has introduced a bill to create a government-run healthcare plan known as a public option or Medicare for all who want it. Craig also supports the traditional U.S.-Israel relationship, voting against an amendment last month that sought to strip U.S. aid to Israel while expressing her dissatisfaction with current Israeli leadership.
Craig has been criticized, however, for being the only Minnesota Democrat to vote for the Laken Riley Act. That bill required ICE to detain undocumented immigrants who are arrested or face charges or who have been convicted of burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law enforcement officer or any crime that results in death or serious bodily injury.
Immigration enforcement is a key issue in Minnesota after federal agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens in the state during the immigration crackdown earlier this year.
Craig has since backtracked on her support of that bill, saying she regrets it in an op-ed in the Minnesota Star Tribune and calling it "the wrong decision" in a debate with Flanagan last month.
Flanagan has pounced on Craig for the vote.
"Voting three days into the second Trump administration for Donald Trump's immigration bill that allowed him to terrorize our communities, the loss of life, the economic impact, the trauma, it's horrific," Flanagan said of Craig's vote during the debate.
Tuesday's Democratic winner is expected to face Republican Michele Tafoya in the general election. Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster, is leading by a wide margin in public polls.
Minnesota will also host a governor's primary on Tuesday, which will likely determine who Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., will face in the general election. The Republican field includes MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell and Minnesota House member Lisa Demuth.

“Faster than originally planned”: Russia wants 292 Starlink-rival satellites by 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:04:47 UTC
03:04:47 KST

Russia is deploying Rassvet satellites, its answer to Starlink, faster than originally planned, Vadym Skibitskyi, Deputy Chief of Ukraine's Defense Intelligence (GUR), told RBC-Ukraine.
Moscow aims to expand the network to 292 satellites by the end of 2027 and 924 by 2035, he said. Existing satellites can already provide intermittent connections as they pass over Ukraine.
Rassvet could give Moscow an independent alternative to Starlink, which Ukrainian forces rely on for battlefield communications and drone operations. Russian forces also used unauthorized Starlink terminals until Ukraine and SpaceX blocked access. Rassvet’s coverage remains intermittent but could eventually support strike drones, prompting Kyiv to consider countermeasures.
Why Russia wants its own Starlink
Ukrainian forces rely heavily on Starlink for frontline communications, drone operations, and command and control.
Russian forces also relied heavily on unverified terminals until Ukraine and SpaceX blocked them on 5 February. The shutdown disrupted Russian communications and assaults across multiple parts of the front. On 10 August 2026, the SBU said it had dismantled two schemes that registered terminals in Ukraine for transfer to Russian forces.
Rassvet could reduce Russia’s dependence on SpaceX and illicit supply networks. Ukrainian experts have warned that a mature network could also relay data to Russian strike drones.
32 satellites up, 260 to go by 2027
Bureau 1440, the Russian satellite developer behind Rassvet, began testing the network with three satellites in 2023. Three larger prototypes followed in 2024 to test upgraded equipment, including satellite-based 5G technology and laser links between spacecraft.
Russia launched its first batch of 16 serial Rassvet satellites on 23 March 2026 after manufacturing problems delayed the mission. A second group of 16 followed in July, Militarnyi reported.
In May 2026, Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a defense technology adviser to the President of Ukraine, said each Rassvet satellite then in orbit passed over Ukraine roughly once daily, providing six to 10 minutes of connectivity. He estimated that continuous coverage would require 200–250 satellites.

The Guardian view on wildfires: firefighters can’t handle this crisis alone | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:04:47 UTC
03:04:47 KST

The wildfire that began on protected heathland in the New Forest in Hampshire on Sunday was reported to be under control on Tuesday. But with temperatures forecast to reach 36C or higher in parts of England on Thursday, the risk of further outbreaks remains high. Firefighters responded to 185 wildfires in the first 10 days of August. In coastal Suffolk, conservationists and locals are counting the cost of the blaze that devastated Dunwich Heath. Its vegetation and rare bird populations are expected to take decades to recover.
Although the immediate cause of many wildfires is litter, the risks are elevated by heat and drought, and repeated warnings from climate scientists do not necessarily lessen the shock and distress caused. As people and governments across Europe assess this summer’s damage, experts including the UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, hope that the fires will focus minds on the urgent necessity of cutting emissions – as well as investing in emergency planning. Europe is currently heating up faster than any other continent, due in part to proximity to the melting Arctic.
The global, existential nature of the climate crisis makes it an awkward fit with Andy Burnham’s current focus on “everyday fixes”. But if he does not find more to say about the summer’s disasters, he is in danger of being left behind. The National Trust has already surpassed its £500,000 fundraising target to restore Dunwich Heath. Conservationists and farmers are publicly debating the best ways to prevent fires. The Fire Brigades Union (FBU) is pushing for 5,000 additional firefighters across the UK, along with new equipment.
In March, the then fire safety minister, Samantha Dixon, said that the fire and rescue service had suffered from “decades of drift and inertia”. Her speech also confirmed that a new College of Fire and Rescue would oversee professional standards, as recommended by the Grenfell inquiry. But three weeks ago Ms Dixon was sacked. If the government wants to avoid an impression that drift and inertia are ongoing, they need to provide an update, along with a response to repeated calls from the fire service inspectorate for new enforcement powers. MPs on the home affairs committee threw their weight behind this idea two years ago.
The fire and rescue service is popular with the public. Even highly critical sections of the Grenfell inquiry report did not significantly undermine confidence in it. This summer’s events seem likely to reaffirm this positive regard, and rightly so: public servants who do dangerous, difficult jobs, when many other people are on holiday, deserve to be appreciated. But scrutiny of the service is also important. An inquiry by the home affairs select committee, which was summarised in a letter to the home secretary in 2024, contained strong criticism of its culture and leadership.
Such concerns deserve a fuller response than they have so far received from ministers. So do the FBU’s call for investment to cope with rising risks, and proposals for a temporary ban on disposable barbecues. Ill-informed and ideological attempts to blame rewilding should also be addressed by ministers. Working groups on how to reduce wildfire risks must produce plans. The latest report from the government’s Climate Change Committee found that existing adaptation plans are not fit for purpose. This summer’s extraordinary heat, drought and wildfires should be a spur to action on both the fire service and the wider climate crisis.

Russia’s Central Bank approves Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT for exchange trading — with limits for retail investors
Russia’s Central Bank has added Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tether (USDT) to its list of cryptocurrencies approved for trading on exchanges, the regulator said in a statement.
Nonqualified investors will have access only to the most liquid cryptocurrencies, with an annual cap of 300,000 rubles’ worth of those assets per intermediary — a broker, a crypto exchanger, or an asset manager.
Qualified investors, by contrast, will be able to buy any cryptocurrency traded on the exchanges without restriction.
Before making a trade, all investors must pass a test and review the risks of crypto investing.
In July, the State Duma passed a law legalizing the circulation of cryptocurrency in Russia. It set rules for using cryptocurrencies and capped the size of nonqualified investors’ portfolios. At the time, the Central Bank clarified that only Bitcoin, Ethereum, and the stablecoin USDT met the criteria for exchange trading.

The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:04:02 UTC
03:04:02 KST

As the huge societal ramifications of artificial intelligence have become clear, some of the tech industry’s most senior figures have taken to writing thinkpieces on what comes next. The latest to do so is Mark Zuckerberg, who this week published 6,500 words making the case for a laissez-faire approach to AI development. Worrying too much about regulation, Meta’s CEO unsurprisingly opines, could lead to the United States falling behind in the race to own the future.
Mr Zuckerberg’s plea for maximum autonomy is, of course, self-serving. Much of his essay – which airily envisions “invention superpowers” for every entrepreneur and “an abundance of jobs in the future” – reads like unadulterated tech-utopianism. But the lobbying at least has the merit of being out there in the open. As midterm elections loom in the US, darker arts are also being used to counter popular concern about what AI will mean for a host of topics, from the labour market to child safety, the environment and cybersecurity.
Replicating a strategy deployed by cryptocurrency backers in the 2024 election cycle, Silicon Valley is pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Super Pacs – groups unaffiliated to political parties or campaigns – to ensure that voices sympathetic to its deregulatory AI agenda get elected. OpenAI’s co-founder and president, Greg Brockman, and Palantir’s co-founder, Jo Lonsdale, have given large sums to Leading the Future, an organisation dedicated to “identifying, maintaining, and growing pro-AI candidates”. Vast amounts are being spent to try to tilt the balance in individual contests, sometimes through disingenuous means.
Earlier this summer, Leading the Future spent $6m on ads attacking Alex Bores, a New York state assemblyman and pioneer of AI regulation at state level. Rather than focus on his AI campaigning, the ads attacked Mr Bores’s progressive credentials, alleging that he had carried out tech work in the past for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which he denies. Running for Congress in a Democratic stronghold, he lost a tight primary race after battling what was in essence a smear campaign.
Countervailing forces are emerging. Guardrails Alliance, a union-backed Super Pac, is attempting to combat Leading the Future’s influence, while a bipartisan groundswell of opposition to datacentres is generating serious electoral clout. But as tech companies and their billionaire owners seek to shape and above all limit the scope of AI regulation, their influence is distorting debate in a political culture where the power of money already holds far too much sway.
In his essay, Mr Zuckerberg urges that AI’s democratising potential be protected from those who believe “a small set of experts … should decide what is best for humanity”. He appears to miss the irony that an unelected tech oligarchy, to which he belongs, is already performing that function by default. Its pressure has been instrumental in persuading Donald Trump to cancel the signing of an executive order which would have given the government the right to review new AI models. Its wealth is now being used to attack and undermine dissenting voices in the public square.
If a democratic debate about the benefits and dangers of AI is to take place, such presumption must be fiercely resisted in the US and elsewhere. The semi-covert manipulation of political discussion is no way to map out an inclusive future in challenging times.

Brazil’s Supreme Court to weigh cases that could weaken Amazon protections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:00:01 UTC
03:00:01 KST

Brazil’s Supreme Court to weigh cases that could weaken Amazon protections
Brazil’s Supreme Court is set to hear several cases that could reshape protections for the Amazon rainforest, after a mostly conservative Congress overrode several of leftist Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s environmental vetoes.
The court will take up the cases on Wednesday, as lawmakers and environmental groups remain divided over how Brazil should balance economic development with environmental protections.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Under Lula, Amazon deforestation falls to lowest level in a decade
- list 2 of 3US to impose new 25 percent tariffs on some Brazilian imports
- list 3 of 3Brazil’s Lula launches fourth-term bid, focuses on national sovereignty
Deforestation in the Amazon has fallen to its lowest level in a decade during the first half of 2026. The cases put some of Brazil’s most consequential environmental fights before the country’s top court.
Indigenous land rights
On Friday, Brazil’s Supreme Court began reviewing final motions seeking clarification of a 2025 ruling that rejected the “time limit” thesis. The legal theory, backed by Brazil’s agribusiness lobby, restricts Indigenous land claims to territories occupied or under legal dispute when Brazil’s 1988 Constitution took effect.
The agribusiness caucus argues that a cutoff date would provide legal certainty for landowners. Indigenous groups say it ignores decades of forced displacement and violence that pushed communities from their ancestral lands. Indigenous communities across the Amazon, including the isolated and uncontacted Kawahiva people, could be affected by the ruling.
The justices are considering motions that seek clarification of the court’s ruling, addressing questions about compensation and possible deadlines for completing Indigenous land demarcations.
The soya farming moratorium
On Wednesday, the court will consider a legal fight over the future of Brazil’s soya moratorium, an agreement that barred major traders from buying soya grown on land deforested in the Amazon after 2008.
The agreement has been credited with helping curb deforestation, even as Brazil became an agricultural powerhouse. But states that are major soya producers passed laws in January revoking tax incentives for participating companies, prompting the Brazilian Association of Vegetable Oil Industries (ABIOVE) to withdraw from the moratorium.
Brazil is the world’s largest producer and leading exporter of soya beans. The Ministry of Environment and Climate Change has defended the soya moratorium, saying it helped reduce Amazon deforestation even as Brazil expanded production.
Environmental licensing
The court will also consider on Wednesday a challenge to a new environmental licensing law that took effect in February.
The law fast-tracks approval for projects including mines, highways and industrial plants, prompting environmental groups to warn that it could weaken safeguards in one of the world’s most important ecosystems.
Suely Araujo of the Climate Observatory said the law is already having tangible consequences in the Amazon, citing the paving of a controversial highway and plans to dredge the Tapajos River without adequate prior environmental review.

FSSAI tightens pan masala packaging norms; bans plastic, foil and synthetic laminates

FSSAI tightens pan masala packaging norms; bans plastic, foil and synthetic laminates
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 11, 2026, 23:29 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Pan masala may now only be packaged in paper, paperboard, cellulose, or other naturally derived materials (Photo: Agencies).
NEW DELHI: India's food safety regulator has barred the use of plastic and plastic-laminated packaging for pan masala, under an amendment aimed at tightening existing packaging norms, according to a press release.The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has specified that pan masala may now only be packaged in paper, paperboard, cellulose, or other naturally derived materials. Such materials must be entirely free of plastic, including polyethene, polypropylene, polyester, polyvinyl chloride (PVC), and other synthetic polymers, copolymers or laminates, as well as aluminium foil or metallised layers, the release said. Tin and glass containers continue to be permitted, it added.The press release further stated that packaging will also need to conform to clauses (f) and (i) of sub-rule 1 of rule 4 of the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, framed under the Environment Protection Act, 1986.The amendment has been incorporated as a new entry in Schedule IV of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations, 2018, which lists suggested packaging materials. It has been placed right after the existing entries at Serial Number 10, the release said.
Notified as the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Amendment Regulations, 2026, the amendment will come into force from the date of its publication in the Official Gazette, according to the release.The regulations were issued by FSSAI in exercise of powers conferred under clause (k) of sub-section (2) of Section 92 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and with prior approval of the Central Government, the release said.
