The Promise We Made to Americans with Disabilities Is Under Attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:58:28 UTC
02:58:28 KST

In the past, Americans with disabilities were sent off to large, isolating, state-run institutions as a matter of course. In overcrowded, understaffed facilities, residents were too often neglected and stripped of privacy, autonomy, or any meaningful connection to their communities. When these conditions were brought to light, they sparked national outrage. That reckoning helped galvanize the deinstitutionalization movement, a decades-long push to create services that support people with disabilities in their homes and communities.
Decades of advocacy to “deinstitutionalize” have fortunately transformed quality of life for people with disabilities, but it wasn’t until just 27 years ago that the Supreme Court's 1999 decision in Olmstead v. Lois Curtis made it so disabled Americans could rest easy knowing forced segregation wasn’t inevitable.
For much of our history, few options existed between mass institutionalization in expensive and confining facilities on one end of the spectrum, and fully independent living absent any supports on the other end of the spectrum. The legal precedent rooted in Olmstead, plus the proliferation of once-nonexistent community-based services, changed that.
Now, however, the foundation that underpins our nation’s wide spectrum of community-based services is crumbling.
Olmstead affirmed that the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) grants people with disabilities the right to live, work, and participate in their communities with the supports they need. That’s why we found it especially egregious that the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) released a legal memo last month coinciding with the decision’s anniversary, calling into question the established right of people with disabilities to receive services in the most integrated setting possible. The memo doesn’t change the law, but it seeks to erode decades of settled civil rights protections.
The DOJ memo follows a range of other actions by the Trump Administration, including significant cuts to federal Medicaid spending set to go into effect next year and the withholding of hundreds of millions of dollars of funding for community-based services in the name of protecting program integrity. In July 2026, the administration paused more than one billion dollars in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, citing fraud but offering little specificity to support their claim. Taken together, these moves seem to falsely imply that home- and community-based services (HCBS) are wasteful, rather than essential.
The Trump Administration has repeatedly questioned the value of HCBS by suggesting that Medicaid is paying professionals to carry out responsibilities families should simply provide themselves. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy told lawmakers that the waivers pay family members “for picking up the groceries, for driving somebody to a doctor’s appointment,” insisting that these family members are “getting paid to do things that they used to do [...] for free.” Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz has echoed that message, describing personal care services as helping “Medicaid patients do something that our families would normally do for us, like carrying groceries.”
Statements such as these have real-world implications and could serve to justify gutting these HCBS services—potentially forcing people with disabilities back into large public institutions, while pushing family caregivers and direct support professionals out of their respective workforces and into poverty.
The debate over how we invest in Medicaid cannot be separated from the debate over civil rights for people with disabilities. Olmstead’s promise of community living is only meaningful if people have access to the services that make community living viable. For millions, Medicaid is a lifeline. It funds the direct support professional who helps someone get dressed each morning. It funds the job coach who helps build skills needed to succeed in the workforce. It funds transportation to medical appointments, support to navigate public transportation, and countless other activities that enable people to participate fully in community life.
These activities are neither optional nor negotiable—they’re the foundation of the inclusion that this country promised through the ADA.
The notion that families should provide care without additional support is unrealistic and shortsighted, especially for families of people with highly complex medical or behavioral needs. Direct support professionals are trained to implement individualized care plans with a person-centered approach, respond to behavioral crises, administer medications, and more.
Moreover, this thinking also ignores reality. For instance, many disabled adults’ parents are elderly or deceased. Many of their spouses work full time, sometimes in multiple jobs to meet their families’ financial needs. Many of their siblings are in the same boat but may live hundreds of miles away. Some have no family to fall back on at all.
Suggesting that people don’t have the right to community-based support while insisting families provide needed care for free risks undoing more than a quarter-century of civil rights progress made possible by Olmstead. Furthermore, dismantling the spectrum of community-based services is expected to have negative down-the-line ramifications. We anticipate that more families will languish on states’ waiting lists for longer, more providers will reduce services or go out of business altogether, more professionals will leave the workforce to fill caregiving gaps, and more people with disabilities will be left with no other choice but expensive, isolating institutions.
All of this threatens to devastate families and local economies. If protecting taxpayers is truly the goal, community-based services shouldn’t be slashed—they should be upheld as the gold standard, especially given the dramatic cost savings they make possible. Supporting someone with an intellectual or developmental disability through home- and community-based services costs about $70,500 per year, versus more than $395,000 annually in a public institution.
While the DOJ’s memo and the administration’s other actions don’t overturn Olmstead, they do place another crack in the fragile foundation on which community living for millions of Americans is built. As we wrote last summer on the 35th anniversary of the ADA, we must reaffirm, not reinterpret or undo, the rights Olmstead upheld.

Here Comes the Sun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:58:00 UTC
02:58:00 KST

The Atlanta Hotel was an ordinary place – a respectable setting for a meeting.
Col. Yevhen Konovalets had some doubts about the man he was meeting, but went anyway. His commitment to Ukraine outweighed concerns for personal safety. He would not turn away from any opportunity to help his embattled nation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
May 23, 1938 was a Monday – a bright spring day in Rotterdam. Just before lunch, Konovalets took a seat in the café at a table near a window overlooking the street. He was 46. He asked for a sherry. The younger man who joined him – 30 years old – ordered a beer. They spoke for only a few minutes. Before leaving, the visitor gave him a gift: a box of chocolates. Konovalets liked chocolate.
Within minutes, Konovalets lay dead – assassinated by an NKVD agent acting on Stalin’s orders. The bomb hidden in those bonbons was meant not only to kill a man, but to decapitate the Ukrainian nationalist movement. Yet the Soviets failed. Col. Konovalets’ name endured.
I first learned about him when I was a young boy. A large photograph of him adorned Kingston’s Ukrainian hall on Bagot Street, a place where our community gathered to remember its history and heroes. I spied that very same image again and again in Ukrainian cultural centers across North America and Western Europe. For most of my early years, I did not fully understand who he was or why he might be worthy of such honor.
Germany Grants Ukraine’s State Emergency Service Nearly €6M in Robotic Firefighting Package
For my parents, like many who devoted their lives to the cause of Ukrainian independence, Konovalets represented a generation who refused to accept that Ukraine’s struggle for independence was over. He believed Ukraine would one day be free. So did they. They were proven right.
Now, almost nine decades after his murder, I am sitting in the Atlanta Hotel café, a sherry to hand. Not far from here, Col. Konovalets’ remains were exhumed at Crooswijk Cemetery – the latest step in his long odyssey to Ukraine, where he will be laid to rest at a military burial ground outside Kyiv. I will not accompany him. I chose instead to remain here, where his life was ended.
As an honor guard accompanies him across Europe, a rare solar eclipse will be visible over much of the continent – the Moon passing partly across the face of the Sun, dimming its light without ever fully extinguishing it. It is a strange coincidence, mirroring the story of Ukraine itself. For more than a century, that nation’s flame has been dimmed time and again – through conquest, famine, terror, occupation, and war – yet it has never gone out. Millions endured decades when freedom seemed beyond reach, and remembering became an act of resistance.
Following the revolutionary years of 1917-21, after Ukrainian statehood was extinguished, many believed this cause forlorn. Its leaders were scattered across the diaspora – imprisoned, hunted, and often killed. But Konovalets refused to accept defeat. Through the Ukrainian Military Organization, and later as the first leader of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, he continued the struggle in exile.
Moscow feared what Konovalets represented. His assassination was part of a wider campaign to suppress Ukrainian resistance. He would not be the only prey. Even after the collapse of the USSR, efforts to silence Ukrainian leaders continued – including the poisoning of President Viktor Yushchenko in 2004. President Volodymyr Zelensky remains a target, as Russia wages a genocidal war against the Ukrainian nation.
The parallel between the colonel’s time and ours is difficult to ignore. That is why bringing him home matters. This is about more than comrades-in-arms honoring a fallen soldier. His return restores a connection across generations – between those who took up arms then and those who fight now, despite overwhelming odds, against those who would deny Ukraine its right to exist.
In Rotterdam, as I think of a brave leader torn away from Ukraine, and of an ideal that could not be liquidated, I also remember what his widow, Olha, said as she grieved by his grave:
“This is for Ukraine...”
Four simple words. They echoed for she foresaw how her husband’s tomb was only temporary – hallowed ground where he would wait until his people came to carry him back to the soil of a free Ukraine. That day has come.
Ukraine’s son has gone home. His limbo is over.
And that is for Ukraine.

====================================================================================================

As Lake Maggiore runs low, Switzerland steps in as Italy faces growing water shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:54:19 UTC
02:54:19 KST

Lake Maggiore is suffering from drought and Switzerland is increasing releases from Lake Lugano. Water is also scarce in Piedmont, Lombardy, Veneto and the Marche: this is Italy's new emergency.
Switzerland is opening the taps on Lake Lugano to help prop up Lake Maggiore. It is an emergency solution that, more than any set of figures, shows how sensitive the water situation in northern Italy has become: more water will be released from the Ceresio towards Ponte Tresa, with the aim of supporting the level of Lake Maggiore and, above all, guaranteeing supplies for the rice fields on the plain.
The discharge will rise from the current 3 to 8 cubic metres per second. The two lakes are connected and a significant share of the extra water will flow into Lake Maggiore.
The measure was discussed within the Italian-Swiss Bilateral Consultation Body on the regulation of Lake Maggiore's levels and the management of water resources in its basin, convened urgently by the Ministry of the Environment on the basis of data from the Po River Basin Authority. The Italian delegation, made up of representatives of the ministry and the Lombardy and Piedmont regional authorities, accepted the Swiss proposal, which could be implemented as early as today.
Switzerland's help and the 'short blanket' problem
The decision taken by Canton Ticino is temporary and will be reassessed in the coming days, but its significance goes well beyond this one-off intervention. The underlying problem is that the available water is no longer sufficient to meet all needs at the same time.
On the one hand are the rice paddies of Piedmont and Lombardy, which at this stage of the season need large volumes of water. On the other are the water supply networks, rivers, lakes and ecosystems, all having to cope with ever lower flows.
It is the classic "short blanket" situation: if you increase the provision for one sector, you have to check what is left for the others. And when the overall resource shrinks, even a seemingly technical decision on how to regulate a lake becomes a strategic issue.
The case of Lake Maggiore is particularly telling. Back in July, the Po River Basin Authority was already warning that the lake was close to its minimum operating level, while agriculture in Piedmont was among the sectors under greatest strain.
The problem is not confined to irrigation water for farmland. In several parts of Italy, scarcity has also started to affect drinking water supplies.
Lake Maggiore, who is in charge?
Lake Maggiore is a transboundary basin, shared between Italy and Switzerland, but its regulation is not by joint management in the strict sense. The lake level is controlled by the Miorina dam at Sesto Calende, on Italian territory, and day-to-day management is entrusted to the Ticino Consortium.
Italy and Switzerland nevertheless discuss and coordinate decisions within the Italian-Swiss Bilateral Body, because changes in the lake's level have consequences on both sides of the border.
The picture is even more complex because the Lake Lugano, also shared between the two countries, is linked to Lake Maggiore via the River Tresa: it is through this system that Switzerland is now providing support, by temporarily increasing flows from 3 to 8 cubic metres per second. So Lake Maggiore is regulated in Italy, but managing the water resource cannot be done without coordination with Switzerland.
Water tankers fill supply gaps
In Piedmont the situation is especially sensitive. By mid-July, the regional authorities reported that around 100 municipalities had already adopted ordinances to curb water use, above all in mountain areas and more isolated hamlets. In around 50 municipalities, with a combined population of 25,000, water tankers were already being used to top up reservoirs serving the water supply networks.
Figures from Arpa Piemonte painted an equally worrying picture: surface water resources were 37 per cent below the seasonal average, while in the first ten days of July many gauging stations were showing deficits of more than 40 per cent. At Isola Sant'Antonio, the Po had an average flow of just 62 cubic metres per second, 75 per cent below its historical reference value.
The heat has made matters worse. June 2026 in Piedmont was marked by temperatures far above the average, with a regional anomaly of about +3.5 °C. Higher temperatures increased evapotranspiration, causing soil and vegetation to lose water more quickly.
The crisis spreads across the Po basin
Piedmont, however, is not an isolated case. The problem affects a far wider area.
At the end of July, the permanent observatory on water use in the Po River District raised its assessment of water stress from "medium" to "high". Flows in the Po had progressively fallen to values below those typical of low-water conditions, and the drought index was indicating severe conditions across most monitored sections, with an "extreme" situation recorded at Cremona.
As early as 21 July, the Basin Authority was reporting problems not only for agriculture but also for water destined for households. In Lombardy, 50 municipalities were struggling, 17 of them supplied by tankers; in the Marche region there were 32. Critical situations were also reported in Veneto and Piedmont.
The picture also includes the Po Delta, where reduced river flows increase the risk of saltwater intrusion from the sea. When the river carries less freshwater, saltwater can push further inland, putting ecosystems, farming activities and water supply installations under strain.
Rice fields, drinking water, rivers: who comes first?
This is where the real issue emerges. The emergency is not just about "how much water there is", but how to distribute it when there is not enough.
Agriculture needs irrigation precisely during the hottest phases of the year. The rice fields of Piedmont and Lombardy are among the most exposed sectors, and Piedmont is one of the areas where the region has most clearly flagged the risk of crop losses linked to limited water availability.
But that same water is needed for water supply networks, to maintain minimum flows in rivers, for ecosystems, for certain industrial uses and, in some areas, for energy production.
Hence the growing need for increasingly sophisticated interventions and agreements between regions and countries. The release from Lake Lugano towards Lake Maggiore is a concrete example: a resource available in one basin is temporarily used to support another water system in difficulty.
And in the South the problem has not gone away
The water crisis, however, is not confined to the North. Conditions vary from region to region and not all of Italy faces the same situation at the same time, but vulnerability remains high, especially in Mediterranean areas and in regions that depend heavily on reservoirs.
ISPRA monitors the severity of water stress in the various Italian districts and defines the "high" scenario as a situation in which, despite preventive measures, the resource may not be sufficient to avoid damage to the system.
It is a snapshot that helps explain why water is becoming one of the most sensitive issues in land management: it is no longer enough to wait for rain. Reservoirs are needed, along with more efficient networks, reduced losses in water supply systems, reuse of treated wastewater, less wasteful irrigation systems and planning that takes account of increasingly variable water availability.

Electric scooter rentals banned in Chernivtsi
Kyiv • UNN
On August 10, the Chernivtsi City Council terminated its memorandums with Bolt, Vevi, and Jet.ua following complaints about parking and traffic violations. The companies have 14 days to remove the scooters; otherwise, they will be forcibly relocated.
The Chernivtsi City Council decided to terminate cooperation memorandums with electric scooter rental operators due to residents’ complaints. This became known from a live broadcast of the council session. 22 deputies voted in favor of the decision, reports UNN.
Details
Electric scooters can no longer be rented in Chernivtsi. The city council adopted the decision to terminate the memorandums during its session on August 10. The operators concerned are Bolt, Vevi, and Jet.ua. 22 deputies voted in favor of the decision.
The companies were given 14 days to completely remove the electric scooters, charging stations, and other equipment from the city.
The main reason for the decision was the numerous complaints from Chernivtsi residents. People complained about the chaotic parking of electric scooters. In addition, regular violations of road safety rules by riders were recorded in the city.
If the companies fail to comply with the requirement within the specified 14-day period, then the vehicles will be forcibly moved to a temporary storage facility.
Reminder
Electric scooters are officially recognized as vehicles, so riders must comply with the traffic rules. In the event of accidents involving children, their parents will be held responsible.

Chiefs WR Rashee Rice: 30 days in a Texas jail a ‘learning experience’ after probation violation
ST. JOSEPH, Mo. (AP) — Kansas City Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice called the 30 days he spent in a Texas jail over the summer a “learning experience” and a “reality check,” one that he got through by rehabbing from knee surgery and watching plenty of comedian Kevin Hart on TV to keep his spirits up.
The 26-year-old Rice was booked into a Dallas County jail on May 19 for violating the terms of his probation, which stemmed from his role in a car crash that left multiple people injured on a Texas highway. He’d had surgery about a week before the sentence to clean up debris in his right knee, which had been causing inflammation throughout much of last season.
Rice was released in June, and he resumed his rehab work alongside Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes — who was rehabbing after his own surgery to repair torn knee ligaments — at their training facility in Kansas City leading into the start of training camp.
“It was tough. It was mentally tough,” Rice said of the jail stint Tuesday, the first time the wide receiver has spoken publicly about his offseason. “They gave me ways to communicate with my teammates as well as my athletic trainer. Besides the hard times in there, just tried to keep positive — as much Kevin Hart as I could to laugh, and communicating with my teammates on the outside.”
Rice has been brilliant for Kansas City when he’s been available, catching 156 passes for 1,797 yards and 14 touchdowns, and helping the Chiefs win the Super Bowl after the 2023 season. But he also missed games to a suspension following the car crash, and several injuries have kept him off the field, resulting in just 28 games played over his first three seasons in the league.
The upcoming season is without question his most important yet.
Not only does Rice has much to prove to a growing chorus of doubters, he’s also entering the final year of his rookie contract. If he wants to land a lucrative, long-term deal in Kansas City or elsewhere, Rice has to not only prove that he can stay on the field but also show that he can consistently be productive for an offense that desperately needs him to be.
“I mean, it’s motivating,” Rice said of impending free agency. “Honestly, just being back on the field with my brothers right now is motivating. That’s in the future. And I’m just focusing on what’s happening right now, and that’s getting better for the team.”
The Chiefs are coming off a 6-11 season in which Mahomes hurt his knee, several others went down with injuries, and what was once one of the NFL’s premier offenses looked like a shadow of itself — even before all those players were sidelined.
Chiefs general manager Brett Veach spent most of his draft capital upgrading the defense, though, including both of his first-round picks, and the biggest move to help the offense was to sign Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III to be their lead running back.
Otherwise, the Chiefs are banking on Rice and fellow wide receivers Xavier Worthy and Tyquan Thornton to take big steps forward in their development, all while hoping that 36-year-old tight end Travis Kelce can still be a reliable and effective pass-catcher.
“We’re going to do some amazing things,” Rice predicted, “not only because we’re great receivers but we have a great coaching staff around us, and a great quarterback and foundation in general.”
Mahomes has certainly looked like his normal self in camp, moving around on his reconstructed knee as if nothing ever happened. That bodes well for Rice, the passing game and the Chiefs in general as they prepare for the upcoming season.
“He was my motivation every morning,” Rice said.
Rice was asked whether he had anything to say to fans who felt let down by his off-the-field problems, or to young players who might be looking up to him. He went back to Mahomes and the teammates that have been with him through thick and thin.
“Find someone that you can lean on. Find someone you can talk to,” Rice said, “and basically don’t be scared to vocalize yourself, or say exactly what’s on your mind, because someone is going through the same thing. There’s too many people in the world for there not to be someone going through the same thing.”
Notes: The Chiefs are signing DE Emmanuel Ogbah, who appeared in 10 games for them during the 2019 season. The veteran spent last season with Jacksonville. “It was disappointing the year we had him. I thought he was coming on and he got hurt, and we didn’t have him at the end of the year,” Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo said. “If he’s part of our group, I’ll be excited.”

Movie Review: ‘The Rivals of Amziah King’ is a Southern fried flick with too many ingredients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:53:02 UTC
02:53:02 KST

Movie Review: ‘The Rivals of Amziah King’ is a Southern fried flick with too many ingredients
It turns out that the honey business isn’t as sweet as it sounds: In the new movie “The Rivals of Amziah King,” beekeepers steal from each other, poison rivals’ insects and rip folk off. “It’s not full of kind people,” the title character warns.
“The Rivals of Amziah King” isn’t as sweet as it thinks it is, either. Instead of picking a single variety to explore, the movie is a maddening mishmash of genres — blending Quentin Tarantino’s sudden brutality, a coming-of-age tale, a heist flick, a revenge fantasy and a sweet, music-filled country hoedown.
Matthew McConaughey returns to the big screen playing the title character in what can only be called Matthew-McConaughey-turned-up-to-11 mode, pure Cheshire Cat smile, rascally wink and buttery, Southern gentlemanly charm. Suspenders and scruff on, cowboy boots snug, McConaughey is the one who makes everyone’s life instantly better just by showing up.
Written by Andrew Patterson and James Montague and directed by Patterson, “The Rivals of Amziah King” follows McConaughey’s honey-producing King as he negotiates his patch of rural Oklahoma until he inexplicably leaves the movie at the hour mark and hands it off to Angelina LookingGlass, making her film debut.
We meet King ordering chicken fried steak sandwiches and cherry Cokes as he plays the banjo in a quartet of musicians at a beloved food joint. That gets interrupted when authorities need his knowledge to find out who abandoned $250,000 worth of honey barrels on the road and King starts to investigate. Then someone gets a chunk of their skull — including ponytail — ripped off in an industrial accident and that takes over. Settle in, the whiplash is just beginning.
King soon connects with his former foster daughter — that’s LookingGlass, fierce and preternaturally grounded — who he gets to mansplain in the local ways, like what to eat at the potluck (“There’s a story in every dish”), life lessons (“Patience is better than being smart”) and beekeeping (“Every queen is a survivor”). Bees here, if you didn’t already get from the clunky writing, represent community, sharing and caring.
Cinematographer M.I. Littin-Menz’s camera techniques never settle down in this movie, like a puppy forever pulling on its leash. Early sequences employ frozen shots irritatingly dropped into the mix and later we have furious close-ups, quick cuts, quirky flashbacks, ethereal river sequences and lingering poetic images of close-up bees like from a documentary, a kinetic approach that seems not to have much faith in the actual story keeping viewers’ interest alive. Music supervisor Winslow Bright swamps many scenes with loud choirs, loud banjo and loud strings.
Maybe that’s because as soon as you’ve settled down for one genre, it gets hijacked by the next. Warm and extended moments of communal song — the great T Bone Burnett had a hand in some of the outstanding Americana tunes like “Quill” with McConaughey exuberant, and “Johnny Come Outside” — are undercut by seeing kids smash their heads on school bus roofs or a cool Western-like tracking of a honey-stealing local rascal that is marred by his horrific, boiling-to-death murder. There are so many montages of honey production that viewers may qualify for a beekeeping certificate.
Great turns are produced by Kurt Russell as a lethal local kingpin who schmoozes his way past the law, and Jake Horowitz, a former Marine who knows how to plan a theft with military precision, mostly shirtless. One brazen theft here is of “O Brother, Where Art Thou?” and, however you liked that movie, you realize now how hard it was to actually pull off.
Patterson likes to remind viewers of his Oklahoma bona fides, but much of the overlong movie was shot in Alabama. And that hints at what’s wrong with “The Rivals of Amziah King” — it just doesn’t feel authentic, either in place or in story. Forget honey, it sort of leaves a vinegary taste behind.
“The Rivals of Amziah King,” a Black Bear release that hits theaters Friday, is rated R by the Motion Picture Association for “language and some grisly images.” Running time: 130 minutes. Two stars out of four.
___
This review has been updated to correct that the former Marine is played by Jake Horowitz, not Owen Teague.

FACT FOCUS: Trump makes false claims as he signs order urging revisions around childhood vaccines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:53:02 UTC
02:53:02 KST

FACT FOCUS: Trump makes false claims as he signs order urging revisions around childhood vaccines
While issuing an executive order on Monday aimed at getting states to revise childhood vaccine recommendations, President Donald Trump and others in his administration repeated several false claims about those vaccines, as well as their relationship to autism.
The order recommends separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate single-disease shots and administering childhood vaccines at separate appointments whenever possible.
But many public health experts expressed concern about the recommendations, saying that spacing out the shots could increase the risk that children would become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit. They noted that childhood vaccines and how they should be given have been rigorously studied around the world for decades, and continue to prove to be safe and effective at protecting children.
Here’s a closer look at the facts.
___
TRUMP: “In many cases, we were requiring 72 jabs for our beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children.”
THE FACTS: That’s misleading. In 2025, the government’s childhood vaccination schedule recommended routine protection against 18 diseases. How many separate injections that added up to between birth and age 18 varied. It depended on things like the brand used, the availability of combination shots and the child’s starting age. But unless you counted once-a-year flu vaccines (which some kids can get as a nasal spray) or COVID-19 shots, the number of injections was closer to three dozen.
Those shots have been proven to protect children from preventable and sometimes devastating diseases. Even so, vaccines were never “required,” as families could opt out. States do require children to get certain vaccines before enrolling in school, but the state lists of school shots were narrower than the federal vaccine schedule, and many states offer different types of exemptions.
The Trump administration in January cut the national vaccine recommendations to injections against 11 diseases, with additional vaccines now separately categorized for at-risk children or as available through “shared decision-making” with a doctor. This drops the total number of injections to about 23 if children receive only the recommended-for-all vaccinations on the administration’s new schedule.
___
TRUMP: “You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they are quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal but just very effective.”
THE FACTS: This is false. Doctors say, and years of real-world evidence prove, that the current combination MMR vaccine is both safe and effective at protecting children from illness. Common side effects are mild and include a sore arm from the shot, fever, mild rash and temporary pain and stiffness in the joints. Doctors point out that separate vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella are not available in the United States.
“I’m concerned about an unintended consequence of people under vaccinating because of fear that giving a single dose of the MMR is going to put their child at risk when there’s no evidence to suggest that’s the case,” said Dr. Aaron Milstone, pediatric director of infection prevention at Johns Hopkins Health System and a fellow with the American Academy of Pediatrics. “There are many, many, many years of scientific data highlighting the safety of vaccines in children.”
___
TRUMP: “Large amounts of vaccine, large amounts of like vats of vaccine are currently pumped into your child’s body.”
THE FACTS: This is false. Dr. Molly O’Shea, a Michigan pediatrician, said amounts vary slightly by vaccine, but doctors give less than 0.5 milliliters per vaccine -- usually 0.1 to 0.3 milliliters per vaccine. By comparison, a teaspoon is about 5 milliliters.
“It’s a teeny amount,” she said. “So there are no vats.”
Trump also said during the executive order signing: “I’ve seen proof of it. Where they have a vaccination that looks like the size of a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body.” A typical plastic bottle of soda contains 500 milliliters, or about 2,500 times more than a typical vaccine.
___
TRUMP: “There’s nothing that we lose with this. The worst thing that would happen would be nothing happens. We’re not going to lose anything.”
THE FACTS: Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit. Doctors say, and real world evidence proves, that vaccinations save millions of lives.
“Vaccines are among the most thoroughly studied, effective tools we have to protect children from serious vaccine-preventable diseases,” said Dr. Willie Underwood, president of the American Medical Association. “Altering a proven vaccination schedule without credible evidence risks weakening public confidence and putting children’s health at risk.”
Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said that “delaying or skipping shots is risky, especially as measles continues to spread and children go back to school.”
Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, but rates are now climbing as vaccination rates decline. The number of cases this year has already surpassed the record-breaking tally for all of 2025, which was the worst year for measles in more than three decades.
___
HEALTH SECRETARY ROBERT F. KENNEDY JR.: “In 1970, the biggest epidemiological study at that time in history was performed. And the university scientists from across this country looked at all the 8-year-olds in Wisconsin, about 900,000 children, and they were looking for autism. And they knew what autism looked like. And they came back with an incidental rate of .8 per 10,000. So less than one in 10,000. The rate according to CDC today in this country is one in every 31 children.”
THE FACTS: It’s true that in the 20th century, only 1 in 10,000 children were diagnosed with autism —- the diagnosis was rare and given only to kids with severe problems communicating or socializing and those with unusual, repetitive behaviors. But the term became shorthand for a group of milder, related conditions known as ″autism spectrum disorders,” and the number of kids labeled as having some form of autism began to balloon.
Health officials have largely attributed growing autism numbers to better recognition of cases, through wide screening and better diagnosis. In April 2025, the CDC said the diagnosis rate was 1 in 31 children.
During the executive order signing, Kennedy and Trump suggested that childhood vaccines may play a role in causing autism. But studies by the CDC and others have ruled that out. A fraudulent single study that claimed a link between the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine was later retracted by the journal that published it.
There are no blood or biologic tests for autism; it is diagnosed by making judgments about a child’s behavior. Research has looked at a variety of other possible explanations, including genetics, the age of the father, the weight of the mother and chemicals in the environment.
“No environmental factor has been better-studied as a potential cause of autism than vaccines,” said Dr. Alycia Halladay, chief science officer at the Autism Science Foundation. “That includes vaccine ingredients as well as the body’s response to the vaccines. All this research has determined that there is no link between autism and vaccines. This is consistent across multiple studies, repeated in different countries around the world, including those mentioned in today’s press conference.”
Last year, Kennedy promised to conduct exhaustive studies to identify any environmental factors that may cause the developmental disorder. He said on Monday that his department will deliver research findings “as soon as they are ready.”
___
AP Medical Writer Lauran Neergaard contributed to this report.

Britain’s Andy Green sets another speed record, this time for fastest run in a hydrogen-powered car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:53:02 UTC
02:53:02 KST

Britain’s Andy Green sets another speed record, this time in a hydrogen-powered car
WENDOVER, Utah (AP) — The only person to break the sound barrier in a car earned another world record Tuesday in a show of force for hydrogen power.
British driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph (653.908 kph) in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines with a combined 1,600 horsepower, setting the record for that vehicle category, according to the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile, the international governing body of motor sports.
The 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot rocketed across the crystalline crust at Utah’s famous Bonneville Salt Flats in a 32-foot (9.75-meter) car engineered by British construction equipment manufacturer JCB. The engines, adapted from those used in the company’s heavy machinery, mix pressurized hydrogen gas with air and ignite it to create bursts of power.
“It’s magic to be able to showcase this technology and to showcase how good the engineering is on the best racing surface in the world, Bonneville Salt Flats,” Green told The Associated Press after the run.
To be clear, Tuesday’s feat didn’t come close to approaching the overall land-speed record, which Green set with jet power in 1997. That year, he climbed into the Thrust SSC, a black needle sandwiched between two cartoonishly large jet engines, and hit 763.035 mph (1,227.985 kph), breaking the sound barrier and achieving a feat no one has come close to matching. His runs in Nevada’s Black Rock Desert produced sonic booms that shook the nearby town of Gerlach.
In 2006, Green also set the land-speed record for a diesel-powered car — 350.092 mph (563.4 kph) — at the Bonneville Salt Flats. He returned there Tuesday with the goal of beating that mark using hydrogen power, which he has called the “fuel of the future.”
In targeting his diesel speed, Green easily topped the previous hydrogen combustion world record of 185.5 mph (298.5 kph). He had a 10-mile (16-kilometer) straightaway to build speed. A few dozen JCB staff members and reporters watched from a distance through cameras and binoculars.
Green said the cockpit of the car he used on Tuesday was “probably a little hotter” than in the jet-powered vehicle from 1997, with temperatures routinely above 122 degrees Fahrenheit (50 degrees Celsius).
“But I have been training four months for that, both training in the gym and actually just getting used to it with hot baths,” he said.
A remnant of a prehistoric lake bed, the Bonneville Salt Flats are about 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of Salt Lake City and sit atop a shallow aquifer that cools the tires. The low-friction surface and dry desert air are conducive to speed and have beckoned drivers since the first race there in 1914.
“It looks like snow, and it behaves a bit like packed snow — it is surprisingly slippery,” Green said.
Green was no stranger to speed when he took his first racing job. He had been flying supersonic military jets when he spotted a 1994 British newspaper ad seeking a high-speed driver to break the sound barrier.
Green did not approach supersonic speeds on Tuesday, but JCB engineers hope his feat with hydrogen power will shake up the clean-energy industry.
The company’s chairman has argued that hydrogen can better handle the demands of heavy industries than electric power.
Hydrogen is only as clean as its source, and the vast majority is currently produced from fossil fuels. JCB signed a deal to buy green hydrogen, which is created using renewable energy but makes up a tiny fraction of global hydrogen production.
The concept and development of such technology has been around for decades, but has had a resurgence over the past several years, said Greg Keoleian, a professor of sustainable systems at the University of Michigan and co-director of the school’s MI Hydrogen initiative.
Many major automakers have already developed hydrogen internal combustion engines or hydrogen fuel cell technology, but the higher cost of hydrogen production compared with gas and diesel is a barrier to wider usage, Keoleian said.
“It represents an important energy carrier for decarbonizing areas of the economy,” he said. “As far as its deployment, it’s influenced heavily by the cost.”
An emerging focus, he said, is extracting hydrogen from natural deposits instead of separating it from water, a prospect that could significantly reduce costs.
___
Associated Press reporter Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed reporting.

Candlelight vigil in Islamabad honors 10 climbers killed on Broad Peak

Candlelight vigil in Islamabad honors 10 climbers killed on Broad Peak
ISLAMABAD (AP) — Mountaineers, diplomats and members of civil society gathered in Pakistan’s capital Tuesday evening for a candlelight vigil honoring 10 climbers killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak, as rescuers described an arduous mission to bring their fellow climbers down from one of the world’s highest mountains.
Rain fell as mourners lit candles and prayed for the dead, shielding the flickering flames from the downpour as they gathered on the open lawns of a sports complex in Islamabad to remember the climbers who never returned from the mountain.
The vigil came days after search teams ended an operation that recovered the remains of eight climbers. Two bodies have not yet been recovered.
Among the dead was renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja. Nepal lost six climbers in the July 30 disaster, when a massive avalanche struck an international expedition.
Nepal’s ambassador to Pakistan, Rita Dhital, joined the vigil and paid tribute to the climbers as candles were lit in their memory. She recalled meeting Purja at her Islamabad home before the expedition and said he would often tell her, “Giving up is not in my blood.”
She thanked Pakistani climbers and rescuers who went onto the mountain in dangerous weather to search for the missing climbers and recover their bodies. Dhital particularly praised renowned Pakistani mountaineer Sirbaz Khan, who led the recovery team, as well as the Alpine Club of Pakistan, the military and government officials involved in the operation.
The bodies of all six Nepalese climbers have been returned to their families, she said.
Khan told The Associated Press that he and his team had set out hoping they would find the missing climbers alive. “I had hoped that I would hug them after finding them alive,” he said. Instead, the rescuers found climbers buried beneath the avalanche. Khan said the team used shovels to dig through the snow and pull out the bodies one by one.
Seeing fellow mountaineers dead on the mountain was difficult, he said, but the rescuers composed themselves and began the equally difficult task of bringing the bodies down, using ropes and makeshift stretchers. Khan said he remained deeply saddened by the deaths but took some solace in knowing that families who had waited desperately for news were able to receive the remains of their loved ones.
Irfan Arshad Khan, president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan and no relation to the rescuer, said the remains of seven climbers, including all six from Nepal, had been repatriated. He said bad weather repeatedly prevented helicopters from reaching the accident site, forcing rescuers to continue much of the search and recovery operation on foot. Eight bodies were eventually brought to a location from where they could be airlifted, he said.
“We have gathered here today to commemorate the passing of our great comrades,” Khan told those attending the vigil. He said the days following the avalanche tested not only the endurance of those searching the mountain but also the courage of rescuers who continued on foot when helicopters could not reach them.
The international expedition included climbers from Nepal, Oman, Pakistan, China, Britain and the United States.
Broad Peak, which rises 8,051 meters (26,414 feet) above sea level in the Karakoram range, is the world’s 12th-highest mountain and lies near K2, the world’s second-highest peak.
Mountaineering accidents are common in northern Pakistan, home to some of the world’s highest mountains.

Lebanon Issues New Charges Against Former Central Bank Chief Riad Salame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:52:00 UTC
02:52:00 KST

Reported by
A Lebanese judge has issued new charges against former central bank governor Riad Salame and a former commercial banker over allegations of financial crimes, including embezzlement, money laundering, bribery, and illicit enrichment, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.
On Monday, Judge Raja Hamouche filed proceedings against 76-year-old Salame and Samir Hanna, 88, the former head of Bank Audi, one of Lebanon's largest banks. The allegations include the creation of shell companies, misappropriating funds belonging to the Central Bank, and the fraudulent use of those funds to purchase shares and bonds in commercial banks. He also charged them with illicit enrichment, money laundering, and bribery.
The Public Prosecutor of Appeal requested an arrest warrant against Salame. Media have reported that he is currently under medical supervision at a hospital in Beirut. He has repeatedly denied all charges against him. His lawyer has not responded to OCCRP’s request for comment.
Hanna, 88, has reportedly already paid a $1 million bail and is not in custody. He could not be reached for comment.
The development marks the second indictment against Salame in Lebanon this year and the third in total.
Lebanese prosecutors took their first formal legal action against Riad Salame in February 2023, charging him with money laundering and embezzlement after years of international scrutiny. Months later, in July 2023, Salame stepped down as governor of Banque du Liban, ending a three-decade tenure at the central bank.
In September 2024, Lebanese authorities arrested Salame in Beirut over his alleged role in a $44.8 million embezzlement scheme involving central bank commissions. He was released on bail in 2025 and placed under a strict travel ban as court proceedings continue.
In January 2026, prosecutors indicted him alongside two legal advisers on charges of embezzlement, forgery, and illicit enrichment for their roles in the embezzlement of $44 million.
European authorities allege that Salame siphoned more than $300 million from the central bank using a front company owned by his brother, which charged exorbitant commissions on commercial bank transactions.
Investigations across Switzerland, France, Germany, and Luxembourg also allege that hundreds of millions of dollars in stolen public funds were funneled into luxury real estate and bank accounts across Europe. Salame has denied those accusations too.
Concurrent with the latest judicial proceedings, Lebanon’s central bank launched legal action in July against additional targets alleged to have played a role in the country’s 2019 financial meltdown. The action followed a complaint initiated by current central bank governor Karim Soueid in January targeting Salame and Hanna, who reportedly stepped down from Bank Audi's board that same month.
The financial authority is also suing Lebanon’s BankMed, alongside several executives and a major investor, according to local media. The claim was confirmed to OCCRP's Lebanese partner, Daraj, by a person familiar with the process. BankMed did not respond to a request for comment.
Under the new leadership Banque du Liban is attempting to recoup funds lost during the 2019 economic collapse, which resulted from a systemic banking failure.
Lebanon had pegged its currency to the U.S. dollar, and to maintain the fixed exchange rate and fund government spending, the central bank lured commercial banks into depositing customer dollars at exceptionally high interest rates. When new dollar inflows dried up, the system collapsed, wiping out the life savings of millions of people. The World Bank ranked the collapse as one of the world's worst economic crises since the mid-19th century.
Badih Moukarzel, the central bank’s lead counsel in the cases, told Daraj that the bank is determined to pursue the matters, calling them key to restoring confidence in the financial system.
“Those who committed financial crimes have to be investigated, and if they are found guilty, they must be tried. I don't see how we can rebuild trust without doing this,” Moukarzel said. He described the financial collapse as a shared responsibility between the state, the central bank, and commercial banks, categorically rejecting out-of-court settlements. “The banks have to pay back. Money has to be returned; we are talking billions of dollars.”

Putin’s motorcade stopped in Novosibirsk for a ‘spontaneous’ crowd of children. They had been waiting more than two hours — by a gas station with no gas.

Putin’s motorcade stopped in Novosibirsk for a ‘spontaneous’ crowd of children. They had been waiting more than two hours — by a gas station with no gas.
Putin stopped his motorcade during a visit to Novosibirsk and got out to greet a crowd of local residents who had been waiting for him along the road. Eyewitness video shows the motorcade halted near an empty gas station where the price board had been switched off.
Pavel Zarubin, a propagandist for the Russian state broadcaster VGTRK, published a video of the encounter. The footage shows people, mostly children, surrounding Putin after his motorcade stopped. He stood with them briefly before leaving. The clip was reportedly filmed on the way to the airport.
From a building near where the motorcade stopped, eyewitnesses filmed another video showing that people had been expecting Putin well in advance. The Telegram channel Intsident Novosibirsk (Incident Novosibirsk) wrote that children began gathering at the spot long before the motorcade passed, some waiting more than two hours. Drivers stopped on a nearby blocked street waited about as long, according to the Telegram channel Govorit NeMoskva (Not Moscow Speaking).
The same video shows that the encounter took place near an empty Teboil gas station where the fuel price board had been switched off. The station had no gasoline at the time, according to the Telegram channel Siberian Express.
The news outlet NDN.Info reported that gas stations charging the highest prices stopped selling fuel on the day of Putin’s visit. Tatneft and Grand, which had sold AI-95 gasoline for 125 and 148 rubles per liter the day before, stopped dispensing fuel; these chains also turned off their price boards at stations along the motorcade’s route. Other gas stations continued operating normally.
A woman who spoke to the independent Russian news outlet Vot Tak claimed that gasoline prices at city gas stations were temporarily lowered for Putin’s visit. Putin’s earlier trips to Irkutsk and Krasnoyarsk were accompanied by temporary drops in gasoline prices.
Novosibirsk residents also complained about traffic jams caused by the road closures. Security forces barred students in Akademgorodok, as well as residents of buildings along the motorcade’s route, from looking out their windows. Eyewitness video shows armed men in camouflage accompanying Putin.
Putin arrived in Novosibirsk in the early hours of August 11 — the fifth city he has visited in the past two and a half weeks, not counting Moscow and St. Petersburg. He had previously traveled to Kazan, Irkutsk, Omsk, Krasnoyarsk, and Ulan-Ude. Before that, he had rarely visited Russia’s regions in months.
Ahead of Putin’s visit, workers hastily repaved roads in Novosibirsk’s city center, laid new sod, and repaired sidewalks and building facades, local residents said.
The Kremlin’s press service often publishes footage of Putin spontaneously chatting with ordinary people during his trips around the country — videos that frequently turn out to be staged.

Fast and fearless: Baltic defence startups innovate to counter Russian threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:48:28 UTC
02:48:28 KST

Fast and fearless: Baltic defence startups innovate to counter Russian threat
As the nature of Russia’s war in Ukraine evolves, Baltic startups are seeking new ways to respond to the hybrid threat from Russia, hoping rapid innovation can have a deterrent effect on Moscow.
One of the lessons of the war in Ukraine is that military technology evolves very rapidly, with the world's first-ever drone war making it harder for conventional armies to make gains on the battlefield.
But they may also herald a new dystopian future, where ordinary civilians become targets of flying objects manned by faraway operators.
Entrepreneurs in Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have taken note.
The Baltic region is already home to several companies that are well known internationally, such as Bolt, Skype and Vinted. Since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, the startup scene has focused on developing defence technologies.
The resulting innovations may be a low-cost and scalable solution to deterring Russian aggression, experts told FRANCE 24.
Faced with technological shifts on the battlefield in Ukraine, “startups tend to be able to equally rapidly develop technologies themselves”, said Tony Lawrence, research fellow at the International Centre for Defence and Security.
“It’s about providing niche solutions that bigger defence primes don’t traditionally have the ability to deal with,” he added.
The startups focus on autonomy – combining AI with hardware, drones and edge computing to operate in environments where GPS or communications have been jammed – as well as domains like software, cybersecurity and electronic warfare.
The Baltic states are quite conscious of their strategic weaknesses in the face of the Russian threat and aware that Moscow has been waging a hybrid war against them for years.
Read moreDrones, sabotage, surveillance: Moscow’s hybrid warfare takes to the high seas
“The whole rearmament process that the Baltic States and NATO in general are going through at the moment is dealing with the potential of a Russian attack on one of the NATO member states, including one of the Baltic states,” said Lawrence.
But the hybrid threat is more of an immediate worry, added Lawrence.
Read moreRussian secret services target Latvia as Ukraine's drone offensive worries the Kremlin
Innovations to counter Moscow
The Baltic states face frequent disinformation and propaganda from Russia. "After Soviet occupation, many people in the region still understand Russian. As a result, it is easier for Russian propaganda to spread its lies,” said Darius Antanaitis, a defence analyst from Lithuania.
One of the most promising AI startups to counter the propaganda is Repsense in Vilnius, according to Antanaitis. “It has developed tools capable of identifying the original sources of propaganda, tracing its dissemination, measuring its impact, and more.”
The company “helps uncover the truth and prevent propaganda from spreading in the future, or perhaps even neutralize it before it spreads”, he said.
Another startup with potential is DefSecIntel based in Tallinn, said Lawrence. The company, which provides surveillance for borders and critical infrastructure protection, helps conceptualize “the hybrid environment and being able to respond to it”.
Faced with a potential US disengagement from its security obligations over the European continent, the Baltic states have massively invested in their defence systems. Lithuania directs more than 5% of its GDP on defence in 2026, the highest share among NATO allies.
Read morePoland prepares to stand its ground with massive new civil defence programme
Yet “not as much money as you would imagine” is trickling down to the startups, said Lawrence. “The three [Baltic] states are spending a lot on defence in GDP terms; but in cash terms, it doesn’t amount to a huge amount. They also have other priorities in terms of conventional armaments, long-range weapons and artillery.”
For startups to be self-sustaining, they must be in the export business, Lawrence explained. “That said, Estonia is encouraging its defence companies more than it did, perhaps, three or four years ago, with various grant schemes that can assist the companies for the domestic market but also for export markets.”
Defence innovation also works in the Baltic states because of the nurturing startup culture that exists there.
A deterrent effect
“The three Baltic states all started from scratch in basically everything when they became independent in the early '90s,” Lawrence said. “That included, particularly in Estonia, e-governance and a digital state. You didn’t have a legacy that it had to maintain. It was starting from scratch. This kind of innovative spirit as to how you might run a state started back then and that kind of culture has been retained.”
Defence also has strong public consensus in the Baltic countries.
“Everybody thinks it’s important and everybody is ready to do their part. Part of that might be finding venture capital to fund startup companies who can make a difference in defence,” he said.
And it is hoped that this sort of rapid innovation will have its own deterrent effect.
Estonia wants Russia to think twice, knowing that it cannot just bring its "war-tested defence technology and use it against Estonia, and expect that Estonia will not have the ability to innovate ... and find countermeasures to what [Russia is] bringing to the game”.

Russia’s Odesa strikes halve Ukraine’s grain export forecast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:47:53 UTC
02:47:53 KST

Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry has cut its forecast for agricultural exports in 2026–2027 by 54% as Russian attacks disrupt shipping through Odesa’s ports, Bloomberg reported.
The ministry now expects 29.6 million tons of agricultural exports, down from 64.4 million. Its wheat export forecast fell by 53%, from 17.6 million tons to 8.3 million tons.
Ukraine grows far more grain than it consumes, exporting 65%–70% of its agricultural output. Bloomberg said the sector generated more than half of Ukraine’s export revenue last year. But Russia’s summer attacks have stalled the sea corridor as the harvest arrives, driving some wheat prices below production costs. Land and river routes cannot match the Black Sea shipping capacity, while sales through neighboring EU states remain politically contested. That leaves farmers with less money for the next sowing and further reduces Ukraine’s export income.
Ukraine has about 59 million tons of grain storage. That storage could be full by early November, leaving the country 11 million tons short of space by the end of fall 2026.
Wheat sells below cost as the silos fill up
Ukraine’s export bottleneck is already hitting its farmers. Port prices fell by another 12-15% in one week, while some farmers sold wheat below production cost. When ships stop, traders either stop buying or pass the higher cost of alternative routes on to producers. That leaves farmers with less cash for fall sowing.
To ease the pressure, the government has approved subsidized loans for agricultural producers. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv would expand storage. Ukraine's Agriculture Ministry has also asked the European Commission for €220 million to help cover interest for small and medium-sized farms.
Ukraine and Moldova are discussing a rail route to Romania’s Constanța port. According to the report, grain was already being redirected through Romania, Slovakia, and Hungary, but these routes cannot replace Odesa’s capacity.
Now the ports and the ships are Russia's targets
The export bottleneck is only part of the problem. Russia’s bombardment also threatens the ports, civilian ships, and crews needed to keep the corridor operating.
The port of Odesa normally handles about 90% of Ukraine’s grain shipments. Russia intensified attacks on terminals and civilian ships in July 2026 as the harvest reached the coast.
On 19 July, three Russian missiles struck the foreign-flagged Golden Leo as it left Odesa carrying corn, killing 10 people, including a Ukrainian sea pilot. Three days later, no vessel passed through the corridor.
Alternative routes offer little relief, as record-low Danube levels were restricting river traffic. Poland continues to bar Ukrainian grain from its domestic market. Those constraints leave more of the harvest inside Ukraine and farmers with less money to plant the next crop.

How viable are Burnham’s plans to free up prison space?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:47:19 UTC
02:47:19 KST

Andy Burnham said on Monday he was “increasingly confident” that PC Andrew Harper’s killers would not be freed in the new year.
Determined to ensure that Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, who were jailed for 13 years in 2020 for manslaughter, serve their full sentences, he has asked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to examine three options for increasing prison capacity.
The options outlined by Burnham are speeding up the deportation of foreign offenders, releasing female prisoners from jail and reviewing indefinite sentences given to “lower-risk” prisoners.
How feasible are they?
Accelerating the deportation of foreign prisoners
There were 10,134 foreign nationals held in prisons across England and Wales at the end of June 2026, according to the most recent Ministry of Justice figures.
Removing them from the UK would therefore be a major political coup for Burnham.
But there are several major obstacles.
Going back to Tony Blair, governments have pledged to clear jails of foreign prisoners, but all have failed.
Andrew Neilson, the director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, said the government would struggle to achieve any immediate relief for the overcrowding crisis by seeking to deport foreign prisoners.
He said: “Reciprocal agreements will have to be drawn up with many of the countries involved and they take time to draw up, and so it does not provide immediate relief to the capacity crisis.”
Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors’ Association, said: “Releasing foreign offenders is difficult because many of them don’t want to go, and quite often they are undocumented. If they have come over on small boats, you do not necessarily know where you might be able to deport them to.
“Many victims will want to see that justice has been served. If someone has been physically attacked or raped by someone from a foreign country which is corrupt, it may well be difficult to guarantee that their attacker’s sentence will be served.”
Emptying women’s prisons and filling them with men
This is an option that has been examined and re-examined by successive governments.
Ministry of Justice officials have been seriously examining schemes to divert female offenders out of jail for more than a year.
Burnham could adopt approaches pioneered by the Greater Manchester authority to steer women away from prison for lower-level offences. These reduced the number being jailed in the region by 55% in eight years.
Turning the biggest women’s prison – HMP Bronzefield in Ashford, Surrey – into a men’s jail would free up more than 500 spaces.
Neilson said: “There should be scope to reduce the number of women in custody, but it is difficult to assess whether Burnham’s plans would work without more detail.”
Wheatley said there would be difficulties in quickly converting women’s prisons so they could hold men.
He said: “Many women’s prisons would not meet the security measures needed for male prisoners.
“For example, some of the prisoner accommodation at HMP Styal is essentially a set of houses within a secure perimeter. The security standards would not meet the requirements needed for men.
“HMP Bronzefield is a newer, secure prison that could be used for men, but it needs to hold women so that women can be brought to London courts.”
Releasing ‘lower-risk’ offenders serving IPP sentences
Imprisonment for public protection sentences were introduced in 2005 for dangerous offenders whose crimes did not warrant a life sentence. They allowed offenders to be detained for a potentially unlimited period until they could prove that they were no longer a threat to the public. If released back into the community on licence, they could be returned to custody.
Although IPP sentences were abolished in 2012, the change was not retrospective, and more than 2,200 people remain in prison despite having served many years beyond their minimum tariff.
Neilson said: “Around 70% of IPP prisoners are in category C or D prisons so the system does not see them as a great risk.
“But identifying them and then putting in place the structures to be able to help people who have been in jail for many years would not be a quick fix.
“People do recognise that people who have been in prison for many, many years will require proper support. It will not free up space immediately.”

Ebola: Over 2,000 dead in DR Congo as virus gathers pace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11

Ebola: Over 2,000 dead in DR Congo as virus gathers pace
August 11, 2026
Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) said on Tuesday that an outbreak of a particularly virulent strain of the Bundibugyo Ebola virus currently raging in the east and northeast of the country has killed more than 2,000 people since the first case was confirmed.
In all, more than 4,380 infections have been recorded.
The current outbreak is the 17th ever recorded in the DRC, with Sania Nishtar of the Gavi global vaccine alliance warning it could become "the largest outbreak ever."
Until now, the worst outbreak recorded in the DRC was the one that took place from 2018 to 2020 when some 3,500 infections led to 2,300 deaths.
The pace of death is gathering momentum this time around, with the virus spreading faster and exhibiting a higher mortality rate than the 2014-2016 West African outbreak — the worst outbreak on record, which logged 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current DRC outbreak was declared on May 15, but health authorities say the first transmissions likely took place in February of earlier still.
The 1,000-death mark was not reached until nine weeks in, now — in just three-weeks' time — that figure has doubled again.
The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is 45.9% compared to 39.6% in the 2014-2016 West African outbreak.
'We haven't reached the peak yet,' says DRC health minister
Though there are vaccines against some strains of the Ebola virus, there are currently none approved for the rare Bundibugyo strain that is spreading across the DRC faster than health authorities can trace it.
Moreover, health authorities face massive logistics challenges due to the volatile security situation in the country, where bad roads and rebel violence coupled with lack of healthcare worker pay and mass strikes make it increasingly difficult to keep tabs on the illness.
"We haven't reached the peak yet," said Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba in an interview shared by the ministry on X. "Within the next three months, we expect to have already brought the spread under control and to start seeing it decline," he added.
Ebola, which is transmitted through physical contact with bodily fluids, causing a hemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past half century.
Authorities in the DRC have placed restrictions on public gatherings as well as closing the airport in Ituri Province, the epicenter of the outbreak. Still, fighting and disease have forced the displacement of masses of people in the DRC, Rwanda and South Sudan.
On Monday, the World Health Organization's (WHO) regional director told reporters that authorities are "chasing the virus… the virus is ahead of us."
What's the latest on bids to treat or vaccinate this Ebola strain?
Clinical trials for two antiviral treatment methods have been ongoing since early July and on Friday the WHO recommended undertaking a full-scale human trial of the Ervebo vaccine.
Although Ervebo has proven effective against the Zaire strain of Ebola, its efficacy in fighting the Bundibugyo strain is unproven. WHO officials are hopeful that it can offer some protection against the DRC strain.
Vaccine alliance Gavi says it has made some 500,000 doses of Ervebo in its stockpiles available for the trial.
Virologists say the new Bundibugyo strain appears to have been transmitted from animals to humans and has changed from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012.
Researchers from Congo, Uganda, Belgium and other countries published findings in the journal Nature Medicine on Monday, suggesting the outbreak began with an animal-to-human transmission event and was then spread between people.
Given the severity of the outbreak, authorities are looking into the possibility that the pathogen may have mutated.
Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa CDC, last week warned that fewer and fewer new cases could be traced back to contacts of existing confirmed patients, with researchers falling well below the WHO's targets of tracking 95% of potential contacts to contain the spread.

The machine reaches a maximum speed of 12 km/h, carries a payload of up to 300 kg, and can tow loads weighing up to 2 tons. It features an operational range of 30 km and can run continuously for 6 hours. In standby mode on a single charge, the system can remain active for up to 72 hours.
In June 2025, the platform was integrated with the Wolly 12.7 combat module carrying a heavy machine gun. Named the Droid Raw 12.7, this vehicle configuration adopted the capabilities of the weapon station, including integration with the 12.7 mm M2 Browning heavy machine gun.
In June 2026, UUT also introduced a version of the Ravlyk ground drone equipped with a combat module featuring the Amulet anti-tank missile system, developed by the Luch Design Bureau.
The anti-tank system is designed to engage both stationary and moving ground targets, including armored vehicles equipped with reactive armor.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian defense technology company WINFLY has unveiled the WINFLY Spider, a reusable interceptor drone designed to neutralize aerial targets using a net and return to its launch point.
Built on the WINFLY 10 Hunter platform, the system can reach speeds of up to 160 km/h and operate at altitudes of up to 5,000 meters.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Novus Ukraine CEO Mark Petkevych stated in an interview with RAU that the destruction of a major distribution hub led to the loss of a significant volume of inventory, which cannot be replaced instantly.

Just hours after the attack, the company transitioned key suppliers to direct delivery models directly to stores and activated backup storage facilities, though overall logistical adaptation remains ongoing.

Online marketplace Rozetka suffered a major blow when its primary fulfillment hub burned down during an overnight attack on August 5.

Over 95% of Ukrainian POWs Face Sexual Violence or Torture in Russian Custody, UN Reports
Former Ukrainian prisoners of war (POWs) and officials have accused Russia of systematically torturing prisoners of war and civilian captives through beatings, electric shocks, and sexual abuse during an informal UN Security Council meeting, Reuters reported on August 11.
Organized by Latvia, the United Kingdom, and Ukraine, the informal Arria-formula session was convened to address Russia’s systematic violations of international humanitarian law, including the abuse of POWs, unlawful civilian detentions, and the coercive recruitment of foreign nationals into Russian forces.
Addressing the meeting, UN Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights Claudia Fuentes Julio stated that monitoring reveals “widespread and systematic” abuse by Russian authorities. The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) has documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian POWs shortly after capture and the deaths of 48 others in custody due to torture or denial of medical care.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Furthermore, UN data shows that over 95% of interviewed Ukrainian prisoners experienced torture or ill-treatment, Reuters wrote.
Fuentes added that more than half also reported sexual violence, including “rape, gang rape, beating while nude, beatings to the genitals, electric shocks to the genitals and nipples, and degrading treatment of a sexualized nature.”
Active Ukrainian soldier Khuan Alberto Levya Garsiya, who survived 1,183 days in captivity, described daily beatings, electrocution, extreme cold exposure, and sexual abuse designed to mentally break detainees. Held in “overcrowded barracks without adequate conditions” in the Donetsk region, where “almost all POWs were ill with dysentery,” and many were starving, Garsiya testified that two of his friends were beaten to death by captors.
Crimean Tatar activist Leniie Umerova similarly recounted being cycled through seven separate detention facilities in what she described as “a carousel of repression,” according to the agency.
Oleg Gushin, representing Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, stated that Kyiv has identified more than 300 detention sites in Russia and occupied Ukrainian territories. While over 9,000 Ukrainians have been returned in prisoner exchanges, thousands remain held incommunicado. Moscow rejected the allegations during the meeting, with Russian Deputy UN Representative Maria Zabolotskaya dismissing the claims as a “disinformation campaign” and alleging that Russian prisoners in Ukraine faced physical and moral abuse, Reuters reported.
While UN monitors also documented instances of ill-treatment against Russian and third-country prisoners held by Ukraine, Fuentes Julio emphasized that those cases occurred on a “fundamentally different scale,” primarily limited to the initial stages of captivity.
In response to the findings, Ukrainian Chargé d’Affaires Volodymyr Pavlichenko urged the international community to increase pressure on Moscow to ensure accountability and secure the release of remaining captives, according to the publication.
These documented abuses extend beyond Ukrainian nationals to foreign captives as well, highlighted by the critical condition of former US Marine Robert Gilman. Imprisoned in Russia since 2022, the 32-year-old was reportedly subjected to torture and injected with mind-altering drugs before being transferred to a civilian psychiatric unit in a “dissociative stupor,” where he now relies on tube feeding.
With Russian authorities barring both US consular officials and Gilman’s mother from visiting him in the hospital, the White House and US State Department have urgently demanded his immediate release for emergency medical treatment in the United States.

Ex-Marine released and returning to US from Russian prison
