EDITORIAL: Energy infrastructure in the AI era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

Taiwan aims to align with global energy trends by proposing to require heavy industrial power users build dedicated power-generation capacity or install energy-storage systems, a critical step in the nation’s efforts to bolster power resilience and safeguard supply stability amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
The legislature’s Economics Committee last week gave preliminary approval to a draft amendment to the Energy Administration Act (能源管理法) that would require large energy users — such as semiconductor companies, data center operators, steelmakers and petrochemical companies — to build on-site power plants or energy-storage systems for new factories or capacity extensions at existing factories. Limited land availability was a major factor in the government’s decision to narrow the amendment’s scope, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said, dismissing environmentalists’ concerns that the change would hinder efforts to optimize power-use efficiency.
In the US, the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge commits leading hyperscalers and AI companies, including Meta and Microsoft, to buy or develop the additional energy generation required for their data centers and to pay for the grid infrastructure, rather than passing that burden on to other energy customers. Comparable, but not identical, constraints are emerging in Ireland and Singapore. The Netherlands tightly restricts hyperscale siting and imposes severe grid-capacity constraints on new projects.
The proposed rules arrive as AI demand causes unprecedented strain on public electricity grids worldwide. Taiwan manufactures the majority of the advanced chips powering AI data centers, and the complex processes and specialized components used to make those chips are highly power-intensive. The nation’s power consumption is expected to grow at an average annual rate of 2.5 percent from this year through 2035, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said in June, much higher than the 1.7 percent average annual growth forecast for the period from last year to 2034. The ministry attributed the change to surging power demand as a result of economic growth, semiconductor industry expansions, data centers and AI, as well as rising temperatures.
Adding to energy concerns, the nighttime reserve margin is expected to remain below the 15 percent benchmark from this year through 2029, falling to 7.1 percent, indicating that electricity supply would be tight, the ministry said, adding that supply pressure has been shifting toward nighttime.
To limit massive power consumption by large data centers, Taiwan Power Co (Taipower) has for nearly three years suspended new power connectors for data centers with capacity of 5 megawatts (MW) or more in Taoyuan and areas to its north. Taoyuan is already home to data centers, including AI facilities, while some are under construction or planned there. The restriction was conditionally eased last month, with some data centers permitted in designated areas. The relaxation came after Taipower added gas-fired units to the Datan Power Plant in Taoyuan’s Guanyin District (觀音), as well as a power plant redevelopment in Keelung.
Details of the proposed energy regulations would remain unclear until implementing regulations are issued, which the ministry said it expects to do within six months of the amendment passing the legislature. Hundreds of companies would be subject to the new rules, the economics ministry said. It said it is considering defining “heavy energy users” based on renewable energy obligations under the Renewable Energy Development Act (再生能源發展條例) and related regulations. In other words, those with Taipower electricity contracts of at least 5MW would be considered heavy power consumers and required to install power plants or energy storage equipment for new factories.
That threshold should be uncontroversial, but local manufacturers have voiced concerns about the size of dedicated energy capacity and how quickly they must meet the requirement. The ministry said it could follow the rules of the Renewable Energy Development Act and request that large power users obtain 10 percent of the 5MW from their own power plants initially and increase the ratio gradually. Additionally, what kind of power plants should they build? All of those considerations need to be factored into their cost structure.
The ministry must work with heavy energy users to establish a feasible schedule, or little would be achieved. Given the costs of power plants, energy storage systems and land acquisition, some companies might consider paying the fines of NT$150,000 to NT$750,000, but repeated fines could add up.
The phrase “at sixes and sevens” refers to being in a state of disarray. How telling it is that the two numbers had a special significance for the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) last week. The TPP was formally established on Aug. 6, 2019. Thursday was its seventh anniversary and it marked the event at the party’s annual national congress meeting in Taichung on Sunday last week. It was also the week that the latest My Formosa public opinion poll was released, showing that the TPP’s approval rating had fallen 6 percentage points since the beginning of the year. The dip in public

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:47 UTC
01:42:47 KST

As the July sun beats down on Taiwan, the heat inevitably pushes us toward lightweight T-shirts. Interestingly, thousands of years ago, the ancient Greeks lived under similar skies and also dressed for the weather.
Around the bright Aegean Sea, the ancient Greeks favored the air circulation and freedom of movement provided by loose clothing. In summer, they preferred breathable linen that felt light against the skin. Clothes were usually made at home by women or household servants. They first wove rectangular lengths of cloth to the required size. Then, with draping, pins and a belt, these plain lengths became elegant, practical outfits.
From this way of wearing cloth emerged three classic styles that are still known today. The first of these was the “chiton,” an everyday tunic, fastened with pins at the shoulders and belted at the waist. Worn by both genders, it was often knee-length for men and ankle-length for women. The “peplos,” a floor-length piece of clothing usually worn by women, had a folded top that created a neat, layered look. For outdoor wear, people added a “himation,” a wide wrap that could offer shade or extra warmth.
Photo: Freepik / 照片：Freepik
However, ancient Greek fashion wasn’t merely about surviving the climate. It reflected deeper cultural values. They valued balance and proportion, so balanced draping reflected their sense of beauty and order. Meanwhile, fabric quality, border designs and skilled draping conveyed social rank. That’s why wealthy citizens wore finer wool and fabrics colored with costly purple dyes, while workers relied on coarser, undyed fabric.
Today, this aesthetic still dominates fashion shows and red carpets. Those flowing goddess-style gowns celebrities love are modern heirs of ancient Greek draped fashion. Ancient Greek clothing teaches us that great style isn’t necessarily about elaboration. In summer especially, with simple fabric and smart draping, suddenly, the heat feels easier to bear.
當七月的太陽炙烤著臺灣時，高溫不可避免地把我們推向輕薄的 T 恤。有趣的是，數千年前，古希臘人生活在相似的天空下，也會因應氣候來穿著。
在明亮的愛琴海周圍，古希臘人偏好寬鬆衣物所帶來的空氣流通和活動自由。在夏天，他們偏好透氣的亞麻布，穿起來輕盈且親膚。衣服通常由女性或家中僕人在家製作。他們先將長方形的布匹織成所需的尺寸。接著，透過垂墜掛法、別針和一條腰帶，這些樸素的布料就變成優雅且實用的服裝。
從這種穿衣方式中出現了三種至今仍為人所知的經典款式。其中第一種是「chiton」，一種日常束腰外衣，在雙肩用別針固定並在腰間繫腰帶。男女都會穿著這種服裝，男款通常是及膝長度，女款則是及踝長度。「peplos」則是一種通常由女性穿著的及地服飾，上方有反折設計，營造出整齊且具層次感的視覺效果。至於外出穿著，人們會加上一件「himation」，它是一種寬大的披巾，可以提供遮蔭或額外的保暖。
然而，古希臘的時尚不僅僅是為了適應氣候。它反映了更深層的文化價值。他們重視平衡與比例，因此平衡的垂褶展現出他們對美與秩序的感知。同時，布料品質、滾邊設計以及精湛的垂褶技藝傳達了社會地位。這就是為什麼富有的公民會穿較細緻的羊毛，以及用昂貴紫色染料染成的面料，而勞動者則依賴較粗糙、未經染色的布料。
如今，這種美學仍然主導著時裝秀和紅毯。那些名人喜愛的飄逸女神風長禮服正是古希臘垂褶時尚的現代傳承。古希臘服裝告訴我們，出色的風格未必需要繁複的設計。尤其在夏天，只要簡單的布料和巧妙的垂褶，炎熱就會頓時變得比較容易忍受。
KEY VOCABULARY
1. inevitably adv. 不可避免地；必然地
If you keep eating junk food every day, you will inevitably gain weight.
如果你每天都吃垃圾食物，你將無法避免變胖。
2. linen n. 亞麻布；亞麻製品
This shirt is made of linen, so it feels cool on hot summer days.
這件襯衫是亞麻布做的，所以在炎熱的夏天穿起來很涼爽。
3. outfit n. 服裝；裝備
Sandra is so fashionable. She always wears the cutest outfits at school.
珊卓真時髦！她在學校總是穿著最可愛的服裝。
4. fasten v. 固定；繫牢
Patty pulled her hair back away from her face and fastened it with a hair clip.
派蒂把頭髮從臉上往後撥並用髮夾固定。

Compal opens new plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:47 UTC
01:42:47 KST

Compal Electronics Inc (仁寶電腦) yesterday said it expects artificial intelligence (AI) servers to account for 30 to 40 percent of revenue next year, up from about 10 percent this year, as it expands production capacity in Taiwan, the US and Vietnam.
In the first quarter, server revenue was NT$10 billion (US$309.8 million), accounting for 5 percent of the company’s revenue, Compal chairman Ray Chen (陳瑞聰) told reporters as the company inaugurated its new plant in Taoyuan.
“We are targeting triple-digit annual growth for our AI-related business this year and next year,” Chen said.
Photo: CNA
The new plant would serve as a key site for Compal’s AI server research, development and production, featuring fully automated production lines for Level 10 (L10) AI server systems and Level 11 (L11) server racks, Chen said.
It should start contributing revenue from next quarter, he said.
Amid strong demand for AI servers, Compal expects the new plant to reach full utilization as early as the second half of next year, Chen said.
The company is evaluating AI server capacity expansion in Taoyuan, although the location and scale have yet to be determined, he added.
Compal’s AI server business remains focused on L10 products, with shipments mainly to neocloud customers such as GMI Cloud and Verda, while L11 shipments are slated to begin next quarter, he said.
Alongside expansion in Taiwan, Compal is increasing AI server capacity in Vietnam and Texas, Chen said.
In Vietnam, where Compal mainly handles Level 6 (L6) server node production, the company operates four surface-mount technology lines and plans to add another six, with construction of its second factory nearing completion, he said.
Compal is building two plants in Taylor and Georgetown, Texas, focused on the production of L6, L10 and L11 models. Trial production is slated to begin next quarter, followed by mass production in the first quarter of next year, Chen said.
The company had planned to ship some L6 products from Vietnam to Texas for assembly, but is adding L6 capacity in Texas as some US customers seek more localized production, he said.
The move would allow Compal to handle production from L6 through L11 rack-level integration in Texas, he said.
The Texas plants would mainly serve US hyperscalers and enterprise customers, while Taiwan primarily serves neocloud customers, Chen said.
The PC industry faces headwinds this year from tight DRAM supply and rising component costs, with International Data Corp forecasting global PC shipments to fall 10 to 12 percent year-on-year.
Chen said DRAM supply is likely to remain tight next year, but rising component costs are pushing up average selling prices, meaning Compal’s PC revenue might not fall at the same pace as shipments.

Two Chinese suspected to have illegally entered Taiwan are being held incommunicado, the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) said yesterday, after a rubber boat was found north of the Port of Taipei last month.
An angler late last month discovered a rubber boat on a beach in New Taipei City’s Bali District (八里), a member of the public wrote on Threads on Monday.
The next day, the angler investigated the boat and discovered that it contained Chinese-made metal oil drums, toilet paper packaging with simplified Chinese characters, an empty soda bottle sold in China and three life jackets, the post said.
Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration
The fisher reported the boat to the authorities, while critics asked why the CGA had not detected it.
The CGA said it dispatched personnel to investigate, while authorities reviewed coastal and maritime surveillance footage.
A court ordered that the two suspects be detained incommunicado and the case has been referred to the Shilin District Prosecutors’ Office.
Since last year, there have been 29 cases of illegal entry into Taiwan involving 71 people, the CGA said.
Sixty-one people in 22 cases were apprehended at the scene, giving the CGA an 85.9 percent apprehension rate, it said.
The CGA said that it has not yet sufficiently upgraded its technological equipment or integrated artificial intelligence systems to identify small targets.
Despite maximizing its workforce and radar sensitivity, it has still been unable to achieve the goal of zero unauthorized entries going undetected, it added.
A CGA task force investigation found that personnel on duty had conducted patrols along the shoreline after the boat came ashore, but overlooked some secluded areas, it said.
The personnel would be held accountable, CGA Director-General Chang Chung-lung (張忠龍) said.

Taitung issues warning on homemade alcohol sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:45 UTC
01:42:45 KST

Alcohol produced at home for personal use cannot be sold for profit, the Taitung County Finance and Economic Development Department said in a reminder to indigenous communities and tourism operators, following complaints that people were allegedly provided with homemade alcohol on paid tours.
During the summer, some indigenous communities in Taitung hold annual harvest festivals, sacred ceremonies to express gratitude and connect with ancestral spirits. Home-brewed alcohol, such as millet wine, plays a vital role in cultural exchange and rituals during the celebrations.
However, homemade alcohol may not be sold or used for commercial purposes under any circumstances, the department said, urging people to be mindful of the regulations while upholding traditions.
Photo: CNA Warning: Excessive consumption of alcohol can damage your health
Under the Tobacco and Alcohol Administration Act (菸酒管理法), people are permitted to brew a limited quantity of alcohol for personal use, up to a combined total of 100 liters of finished and semi-finished products per household annually.
Indigenous tourism has grown in popularity in the past few years, with many businesses offering paid tours that combine cultural activities, ecological tours and traditional experiences, the department said.
In some cases, operators were accused of selling homemade alcohol as part of such activities; such sales fall outside the scope of personal use and could contravene Articles 45 and 46 of the act regarding the production and sale of illegal alcohol, as paid tour programs involve commercial transactions, it said.
Tour operators who wish to provide alcoholic beverages as part of their services should use products manufactured by licensed alcohol producers to protect consumer rights and maintain a lawful business environment, the department said.
While respect for indigenous culture is important in tourism development, the county government hopes to promote indigenous traditional lifestyles as while ensuring market order and consumer safety, department Director Chang Cheng-wen (章正文) said.
Typhoon Dolphin is expected to enter the East China Sea on Saturday and intensify rainfall in western regions over the weekend as the typhoon’s outer circulation sweeps across the sea north of Taiwan, independent meteorologist Daniel Wu (吳德榮) said today. The eastern coast should prepare for extreme heat caused by downslope winds over the weekend, while southwesterly winds from Monday would bring localized heavy rain to the southwest, he said. As Typhoon Dolphin’s outer bands move past northern Taiwan over the next couple of days, northern, central and southern areas would experience showers tomorrow, he said. Rheinmetall Plans to Deliver First Batches of Its Own ATACMS Missiles in 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:45 UTC
01:42:45 KST

German defense contractor Rheinmetall plans to begin production of U.S.-made ATACMS ballistic missiles at its facility in Unterlüs and expects to see the first profits from the project in 2028.
This was announced by the company’s CEO, Armin Papperger, during a conference, according to hartpunkt.
The production line is scheduled to be deployed in 2027, and serial assembly is expected to begin at the end of that same year.
It was previously reported that production of rocket engines and guided missile components at the German facility is planned to begin as early as 2027.
As part of the project, the companies have established a joint venture with the support of the U.S. and German governments, which will serve as a European center for the production, integration, and maintenance of missile systems for the armed forces of NATO countries and allies.
The relocation of production capacity is driven by Lockheed Martin’s need to free up its own assembly lines in the U.S. for the production of the new Precision Strike Missile (PrSM), which is replacing the ATACMS in the U.S. Army’s arsenal.
This decision means the complete relocation of U.S. production of these ballistic missiles to Germany, unlike the production of PAC-2 GEM-T anti-aircraft missiles in Schrobenhausen, where the U.S. production line continues to operate in parallel.
The site in Unterlüsse (Lower Saxony), where Rheinmetall already manufactures 155 mm artillery shells, will also be expanded with a new rocket engine plant, which is scheduled to begin operations in the first quarter of 2027.
Development of the operational-tactical system began in the late 1970s in the U.S. to engage the enemy’s second echelon of troops. The program was launched in 1982 under the name ATACMS.
The missile is approximately 4 meters long and has a diameter of 610 millimeters. Its solid-fuel engine allows the missile to accelerate to speeds exceeding Mach 3 during flight. It is launched from M270 MLRS tracked launchers or M142 HIMARS wheeled systems.
The first version, the MGM-140A Block I, had a range of 128 km and a cluster warhead containing 950 submunitions. The MGM-140B Block IA variant features GPS satellite navigation, a reduced cluster warhead with 275 submunitions, and a range of up to 300 km.
The current version, the MGM-168A Block IA QRU, is equipped with a 230-kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead and has a range of up to 300 km.

Ebola death toll in DR Congo outbreak rises to over 2,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:43 UTC
01:42:43 KST

An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) has killed 2,011 people out of 4,381 confirmed cases of the virus, officials said yesterday.
The latest toll puts it close behind the nation’s deadliest Ebola outbreak in 2018 to 2020 when nearly 2,300 people died out of 3,500 recorded cases.
The Ebola outbreak, which has hit the nation’s conflict-plagued eastern and northeastern regions, was declared on May 15, but is thought to have already been spreading for several weeks.
Photo: AFP
It is the DR Congo’s 17th surge of the highly contagious disease and is already considered the largest in the country’s history “and could well become the largest outbreak ever,” Sania Nishtar, chief executive of the Gavi global vaccine alliance, has said.
The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is estimated by Congolese health authorities to be 45.9 percent.
On Friday, WHO vaccine experts recommended a full-scale human trial of Erbovo, the only existing approved Ebola vaccine, to see if it offered cross-protection against the strain of Ebola currently spreading in the DR Congo against which no specific vaccine exists.
The Ervebo vaccine has proved safe and efficacious against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola virus and WHO experts said that early data, notably from animal trials, showed it might also give some protection against the rare Bundibugyo strain exploding in the DR Congo.
Two potential Bundibugyo vaccines are in the early stages of clinical trials on humans, while a third is being worked on to bring it to that stage.
Ebola is spread by contact with bodily fluids and causes a hemorrhagic fever.

In Lam’s first trip to the country as party chief and president, the two sides pledged to increase trade and investment, and support “resilient supply chains in areas such as critical minerals, semiconductors, clean energy,” they said in a separate statement.
Photo: EPA
The two nations “expressed concern” over the situation the South China Sea and reaffirmed the importance of maintaining peace, security and stability, and freedom of navigation and overflight.
They called for disputes to be resolved peacefully through legal and diplomatic processes, without the threat or use of force.
Australia and Vietnam have expanded maritime-security cooperation in the past few years, as they confront increasing Chinese aggression in the contested waters of the South China Sea. Following a visit to Danang in April, the HMAS Toowoomba trained with Vietnam People’s Navy Ship 275 off the Vietnamese coast, including search-and-rescue and ship-handling exercises.
Among the agreements reached, Vietnam would reinstate access for Australian kangaroo and deer meat, and Melbourne’s RMIT University is to expand its presence in Vietnam, with plans for a new Hanoi campus and broader operations in Ho Chi Minh City.
Two-way trade stands at more than US$14 billion, the Vietnamese government said.
Australia is also a major provider of official development assistance, supporting infrastructure and climate change resilience, it said.
Vietnam and Australia established diplomatic relations in 1973 and upgraded ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership in March 2024.
To mark the visit, Vietnamese budget carrier Vietjet Aviation JSC on Monday announced a new direct service between Ho Chi Minh City and western Sydney, scheduled to start from January next year with two round-trip services per week.
From Australia, Lam heads to New Zealand, the first visit by a Vietnamese president since 2007, where he is expected to focus on trade, investment, technology, agriculture and other areas.

====================================================================================================

Allure of 2028 Olympics draws in old guns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:42 UTC
01:42:42 KST

For those who have competed — or nearly competed — under the Olympic rings, the fear of missing out the next time the Games beckon is real, regardless of the venue, regardless of the sport.
Athletes who try to run it back following a lengthy sabbatical or retirement is hardly new. The list is filled with famous names, from Mark Spitz to Michael Phelps, from Lindsey Vonn to Simone Biles.
Still, the steady drip is becoming more of a torrential flow as Los Angeles 2028 approaches. The pull of the Games combined with the chance to compete at home on the world stage under the white-hot spotlight only the Olympics provide is already proving too tempting to ignore for a generation of American stars who have won medal after medal on seemingly every other continent but their own.
Photo: AP
Track icon Allyson Felix is mounting a return in her early 40s. Six-time Olympic medalist and 2020 Olympic gymnastics all-around champion Suni Lee announced last month she has started training for a shot at her third Games. Two-time Olympic gold medalist Jade Carey is back, winning the vault and finishing fifth in the all-around at the US championships over the weekend.
Asked how much of a factor the chance to compete on American soil played into her decision, Carey just smiled.
“I probably would have gone for it regardless,” said Carey, who will be 28 when the flame is lit at the Coliseum in Los Angeles, “but it does make it a little extra special that it’s in the US.”
Or maybe a lot more special. Oh, and conceivably a lot more lucrative too.
Olympic success at home can be life-changing
The media landscape has shifted dramatically since the 1996 Games in Atlanta. The rise of social media allows athletes to easily tell their stories directly to new audiences, and the ability to create and curate their own brand opens sponsorship opportunities that did not exist a generation ago.
Finding your way onto the medal stand at the Olympics anywhere in the world can make you a hero. Doing it in the US could turn you into a legend. Mary Lou Retton, Mike Eruzione and Kerri Strug know how that goes.
Longtime agent Sheryl Shade, whose list of clients over the last 30 years has included a “who’s who” of Olympians, from gymnasts Nastia Liukin and Shawn Johnson to soccer pioneer Mia Hamm and figure skater Tara Lipinski, called the opportunities for athletes to capitalize on success in Los Angeles “exponentially” greater than any Games that have come before.
“It’s going to be long-range too,” Shade said. “Because now it doesn’t end at the Olympic Games. That’s why LA is so important. This is about legacy.”
Look to “The Magnificent Seven” for proof. Three decades ago, the members of the 1996 US women’s Olympic gymnastics team walked onto the floor of the Georgia Dome for the team final as underdogs. They walked off it with gold medals around their necks, their lives forever altered.
“I mean, we all knew that was going to be special,” team captain Amanda Borden said.
Even if they had no idea how special at the time. While the group, all teenagers that summer, eventually retired and went on with their lives, to this day they get stopped by fans who remember where they were that memorable July night when the injured Strug gingerly stuck her vault landing to secure gold for the US.
They have lived the dream. In some ways, they are still living it. So no, they are not surprised that so many who have “already been there, done that” want to give it another shot.
“I can promise [for] every athlete that makes the team, this Olympics will be one of the greatest moments of their careers,” seven-time Olympic medalist Shannon Miller said.
Her advice to anyone considering it: go for it, even if things do not work out exactly as you planned.
Miller decided less than a year before the 2000 Games in Sydney to give it one final shot at age 23 — considered ancient for a gymnast at the time, although less so now. An injury at the Olympic trials ended that dream. Miller has no regrets, and a quarter century later it is considered a footnote for the most-decorated American women’s gymnast after Biles.
The attempt comes with considerable risk to mental and physical health. For every athlete that makes it, there are countless others that will not. And for those that do, the burden to succeed is ratcheted up to a level they have likely never experienced.
Dominique Moceanu, the youngest member of the Magnificent Seven, described it as a “double-edged sword.”
“You have to understand that it will be probably the biggest moment of your life,” Moceanu said. “Whether it’s because you put it on yourself or you feel the enormity of the weight of the country and the expectations. That does something to people, right?”
It does. Biles brought the discussion around mental health to the forefront of the Games in Tokyo when she removed herself from multiple nights of competition to protect herself while dealing with “the twisties.”
She took time off before returning in 2023, capping the perhaps final chapter of her career — Biles remains noncommittal about her future — by winning a second all-around gold in Paris a year later.
Skye Blakely watched Biles’ triumph from afar after her bid to make the 2024 Olympic team ended when she tore her right Achilles while training at the Olympic trials, three years after her outside shot at making the 2021 squad ended with an elbow injury at the same meet.
That has not stopped her from throwing herself into the mix once again. When describing why she continues to press on, Blakely sounds like so many American athletes across the spectrum — regardless of their resume — who feel the Games’ unique gravitational pull.
“Having a dream is always a risk if you’re going to go after it,” she said before finishing seventh in the all-around at the US championships, her first elite all-around meet in two years. “And I feel like the want for that dream has to be more than being afraid of that risk. And for me it is.”

Fourie back to Springboks  in time for New Zealand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:40 UTC
01:42:40 KST

Three years after his last cap for South Africa and two years after an ACL injury he thought would end his career, Deon Fourie is back in the Springboks.
Fourie, turning 40 next month, was summoned by South Africa on Monday and set to join the squad yesterday in Johannesburg to prepare for the four-match Greatest Rivalry test series against New Zealand starting on Aug. 22.
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was moved to recall Fourie after he rolled back the years for the Stormers in New Zealand’s tour opener in Cape Town on Friday.
Photo: AP
In his first match in 13 weeks, Fourie scored the Stormers’ first try, grabbed two turnovers and amazed Stormers coach John Dobson with three tackles in 15 seconds. Fourie was replaced after an hour with the score 14-14. The All Blacks prevailed 38-21.
Fourie’s value as a hybrid flanker and hooker was “invaluable,” South Africa Rugby said on Monday.
The oldest player to make his Springboks debut at 35 in 2022, Fourie played his 13th and last test in the 2023 Rugby World Cup final against New Zealand in Paris. He replaced hooker Bongi Mbonambi in the opening minutes, injured his shoulder but feared coming off and making South Africa vulnerable in the front row. They won 12-11.
Since then, he has primarily been rehabilitating.
A ruptured ACL sidelined him in 2024 from April to December. An ankle issue followed. Last season he was out from October to March with a bicep injury. In May, a croc roll tackle sent him into knee surgery.
“Over the last two years I’ve had terrible luck with injuries, and I didn’t know whether I’d be able to play this year,” Fourie said at a news conference last week before the All Blacks game.
“I’m definitely raring to go. I’ve been looking forward to this match since it was announced,” he said. “To represent your club, where I’ve spent almost my entire career, against a test side like the All Blacks is such a big occasion. To face the haka is something every little boy dreams of when they start playing rugby.”
He might get another chance in the next month.

China rocket launch fails: reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:40 UTC
01:42:40 KST

A Chinese rocket carrying a communications satellite failed in its launch, state media said, attributing the failure to a “flight anomaly” as reports and videos suggested the spacecraft had exploded in mid-air.
Beijing has plowed billions of dollars into its space program in the past few years to achieve what Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) calls the country’s “space dream.”
Monday’s rare launch failure involved a Long March 7A carrier rocket, which lifted off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China’s southernmost province of Hainan at 8:02pm, state news agency Xinhua said.
Photo: Social Media, Reuters
An “anomaly” occurred when the rocket, which was carrying the Zhongxing-4B communications satellite, was in flight, Xinhua added.
The cause of the failure is under investigation, it said.
Singapore-based broadcaster Channel NewsAsia said in an Instagram post that the rocket had exploded and posted footage from the scene of awestruck crowds watching a fiery ball in the sky.
One video, posted a few hours after the launch by a social media profile in Hainan, showed a rocket exploding into flames about 85 seconds after it blasted off, leaving behind a cloud of gray smoke as debris fell to the ground.
China successfully landed a reusable rocket for the first time last month, its space agency said, marking a major step in its space ambitions and in reducing launch costs.
The country is aiming to land astronauts on the Moon before 2030, a race in which the US is also competing with its Artemis program.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, commenting on a post about Monday’s failed launch on X, said that “rockets are insanely hard.”
“I hope they have a speedy recovery,” he added.
A 4-tonne piece of a SpaceX rocket was believed to have unintentionally crashed into the Moon on Wednesday last week, a collision expected to leave behind a lunar crater.
China’s maiden launch of the Long March 7A from the Wenchang site in 2020 was also unsuccessful after “a malfunction occurred,” Xinhua reported in March that year.
Beijing has quietly confirmed the deaths of two Chinese sailors in a collision in the contested South China Sea, according to government statements nearly a year after the incident. In August last year, a China Coast Guard ship collided bow first with a Chinese naval destroyer while chasing a Philippine patrol boat near the disputed Scarborough Shoal (Huangyan Island, 黃岩島), video footage released by Manila showed. A China Coast Guard spokesperson confirmed at the time that there had been a confrontation, but did not mention the collision, nor injuries or deaths. The Chinese People’s Armed Police Force said on social media on Wednesday

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:40 UTC
01:42:40 KST

Siliconware Precision Industries Co (SPIL, 矽品精密) commenced construction yesterday of a new NT$100 billion (US$3.1 billion) chip-packaging plant in Yunlin County’s Douliou City (斗六) to scale up capacity amid artificial intelligence (AI)-driven supply bottlenecks.
The Taichung-based company plans to offer advanced chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) packaging services at the new plant after it begins first-phase operations in 2028, SPIL vice chairman Chang Yen-chun (張衍鈞) said in a statement.
It would be a new growth engine for SPIL and allow the company to play an indispensable role in the global AI supply chains, Chang said.
Photo courtesy of Siliconware Precision Industries Co
SPIL is a major subsidiary of ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控), the world’s biggest chip packaging and testing service provider, and both have benefited from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (TSMC, 台積電) limited CoWoS capacity amid the AI boom.
The Douliou plant, SPIL’s second advanced packaging facility in Yunlin County, is expected to create 1,300 jobs upon the launch of its first-phase production, with the figure rising to 2,200 jobs after the plant is fully online, the company said.
In September last year, SPIL began operations at its first Yunlin plant in Huwei Township (虎尾).
The new investment would enhance SPIL’s advanced packaging capability and improve the company’s production efficiency and yield, Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said in the statement.
It would elevate and safeguard Taiwan’s position in the global semiconductor supply chains, Kung said.
Over the past two years, SPIL has invested about NT$200 billion in new facilities in Taichung, Changhua County, Yunlin County, Hsinchu City and Tainan, creating 8,000 jobs, the company said.
The company plans to raise NT$16.19 billion by offering 810 million new shares to support its raw material purchases and capacity expansions, with ASE set to subscribe to all of the new shares, SPIL said in filings with the Taiwan Stock Exchange on Monday.

The company, a key supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips to Nvidia Corp, is speaking with prospective advisers to help review the business, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. A potential stake sale could value the facility at about US$3 billion, the people said. Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:42:39 UTC

Sharks coach JP Pietersen has defended his decision to pick All Blacks great Ma’a Nonu to play against New Zealand.
“His name says it all,” Pietersen said on Monday, the day before the Sharks host the All Blacks’ second tour match at Kings Park.
The 44-year-old Nonu arrived at the Sharks only last week primarily to mentor and help develop their younger players. His selection in the reserves for a side without eight senior Springboks and impacted by injuries turned heads, even among the touring All Blacks.
Photo: AP
Local critics jumped on the irony of Nonu coming to help player development while playing in a milestone match at the possible expense of a young Shark.
Pietersen said Nonu was not denying anyone a spot, the midfield choices were limited, and he had to respect what he called “a massive and awesome” occasion as the Sharks host the All Blacks for the first time in 30 years.
“This is our strongest team,” Pietersen said. “It’s great he’s here with us and giving our young boys just a feel of what the All Blacks may give to them. He’s slot in like he was here for a long [time] and the boys love him.”
“It’s going to be an emotional game for Ma’a because it’s the first time he’s playing against the All Blacks,” Pietersen added. “It’ll be awesome to see tomorrow.”
Nonu retired from the All Blacks in 2015 as a two-time World Cup champion with 103 caps. He has continued to play for clubs around the world.
Pietersen, a former Springbok opponent of Nonu’s, has urged his youngish side, which has not played since May 16 and was in preseason training, to “make a memory” to talk about for the next 30 years.
The Sharks include Vusi Moyo, who became the youngest flyhalf in Springboks history at 20 last month in the win against Wales. They have six players from the South Africa A side which beat Zimbabwe 40-0 in June. They had seven but lock Vincent Tshituka withdrew on Monday due to concussion.
“We will not be at 100 percent, at best at 70 or 80 percent, but we’ll give it everything we can,” Pietersen said.
Rain is forecast for the entire match.
The All Blacks beat the Stormers 38-21 in Cape Town on Friday in their tour opener.

A lawyer has been indicted for allegedly fabricating information to help Chinese enter Taiwan under false pretenses, the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office said yesterday, citing potential threats to national security.
Chen Chen-wei (陳振偉), a lawyer who owned an immigration consulting agency, and others drew up false business plans to secure permits from the National Immigration Agency (NIA) for four Chinese nationals to enter Taiwan in 2023 and 2024, prosecutors said.
Instead of visiting Taiwan for business purposes, three of the Chinese were in Taiwan to apply for Belizean passports at the Central American country’s embassy in Taiwan, prosecutors said.
Photo: Wu Sheng-ju, Taipei Times
Chen’s group was paid US$80,000 to help applicants secure Belizean passports, the indictment said.
The actions contravened the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (臺灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例), it said.
The act stipulates that before Chinese citizens travel to Taiwan on business, the organization in Taiwan that has invited them must apply for entry permits on the NIA Web site and provide supporting documents, including proof of employment, a guarantee, power of attorney, a business-related activity plan and itinerary and a copy of the contract, as well as the inviting organization’s company registration form and its corporate income tax return for the previous year, it said.
However, Chen’s group used their individual company seals to create fraudulent business plans and itineraries, while falsifying other documents to submit to the NIA Web site, the indictment said.
The allegedly fake documents enabled Chinese nationals identified as Zhu Naixian (祝乃賢) and Sun Tao (孫濤) to secure entry permits from the NIA and enter Taiwan in 2023, and another Chinese citizen named Lu Tao (陸濤) to gain entry into Taiwan in 2024, prosecutors said.
Another Chinese citizen allegedly involved in the scheme, Li Fengxiang (李鳳祥), was denied entry in 2023, as he is a former member of China’s National People’s Congress, prosecutors said.
While all of the members of Chen’s group were indicted, prosecutors singled out Chen, saying that his alleged actions undermined the NIA’s border management and created potential national security loopholes.
They recommended a heavy sentence for Chen.

Revamp to replace Taipei station’s iconic floor tiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:37 UTC
01:42:37 KST

Shin Kong Mitsukoshi Department Store Co’s plan to invest at least NT$1 billion (US$30.98 million) to renovate commercial and public spaces at Taipei Railway Station would involve removing the iconic black-and-white flooring in the main hall, the company said yesterday.
In April, Shin Kong Mitsukoshi, the nation’s largest department store chain, was selected as the new contractor to manage the station’s commercial area. Breeze Center was the previous operator.
Shin Kong Mitsukoshi took over commercial operation at the station on July 25.
Photo: Huang Yi-ching, Taipei Times
The rehabilitate-operate-transfer project would be carried out in phases over the next two years and eight months, Shin Kong Mitsukoshi executive vice president Wu Hsin-chang (吳昕昌) said at an event at Regent Taipei to mark the beginning of the renovation.
The renovation aims to update the station’s image, enhance its food and shopping offerings, promote international tourism, create public-interest spaces, improve safety and introduce artificial intelligence technologies, he said.
“As more than 600,000 people access Taipei Railway Station daily, our vision is that it should serve as a ‘window to the world,’ allowing international tourists to see Taiwan and railway travelers to see the world,” Wu said. “We will introduce a wide variety of products and enrich the decor with Taiwanese culture and art.”
Photo: CNA
He also confirmed that the station’s signature black-and-white flooring in the lobby would be removed, and lighting in the lobby would be changed as well.
Under Shin Kong Mitsukoshi’s initial plan, food and beverage businesses would occupy less than 70 percent of the commercial area and include international restaurant chains, as well as eateries serving Taiwanese cuisine.
The remainder would be devoted to everyday services for passengers and visitors.
A 600-inch LED screen would be installed in the main lobby to show videos highlighting Taiwan’s culture and natural scenery, Wu said, adding that it would broadcast international competitions featuring Taiwanese athletes.
A new station clock would be placed in the lobby, serving as a new landmark, he said.
The renovation would add kiosks at each floor, some of which would feature AI services, emergency equipment and call buttons, drinking-water facilities and ATMs, Wu added.
The bathrooms would be renovated as well, and outfitted with a system to issue an alert if a passenger remains in a stall for more than 30 minutes, he said.
To facilitate access for people with limited mobility, the contractor plans to build elevators from the first underground floor to the second floor, Wu said, adding that it would discuss the feasibility of that change with Taiwan Railway Corp (TRC).
Currently, passengers using elevators must transfer on the first floor to travel between the first basement floor and the second floor.
Part of the commercial area would be reserved for showcasing artists.
TRC chairman James Jeng (鄭光遠) said that the railway company would work closely with Shin Kong Mitsukoshi to ensure that at least 70 percent of the commercial area remains operational during construction.
Wu said that TRC, Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp and Taipei Rapid Transit Corp would need to work together to maintain safety during the renovation.
“During the renovation, construction and passenger traffic will be completely separated to ensure the safety of both workers and passengers,” he said.

AUSTRALIA
Birds to get flu vaccine
Authorities yesterday said they would vaccinate bird species deemed to be especially vulnerable to the highly contagious H5 bird flu virus. The country was for years the only continental landmass free of the H5 strain. The first domestic case was discovered in a migratory sea bird in June and last week the government reported its first mass mortality event in wildlife. Officials said they would roll out targeted vaccinations for captive and wild species. “It is difficult to vaccinate birds in the wild — it does take two vaccination doses to vaccinate birds,” Minister for the Environment and Water Murray Watt said. “Where it is possible to vaccinate wild birds, we will do so, but the priority is to vaccinate birds that are in captivity.”
SWITZERLAND
World disaster losses fall
Economic losses from natural catastrophes worldwide are estimated to have reached US$100 billion in the first half of the year, reinsurance group Swiss Re said in a report yesterday, a sharp decline from a year earlier. Despite severe storms in the US and the deadly earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June, the losses were well below the US$152 billion recorded in the first half of last year, it said. The losses were also 10 percent below the 10-year average for the period. However, losses from natural disasters often increase in the second half of the year, mainly due to hurricanes in the North Atlantic ocean, Swiss Re said. “A less costly first half of the year does not mean the risk has gone away,” said Balz Grollimund, the group’s director of Catastrophe Perils. “One major hurricane, earthquake or wildfire can quickly change the picture.” Severe heat across Europe since June has sparked an early wildfire season in France and Spain that has already destroyed thousands of homes and businesses as well as infrastructure. “Wildfire risk has so far accounted for only a relatively small share of insured losses in Europe. Yet it is the fastest-growing weather peril globally,” the company said.
THAILAND
PM suspends gun licenses
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul yesterday suspended the issuance of permits to buy firearms and said existing licenses would be reviewed, days after a 14-year-old gunman killed nine people. Anutin directed a deputy prime minister overseeing legal affairs to expedite a new gun control law, with stronger controls and significantly harsher penalties. Police were ordered to stop renewing permits that enable people to buy firearms. Registered firearms must be kept at home and cannot be carried in public, Anutin said, reiterating the current law. For illegal firearms, studies are under way to enact legislation requiring their return to the state within a specified period, he said.
SOUTH AFRICA
14 miners found dead
A rockfall at an illegal mine northwest of Johannesburg killed 14 clandestine miners, most of them from Lesotho, police spokeswoman Colonel Adele Myburgh said yesterday. Thousands of unregistered miners known as “zama zamas” operate in the nation, scavenging abandoned mines for gold and other minerals in arduous and often perilous conditions. “Eight others were hospitalized and an unknown number of illegal miners are currently possibly stuck under the ground. Police are on the scene, and the scene is still active,” Myburgh said in a statement. Officials were headed to the site of the disaster at Nkaneng, near the town of Rustenburg, in North West Province. The incident was reported late on Monday.

A China Coast Guard spokesperson confirmed at the time that there had been a confrontation, but did not mention the collision, nor injuries or deaths. Electronics overtime hits monthly record for June
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:34 UTC
01:42:34 KST

Overtime hours at Taiwan’s electronics companies hit their highest level for June since records began in 1980 as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom continues to drive demand, data released on Monday by the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) showed.
Employees in the electronic components industry worked an average of 28.7 hours of overtime in June, far beyond the national average of 9.1 hours across the industrial and service sectors, the DGBAS said.
Average overtime in the computer and optoelectronics industry also reached a record high for June at 17.7 hours, the highest since 1980, the data showed.
Photo: Huang Shu-lei, Taipei Times
The DGBAS said sustained global enthusiasm for AI has driven a surge in orders received by technology companies, prompting employers to rely heavily on overtime. It said that overtime hours are often a barometer of activity in the sector.
In June, average overtime in the manufacturing sector stood at 18.0 hours, up 0.5 hours from a year earlier, but down 0.3 hours from May. Across the industrial and service sectors, average overtime was 9.1 hours, up 0.5 hours year on year but down 0.2 hours from the previous month, the agency said.
For the first half of the year, average overtime nationwide stood at 9.1 hours, up 0.4 hours from a year earlier, while average overtime in the manufacturing sector rose 0.8 hours year on year to 17.8 hours, it said.
Employment in Taiwan’s industrial and service sectors was 8.58 million at the end of June, up 10,000, or 0.12 percent, from the end of May. Manufacturing reported the largest monthly increase, adding 4,000 jobs, the DGBAS said.
Within manufacturing, employment trends varied in June: The number of workers in the electronic components industry rose 0.6 percent from a month earlier and the number of employees in the computer and optoelectronics industry rose 0.27 percent, while employment in the rubber and plastics products industry fell 0.37 percent and employment in the plastics industry declined 0.13 percent, the data showed.
DGBAS Census Department Deputy Director-General Tan Wen-ling (譚文玲) said employment declines in some traditional industries indicated that conditions in those sectors needed time to improve.

Taiwan slams China’s typhoon tactics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:34 UTC
01:42:34 KST

China’s use of typhoon disaster prevention as a pretext to exercise traffic control over vessels in the Taiwan Strait was unacceptable, the Maritime and Port Bureau said in a statement on Monday.
The bureau issued the statement after China’s Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration on Thursday last week unilaterally said that it would enforce traffic controls over northbound vessels in the Taiwan Strait due to Typhoon Dolphin.
The bureau said that following the Chinese announcement, it had immediately issued maritime safety notices via coastal radio and maritime safety centers to inform vessels operating near Taiwan that the Taiwan Strait is international waters.
Photo: AP
Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), China has no right to exercise any form of control or jurisdiction over waters around Taiwan, the bureau said, urging vessels in the area to disregard China’s maritime traffic control requests and independently seek safe waters to shelter from the storm.
Ahead of the issuance of the Chinese announcement, the bureau had broadcast disaster-prevention alerts through multiple channels, including news releases, coastal radio and the automatic identification system, to warn vessels operating in waters near Taiwan, it said.
It also activated a clearance measure for a 12 nautical mile (22.2km) coastal security zone on Thursday last week, urging vessels in the designated areas off northern and eastern Taiwan to leave the zone and seek shelter farther offshore, it said.
It coordinated with the Coast Guard Administration to carry out vessel-evacuation operations, it said, adding that all vessels were clearly informed that those remaining in the restricted zone could be prohibited from entering Taiwan’s commercial ports, as stipulated in the Commercial Port Act (商港法).
As a result, no maritime incidents were reported while Dolphin passed through waters near Taiwan, it said.
The Republic of China (Taiwan) has legally recognized sovereign rights to the area under the UNCLOS and has the authority to implement maritime traffic control measures for vessels, the bureau said.
The Taiwan Strait is international waters and, as stipulated in the UNCLOS and other international rules, the principle of freedom of navigation applies beyond territorial waters, it said.
China has no right to impose traffic controls on Taiwanese or foreign vessels in such waters, the bureau said.
The Coast Guard Administration and the Mainland Affairs Council issued similar statements condemning the Chinese announcement.
A US Department of State spokesperson on Monday told the Central News Agency that “the United States opposes any actions that interfere with the freedoms of navigation and overflight applicable in the Taiwan Strait.”
Late last month, the China Coast Guard said it had launched “routine law-enforcement patrols” in waters east of Taiwan.
The State Department at the time said it was concerned about China’s actions, adding that Taiwan has peacefully administered the waters for more than 70 years.
China’s claims of jurisdiction over the waters would only heighten tensions, it said, calling on Beijing to stop pressuring Taiwan.

Diplomatic lessons in Nagasaki
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

Three days can reveal a great deal about diplomacy.
Representative to Japan Lee I-yang (李逸洋) on Thursday last week attended the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Ceremony, seated in the area for diplomatic representatives. Three days later, he declined to attend the Nagasaki ceremony after the Taiwanese delegation was placed outside the main diplomatic section.
Nagasaki officials said that seats in the special guest area were limited and that Taiwan had been assigned to an “overseas” section, which was not intended to downgrade Taiwan’s status.
From Taipei’s perspective, the question was difficult to avoid: If Hiroshima could accommodate Taiwan alongside diplomatic delegations, why could Nagasaki not do the same?
Lee’s decision to stay away was understandable. After Taiwan raised objections to a similar arrangement last year, accepting it again could gradually turn an unsatisfactory practice into precedent.
Yet the incident deserves to be examined beyond the immediate dispute over diplomatic dignity.
Anyone familiar with Japan knows that Tokyo is not Japan in its entirety. Japanese politics is strongly shaped by local institutions, administrative traditions and jimoto — the deeply rooted sense of local identity and community. Mayors, prefectural governors, local assemblies, bureaucracies, business organizations and civic groups have networks and political calculations of their own.
This does not mean that local governments in Japan can act independently on national foreign policy issues. Nor should every unfriendly decision toward Taiwan be attributed to Chinese pressure.
It does mean that stronger Taiwan-Japan relations in Tokyo do not automatically produce equally strong relations throughout Japan.
Nagasaki illustrates the problem particularly well.
The city has centuries of historical connections with China and has maintained a friendship-city relationship with Fuzhou since 1980. China also maintains a consulate-general in Nagasaki. Such relationships do not prove that Beijing instructed Nagasaki officials how to arrange Taiwan’s seat.
Indeed, the more important point might be that direct instructions are not always necessary.
Diplomatic influence accumulates through institutions, personal relationships and repeated exchanges. Officials learn which decisions create friction and which preserve established relationships. Political preferences can eventually become embedded in seemingly technical administrative choices.
For Taiwan the lesson should not simply be to protest more forcefully. It should be to invest more seriously in Japan’s local diplomacy.
Former representative to Japan Frank Hsieh (謝長廷) understood this particularly well. During his years in Japan, considerable effort went into relationships not only with national politicians in Tokyo, but also with prefectures, municipalities, local assemblies and civic networks. Taiwan-Japan exchanges among local legislators and governments expanded significantly during this period.
Such work is rarely glamorous. A meeting with a mayor or local assembly member attracts less attention than a photograph with a prime minister. Yet diplomacy is often built precisely through these accumulated relationships.
Taiwan needs to map Japan more carefully: Where are Taiwanese networks strong? Where has China spent decades cultivating local relationships? Which municipalities matter because of ports, technology, education, tourism, disaster relief or their proximity to Taiwan?
Where those connections are weak, Taiwan needs to show up — repeatedly.
Invite local politicians to Taiwan. Expand university and youth exchanges. Build partnerships in disaster relief, public health and maritime affairs. Engage chambers of commerce, civic organizations and local media.
The objective is not to force every Japanese municipality to become “pro-Taiwan.” That would misunderstand diplomacy and Japan.
The objective is to ensure that when local officials encounter Taiwan, they see an established partner rather than an inconvenient diplomatic exception.
Defending dignity sometimes requires refusing a seat.
Good diplomacy means building relationships so that, eventually, there is no need to refuse one.
Bonnie Yushih Liao is an assistant professor in Tamkang University’s Department of Diplomacy and International Relations.

The issue of Morocco halting its visa confirmation letter application service for Taiwanese is being negotiated, while visa suspensions and entry bans for residents of Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) would be reassessed at the end of this month, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) said yesterday.
Department of West Asian and African Affairs Director-General Yen Chia-liang (顏嘉良) said the Moroccan government on July 20 instructed its embassies and consulates worldwide to stop processing visa confirmation letter applications from Taiwanese seeking to travel to Morocco.
Taiwanese are required to obtain the letter before traveling to the north African nation.
Photo: Huang Ching-hsuan, Taipei Times
Based on the principle of reciprocity, Taiwan on July 30 suspended processing of visa applications from Moroccan nationals, aside from special approved cases, Yen said.
There are four main situations in which special approval is considered — family visits, study, diplomatic or official business and medical treatment, Yeh added.
Asked why Morocco had changed its policy, Yen said the reason is unclear.
It is not solely Taiwanese nationals who need a visa confirmation letter to travel to Morocco, so the policy might not be specifically targeted at Taiwan, he said.
However, the ministry would stay in contact with Moroccan authorities through multiple channels, including by asking like-minded countries to help gain an understanding of the situation to hopefully solve the issue swiftly, he said.
“The ministry urges the Moroccan government to maintain convenient travel arrangements for people from both sides and restore normal non-governmental exchanges as soon as possible,” he added.
In other matters, the ministry recently received reports of two cases of Taiwanese whose passports were seized by immigration officials and denied entry when they arrived at Entebbe International Airport in Uganda, Yeh said.
The ministry is aware of the situation in the African nation and offered prompt assistance, he said, adding that one of the Taiwanese has left Uganda, while the other is awaiting an outcome.
“Our preliminary understanding is that the decision by Ugandan officials is associated with our government on June 2 suspending visa issuances and entry for Ugandan nationals due to an Ebola outbreak,” Yen said.
The conditions also apply to DRC passport holders.
However, the ministry does not rule out the possibility that the Ugandan government has adjusted its policy for Taiwanese in accordance with its “one China” policy, he said.
Taiwan’s representative office in Somaliland would continue to negotiate with Ugandan officials on the matter, and it will provide necessary assistance and care to Taiwanese nationals, he added.
The ministry and the Ministry of Health and Welfare would hold meetings to re-evaluate the pause on visa issuances and entry for residents of Uganda and the DRC at the end of the month, Yen said.
People planning to travel should assess the visa polices of their destination countries before departure and call the foreign ministry’s emergency hotline it they face critical situations abroad, he said.

====================================================================================================

Mine strategy needs an exit plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:28 UTC
01:42:28 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) on Thursday last week stood at a loading area at the Port of Taipei to watch soldiers from the army’s 53rd Engineer Group rehearse mine deployment. The demonstration, staged on the second day of the annual Han Kuang exercises, was meant to signal that Taiwan takes mine warfare seriously. It did. It also raised a question that no public drill has yet answered: If Taiwan can close its ports with mines, can it reopen them?
The logic behind Taiwan’s mine investments is sound. Defensive mines would complicate an amphibious assault by forcing the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Navy to slow down, sweep channels and absorb losses before any landing craft reaches shore.
The Republic of China (ROC) Navy’s Min Jiang-class minelayers, four of which entered service in January 2022, are purpose-built for rapid coastal mining. Six more are on order, with the fleet expected to reach 10 vessels by next year. Each ship can carry 32 to 64 mines per sortie, depending on the type deployed. At full strength, 10 minelayers conducting two sorties each could sow between 640 and 1,280 mines across the approaches to Taiwan’s major harbors — a meaningful obstacle for any invasion fleet.
However, minelaying is the easy half of the mine-warfare cycle. The hard half — mine clearance, hydrographic charting of mined areas, command-and-control coordination, deconfliction with friendly naval forces and reopening ports once the immediate landing threat recedes — has received far less investment and virtually no public exercise time.
Taiwan’s mine countermeasures fleet tells the story. The ROC Navy operates four Yung Feng-class minehunters built in Germany in 1991, and two Yung Jin-class minehunters acquired secondhand from the US. These vessels are capable of limited coastal mine clearance under permissive conditions: calm seas, no hostile fire and known minefields. None are equipped to handle rocket-rising mines, smart mines with anti-sweep features or mines with target-discrimination algorithms.
There is no replacement on the horizon. The NT$35.85 billion (US$1.11 billion at the current exchange rate) Ching Fu contract to build a new class of minehunters collapsed in a corruption scandal in 2017. Nine years later, no successor program has been announced.
Taiwan is an island economy, and mines do not discriminate between enemy warships and friendly merchant vessels. The Port of Kaohsiung handles more than 60 percent of Taiwan’s container throughput. If Taiwan mines its own port approaches to deny a PLA amphibious force — and it should — it must also be able to clear safe channels for its own navy to sortie, for allied reinforcements to arrive and for commercial shipping to resume before stockpiles of fuel, food and ammunition run dry.
The current posture creates a strategic paradox: A mine barrier designed to buy time could become a self-imposed blockade if clearance capacity cannot keep pace with deployment.
Some observers might say this problem is secondary. If mines prevent a successful PLA landing, the war is won regardless of port access. That assumption collapses under scrutiny. A cross-strait conflict is unlikely to end with a single repelled assault. It would be a sustained campaign in which logistics, resupply and the ability to receive external support determine the outcome as much as any beach defense.
A Taiwan that cannot reopen its own ports after mining them is a Taiwan that cannot be resupplied — and a Taiwan that cannot be resupplied is a Taiwan that loses slowly instead of quickly.
There is also a command-and-control dimension that the Han Kuang exercises have yet to test publicly. Would Taiwan’s political leadership authorize mining operations before the first shots are fired? Pre-conflict mining is vastly more effective than mining under fire, but it also risks escalation. If the answer is that mines would only be deployed after hostilities begin, then the exercises should simulate contested deployment — minelayers operating under air and missile attack, with the PLA’s reconnaissance satellite constellation tracking every naval movement in the Taiwan Strait.
The Han Kuang drills should test the full mine-warfare cycle, not just the deployment phase that Lai observed last week.
Three priorities stand out.
First, the exercises should simulate mine clearance under combat conditions — contested waters, degraded communications and the assumption that some of Taiwan’s own mine countermeasures (MCM) vessels would be damaged or destroyed before they can begin clearing.
Second, Taiwan needs a credible timeline for MCM fleet modernization. Every year without a replacement program is a year in which Taiwan’s ability to reopen its own ports after mining them erodes further.
Third, mine-warfare authorization protocols should be exercised under realistic political conditions. The question of when to mine — before an attack, during an attack or after a landing has begun — is not purely military. It requires coordination between the Presidential Office, the Ministry of National Defense and naval fleet commanders that is best rehearsed in advance rather than improvised under fire.
Lai’s visit to the Port of Taipei demonstrated that Taiwan understands the value of laying mines. The harder question is whether it has a plan for lifting them. A mine that cannot be cleared is not a weapon. It is a wall — and walls work in both directions.
Ethan Connell is an assistant director at the Taiwan Security Monitor and a graduate student at George Mason University’s Schar School of Policy and Government.

Trump vaccine order sparks WHO warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:27 UTC
01:42:27 KST

The WHO yesterday defended the science-based process used to determine childhood immunisation schedules after US President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccinations in the US.
Trump on Monday signed an executive order calling for a reduced childhood vaccination schedule of 11 immunizations.
‘GOLD-STANDARD’
Photo: AFP
He said the move would provide US children with “gold-standard” protection and align the US more closely with other developed countries that recommend fewer shots.
Vaccine experts say that other developed countries that may recommend fewer shots face different disease risks and have different healthcare systems.
The order advances a long-standing objective of US Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr, who has questioned vaccine safety and promoted claims linking vaccines to autism even though scientific studies and public health authorities have found no evidence of a link.
WHO spokesperson Tarik Jaarevi told a press briefing in Geneva that vaccination recommendations were based on more than 60 years of research by the global body, national authorities and independent expert groups.
The timing of individual vaccines was determined through extensive scientific review of when people were most vulnerable to particular diseases and the development of the immune system, Jaarevi told reporters in Geneva.
EXPERTS’ ADVICE
Jaarevi said countries typically relied on national immunization technical advisory groups made up of multidisciplinary experts who provided independent, evidence-based recommendations to governments and vaccination program managers.
Those groups draw on guidance from the WHO’s Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization when establishing national schedules, he said.
“What comes out from WHO is science-based,” Jaarevi said.
“We hope that all countries will use this best scientific evidence that we have.”
Trump’s executive order has drawn criticism from medical associations, public health experts and vaccine manufacturers, who say there is no new scientific evidence to justify the changes, and that the existing US schedule reflects decades of evidence and the specific health needs of Americans, rejecting the comparison to other countries.
Physicians have warned that reducing the number of recommended vaccinations could leave more children vulnerable to preventable diseases and create confusion among parents about when children should be immunized.
SEPARATE MMR SHOTS
The Trump order also recommends separating the combined measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine into three individual injections.
Vaccine maker Merck has said there is no published scientific evidence showing a benefit from splitting the shot and warned that requiring separate visits could increase the risk of delayed or missed vaccinations.

Fintech, stablecoin can help speed up AI supply chains: Industry leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:25 UTC
01:42:25 KST

Financial technology (fintech), including stablecoins, could help accelerate the movement of funds across global semiconductor and artificial intelligence (AI) supply chains, allowing manufacturers to operate more efficiently, industry leaders said yesterday.
Speaking at a news conference in Taipei ahead of the second edition of the Asia FinTech Alliance (AFA) Summit, AFA chairwoman Jaclyn Tsai (蔡玉玲) said Taiwan is the "heart" of semiconductor and AI server manufacturing, and that faster production must be matched by faster financial transactions.
"We cannot just move goods around quickly. We have to move the money quickly as well," she said, adding that fintech could improve supply chain efficiency and strengthen the competitiveness of manufacturing economies.
Photo: CNA
Echoing Tsai, Etron Technology Inc chairman Nicky Lu (盧超群) said speed is critical for technology companies operating across different time zones, where banking and settlement hours could delay transactions.
"How quickly can we pay? How quickly can we receive?" Lu said, adding that financial delays could affect production, deliveries, suppliers and customers across several countries when transactions are held up by banking cut-off times.
"In Taiwan, 3:30 in the afternoon is like a cut-off point for everything about semiconductors. We have to wait for the next day," Lu said, referring to the afternoon transaction cut-off observed by many local banks.
He said the financial infrastructure supporting global technology supply chains therefore needs to become faster while maintaining "security, reliability, and resiliency."
During a Q&A session, Tsai said emerging technologies including AI, blockchain and virtual assets could offer new tools to improve manufacturing and supply chain efficiency.
She said regulatory approaches across Asian economies are also becoming more aligned, creating opportunities for greater interoperability in areas such as stablecoins and cross-border payments.
Stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value, typically by being pegged to a fiat currency such as the US dollar. The Legislative Yuan passed the Virtual Asset Services Act (虛擬資產服務法) on June 30, establishing Taiwan’s first legal framework governing stablecoin issuance.
Tsai said the framework could allow both New Taiwan dollar and foreign currency-backed stablecoins, although there has yet to be a decision on which type would be more widely issued.
Pointing to their potential use in supply chains, Tsai said a Taiwanese company could, for example, receive a US dollar-backed stablecoin from an overseas customer and convert it into a NT dollar-backed stablecoin to pay suppliers, employees and other expenses.
Stablecoin payments, which could help make cross-border transactions faster by providing a "new rail" for settlement alongside traditional payment systems, are "very likely" to become more common as early as next year, not only in Taiwan but also in other countries, she added.
Founded in 2023, AFA brings together fintech associations from 16 Asian economies, with one association from each, and promotes cross-border collaboration, regulatory dialogue and financial innovation.
The inaugural AFA Awards will be held in Taipei on Sept. 1, followed by FinTechOn 2026 and the second edition of the AFA Summit on Sept. 2-3, with a focus on virtual asset and fintech regulation, global supply chains, cross-border payments and AI.

Exclusive: Qaani holds secret Iraq talks on militias and Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:40:28 UTC
01:40:28 KST

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Qaani in secret Iraq visit as Baghdad seeks Hormuz guarantees
The commander of Iran’s Quds Force made an unannounced visit to Baghdad on Monday, carrying a message to Iran-aligned armed groups to avoid confrontation with Iraqi security forces as the government faces a looming deadline to bring weapons under state control.
Brig Gen Esmail Qaani held a series of separate meetings with senior figures in Iraq’s Shia Coordination Framework and leaders of armed factions during the hours-long visit, according to sources familiar with the talks who spoke to The New Arab.
But the discussions extended beyond the increasingly fraught question of the factions’ weapons. Iraqi officials also used the meetings to press Tehran for firm guarantees that Iraqi oil tankers would be allowed to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the sources said, as mounting financial pressures begin to weigh on Baghdad’s ability to meet its obligations, including public-sector salaries.
The request underscores Iraq’s precarious position as it tries to insulate its economy and domestic politics from a widening regional confrontation while navigating its close relationship with neighbouring Iran.
At the centre of Qaani’s visit was one of Iraq’s most politically sensitive issues: the government’s effort to establish a state monopoly over arms.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government has set 30 September as the deadline for Iran-aligned factions to hand over their weapons, however the process has so far produced little visible evidence of disarmament.
According to the sources, Qaani urged faction leaders to avoid any armed confrontation with Iraqi security forces, amid concerns that Baghdad could resort to tougher measures, including force, if groups refuse to comply.
But Qaani gave no indication that Tehran had accepted the demand for the factions to surrender their weapons. Instead, he portrayed the disarmament push as driven by American pressure, the sources said.
He also stressed the importance of preserving the factions’ military capabilities in the face of what he described as growing US threats against the Iran-led regional alliance known as the “Axis of Resistance”.
The message appeared to reflect the difficult balance Tehran is seeking to maintain in Iraq: protecting the armed groups that have long formed an important pillar of Iranian influence while preventing a confrontation that could pit those factions against the Iraqi state or US forces.
Hussein al-Asaad, an expert on strategic affairs, said Qaani’s personal intervention showed how seriously Tehran viewed the debate over the future of Iraq’s armed factions.
“The Iranian intervention in this issue is not new, but the presence of the Quds Force commander personally in Baghdad at this stage sends a message that Tehran considers the factions’ weapons a strategic issue affecting its influence and interests in Iraq,” Asaad told The New Arab.
Iran, he said, appeared to be seeking a compromise under which the factions would avoid fighting Iraqi forces without entirely surrendering their military capabilities.
Such an arrangement could involve reorganising the factions’ relationship with state institutions while preserving some of their influence, he added.
The stakes have risen as the September deadline approaches. Despite government claims that some groups have already begun handing over weapons, no images of arms being transferred have been made public, including by factions that have said they are prepared to comply.
The government has also not disclosed what types or quantities of weapons have been surrendered, or issued detailed statements documenting the process.
Several of Iraq’s largest and most heavily armed factions continue to resist the demand, raising questions over what Baghdad intends to do if they refuse to comply.
During a visit to Washington in mid-July, Zaidi said after meeting US President Donald Trump that some factions had already surrendered “many weapons” and that after 30 September there would be no need for any armed factions to remain.
He provided no further details.
Asaad warns that the dispute could move from political negotiations to confrontation on the ground if no agreement is reached.
Iranian calls to avoid clashes could reduce that risk, he said, but they should not be interpreted as Tehran accepting the complete disarmament of its Iraqi allies.
“Iraq faces a real test of its sovereignty and its ability to make security decisions free from the influence of outside powers, whether Iran or the United States,” he said. “The decision to place weapons exclusively in the hands of the state must be an Iraqi decision.”
For Baghdad, however, the dispute over weapons is unfolding alongside a more immediate economic concern.
During Qaani’s meetings with political leaders, Iraqi officials sought what the sources described as a “real and serious” Iranian commitment to guarantee the passage of Iraqi oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz.
The request reflects growing concern over Iraq’s finances and the vulnerability of an economy heavily dependent on oil exports. The pressures have already begun to raise concerns about the government’s ability to meet financial commitments, including the payment of state salaries, according to the sources.
