====================================================================================================

‘Real struggle’ to tame New Forest blaze as UK set for hottest summer on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:49:18 UTC
00:49:18 KST

The battle to contain a large wildfire spreading across the New Forest will go on for several days, experts have said, as wind changes and a desiccated landscape fuel the flames.
Smoke billowed above the deserted A31 road, the main tourist route into the New Forest national park where tens of thousands of families are on holiday, late on Tuesday while a helicopter flew above the blaze. Firefighters at the scene said they were trying to contain several hotspots across the more than 100 hectares (247 acres) of dried heathland as winds swirled over the area.
Roads, including the A31 dual carriageway, will remain shut until at least Thursday, Hampshire’s fire service said, adding that “significant” repairs were needed to the surface, barriers and fencing.
One source at the scene said: “They are really worried that as they dampen down the top, the peat underneath is still alight and spreading the fire. It is too dry, too windy, and it is a real struggle.”
July was the busiest month on record for wildfires, the National Fire Chiefs Council said on Tuesday. Its services have responded to 966 wildfires this year, including 458 in July alone.
Parts of England are bracing for a fifth heatwave of the summer this week as climate breakdown makes extreme heat, drought and wildfires more likely. The Met Office said on Tuesday that the UK was on course for its hottest summer on record by average temperature. On Monday, authorities declared almost three-quarters of England officially in drought.
Hampshire fire and rescue service said it was facing many challenges, including maintaining a water supply and dealing with difficult terrain and changes in wind direction, but it was trying to mount a larger-scale attack on the blaze. Britain owns no dedicated water-bombing aircraft of the kind used by fire crews in Europe.
“Thanks to the efforts of firefighters, we are managing to contain the fire,” it said. “We have been using a mix of fire engines and off-road vehicles to damp down and cool the edges of the area … to prevent spread and escalation. The police drone is being used to enable us to prioritise hotspot areas and manage flare-ups.”
As the emergency services worked through the night, a spokesperson for the Fire Brigades Union said it was calling for the recruitment of 5,000 more firefighters to cope with the extreme climate conditions.
Firefighters have been at the scene since Sunday evening when a lorry caught fire on the A31 at Ringwood at about 5.21pm, sparking the blaze.
Each summer, millions of tourists camp, hike and cycle in the New Forest national park. This year the human-caused climate crisis, which is driving extreme heat, has turned the green English heartland of Hampshire – which has not had rain for 59 days – into a landscape more akin to Arizona in the US.
The A31 dual carriageway, which in August is normally nose to tail with tourist traffic, remained closed on Tuesday with no timetable for when it would reopen. Along the abandoned route, two Shell petrol stations stood empty and closed outside the village of Burley.
A yellow high-pressure water pipe stretched 5 miles along the empty highway from a stream near the village to the blaze, where more than 120 firefighters from stations across the country continued to try to contain the blaze.
Debbie Tann, the chief executive of Hampshire and Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust, said: “It is devastating. It is just dry tinder across the whole forest. It has spread really quickly because of these dry conditions. The New Forest is one of the most important habitats in Europe. It has so many rare species in the heathland – reptiles, adders, lizards, and then the birds like nightjars. This is going to have a devastating impact.”
Sue Oatway, who lives in Burley, said people had come together to support the firefighters, many of whom are volunteers, collecting food and drink for them. On a community WhatsApp group, firefighters thanked the “amazing community” for the support.
Outside Oatway’s home, New Forest ponies sheltered from the heat under brown, dried-out trees amid withered bracken. Oatway said: “I have never seen it so dry here. Someone posted a world map today on a social media group. I knew about the wildfires in Canada and Europe, but the scale of them in the United States I didn’t know. They are everywhere, and now here on our doorstep.”
With the A31 closed, tourist traffic was forced on to back roads through the forest, causing jams on narrow lanes. Holidaymakers were continuing to try to enjoy their break but as the battle to contain the wildfire entered its fourth day, the reality of the threat was becoming clearer.
Jason Bunsell had been camping with a friend at Ashurst on Sunday night when the fire began. “We were coming back on our bikes and saw this big thick black cloud above, we thought it was a storm,” he said. “Then we got back to our campsite and my wife sent a message to me saying: ‘How far are you from the fires, are you all right?’”
Ian Buckman, a district lead volunteer for Arundel and Littlehampton Scouts, who was guiding 26 scouts and explorers on a cycle ride through the forest outside Burley, said: “I have never seen the forest so dry. The environmental impact is massive.”
Tourism is the largest single industry in the local economy. Within the national park boundaries, leisure and recreation trips account for £107.6m in income each year. But the threat of fire spreading and the impact of air pollution have prompted appeals for tourists to stay away.
Forestry England, which manages about half of the national park, said the operation to contain the fire could last for several days. Its spokesperson Esta Mion said: “We are very much asking people to stay away … it’s unpredictable. We just don’t know how long this incident could go on for. We’re certainly thinking it could be the next few days, for sure.”
Emma Howard Boyd, the chair of the independent National Heat Risk Commission and a professor in practice at the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, said: “As the prime minister tours every region of the UK, it will be hard to miss the impacts of this extraordinary summer: wildfires, drought, parched farmland and people struggling to work in extreme heat. The government must now act with urgency to prepare the country for a hotter climate, cutting emissions while investing in the resilience of our homes, infrastructure, farms and public services.”

Norway wealth fund manager says fund collapse not impossible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:49:12 UTC
00:49:12 KST

Norway wealth fund manager says fund collapse not impossible
- Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, worth over US$2 trillion, could potentially collapse due to global tensions and extraordinary growth that may not continue, warns CEO Nicolai Tangen.
- The fund, built from oil and gas revenues since 1996, invests globally in equities, bonds, and property for long-term benefits and allows a 3% annual government withdrawal.
- Tangen highlights risks like nuclear war, biological terrorism, or an "AI bubble" burst combined with US-China trade wars, which could cause losses up to 80% of stock market investments.
AI generated
OSLO – Could Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, the largest in the world with over US$2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion) in assets, go up in smoke? On Aug 11, its manager said it was a possibility and that current global tensions made the prospect less implausible.
Fuelled by the Norwegian state’s oil and gas revenues, the sovereign wealth fund – commonly called the oil fund – has seen its value rise from under 2 billion kroner at its inception in 1996 to more than 22 trillion kroner (S$2.96 trillion) today.
Nicolai Tangen, chief executive officer of Norges Bank Investment Management which manages the fund, on Aug 11 warned that the phenomenal and extraordinary growth, partly due to luck, was not something that could be expected to continue at the same pace in future.
“Can the oil fund disappear? The answer is yes. And the worst thing is that in the world we live in today, it’s not totally improbable,” he said in a speech in Arendal, a town in southern Norway where the country’s elite is gathered this week.
“No country in history has managed to maintain such a vast fortune over the long term. Fortunes always end up disappearing,” he argued, citing historical examples such as Spain and the United Kingdom.
Invested in equities, bonds and properties across the world, the Norwegian fund is designed to be a long-term undertaking and to benefit future generations.
To balance public finances, which would otherwise be in deficit, the government is currently allowed to draw up to 3 per cent from the fund each year, a ceiling that corresponds to the estimated annual return on investments and therefore does not eat into the nest egg itself.
Among potential risks, Tangen mentioned extreme scenarios such as a nuclear war or biological terrorism, but also that of a prolonged depression triggered, for example, by the bursting of an “AI bubble” – referring to the high prices of stocks linked to artificial intelligence – combined with a trade war between the US and China.
Even though more safeguards are now in place, the latter scenario would be comparable to the great economic depression of 1929 and could wipe out “at least 80 per cent” of the value of stock market investments, Tangen said. AFP

Al Jazeera Untangles
Rwanda: The genocide against the Tutsi
How colonial identity, extremist politics and ‘hate radio’ helped turn Rwanda’s genocide into organised mass murder.
This episode on the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda examines one of the few mass atrocities universally recognised under international law. It traces how colonial rule hardened fluid social categories into fixed Hutu and Tutsi identities, and how post-independence politics turned these into a racialised hierarchy of fear.
It also explores how economic crisis, civil war and the Arusha peace process created space for extremists, who used newspapers, churches and “hate radio” to prepare people for mass murder.
Through testimony and archive footage, the film follows how local officials, militias and neighbours organised killings at terrifying speed, and how international actors failed to intervene. It also looks into how courts, memorials and political power have since shaped Rwanda’s official narrative of the genocide.

The Mecca Agreement – Q&amp;A
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:49:00 UTC
00:49:00 KST

Q? So why the Mecca Agreement, what are the key drivers?
Answer – Quite obviously, I think the main driver for the Mecca Agreement (MA) is the newfound insecurity felt by all three signatories, but particularly by Saudi Arabia, in the context of the ongoing Iran war. MBS has developed the Vision 2030 for Saudi Arabia to transform the country economically, but I think also as a means to cap social and political risks within the system; the key requirement for successful social and economic development of Saudi Arabia is security. MBS had assumed that he had assured security for Saudi Arabia via cementing the existing US military backstop – by pandering to Trump’s desires for big investments into the US, and through economic engagement and normalization with Iran. The latter was brokered by China in the landmark Saudi – Iran deal in March 2023. MBS wrote big cheque commitments to Trump to invest in the US economy and he assumed that when push came to shove the US military would provide a defensive shield for Saudi Arabia as it had during the Gulf War. Never did Riyadh imagine that, not only when Iranian missiles began to head to Saudi Arabia, the US would fail to provide adequate air defense for Saudi Arabia, but that US belligerence had in many ways pushed the region into war – the US & Israel attacked Iran in the midst of peace talks in February 2026. Even prior to that, though the fact that the US failed to stop Israel in its missile strikes against Hamas officials in Qatar, I think, demonstrated to Riyadh that for the US, Israel came first, and that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states fell low down its pecking order, while there was actually little restraint in Israel. Israel could attack anywhere in the Gulf unconstrained, and many saw Israeli policy as actually favoring a zone of instability around it, which suggested rolling attacks across the region – which would be counter to MBS’s core need in Vision 2030 for security. All this further affirmed by limited provision by the US of air defense missiles for Saudi Arabia et al, at their hour of need, while supply to Israel was prioritized.
Russia Preparing Mass Mobilization for Fall, Zelensky Says
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
And when it came to the normalization with Iran, the war proved that even that had limits, and when Tehran faced an existential threat – spelled out by the US and Israel in their prior call for regime change – the Islamic Republic would do whatever it needed to do to survive, and to take the war to the US, which meant causing global economic impact through retaliatory strikes against Gulf states, and blocking the Straits.
The writing had already been on the wall for efforts by Saudi Arabia to diversify its security arrangements, as seen by the Saudi – Pakistan strategic defense agreement concluded just after the Israeli strikes in Qatar, but before the latest Iran war, but the Mecca Agreement looks to go beyond and expand that, creating a new regional defense arrangement for Muslim Sunni states, led by Saudi Arabia.
More broadly I think the agreement signals that former US allies are no longer trusting of the US and are looking to diversify their own security arrangements. I think in this the MA signatories are no different from US allies in Europe, or Canada, Japan and South Korea. In the war in Iran, the US, or rather Trump, acted in its/his interests, very much against the interests of key allies in Europe, Asia or the Gulf. The war elevated energy prices against the core economic interests of Europe or Asia. The war undermined security in the Gulf against the interests of Gulf states, Pakistan, or Turkey. The war depleted critical supplies of US munitions against the interests of all US allies – and as now seen with Ukraine’s mission critical shortage of Patriot air defense interceptor missiles. The US failed to adequately consult with key allies, aside from
Israel, prior to launching its strikes on Iran, and seemingly where it did, it failed to listen to their best advice. So if the US fails to take the interests of key allies into account, they need to look after their own best interests which means developing greater defense autonomy, either alone or with new allies.
Why the enthusiasm by Pakistan and Turkey?
Answer – I think both share Saudi’s concerns around the regional security setting, and a nervousness over the reliability of the US, albeit I think the leaderships in both countries have done wonders in playing to Trump’s ego to keep him onside for their own national security interests. I think that is hedging: play nice with Trump, while looking for new defensive partners and alliances. In Pakistan and Turkey’s case though both have fragile economies, and the prospect of a defense pact that opens the way for potentially huge investments in their economies from KSA is a huge win for both. Pakistan is still recovering from a near default scenario a few years back, has large annual financing needs and limited FX reserve cover. Turkey is similarly coming out of a decade–plus of perennial balance of payments crises prior to the recent Simsek stabilization. Simsek has managed to stabilize the BOP, and rebuild reserves, but they are still not at comfortable levels. And a strong FX reserve backstop is central to the CBRT’s policy of using real FX appreciation as central to its disinflation drive, and inflation is the number one economic problem in Turkey. A big slug of investment, or financing from KSA, would go a long way to assuring Turkey’s financing position to hold the FX to enable inflation to push much lower, and that would certainly help Erdogan’s reelection chances. But for Turkey and Pakistan they face military threats on numerous fronts, and need financing to fund upgrades to their militaries and defense tech capability. In Turkey’s case Erdoğan has announced plans to invest $22 billion in a new Steel Dome air defense program, and an additional $140 billion in defense spending over the next decade but it is unclear how that will be financed. Turkey is developing the Kaan fifth–generation fighter jet, but needs to develop an indigenous engine, on par with the UK’s Rolls Royce, which will be hugely expensive. Plus Turkey wants to develop long–range ballistic missiles, and to cement its lead already in drone space. All this costs big bucks, which Turkey does not really have. But cooperation with Saudi Arabia could potentially provide that – imagine, KSA has huge sovereign wealth assets ($1 trillion plus in SAMA and the central bank), assets in Aramco of circa $1 trillion, and with a relatively lowly debt ratio and ability to leverage up further. And if MBS rationalizes the Vision 2030 program away from spending on social infrastructure to defense and logistics, then Turkey, and Pakistan potentially would be huge winners via new defense orders. And on logistics and energy, the room for cooperation is immense. Both Turkey and Pakistan are huge energy importers, but in Turkey’s case it offers KSA a chance of diversification of pipelines and logistics chains away from the Straits and to Europe.
Actually, I think the core of the MA is the recognition by all three MA signatories that by cooperating they can all improve their individual military capabilities. In a way it is not like NATO where pooling resources, common procurement and standardization, and cooperation have, if anything, enabled NATO members to do more with less. I think with MA members that cooperation can moon shot their individual defense capability. Each wants their own autonomous air defense capability, their own fifth–generation fighter jet et al, but by using each other’s respective strengths in finance, or technology, or frontline battle experience, they can all get much better systems at a better price through cooperation.
Financing linked, but for Turkey a deepening in ties with KSA offers the prospect of increased Saudi engagement in the peace process and reconstruction in Syria, potentially Iraq, as well as domestically in Turkey as the Kurdish peace process of rolled out.
Lebanon, Gaza and the West Bank are also areas where the three could further cooperate – albeit therein much to the consternation of
Israel.
Do you think other US allies will seek similar agreements to the MA?
Answer – absolutely, particularly in Europe, and therein we are seeing a redesign of security architecture. Ukraine, I think, will be central to thinking therein in Europe, given the huge strides it is making in defense but also in defense technology, and particularly drones. But I think we are seeing efforts at more bilateral defense cooperation within Europe, and between Canada, Turkey, the UK, and Europe, as an alternative to the US. Autonomy and diversification are now the keys to a country’s defense.
Why the need to sign the agreement in Mecca?
True, it could have been signed in Riyadh, but I think by signing the agreement in the holy city of Mecca, the Saudis signaled both their own leadership of the entity as the protector of the Holy sites, but also that they want to lead a Sunni Muslim entity, and that certainly provides a strong signal to Iran.
It is interesting though that Iranian officials seem to have reacted quite positively to the new MA – suggestive that they don’t see it as a direct threat to themselves but as a welcome reflection of reducing US influence in the region.
Q? Is Egypt likely to be the next country to join the MA?
Well, Egypt was part of the earlier strategic partnership talks, including KSA, Turkey and Pakistan, but seems to have pulled away from signing the tighter defense and security arrangement, and as Hakan Fidan, Turkey’s foreign minister, has argued, NATO Article 5-like commitments. Fidan has also suggested that Egypt is welcome, even expected to join, pending resolution of certain ‘technical issues’. There is recognition, I think, that Egypt brings a lot to the table, in terms of its weight of population, and scale of its military, plus its leverage with the US, and the wider region, and role in any Palestinian settlement. But I think Egypt likely is minded not to be seen to ally with a KSA-led group, as it has put much effort in building relations with the UAE, and has benefited therein from huge UAE financial support for its fragile economy and would not want to put these flows at risk. There are also long-running tensions and rivalries between Egypt and Saudi Arabia that are still grist to the mill in terms of Egypt signing up to a Saudi-led security entity.
Q? What are the threats or dangers to the MA for the signatories?
Answer – the mutual defense, the NATO Article Five, component is the key strength and weakness of the new arrangement. Signatories have made much of the new pact as a defensive arrangement, but if there is an Article Five component, then an attack on one is an attack on all. What does that mean in practice? If Houthis in Yemen attack KSA, as they have done in recent days, does that mean that Pakistan and Turkey will be dragged into the Yemen war? Similarly, what happens if Iran attacks Saudi Arabia? Do Turkey and Pakistan then have to take up arms for Saudi Arabia in such a conflict?
Likewise, if India attacks Pakistan, would Turkey and Saudi then be drawn into such a future conflict? Signatories, I think, would hope that the MA, through its signaling, will act as a greater deterrence against future wars, so no need to be put in a place of deciding whether to honor the Article Five commitment. But say in the case of
India, if there are attacks in Indian controlled Kashmir against
Indian troops and Modi’s domestic politics suggests a response, is Modi really going to hold back for fear of a wider war against Turkey and KSA? I doubt it. But in any event I think Turkey, and China, both provided very significant support to Pakistan in the recent India – Pakistan war without directly joining the conflict, and I would assume the MA would suggest a similar high level of military support but a level, or levels, below direct military involvement. I guess as with NATO Articles IV and V, it’s for the country being attacked to determine when it invokes the requirement for mutual defense. That actually can be quite a high bar. In the case of an India – Pakistan war, at what level realistically would Pakistan seek to invoke the mutual defense clause with KSA and Turkey, knowing full well the ramifications of such a move, as a much wider global war? Again, I think it would be a high bar.
Critics have also argued that in signing the MA, NATO member Turkey is tying the rest of NATO to security threats and risks for KSA and Pakistan. Again, note the bar for Turkey invoking Article Five in reality is likely quite high. And note there that various NATO members, including the US, have very close defense ties with other non-NATO members which could similarly risk dragging in the rest of NATO to broader conflict. In the end, who goes to war with whom is a bit subjective and depends on a much bigger geopolitical map of the world.
Perhaps a good example of the above is the Falklands War. The territory of a NATO member, the UK, was attacked, but did it invoke Article Five? No, partly as it was unsure as to the response – would NATO members come to the defense of the UK for a disputed territory? Probably not, and the UK knew that invoking Article Five and failing to see a response would have been a body blow to NATO, a core pillar of UK defense, arguably more important than the Falklands. Indeed, during the Falklands war, even the US was less than enthusiastic about assisting its supposedly core allies, with a special relationship.
I guess now even within NATO European members are questioning the reality of the Article Five assurance with respect to the US. If the Baltic states are attacked by Russia, would the US come to their defense? I doubt it under Trump, and I know many Europeans also doubt it. But the Article Five assurance still has some value, as the assumption is that Russia is still unsure as to whether the US would come to the Baltics’ defense, and while Russia is unsure, it might then not risk an attack. An Article Five assurance might no longer be cast iron, but its mere presence is a deterrence, I would think.
Look, in summary of the above, the MA is a political, security, defense agreement with Article–Five–like elements, but in the end, whether or not members ride in to the defense of their newfound allies will depend on the situation. But the members see value in working more closely together in the defense and security field, and see benefit in signaling to others, potentially adversaries, that in taking on the members they could potentially risk confrontation with the wider group. But I would expect, for example, Turkey and Pakistan to assist Iran with air defense, and naval capabilities to assist it in its defense against attacks by Yemen. Do I expect Turkey and Pakistan to deploy ground troops in Yemen in support of KSA? Absolutely not. But they might deploy ground troops to KSA to free Saudi troops for deployment then to Yemen.
The key here is that signatories signal to the wider world a new commitment to cooperate much more in defense and security, and come to each other’s aid in time of attack, and others have to figure out how seriously the Article 5-like assurance is in practice. But adversaries will have to take note.
In the latter context, it is interesting that both Israel and India have seen the MA as a huge strategic defeat, and wins for Pakistan and Turkey particularly. And note above that Iran has been quite sanguine. Perhaps this is explained by the fact that both Israel and India see Turkey and Pakistan as enduring, primary threats, whereas for Iran I think the US and Israel rather than any of the three signatories to the MA are primary threats.
Q? What about the US, how does it view the MA?
Answer, well the Trump administration, rather like Iran, appears sanguine, strangely, even supportive of the MA. I think the view is that any structure where regional partners step up and assume a greater responsibility for their own defense is a positive, as it will mean less reliance on the US for their defense. Trump, personally, I think, as noted above, has strong personal bonds with leaders of all three MA signatory states and perhaps thinks that a strong MA organization or defense/security entity could help the US find solutions in places like Syria, Lebanon and Gaza, and the West Bank. Likely Trump would appreciate MA members’ participation in the security agency looking to deploy to Gaza to help implement the Trump peace plan. But likely that is why
Israel is so unnerved by the new MA, as it could well bring forward the possibility of the nightmare scenario of the deployment of Pakistani, and especially Turkish troops to Gaza as part of a Trump peace process. Notable in the commentary from US deputy undersecretary for defense, Elbridge Colby, seemingly playing down prospects for middle-level power development and cooperation, suggesting that in the end there was no alternative to US power, so I guess Colby does not see entities such as the MA as a threat but a captive market for US military kit. And if the MA enables Saudi cash to connect with Pakistani and Turkish technology to improve the military capability of all three, as US allies, this has to be a good thing.

Officials in southern Russian city urge residents to avoid driving amid fuel shortage

Officials in southern Russian city urge residents to avoid driving amid fuel shortage
Sochi authorities have urged residents and tourists to avoid traveling by personal car amid a fuel shortage, saying the measure would help “reduce the burden on gas stations and speed up a return to normal operations,” the city administration stated.
Authorities warned that if lines form at gas stations, drivers must follow traffic rules.
The city issued the appeal after a meeting on the fuel situation. Officials said major gas station operators have limited fuel dispensing “due to logistical disruptions,” and that some stations have restricted gasoline sales to individuals “due to a resulting rush.”
The Sochi-based news outlet Sochi1.ru reports that the city has faced fuel shortages for a third straight day, with hours-long lines at gas stations creating traffic jams on city streets. Some tourists have been unable to leave for home because of the gasoline shortage.
Russia’s fuel crisis has worsened due to Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities. On August 8, Ukrainian drones attacked the Ilsky oil refinery in Krasnodar region.
The peak of the fuel crisis fell in June and early July. Russian regions introduced various restrictions on gasoline sales, and people were forced to stand in hours-long lines at gas stations. After Ukraine shifted its strikes from refineries to warehouses of the Wildberries marketplace, regions began lifting fuel sale restrictions.
However, in recent days active strikes on refineries have resumed. According to estimates from the outlet 7×7, residents of at least 15 regions have once again faced hours-long lines and shortages of 92 and 95 octane gasoline at gas stations.

A fire in the Rivne region caused localized air pollution; the level is not critical
Kyiv • UNN
In the village of Varkovychi, increased concentrations of pollutants were recorded after a fire at an enterprise; the levels are not critical. In other settlements, no exceedances of the maximum permissible levels were detected.
Due to a fire at an enterprise in Rivne region, local atmospheric air pollution was recorded, UNN reports citing the Rivne Regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
Details
Specialists from the Rivne Regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention monitored atmospheric air quality in connection with a fire that broke out on the premises of one of the enterprises in Dubno district.
According to the results of the laboratory tests conducted, atmospheric air pollution is local in nature—in the village of Varkovychi, increased concentrations of certain pollutants were recorded; however, the levels are not critical
Specialists also measured atmospheric air quality in the settlements located near the site of the fire: Ozeriany, Molodizhne, Zdovbytsia, Mizoch, and Velyka Omeliana.
According to the results of the tests, concentrations of harmful substances in these settlements do not exceed the permissible maximum levels.
Atmospheric air quality in the regional center is also satisfactory. If the indicators change or new results are obtained, additional information will be provided.

Yemen govt says four killed in Houthi strike on ship in Red Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:46:49 UTC
00:46:49 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen coastguard says six killed in Houthi strike on ship in Red Sea
Yemen's coastguard on Tuesday said alleged strikes by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels on a cargo vessel killed at least six people near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait off the country's southern coast.
The strikes are the latest in a number of deadly attacks against shipping in the entrance to the Red Sea since the Houthis announced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia last month.
The coastguard from Yemen's internationally recognised government said four sailors aboard the cargo vessel -- identified as the "Tihamah" -- were among the dead along with two members of the forces deployed during a rescue mission to evacuate the ship.
The initial salvo targeting the ship "caused a fire to break out aboard the vessel and inflicted extensive damage, in addition to causing deaths and injuries among its crew, including three Pakistani nationals and one Indonesian national killed," the coastguard said in a statement.
A second strike targeted the vessel as rescue workers carried out a mission to evacuate the ship.
"The attack struck the site of the rescue operation and resulted in deaths and injuries among the forces participating in the response operation," the coast guard added, saying 10 people were injured over the course of the strikes.
The statement came hours after the Yemen government's transport ministry accused the Houthis of launching the strikes that hit the vessel.
The ministry gave a slightly smaller toll, saying four had been killed.
The transport ministry in its statement said it "held the Houthi terrorist militias fully responsible for the deaths, injuries and damage inflicted on the commercial vessel 'Tihamah' as well as for the serious consequences resulting from these attacks".
There was no official comment from the Houthis about the alleged attack.
The incident comes after a years-long truce in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government collapsed last month as fighting flared between Iran and the United States.
The breakdown of the UN-backed 2022 accord came as the Houthis announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, hitting Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and the kingdom's oil infrastructure, in parallel with Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Syria agrees to surrender Assad-era nuclear material to IAEA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:46:38 UTC
00:46:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria agrees to surrender Assad-era nuclear material to IAEA
Syria has agreed to surrender its remaining stockpile of nuclear material to the UN's atomic watchdog, but the breakthrough is unlikely to bring Damascus and Israel any closer to a security agreement, a senior Syria analyst told The New Arab, as negotiations remain stalled over Israeli occupation and withdrawal demands.
"The legacy reactor residue unlocks none of that," Nanar Hawach, senior Syria analyst at the International Crisis Group, told TNA, saying the nuclear file was largely separate from the disputes that have frustrated US attempts to broker an agreement between the two countries.
The assessment comes after US and Israeli officials told Axios that Syria had agreed to hand the material over to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) under a US-brokered deal reached several weeks ago, following weeks of Israeli threats to bomb Syrian facilities.
The Trump administration and the IAEA had raced to secure the material amid concerns that the issue could provoke a new crisis involving Israel, Syria and potentially Turkey.
The stockpile is a remnant of a secret nuclear programme pursued under the Assad regime more than two decades ago. The material was reportedly connected to the Al-Kibar nuclear reactor in Deir Ezzor governorate, which Israel destroyed in 2007, although several storage and research and development sites remained intact.
A US official said the material included powdered uranium ore known as yellowcake, which can be enriched as part of the process of producing nuclear fuel or weapons and could also potentially be used in a "dirty bomb".
Six months after Bashar al-Assad's overthrow, Syria's new government agreed to give the IAEA unrestricted access to the facility and several other sites connected to the former government's nuclear programme.
But Israeli officials later said they had detected possible attempts by Syria's new authorities to access material at a facility known as Site 99 and suspected they were receiving assistance from Turkey.
When questioned by the Trump administration, Syrian officials said they had been unaware that nuclear material was stored at the site.
"We think everybody is happy with the result. Hopefully we will be able to kick off the removal process soon and end it before the end of the year," the US official told Axios.
The harder question of Israel-Syria talks
For Washington, removing the material may close one sensitive file inherited from the Assad era. But it does little to resolve the disputes at the heart of negotiations between Syria and Israel.
"I expect the handover to have little to no impact because it speaks to Washington's non-proliferation agenda while the negotiations themselves are stuck on territory, Israeli withdrawal lines, the demilitarised zone and the Druze question," Hawach told TNA. "The legacy reactor residue unlocks none of that."
Relations between Damascus and Israel have sharply deteriorated since Assad's overthrow. Israel seized strategic areas of southern Syria after his fall and launched extensive attacks that destroyed much of the country's remaining military capabilities.
Israeli forces continue to occupy parts of Quneitra, Daraa and Damascus provinces and carry out regular raids in villages near the occupied Golan Heights.
President Ahmed al-Sharaa has spoken favourably about reaching a security agreement with Israel, but negotiations have struggled to make progress amid disagreements over Israeli forces remaining on Syrian territory.
Hawach said the nuclear agreement could nevertheless strengthen the position of US officials advocating continued engagement with Syria's new authorities by demonstrating Damascus's willingness to resolve an inherited security issue through negotiation.
"The deal shows Damascus is willing to resolve inherited files through cooperation while Israel's approach continues to rest on indefinite deployment and strikes," he said.
Other Syrian analysts similarly see the agreement as part of a broader effort by Damascus to remove potential Israeli pretexts for further attacks while distancing the new government from the military programmes it inherited from Assad.
Rashid Hourani, a researcher specialising in security and military affairs, told TNA that Syria's new authorities had adopted a more open approach to the nuclear file and cooperation with international organisations, in part to demonstrate that Damascus does not pose a threat to neighbouring countries or the wider region.
The government also hopes its cooperation over the nuclear and chemical weapons files will help secure greater political and economic support for Syria's recovery, he said.
Hourani cautioned, however, that the new authorities could face difficulties establishing exactly what remains of the former government's nuclear programme, with conditions on the ground not necessarily matching existing documentation after the disorder surrounding Assad's fall.
Some documents or materials may have been removed by the former government or its allies during that period, he said, adding that cooperation with the IAEA could help resolve those discrepancies over the short and medium term.
Khaled Khalil, an expert on Syrian-Israeli relations, said Damascus's cooperation with the IAEA had also deprived Israel of one potential justification for military action.
He described the agreement as evidence of a Syrian policy based on "realism and clarity" in handling sensitive security issues, contrasting that approach with Israel's continued military operations inside Syria.
"Damascus sent messages of reassurance to the region and was not a source of concern," Khalil told TNA, arguing that Syria had increasingly presented itself as a partner in regional security.
Through active diplomacy, he added, Damascus had succeeded in "taking many cards out of the hands of the Israeli occupation", even as Israel continued trying to impose facts on the ground and intervene in Syrian affairs.
The Trump administration has meanwhile moved rapidly to build ties with al-Sharaa's government, lifting Assad-era economic sanctions, reopening its embassy in Damascus and supporting Syria's diplomatic and economic reintegration.

Swarming jellyfish overrun French nuclear plant on same date two years in a row
The jellyfish invasion is the latest in a series of climate change-driven incidents that have affected a record number of French nuclear reactors over the summer.
Aug. 11 is quickly becoming jellyfish invasion day at the Gravelines nuclear power plant in northern France.
Despite spending hundreds of thousands of euros to protect the plant from a jellyfish swarm like the one that saw reactors shuttered on Aug. 11, 2025, French utility provider EDF on Tuesday was again forced to bring the parts of the facility offline due to the presence of “several dozen tons” of jellyfish blocking pumping systems.
“On-site teams are fully mobilized to ensure the safety of the facilities and to reconnect the reactors to the national power grid,” EDF said in a statement.
Advertisement
Three fishing vessels are now “constantly patrolling off the coast of the plant" to conduct "preventive fishing operations [...] 24/7,” the company added.
Tuesday’s jellyfish invasion comes a the latest in a series of climate change-driven incidents that have affected French nuclear energy during a particularly infernal summer.
Nuclear power plants are typically built by rivers or on coastlines so they can use nearby water sources to cool their reactors. But a record number in France this summer have been forced to temporarily shut down due to heatwaves and droughts affecting their water supply.
Rising sea temperatures have made jellyfish swarms more common along the French coast in recent years, and those swarms can affect a plant’s ability to bring in seawater — which is what happened at Gravelines. Following last year’s incident at the plant along the North Sea, EDF installed cameras and deployed fishing boats to monitor the situation.
While the vessels “prevented a massive influx of jellyfish” on Saturday and Sunday, they were eventually overwhelmed as the swarm grew from “about 100 kilograms” to “several dozen tons,” the French state-owned utility giant said.
Opponents of nuclear energy were quick to jump on the incident.
“This only highlights that nuclear power plants are ill-equipped to deal with the consequences of climate change,” the French branch of Greenpeace said in statement.

DARPA Lift Challenge ends with a surprisingly old-fashioned winner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:45:01 UTC
00:45:01 KST

- DARPA's Lift Challenge concluded after seven days, with Team Avidrone winning first place at a 3.84 to 1 payload-to-weight ratio.
- Avidrone's Katana helicopter drone carried 112.4 pounds (51 kilograms) while weighing 29.3 pounds (13.3 kilograms), earning $1.25 million.
A team of engineers have proved that a helicopter design older than most of their grandparents can still out-fly the strangest, most futuristic drone shapes engineers could dream up. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the Pentagon’s advanced research arm known for funding technologies that eventually reshape entire industries, announced that its Lift Challenge had wrapped after seven days of competition, crowning Team Avidrone the winner with a payload-to-weight ratio of 3.84 to 1.
DARPA launched the Lift Challenge last November with a prize pool of $6.5 million and a single, brutally simple goal: build a drone that can carry a payload weighing more than four times its own body weight, a threshold no existing heavy-lift drone comes close to reaching. Conventional delivery and cargo drones on the market today typically top out at payload ratios well under 2 to 1, meaning a drone that weighs 50 pounds (23 kilograms) might struggle to carry even 100 pounds (45 kilograms) of cargo. DARPA’s bet was that opening the challenge to unconventional designs, rather than dictating a specific engineering approach, would push someone past the 4 to 1 mark the same way earlier DARPA competitions produced breakthroughs in autonomous vehicles and computer networking.
The competition unfolded at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force in Dayton, Ohio, where DARPA had invited 124 teams to compete and 76 actually made it to the flight line, according to DARPA’s own accounting of the event. Teams flew a five-nautical-mile (9.3 kilometer) circuit course in head-to-head live trials, taking off with a loaded payload, flying a set distance, dropping the cargo, and completing the remaining distance empty, all within a 30-minute time limit. The format rewarded not just raw lifting power but reliability, since a single failed run eliminated a team’s chance at that day’s ranking.
Avidrone Inc. entered a design that stood out precisely because it wasn’t exotic. While rival teams flew multirotor drones and experimental configurations built specifically to chase the payload-to-weight metric, Avidrone’s aircraft, named Katana, used a conventional single-main-rotor helicopter layout with a tail boom, the same basic configuration that has defined production helicopters since the 1940s, according to DroneXL‘s reporting on the event. The Katana weighed 29.3 pounds (13.3 kilograms) and carried a payload of 112.4 pounds (51 kilograms) of cast iron around the course, producing the 3.84 to 1 ratio DARPA confirmed in its announcement. DroneXL and DefPost both reported that Avidrone completed its winning run in 19 minutes and 17 seconds, well inside the 30-minute limit, and DefPost added that the Katana’s aircraft platform, propulsion system, and flight-control technologies were all developed in-house by the company. A component list published by DefPost pointed to battery-electric propulsion, with battery modules supplied by Titan Batteries powering motors run through separate speed controllers.
No team reached the 4 to 1 target DARPA set when it opened the competition, a fact that triggered a prize rule DroneXL had flagged before the event’s first weigh-in: because the top ratio fell short of the stated goal, every podium payout was cut in half. Avidrone collected $1.25 million instead of the $2.5 million top prize, MTech Operations LLC took second place with a 3.64 to 1 ratio for $750,000, and Xtreme Aerial Concepts finished third at 3.45 to 1 for $500,000, according to DroneXL’s reporting.
The runner-up and third-place finishers took very different paths to their results. Coverage from ENGtechnica noted that other competitors explored configurations far removed from anything flying commercially today, including a design from RotoWings built around two radio-controlled airplanes connected together to form one large rotating system, and a tandem-rotor aircraft from Phoenix Drone LLC built to resemble a scaled-down Chinook.
That range of approaches, from Avidrone’s deliberately conventional helicopter to designs that looked nothing like any aircraft currently in service, captures what DARPA challenges are built to surface: not a single predetermined answer, but a wide field of competing ideas tested against the same unforgiving standard.
Aviation Week, which covered the competition’s final days, framed the results as falling short of DARPA’s stated goal while still meaningfully resetting expectations for what small drones can carry, noting that the event ran from August 4 through 9 at the Dayton museum.
What DARPA proved this month goes beyond a single number on a scoreboard, showing that the agency’s decades-old formula, hand a hard problem to dozens of competing teams and let the best design win, still works even when the winning idea looks less like science fiction and more like something that has been flying since before jet engines existed.

North Korean ballistic missile kills 7 steelworkers on their way to shelter, shuts down Zaporizhstal plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:44:16 UTC
00:44:16 KST

A Russian ballistic strike on Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, killed seven employees of the Zaporizhstal steel plant and injured 21 others, Ukrainian steelmaker Metinvest, the plant’s majority owner, said on 11 August.
The workers were on their way to a shelter after an air raid alert was announced when the strike hit the industrial site, according to the company.
Metinvest said the attack also damaged energy facilities and infrastructure, as well as the main and auxiliary facilities of the plant’s coke and blast-furnace operations.
Russia’s ballistic missile strikes leave very little time between threat detection and impact for people to react and reach shelter. Several people have been killed from strikes across the country while on their way to bomb shelters.
Zaporizhstal shuts down after strike
Metinvest said Zaporizhstal has been completely shut down following the attack, while its other production sites in the city are operating at reduced capacity.
Company specialists are assessing the damage and determining the scope and timeline of repairs. Emergency and restoration work is already underway, according to the statement.
The company said its Zaporizhzhia facilities are civilian industrial sites that employ tens of thousands of people and produce steelmaking and coke-chemical products.
Metinvest said it is providing medical assistance and support to the 21 injured employees and staying in contact with the families of those killed and wounded.
The company's facilities will fly flags at half-mast on 11 and 12 August in mourning for the seven Zaporizhstal workers killed in the attack.
North Korean missiles used against Zaporizhzhia
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Zaporizhzhia was targeted overnight with North Korean ballistic missiles, Russian Zircon missiles and guided aerial bombs.
Zelenskyy said the attack was designed to cause maximum damage to civilian infrastructure.
Ukraine's military intelligence said on 5 August that a North Korean missile unit had begun deploying to western Russia, potentially adding up to 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers to Russia's arsenal.
According to Ukrainian intelligence representative Andrii Cherniak, North Korea has supplied Russia with around 150 KN-23 and KN-24 missiles since late 2023, including a recent batch of 40 missiles.
The missiles have been linked to attacks with high civilian casualties, including a July strike on Radushne in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast that killed an entire family.
Ballistic threat is growing
The strike comes as Russia has increasingly relied on ballistic missiles in attacks on Ukrainian cities. Unlike drones and cruise missiles, ballistic missiles travel at very high speeds and are much harder for Ukraine to intercept, particularly because Kyiv has a limited supply of the advanced air defense interceptors needed to counter them, mainly US-made Patriot systems.
Ukraine has reported that most ballistic missiles launched in recent mass attacks have penetrated its air defenses, contributing to severe destruction and civilian casualties.

Source: European Pravda, citing the German embassy in Ukraine

Colombia earthquake strikes at challenging time for aid response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:40:49 UTC
00:40:49 KST

Share & more
Aid organisations responding to the powerful earthquake that hit Colombia on 10 August face significant challenges, including difficulties accessing some of the worst-hit areas in remote western regions that have been seeing rising violence.
Emergency response teams are still assessing the damage, but at least 181 people have already been reported killed and nearly 1,250 injured. It is feared the toll could rise significantly, with many more trapped under the rubble or missing.
Speaking at a press conference hours after the 7.4-magnitude quake struck at 7:34am on Monday, President Abelardo de la Espriella, who only took office last week, said more than 1,500 residential buildings, 18 health centres, and 52 schools had been damaged. An update on 11 August from the Colombian Association of Capital Cities (Asocapitales) said 153 buildings had collapsed.
The earthquake comes at a tough time for Colombia. The country was already facing its worst humanitarian crisis in years, with rising violence by armed groups making it increasingly difficult for aid groups to address mounting needs in conflict zones.
“Local communities were already facing armed conflict and high levels of poverty long before the ground began to shake,” Nicole Kast, the International Rescue Committee’s country director for Colombia, Venezuela, and Ecuador, said in a press release issued on the day of the quake. “We are deeply concerned that today's natural disaster will make the needs on the ground even steeper as people lose access to health care and other essential services."
In Chocó department, where the earthquake’s epicentre is located, restrictions on humanitarian aid are common. The region is not only one of the poorest in the country but also one of the hardest hit by armed conflict, with more than 21,000 people experiencing forced confinement – the highest number in the country, according to Colombia’s Ombudsman’s Office.
Armed groups have sought to increase their control over communities as they fight each other for control over key territories, leaving remote communities even more isolated. The quake has now rendered some of them – including Chocó’s San Juan and Baudó river regions – completely unreachable.
“Chocó subregions such as San Juan and Baudó are currently inaccessible and isolated,” Shirley Hidalgo, senior director of operations of World Vision in Colombia, told The New Humanitarian. “The local authorities are asking for urgent medical supplies and support to address the needs of this department.”
But it may be hard for aid to arrive soon. And not only in Chocó. The situation in that department is mirrored in other places affected by rising violence.
According to the UN’s emergency aid coordination body, OCHA, more than 1.6 million people in the country were affected by violence and armed conflict last year – three times the figure in 2024. Some 96,000 people were forcibly displaced and 155,000 were confined by curfews, armed strikes, and drone attacks, as armed groups waged war for territorial control over strategic trafficking routes and illicit economies.
Meanwhile, 416 “humanitarian access restrictions” were registered, including threats and violence that impeded humanitarian personnel and their services to civilians – a 13% increase on 2024.
“In the past two years, the context has been characterised by the expansion and strengthening of Non-State Armed Groups (NSAG) in different territories of the country, an increase in territorial disputes… and in high-impact armed actions,” Yann Cornic, director of the Danish Refugee Council office in Colombia, told The New Humanitarian in an email exchange last month. “These factors have created greater risks for the affected communities and have significantly complicated the conditions for providing humanitarian assistance and protection.”
Who do aid agencies engage with?
Colombia has been gripped by a decades-long cycle of internal conflict, despite repeated efforts to address it. A landmark peace accord signed in 2016 led to the demobilisation of the FARC guerrilla group and a temporary lull, but new and more numerous armed groups filled the void and fighting has surged over the last decade.
During his 2022-2026 presidential term, De la Espriella’s predecessor, Gustavo Petro, sought to move away from predominantly military responses and pursue dialogue with armed groups through his so-called “Total Peace” plan. But the policy yielded little progress and a dramatic rise in violence has since triggered a cascade of new humanitarian needs.
Instead, De la Espriella, who took office on 7 August, has pledged to take a hardline stance against armed groups. He joined US President Donald Trump’s “Shield of the Americas” security alliance, and the US has pledged $1 billion in security assistance to Colombia.
De la Espriella has also vowed to restart Plan Colombia – a US-backed anti-drug military programme launched in 2000 that displaced hundreds of thousands of civilians – and to launch a new military offensive against armed groups. The latter is part of his so-called “Patriot Plan 2.0” – billed as a revamped version of an iron-fisted crackdown on armed groups launched in 2003 by Álvaro Uribe – a populist right-wing president.
Aid organisations worry that all this could bring a new escalation of violence, driving greater humanitarian needs and additional risks for their operations.
“For us, the situation will become much more difficult because the context will be harsher, and the [armed] groups will tighten their control [on territories],” said Etienne Malingrey, director in Colombia of the International NGO Safety Organization (INSO), which opened a new office in the country last year.
Experts say the fragmentation of armed groups has not only led to more fighting but also to changes in their structure and leadership. This, in turn, has made it more difficult for aid groups to identify who to engage with at the local level to obtain access to communities in need.
In the past, humanitarian organisations had to negotiate access with one or two main armed actors, but coordination is harder now that there are more. The rising number of ongoing conflicts and military operations only compounds that problem as it means more turnover in command positions within armed groups.
“It's becoming increasingly difficult to identify who's in charge within [armed] groups. Changes [in leadership] are happening much more quickly, the people involved are very young, and the operational chains aren't as clear,” explained Malingrey from INSO.
When they do engage with them, the risks are also higher, as this new generation of fighters often pays little heed to the underlying rules of humanitarian work. “These are people who are unfamiliar with international humanitarian law and human rights,” said Ángela Olaya, director of Conflict Response, a Bogotá-based organisation studying the armed conflict.
In this context, aid groups are often forced to call on community leaders to obtain access. But it is an approach that puts locals “at considerable risk”, and isn't necessarily efficient, Malingrey said. “The response is somewhat slow, and the reliability of the information we receive from leaders in certain contexts is also limited.”
As conflict deepens, mistrust grows
The past year has been particularly difficult.
As conflict has intensified, rival armed groups have sought to tighten their control over entire communities. In the Norte de Santander department, for instance, the National Liberation Army (ELN), one of the country´s main armed actors, started fighting a FARC dissident group in January 2025, displacing more than 138,000 people and confining over 12,000 over that year.
Constant ambushes, confrontations, and military operations have made armed groups increasingly suspicious of humanitarian actors.
“The command structures and internal cohesion within these groups are much more fragile and dynamic, the sense of mistrust toward everyone – including humanitarian actors – is pervasive,” Olaya explained.
As a result, many humanitarian access restrictions are related to interference with the movement of humanitarian personnel or agencies, with 51 cases reported between January and July 2026 – 20 more than in the same period of 2025.
“In Cauca, Norte de Santander, Bolívar, and Guaviare, the main issues or restrictions arise because a particular armed group is suspicious, imposes last-minute rules, or because… conflict actors [suddenly] become active, and it is no longer safe to provide assistance to the population,” said Cornic.
In March 2026, the Estado Mayor Central (EMC), a FARC dissident group present in at least 133 municipalities across the country, announced it was forbidding the UN Verification Mission, the Organisation of American States Mission to Support the Peace Process in Colombia (MAPP), and the Colombian Ombudsman’s office from carrying out activities in areas under their control. The group cited “violations of trust and neutrality”, claiming humanitarian assistance and verification missions had been used to gather intelligence to facilitate military operations against them.
The announcement was not the first of its kind.
In June 2025, a faction of the same group, the “Bloque Amazonas”, published a pamphlet “reminding” UN bodies and the MAPP that their access to areas under their control was restricted. A similar message was sent in Cauca in May 2025.
Barriers are sometimes more concrete. In Norte de Santander, humanitarian convoys have been forced to turn back several times when deploying in the field, with armed groups going as far as checking humanitarian staff´s personal phones. In southern Bolívar and the mountainous area of Nariño, some humanitarian teams have been asked to provide identification papers, letters of acceptance by community members, or access permits signed by armed groups.
The growing risks on the ground
Violence against healthcare workers has also been on the rise.
In February, a doctor and a nurse were kidnapped in Norte de Santander and forced to provide medical care to injured members of the ELN after a bombing by Colombia’s armed forces in the small town of Tibú.
A similar situation was reported in the violence-ridden southwestern department of Valle del Cauca in April. And in Briceño, in northwestern Antioquia department, an ambulance was stopped by members of an armed group who forced the medical personnel out of the vehicle and killed the patient.
According to data shared by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), there were 595 incidents of violence against medical missions in 2025 – 16 more than in 2024. Recorded incidents this year include threats against healthcare personnel, restrictions on access to services, demands for care under inadequate conditions, and obstruction of efforts to treat the wounded.
The theft of humanitarian vehicles is also becoming more common. At least six were reported stolen in 2025, and 10 so far in 2026, according to OCHA’s data. Armed groups use them for logistics but also because it allows them to move around under cover for criminal purposes.
“Between the reporting of the theft and the moment the truck is recovered [by the police]... there’s enough time for them to do what they need to do with it,” Olaya said.
Another source of concern is the greater use of drones carrying explosives. Although aid workers are not directly targeted, Malingrey said that there were five or six incidents last year in which humanitarian teams were on the ground when drones exploded only 300 to 500 metres away.
On 18 June, in Tibú, a drone attack during confrontations between armed groups forced a humanitarian organisation to suspend its activities and seek shelter. According to the Colombian Ministry of Defense, 333 attacks involving weaponised drones were registered in 2025, a 445% increase from 2024. OCHA recorded 158 drone attacks between January and July 2026, especially in Cauca, Norte de Santander, and Antioquia.
Aid groups are still looking for ways to cope with these new dynamics. In some areas, humanitarian workers have had to take alternative – often much longer – routes to avoid conflict zones or armed groups' checkpoints. They also avoid going to the field with personal phones.
Stijn Houben, head of operations at the ICRC’s regional delegation in Bogotá, said they are trying to adjust their strategies based on the experience of other countries.
“We’re making a huge change internally… where we learn best practices from other contexts that may be much more advanced in these issues – such as Ukraine – and try to adapt and implement them here for our teams,” he said.
Uncertainty about the impacts of the new government’s announced military offensive is already affecting humanitarian work. A staff member of one organisation who asked to speak anonymously because they weren’t at liberty to speak about this topic, said “armed groups don’t know what’s coming and are already increasing restrictions”.
“There’s more mistrust with humanitarian organisations too, so we’ve tightened our security and focused on building trust with communities,” they added. How all these complex dynamics will impact the response to the earthquake remains to be seen.

Jury in Luigi Mangione's insurance CEO murder trial to be anonymous

The jury in Luigi Mangione's murder trial next month on charges of gunning down a health insurance executive on a Manhattan sidewalk will be anonymous, the judge overseeing the case said at a hearing on Tuesday.
New York State Justice Gregory Carro did not explain why jurors would remain anonymous. While not the norm in US criminal trials, judges often decide to shield jurors' identities from the public in high-profile cases where there is concern jurors may be subject to harassment or intimidation.
Mangione, 28, is accused of shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson outside a hotel in December 2024. The killing was widely condemned by public officials but became emblematic of many Americans’ frustration with health insurance industry practices.
Mangione has pleaded not guilty to murder, weapons, and forgery charges brought by Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg. He also pleaded not guilty to stalking charges in a separate federal case.
At Tuesday's hearing, Carro also ruled that an overflow courtroom would be made available for the press and the public to witness the trial if the main courtroom fills to capacity.
Prosecutors say they can prove Mangione’s guilt with hundreds of hours of surveillance video, fingerprints, DNA, a cellphone, a gun with matching ballistics and a notebook in which Mangione allegedly wrote of hating insurers and wanting to kill.
Mangione’s lawyers have revealed almost nothing about their potential trial strategy, though a July court filing indicated they might argue Mangione lost control of his actions due to an extreme mental health breakdown. They have not conceded that he was the shooter.
Former UnitedHealthcare CEO shot dead outside hotel
Thompson led UnitedHealth Group's insurance unit before he was shot dead in the early morning outside a hotel where an investor conference was taking place.
Graphic footage of the killing and a five-day manhunt for a suspect made the case a media fixture and social media sensation. Mangione was arrested in Pennsylvania.
His trial in the federal case is scheduled to begin in January.

Venture capital firm OurCrowd has appointed Cali Chill as chief executive officer, formally placing the seven-year company veteran at the head of the Jerusalem-based venture investment platform after he served as acting CEO since mid-2025.
Chill had been serving as acting CEO and chief operating officer after OurCrowd founder Jon Medved stepped back from day-to-day management for medical reasons. The company’s board of directors has now appointed Chill to the role on a permanent basis, OurCrowd announced Tuesday.
“I am honored to lead the next chapter of the OurCrowd story,” Chill told The Jerusalem Post. “The company is made up of some extremely talented and hard-working people, and it will be thanks to their true dedication and unwavering commitment that we take the OurCrowd investment platform to new heights.”
Chill added that he was “energized by what we can all build together from here.”
Company working to introduce more AI tools into its investment and asset-management process
The formal appointment follows a year in which OurCrowd said its leadership team focused on stabilizing operations, narrowing its investment strategy toward fewer high-conviction deals and assessing options for monetizing parts of its existing portfolio. The company has also been working to introduce more artificial intelligence-based tools into its investment and asset-management processes.
Earlier this month, OurCrowd announced one of the largest exits in its portfolio after Visa agreed to acquire Israeli fraud-prevention company BioCatch in a deal reportedly valued at $2.4 billion.
OurCrowd was an early investor in BioCatch and continued investing in the company as it grew. The acquisition remains subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions and is expected to close by the end of Visa’s fiscal second quarter of 2027.
Ben Plotkin, chairman of OurCrowd’s board of directors, said the board had been encouraged by the company’s performance since Chill took over its day-to-day management.
'I am excited about OurCrowd’s prospects'
“I am very pleased with the company’s progress and accomplishments over the past several quarters,” Plotkin said. “Since Cali took charge of the operation, the firm has been managed with increasing financial discipline and operational focus.”
“Having worked closely with Cali since the leadership transition of 2025, I am excited about OurCrowd’s prospects, and the board has full confidence in Cali’s ability to lead the firm through this next chapter,” he added.
Chill joined OurCrowd seven years ago as general counsel and later served as chief legal officer. He subsequently became head of funds, overseeing the company’s in-house and third-party investment funds, before serving as chief investment officer and chairman of OurCrowd’s investment committee.
Before joining OurCrowd, Chill served as general counsel of Nasdaq-listed Answers Corporation and AFCV Holdings, a private-equity-backed technology investor.

Severe heatwaves in Bulgaria reveal ancient Rome's Constantine Bridge hidden under Danube's waters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:40:01 UTC
00:40:01 KST

Exceptionally low water levels on the Danube have exposed parts of the foundations of the ancient Constantine Bridge, giving Bulgarian archaeologists a rare opportunity to document what they describe as one of the Roman Empire's most impressive engineering achievements.
A succession of record-breaking heatwaves in Europe this summer has caused a severe drought in parts of the continent, affecting major waterways such as the Danube and the Rhine.
"For archaeologists, these moments are extremely valuable because nature briefly reveals an object that is hidden beneath the Danube for most of the time," said Pavel Popov of the Regional Historical Museum in Pleven. "It gives us a rare opportunity to observe, document and study it in its real environment."
The bridge, commissioned by Emperor Constantine I and inaugurated in 328 CE, linked the ancient city of Ulpia Oescus with Sucidava in what is now Romania. Stretching more than two km (1.2 miles), it is regarded as one of the longest bridges of antiquity, though short-lived. It is believed to have been largely destroyed around 367 CE.
A team from the Pleven museum carried out aerial photography and documentation of visible bridge remains, close to the village of Gigen in northern Bulgaria.
Researchers used drones to map and photograph the exposed remains, tracing the line of visible foundations and assessing their condition.
The Danube's water levels have been receding all across Europe, revealing finds from as far back as the Ice Age.
Near the Serbian port of Prahovo, the Danube’s receding water levels have revealed dozens of German battleships sunken during World War II.
At least 20 warships can be seen emerging from the Danube, according to CBS News, adding that they are believed to have belonged to Nazi Germany’s Black Sea fleet, sunken by the German’s during their retreat from Romania near the end of the war.
Remains of two Nazi soldiers found in Budapest
On the riverbank near Batthyány Square in Budapest, the German War Graves Commission (Volksbund) announced last week that the skeletal remains of two Nazi soldiers had been found alongside a World War II DKW NZ 350-1 motorcycle.
The dog tags of both soldiers are complete, Volksbund noted, explaining that this likely meant the two soldiers had been declared missing as no offical notice of their deaths had been recorded at the time.
The two are expected to be buried in the Budaörs German Soldiers Cemetery outside of Budapest.
Ice Age mammoth remains unearthed in Bulgaria
Two weeks ago, the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) reported that the remains of the ancient mammoth (Mammuthus primigenius) were found in northern Bulgaria after Danube's water levels receded to a record low.
The animal's remains were found by a local resident of the Ryahovo village, who noticed the unusual find on the river bed. Villagers then alerted specialists in the Regional History Museum in the nearby town of Ruse.
Ryahovo Mayor Hristina Ivanova shared with BTA that the area was particularly interesting from a historical perspective, and that over the years, “various finds have been discovered here, including animal remains, vessels and other objects.”
Miriam Sela-Eitam contributed to this report.

Chinese citizen pleads guilty to attempting to smuggle US military equipment to PRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:40:01 UTC
00:40:01 KST

A Chinese citizen pleaded guilty in federal court to charges related to attempting to smuggle US military hardware to China in violation of the US Arms Export Control Act, according to the US Justice Department (DOJ) on Monday.
Dingwei Chen, a 29-year-old citizen of the People's Republic of China (PRC), tried to purchase US-manufactured military-grade communications hardware, such as radios and satellite modems, on the black market.
Chen worked with individuals in China to acquire the communications systems from foreign arms dealers, eventually making a down payment of $40,000 to secure the technology.
The co-conspirators then made another payment in cryptocurrency, equivalent to $30,000, for the purchase of 10 satellite modems.
Chen, co-conspirators attempted to avoid law enforcement detection
Chen and his accomplices shifted to using cryptocurrency because, according to the DOJ, they noted that cryptocurrency wallets “are essentially anonymous bank accounts. Each transaction processed through them is private and untraceable.”
Using encrypted apps to communicate in an effort to avoid detection, Chen claimed that the purchase of 10 modems was just an initial deal, and that he had enough funding to obtain tens of millions of dollars worth of military technology.
Chen and the co-conspirators also discussed plans to covertly export the hardware to China, initially weighing shipping them through Switzerland or retrieving them in Saipan in the Northern Mariana Islands. Eventually, they agreed to smuggle the military equipment through Mexico.
Such hardware is illegal to export without a license issued by the US Department of State’s Directorate of Defense Trade Controls, the DOJ stated.
Chen’s guilty plea was accepted by a federal court in Salt Lake City, and he faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.
Smuggled equipment may have been used against US
Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg asserted that if Chen had been successful in diverting the communications equipment to China, it may have been used against the US in the future.
“Today’s guilty plea underscores the serious consequences for those who attempt to illegally procure, export, or transfer sensitive US-origin military equipment,” Acting Special Agent in Charge of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement Investigations Spiros Karabinas added.
“Protecting American innovation and preventing critical technologies from reaching foreign adversaries, terrorist organizations, and transnational criminal organizations is a core national security mission,” Karabinas continued, praising law enforcement agencies for their collaboration on holding Chen accountable.
